item.title: [Bits + Bips] 'We're Not Carnival Barkers': Who Wins the CFTC's Prediction Market Brawl?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"波动率虹吸"：Bessant如何把国债市场的病灶变成比特币的养料

大部分人在讨论Bessant的长债回购时，纠结的是"这算不算QE"、"4亿够不够"。但节目里Gordon透露了一个更隐秘的机制——波动率的跨资产传染。国债市场的坏胆固醇（bad cholesterol：on-the-run/off-the-run错位、swap spread异常、TIPS的蝴蝶失衡）正在系统性地把"方差风险溢价"推向右尾。

这里有个反直觉的对称性：利率的波动率下沉在零附近（有下界），而向上无界，其对数正态分布的右尾在被重新定价；比特币的波动率结构正好相反——价格下方接近历史底部十分位，右尾同样在被重新定价。 换句话说，国债市场的"晕船"和比特币的"起飞"共享同一个数学骨架——skewness在往同一个方向漂移，只不过一个是灾难信号，一个是狂欢信号。

这其实揭示了一个更深的模式：当一个庞大的、被视为"无风险"的市场开始定价尾部风险时，它释放出的方差不会消失，而是会寻找那些天然"喜欢波动"的资产作为宿主。比特币在这个循环里，扮演的不是"数字黄金"，而是波动率的排污管道。

二、Kalshi vs CME这场"拳击手 vs 芭蕾舞者"的真正战场，不在预测市场本身

节目表面上讨论的是Terry Duffy和Luana Lopez Lara的口水战，但真正被埋在Gordon那段"parametric insurance"论述里的洞见是——预测市场的原语（liquidity aggregates around outcome projections）正在悄悄解构一个远比预测市场大得多的产业：再保险。

跨领域的连接在这里：预测市场和ILS（保险连接证券）本质上是同一门数学的两种社会包装。它们都在解决"如何为二元/参数化事件定价"。Kalshi赚的每一分钱，本质上是在替帕胡罗农田的干旱、玻利维亚水坝的水位、加州山火的风速这些至今仍被寄生性经纪人把持的巨大市场做技术验证。

但Austin立刻从ILS老兵的视角丢出一个反杀：参数化触发器最大的问题不是价格，而是"basis risk"——参数触发和实际经济损失往往同向移动，让保险公司在赚了参数化的钱后，反而更接近破产而不是远离。这解释了一个吊诡的现象：为什么预测市场的数学如此优雅，但保险公司死活不肯买单？ 答案是监管层不给"参数化再保险"完全的准备金抵免，于是价格永远达不到市场出清。

真正的机会窗口不在保险，而在Gordon点破的那句话里——"local disruption events"。预测市场如果要真正吃掉一块万亿级市场，它需要去的不是Lloyd's of London，而是那些至今没有对冲工具的、颗粒度过细、传统承保商懒得看的场景。这是一个被所有人误读的战场。

三、AI能耗政治化：加密行业已经把剧本写好了，AI公司却还没读

节目最后的AI讨论里，一个惊人的类比被埋得很深——Gordon把AI数据中心的电力困境，直接对标2021-2022年的比特币矿工。当年矿工信誓旦旦说"北美有3-4分钱的电力从现在到永远"，结果被现实教育。

这里的跨领域洞见是：AI行业正在重演加密行业2018-2022年的政治周期，但速度快10倍，且他们完全没有意识到自己在重演。加密行业花了五年时间，才学会如何面对Elizabeth Warren、如何组织Fairshake PAC、如何构建"我们创造就业、我们是基础设施"的叙事。而AI公司还在用"我们要毁掉你的工作，但我们的机器神会统治社会，请信任我们"这种最灾难性的话术。

更隐秘的观察是Rahm提出的那个数据点：中国民众对AI的好感度85%，美国35%。这个鸿沟不是技术差距造成的，而是叙事结构差距——中国把AI定位为"公用事业"，美国把AI定位为"取代你的存在性威胁"。这里有个反直觉的推论：如果AI公司想赢得中期选举周期，它们需要的不是更好的模型，而是雇一批加密行业的合规和政策老兵。因为这些人已经在Warren的听证会上被暴打了五年，他们知道那些电力争夺、NIMBY反抗、"你在毁掉小镇"的叙事该怎么破。

而这直接连回一个更深的模式：Bessant、CFTC主席Selig、Trump对hyperliquid的表态——所有这些"意外的加密友好信号"，其实都是加密行业花了五年时间、几亿美元PAC资金、无数次听证会痛击后才换来的"政治学习曲线"红利。AI行业现在站在的位置，是加密行业2019年的位置。它们还有大约36个月的时间来学习——或者被同一套政治机制碾过一次。

开场引子

"If you're an executive at Poly Market or Kalshi, call me up we can talk about it — parametric insurance. Right? Why aren't these guys building in this space? Because that is a highly illiquid, opaque and I would say unsubstantial marketplace that doesn't live on chain, doesn't have smart financial quants trying to solve the problem through DeFi, and is more or less trafficked by a bunch of parasitic brokers and large balance sheet players."

Hey everyone, welcome to Bits and Bips — where we explore how crypto and macro collide one basis point at a time, or I guess today, tens of basis points at a time.

We're here to discuss the latest stories in the worlds of crypto and macro. As a reminder before we dive in, Bits and Bips has its own channels now. If you're listening on the Unchained feed, come subscribe to Bits and Bips directly so you don't miss an episode.

And before we begin, a word from one of our sponsors. This episode is brought to you by 1inch Aqua, the shared liquidity layer from 1inch. Back multiple liquidity positions with one wallet balance and keep your tokens in your wallet until a swap fills. See how it works at 1inch.com/aqua.

Not listening to Bits and Bips yet? It's our weekly crypto and macro market show with Ram Ahluwalia, Austin Campbell, and Chris Perkins. Search Bits and Bips and subscribe.

市场快照

All right, everybody. Quick market snapshot because we're going to be talking markets today.

Bitcoin touched 80K, currently is hovering in the high 7,800s as I'm looking at my screen here — extending last week's run. Spot Bitcoin ETFs flipped hard to inflows. We've seen billions of dollars across the entire week: over 500 million Wednesday and Thursday and over 300 mil on Friday from the numbers I have in front of me.

The 30-year Treasury yield remains elevated in the 5.2s — highest basically since 2007. 10-year not much lower at 4.65. So where we are with all of that is Bitcoin is now only 37% below its all-time high.

For today, as always, I'm your host Austin Campbell, high scholar of Zero Knowledge Group. I'm here with my two usual co-hosts Ram Ahluwalia, maester of wealth, the leader of Lumida, and Chris Perkins, the golden hand of Franklin Crypto. But today I am particularly excited because we have Gordon Grant with us, portfolio manager, head of derivatives at Bitwise.

So to lay everything out before we start talking markets, everybody remember we've got Bitwise on here, we've got Franklin on here, and I used to run stablecoins at Paxos. So all of us have views.

一、Bessant的长端回购与波动率的跨市场传染

Let's start with some framing and then I want to talk markets, guys. So the tape last week turned pretty hard. Bitcoin topped 75K and kept running over the weekend and into today. As we said, the ETF flows flipped.

The catalyst appears to have been the Treasury. They started doing long-end buybacks — talking 30-year sector with maybe some in the 10 to 20 year. They were looking at 2 billion up to 4 billion, maybe more as of today, and 30-year yields ran up. 4 billion is limited relief in a 32 trillion market. But there are some people who are saying this is positive.

Arthur Hayes on Laura's Unchained interview said: "I think this is the beginning of a major move on Treasury buyback change. Warsh and Bessant are running the Powell and Yellen playbook. Keep the short end cheap so the Treasury can issue short and buy back long — a sort of operation twist. They are going to start printing money and the buyback is meant to scare the market into believing 5% on the long bond is the level we'll defend it at."

ETH cleared 3,000 on that, but other analysts have stressed the buyback is not QE. The Fed did not turn on the printer, and that the bond market moved first, and it was a short squeeze that did the rest.

Gordon：波动率的连接被打通了

I want to start before we get into some of the other commentary — since we have a few people here who know a little bit about these markets — and Gordon, I'll go to you first. When you're looking at what Bessant is doing and what it's doing to perceptions and volatility in the market, what are you seeing here?

Gordon: I feel like Bitcoin was kind of the last of large cap liquid assets ex-crypto to pick up on the volatility bug that's been percolating, permeating, pervading the macro space for the last several months. We had chips and GPUs and data center players and large cap fintech, and then the energy markets earlier in the year, and rates themselves.

I think what Bessant has done, from my perspective, right — sitting here and trying to run a number of significantly sized Bitcoin and crypto volatility books — is make a connection between TradFi rates volatility and now crypto volatility in a way that is meaningful to institutional participants and that a narrative can be built around.

The market reaction is really saying not much more than that: as you pointed out Austin, volumes are not so significant from this perhaps redux of operation twist and the context of the size of the market. But signals can be as effective as sizes. We saw this a little bit with the way MicroStrategy's own policy articulation played out earlier in the year — when signaling wasn't effective, it took some size to finally get things moving. Here, it's a bit of the opposite.

The expectations around what it could mean if there's a steep yield curve — and exactly the type of behavior that you meant — people hear, think, see and project in terms of price and their participation, even if the liquidity is not yet hitting the system. And probably from a delta or second-order perspective it matters more, because most folks who are watching might have started to sense palpably that the tide was going out on liquidity. And this matters in some substantive way.

Ram：这是一个平行宇宙

Austin: Ram, I want to flip over to you as somebody who's been following markets for a while here. What are you making of the price action over the last week?

Ram: Well, it's extraordinary. There's a lot happening.

Number one: after Bessant had the intervention into the long end market, that set commodities racing again. If you look at the SPY versus gold chart, for example, commodities just outrunning — that's called the debasement trade.

And then you had Trump's comments around crypto which has sparked an incredible short squeeze in Bitcoin. And you have the Treasury Secretary talking about Hyperliquid. It's like we're in a parallel universe — I mean, it's as strategic apparently as like Taiwan Semiconductor.

I still continue to think that is the asset of this cycle. It's got all sorts of interesting properties around it. We talked about this a few months ago, the Circle and Coinbase deal with them.

Bitcoin is a momentum asset. It does have momentum now, and unlike other assets, momentum assets just kind of tend to keep going. So when they have momentum, you don't want to fade that. It is at a very interesting juncture right now and you really have to manage this like day-to-day. There seems to be a bit of waning momentum around there but you don't have any red bars yet.

So there's like a tactical view and then strategic view. I even think that Hyperliquid is the better asset in the category. Trump also has midterm elections coming up. He doesn't want investigations from the House. And who got him elected? Fairshake PAC. So the timing around this intervention plays to the political cycle as well. Clarity Act has been challenging. This is a way to deliver a win and potentially juice up those coffers to set up for the next midterm fight.

Chris：新的财政部-联储协议

Chris: Yeah, I was going to say — did you guys see the Bitcoin-gold chart? It's been pretty much vertical, which I think is a good story for Bitcoin.

Just to unpack some of the stuff you guys said: we've been talking on this show for a long time about the new Treasury-Fed accord. I think you're going to see more of this in action this week as Warsh ends up in Jackson Hole. Probably not going to say a ton because he told people he's not going to say a ton, but what are you seeing? You're seeing these two guys working in very close coordination.

And what have we known since the beginning? Bitcoin, crypto — it's very very responsive to liquidity. It's very very responsive to rates. I think people are starting to see that Warsh may say some things, maybe he'll be hawkish, but we just don't see him moving rates anytime soon. He was not put in the seat if the president thought he was going to raise rates in any way, shape, or form.

You're seeing a lot of the yield curve — I guess I don't want to say control — but action being a function of Bessant. Is this the beginning of a new regime? Well, it's pretty clear to us that Bessent himself is very focused on keeping rates in check. He talks often about the 10-year. Maybe this time he went out a little further on the curve.

This also plays very nicely into the stablecoin story. If we can get stablecoins going — because if we can move debt to the front end of the curve, short-term Treasury bills, we can issue more stablecoins, we can have people consume those stablecoins, yields will stay nice and tight. That's good if you're running a government and you want to keep your interest rates in check. You don't want to pay all that interest.

二、财政主导、期限溢价与"坏胆固醇"

Austin: So I think an interesting dynamic that's emerging there, Chris, to piggyback on your comments: if we look at the setup — we have Bessant talking about buying back the long end and issuing at the short end. We still have above-target inflation for the Federal Reserve, but we also have significant amounts of outstanding current Treasury debt.

It puts us, if you really zoom out and think about government finances in the simplistic way possible — which is to say dollars in, dollars out — a very funny situation where I might say fiscal dominance. That is to say, the spending of Congress and the outstanding debt load means raising rates also strangely shoots more money out of the fire hose. If you are quickly reinvesting all of this in short-term debt, there's more money going from the government into the private sector.

One of the things that I've been keeping an eye on here — and Gordon, I actually want to flip this back over to you — is the increasingly divergent behavior between the front end and the long end of the curve. Like we see this behavior in EM historically where the government starts doing things and kind of regardless of what they do, people lose confidence and the long end just starts going up and up and up. We're seeing a little bit of that in the United States and that also tends to be volatile. So what are you making of this whole situation through that lens?

Gordon：过度方差、买家罢工与"坏胆固醇"

Gordon: Yeah, bingo. In a classical economics course, you talk a lot about liquidity preference. I liken this to excess variance causing a buyer strike. And that's really the problem here.

There's actually nothing in common between 30-year rates and the front end, just as there's very little in common between one-month implied vol and one-year implied vol. Sometimes they're the same level, and sometimes they're different by many factors or even orders of magnitude depending on the asset class.

That excess variance has now caused liquidity to worsen — it's not the same as it was when rates were a lot lower. I think it's also caused a knock-on effect in disparities based on what I read. Again, I'm not in the Treasury market all day every day like I was when I was at a macro shop for a long time. But the on-the-run, off-the-run stuff appears to be rearing its head again. It's also showing up as it seems a little bit in some of the swap spreads.

All of that is kind of signs of bad cholesterol, as my former mentor and boss at NWI used to call it. An operation twist, a jawbone policy articulation out of the Fed, might be intended to bring down some of that LDL — or at least change people's perceptions and say, "Is this really LDL, or maybe there's a little bit more HDL in that mix than you think, and you shouldn't be as scared of it."

Now, are they going to get — and this is going to open Pandora's box for our calls, so forgive me — but are they ever going to be able to get the international community, not ever, but in the near future, back into the long end in a big way? What would it take to convince some of the most significant international participants in the Treasury market to say, "Hey, take that bet on US policy orthodoxy, US rhetoric consistency, US decision-making hierarchy" in a way that would inspire people to come back into the long end in a big big way?

Not sure that's the case. It's kind of a low credit quality perception that we're going to have to deal with here. Of course, there is no credit quality because they can always pay back and in their own currency. But the credit quality for them is the variance. And it is something that you tend to see in junk issuers and high yield, where even at higher levels of yield, there's higher levels of yield and price variance. And that's kind of making the Treasury market seasick.

比特币爱波动率，利率恨波动率

There are some markets that thrive on vol. Bitcoin — people tend to like when the vol picks up. When the vol is low, it's not good for Bitcoin. That takes us to Dec '22, Jan '23 when front-end Bitcoin vol is in the teens and 20s, when price at that time was in the teens and 20s. Takes us to where we were until August 19th at about 9:30 in the morning, where Bitcoin is hanging around its bottom decile of price and bottom decile of vol. High vol gets people excited about it because it starts to inflate the right tail of distribution.

And rates — it kind of works the other way. Rates are bounded at zero. They're unbounded to the top side. And so this kind of vol starts pricing in not just greater gyrations around some mean-reverting tendency but the skewness of the distribution. You go: "Hey, the log-normal adjusted probability of 30-year rates going back to four is now going to be more equivalent to like 30-year rates — or let's say 20-year rates 10 years forward — hitting 6, 7, 8." And that starts to scare people.

You've got that skew moving the wrong way and you've got that convexity premium in the tails of the distribution moving the wrong way. It's interesting to see how that's being detrimental for Treasury market stability, but it's actually creating momentum behind Bitcoin.

For those of you that play in longer-dated volatility in Bitcoin, we've been of the view for a little bit of time that the long end was just inappropriately priced — where you had stuff like one-year almost sub-10 delta strikes at, take your pick, 40, 42, 43 vol. And that started to move the other way. So the at-the-money vol is now higher and the out-of-the-money options vol is higher. And that's exactly what's happening in Treasuries just in the opposite way.

Chris：Basis回归对现货是极大利好

Chris: Hey Gordon, the other thing I would add is: in our space, the crypto space, when that volatility results in basis — where you have the future price higher than the spot price — all the big boys want to come in. Because when that gets attractive, crypto has been proven to be a very lucrative place to play the basis trade.

Basis trade is very very good for spot assets, because what you do is you buy the spot, you sell the future. When you have more buyers and sellers, what happens? Price goes up. So that's another thing to really watch. That is very very healthy for our markets.

Gordon: Big time. And been a long time coming, right? For us to get back —

Chris: Been a long time. It's been awful — no basis trade, no reason to buy spot, sell future.

Austin: And this was a big trade during the last cycle and I think it was one of the things that drove assets pretty high.

Austin：TIPS市场里那些"奇怪的褶皱"

So to pile in here on what's going on in Treasury markets, there's a weird little corner pocket of the Treasury market most people don't think about too often called TIPS — the inflation-protected Treasury market. We're starting to see some weird and chunky things moving around in the TIPS market, which is also usually a good sign something is getting creaky in there.

You're seeing very bizarre stuff like a one-year, two-year, three-year butterfly action, which means the twos are much shallower than the ones and threes. You're seeing bizarre steepeners. Real yields hitting some highs since the crisis. All of these are basically signs to me that people are starting to think the endgame of some of the US fiscal imbalances may be closer than people think.

Because if you look at the timing framework, we're probably now five to six-ish years off having to do something about Social Security — either just straight up cut benefits, or start modifying programs, or change behavior, or just straight up print money. And when you're already going into that with a debt-to-GDP of 100 plus, you typically end up in one of two places historically.

One of those is inflation — where what happens is they'll hold rates down below what essentially real inflation is, to work your way out of this over a, you know, however long period, call it a decade or two. And for those who think that hasn't happened before in the United States, look at the post-war aftermath in the 40s, 50s, and then look at the 70s. Like, we've done this repeatedly.

The other one is default. But again, the US is denominated in dollars, controls all its debt in dollars, the dollar is used globally. Here, I think inflation is the much easier political choice. So I don't really see people going with default in this case.

And that leads, I think, Ram, all the way back to you — which is to say you're talking about Bitcoin as a momentum trade here. And by the way, I do agree there's definitely momentum in crypto markets, because while the fundamentals have definitely improved for something like Bitcoin here, it's hard to look at like Cardano rallying in sympathy a significant amount and be like, "Cardano has tens of users. I'm not seeing people piling in and more builders there." This is just a momentum trade. So there's going to be some breaks and mean reversion within the category. But where I wanted to get to is: is this momentum, or put differently, when everything is rallying like this, is it just inflation?

Ram：不要过度担心美债

Ram: Well, let me pull back to your point on Treasuries. You're actually channeling Ray Dalio there — it's interesting analysis.

I don't think you're going to see end-bond vigilantes breaking the US Treasury market. It's the most liquid market in the world. It's the least dirty shirt in the laundry basket. The productivity growth is here. The earnings growth is here. Nominal GDP growth of the United States resembles like China a few years ago — meaning we're the Asian tiger now.

So I wouldn't get overly concerned about rates. I've noticed that in the equity markets, rates-sensitive names aren't going down anymore. In fact, I don't think Bessant even needed to intervene. Markets were settling of their own accord. His intervention might have actually spooked investors.

How I see this playing out: if rates go to 5% on the 10-year, that's the top in rates and you buy whatever you can. That might be the time to buy bonds — or somebody out there, not me, but somebody, I could get behind that logic. But if that happened, risk assets would be very cheap. I wouldn't be surprised if in 6 to 9, 12 months, the 10-year is lower than 4.79, because you are seeing disinflation, you are seeing productivity growth. So yeah, I think this is much ado about nothing.

You also have this August. It seems like policymakers always like to scare markets. August: dump all the bad news here. They do the interventions here. Moody's does something around now also.

On Bitcoin momentum — it's funny, the four-year cycle is in a way starting a little bit too early. So I don't think — a lot of people are offsides on this as well. Bitcoin didn't deliver what it should have this past cycle. That's just a fact — versus where you were four years ago, versus the prior cycle high. So I think the dynamics that play out in crypto are going to be very different. It does have significant competing narratives against it, including physical AI. Everywhere you look, you got a robot outrunning Usain Bolt. Now you got Travis Kalanick building physical robots to do mining, to do cloud kitchens, to do autonomous vehicles. So I still think a lot of attention and capital will be more focused in those areas.

Gordon：EM剧本与NTNB的启示

Austin: Gordon, what do you make of the Dalio parallel there? I knew Ram might drop that one. I'm curious as to your thoughts.

Gordon: I'm going to kind of pull out the EM playbook to which you alluded and I think is appropos here. I'll be the devil's advocate.

How likely could it be that US inflation-index product could start to get looked at such as something like Brazil's NTNB market? For those of you that have played in that space — I remember it being 2011-12 era going into the taper tantrum. I was at NWI. We had one of the world's biggest asset managers come to us and go: "What's wrong with the inflation-linked product in Brazil, Mexico, South Africa, you name it? Is there an opportunity here for alpha?"

We debated it and they created a $100 million SMA to go out and do currency-lite hedged investments into inflation-index product in all of those jurisdictions. It took a minute for that to kind of come right round. NTNBs have crazy duration — you can get it even longer than the flavors in North America and G10 markets. But eventually it did, because they went through a period of significant belt-tightening, monetary tightening, other forms of austerity. And they left behind some of the vicissitudes of policy heterodoxy, fiscal heterodoxy.

That's not unlike what we're seeing here — where although productivity is a big driver, although rates up at this level in the long end are starting to impose some degree of tightening of financial conditions, along with energy markets. And by energy markets, what we really talk about are the product markets. Total CEO out there today talking about the bifurcated physical crude and physical products markets — not unlike the front end and the long end of the bond curve. These don't appear to exist in the same zip code, maybe not even the same continent anymore.

But I do see Ram's POV there, which is to say — 5% tens, it's either this thing comes back down or we're all going to hell in a handbasket, because it just can't absorb that. And that should be the top of real yields, the top of nominal yields, minus or plus some variance buffer.

Austin：路径依赖与远期曲线

Austin: Yeah. I look at this through the lens of: if we're at 5% in the 10-year, either, as you said, rates are going way up to start handling this, or they're coming back down and we're going to financially repress people in some way. And you'd want to be owning the inflation products, or you want to be owning gold and Bitcoin in those cases — because you are either playing the game as aggressively as possible, or you don't want to be playing that game at all. Those are kind of the two vectors. It's not staying at 5.

But I think what was most interesting to me watching Bessant and then the market reaction is: right now I'm not sure we could tell from the market signals which way people are predicting things will go, because this is probably a net improvement in either of those outcomes right now. But where are we going to be three months from now, six months from now, a year from now? There's some iterativeness to this game and I wonder how much people understand that.

Gordon: Path dependency in full force. And you raised a great point about optionality. Probably worthwhile to dust off your Bloomberg — I need to do it myself — and check out where the forward curve is. Where's the 10-year 10-year, 20 or 20-year? The old playbook, the macro playbook, comes out — at-the-money spot, at-the-money forward, receiver spreads, things of that nature could be interesting. Not a recommendation to make an investment or withhold from taking action, but I'm curious to what are the payoff ratios for those types of strategies at this level of rates, especially in forward space.

Austin: Yeah, and I think we've seen some movement recently — like front-end/back-end and breaks in the inflation market for instance. All those little granular bond things are coming back and mattering now that the whole curve is not laying flat close to zero.

All right, before we get any further into the bond market, because we're going to lose everybody if Gordon and I keep talking about that, we are going to go ahead and take a quick commercial break.

广告插播

$540 million. That's how much concentrated liquidity sat idle in a given week in the first half of this year — about 30% of the DeFi TVL if you're wondering. That's according to Dune Research commissioned by 1inch.

But there's a solution. 1inch Aqua is the new shared liquidity platform. It lets LPs back multiple positions with the same token balance and keep their tokens in their wallet till a swap comes. Why does that help? Because the LPs don't have to split their tokens across positions. They can cover more market conditions and pairs with their full balance. That means more activity across deeper liquidity. See how it works at 1inch.com/aqua. Remember that providing liquidity carries risk and fees aren't guaranteed.

Heads up everyone. We've now fully transitioned Bits and Bips to its new dedicated channels. If you're not yet subscribed to the new Bits and Bips channels on X, YouTube, Spotify, Apple Podcast, or wherever you get your podcast, go there and subscribe now. For the next few weeks, we'll play segments of the full interviews on Unchained as a reminder. But for now, you'll only hear those short segments of Bits and Bips on Unchained — no more full episodes. You can get links to all of the dedicated channels with the full episodes at unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips.

三、CFTC的预测市场之战：拳击手 vs 芭蕾舞者

All right, everybody. Welcome back. Now we're here to talk about people fighting — specifically the CFTC.

At the CFTC's inaugural innovation advisory committee meeting in DC on August 21st, CME chairman Terry Duffy and Kalshi co-founder Luana Lopez Lara traded — shall we say — insults over prediction market oversight.

Duffy was saying: "We're not a bunch of carnival barkers at a circus." And warned, "Some event contracts are open to manipulation." He said again: "I have more people in my regulatory department than you have in your entire company." To which Kalshi's CEO responded: "Maybe you should learn a little bit about efficiency then." And Duffy said: "Maybe you should learn about credible markets."

Now before we get into the brawl between them, let's also talk about Mike Selig and his comments here, chair of the CFTC. "Congress gave the CFTC exclusive authority to regulate prediction markets," he said, and that the agency will defend its jurisdiction against states seeking to nullify federal law. He said: "We've crossed the Rubicon and are standing at a new frontier in finance." And framed the prior era as "anti-crypto armies, doomers, and decelerationists."

So this is a hell of a brawl.

Chris：终于看到创新在岸发生

Austin: Chris, I want to start with this one for you since I know you're a derivatives markets guy as well. What do you make of the sparring between the CFTC and Kalshi? Do you think each argument has validity? Is somebody solely talking their book?

Chris: I mean, I'm actually thrilled to see this dialogue happening. I was in this market for so many years, and after the global financial crisis, any kind of creativity, any type of innovation kind of died in derivatives markets. There was nothing. The biggest innovation was like the regulated businesses that we built, which is like not really innovative — you do stuff around the edges.

You finally, finally, finally, after years, we finally have these two new innovations coming out at the same time. They've been around for a little while, but now you're finally seeing product-market fit. And guess what? This is another — we always talk about convergence. We're seeing more and more the crypto market is exporting stuff into traditional markets, whether it's 24/7 markets, whether it's perpetuals (and notice I didn't say futures or swaps — kind of think they're futures). And also prediction markets. These are things that have really been a part and parcel to crypto markets, where they had product-market fit.

I am thrilled. I am thrilled that we're seeing this innovation. I'm thrilled that we're starting to see this innovation happening onshore. Sadly, all this innovation happened offshore because people were scared. I had portfolio companies that were literally put out of business when they tried to build onshore, because the technology didn't reconcile with what we have.

We talked about market moves earlier — we said macro caused a lot of it. We also saw the president say, "Hey, Chairman Selig and I are going to work to get Hyperliquid onshore." And I think you have to say that a lot of the Hyperliquid move was idiosyncratic, related to that subject.

Now, as these perp DEXes are coming onshore, what can they do? Number one, they can follow the old way, which is get what I like to call the cocktail of derivatives licenses: DCO, FCM, DCM. Or maybe the CFTC is going to be bold enough — and if anyone can do it, it's Chairman Selig — on finding ways to align with the principles of the regulation, disclosures, controls, etc., with the technology as it works. I testified in Congress a bunch of years back saying, "You know what? We don't really need intermediaries with this technology. You may want them but you don't need them."

Regarding this hearing — so you have Lana from Kalshi, you got Duffy from CME. The first thing that I love about it is the visual. You can't get two more opposite people, right? Just look at them. Terry — the CME has been a dominant factor. They're an incredible business. And lately their stock price has been taking a hit because of some of this disruption. When you're an incumbent, you have to make a decision, and it's a tough decision. Do you try to fight? Do you try to put up regulatory gaps? Do you try to do whatever it is to keep the status quo where you're doing quite well? Or do you swim with it and have partnerships?

It looks like Chairman Duffy is looking to fight right now. Terry was very critical of prediction markets, saying that they're prone to manipulation. Well, I've got news for you: it's illegal to manipulate derivatives markets. And to the extent somebody manipulates a derivatives market, the CFTC is going to hold them accountable. So guess what guys, don't do it.

And you know, the other thing is they'll immediately go and say, "You know, FTX this or FTX that." Let's just look at history. FTX blew up overseas. When we have a thoughtfully regulated market, which you want to see here, that's a good thing.

Lana's right — if she's able to accomplish these things with more automation, probably pretty awesome than rather have a lot of people manually going around checking things. So at the end of the day, what am I a fan of? I'm a fan of innovation. I'm a fan of markets that are not subject to manipulation. To the extent there is fraud, manipulation, or abuse, let's get after 'em, Chairman Selig — and that's exactly what he's doing. I'm a fan of automation. Automation is the way that we can scale.

Let's accelerate these derivatives markets. ICE has been very thoughtful as well in their embrace of the technology. They did the deal with Polymarket. My personal sense is that Terry Duffy is probably not consensus right now. I'm seeing a lot of the other exchanges actually moving very fast to embrace prediction markets.

Oh, last thing guys — let's just remind each other: derivatives rule the world. Spot markets don't really matter that much. It's derivatives that rule everything. All right, I've said my piece.

Gordon：拳击手与芭蕾舞者

Gordon: I like to call this the pugilist and the ballerina. That's what I think yesterday's name was all about really. And it's all there in it — you've got youth, elegance, and then you've got the kind of swaggering prize fighter looking to take back the title belt. That dynamic is totally understandable.

But I think it's going to be grace and elegance, intelligence, suave panache poise that ultimately wins here. You said it right, Chris, about derivatives markets ruling the world.

Speaking of fighting — not just CFTC fighting — if you want to see an instance for how these markets sometimes have inappropriate activity, such as the betting that happened around a conflict and kinetic outcomes in the Persian Gulf, those are actually quickly spotted. People were slapped on the wrist and I think you're going to face significant penalties for placing wagers on things for which they had asymmetric and material non-public information.

So while I'm not going to say that I see no point in the points that Duffy has made, I'm going for the ballerina to take the belt home in this discussion.

Chris: I want to say she was a classically trained ballerina, by the way.

Gordon: Oh, 100%. That's absolutely right.

Austin：市场操纵在传统衍生品里也发生过

Austin: I was gonna say — it's not like there hasn't been manipulation in traditional derivatives markets. So, war did not happen. Everybody memory-hole that thing. It's not real. It's totally not the case that hedge funds have taken position in derivatives and then hammered thinly-traded spot on people in the CDS market. Like, none of those things have ever happened. It's fine. It's fine.

But like all nonsense aside there, I was watching this and it's interesting to me to see the fight being between Kalshi and the CME because I want to take the opposite side. The dominant voice here who should probably be determining this is actually the customers. Because if we're thinking about what makes markets valuable, it's: can people use them for purposes that actually have utility? Are we hedging? Are we speculating? Are we raising funds? Are we engaging in things that ultimately lead to productivity? Because I have an old economics professor who used to say if you're not doing those things, that actually is gambling. But if those activities are at sort of the core of what your markets are doing, at least in some amount, then you have real capital markets.

I'm curious as to where this debate goes based on how people vote with their money and vote with their feet. Because the reality is the CEOs of Kalshi and CME can say whatever they want, but you still got to win the game to get the trading volumes and deliver the best product to people. And isn't that ultimately what we should be following?

Ram, for you as an investor, when you see this fight breaking out, how are you thinking about this on a forward basis — who's winning and who's losing?

Ram：产品不错，但对消费者是负期望值

Ram: Well, on the one hand, having these prediction markets to price events, including election outcomes, is truly extraordinary. It's great to see that.

On the other hand, of course those markets are manipulated. Of course, it's negative expected value for the consumer. I don't think it's a healthy product for the vast majority of consumers.

From an investor standpoint, the question is: can Kalshi translate in a boarding event like the World Cup and make that customer sticky and then adopt new categories? We'll see. That's hard to do. I'm not terribly excited about those businesses given where their valuations are. I think one of these businesses just doubled their valuation after the World Cup and raising money. I look at that as: if you're an insider, you should be selling. I think that's what some of these folks are doing.

So on the one hand — great for the innovation — I just don't think they're great products for consumers or investors.

Austin: How long, Ram, do you think — you use prediction markets as part of hedging strategies? And Gordon, you guys doing that already?

Ram: It's great for getting information and insight — that's how I would look at it. But the best hedge for a risky asset is to sell the asset. That's the first thing you do.

Gordon：参数化保险的机会

Gordon: Yeah, so I agree with Ram about using the information that you get from the markets today. That's what they're useful for, because we've got liquid, transparent, functional, scalable, linear and nonlinear derivatives markets. That's the space I play in. And that's where I think I find positive expected value, consistent alpha, let's say, across a volatility surface.

Unless I'm thinking about running an ARB strategy — let's say between binary outcomes in prediction space and vanilla options outcomes, which is not yet within my mandate — but if I were back at Genesis running a regulated derivatives business, we probably would have had a healthy slice of that in the prop book.

But looking forward — what are the products that could be healthy for the customer base? I got one for you. And if you're an executive at Polymarket or Kalshi, call me up. We can talk about it: parametric insurance.

Why aren't these guys building in this space? Because that is a highly illiquid, opaque, and I would say unsubstantial marketplace that doesn't live on chain, doesn't have smart financial quants trying to solve the problem through DeFi, and is more or less trafficked by a bunch of parasitic brokers and large balance sheet players.

The primitives that have been discovered through Polymarket and Kalshi tell us one thing: liquidity will aggregate around outcome projections. Whether those are fairly priced or not is a separate discussion. But when you look at the world today — and Chris, you and I and our little Ted had this discussion — you are all about making entropy great again. And I'm right there with you. I think the way that we make MEGA happen is by creating mechanisms for decentralized financial risk mitigation that disintermediates a lot of the sclerotic interstitial tissue that has held back financial innovation.

A derivatives market where you could, let's say, get parametric coverage for — I don't know — a Bolivian dam operator that's facing a perhaps existential drought, and he's not going to be able to get his favorite XYZ broker or underwriter to approach that, is a great thing. And other types of nat-cats and other types of hard-to-categorize binary outcomes around which we can build oracles that are robust to manipulation — that's really interesting stuff.

I do think also that working with financial parameters as a start — and not just event parameters, RWEs — is helpful because it starts to drive convergence. There can be manipulation, let's say, in things like the 15-minute epochs on Bitcoin outcomes on a predictive marketplace. But guess what? Once they get liquid enough, the vanilla options and linear derivative guys are going to come in and try to arb it. And that's going to drive convergence in a cubrious way.

Ultimately what I've kind of intoned about — insurance potentially in a parametric fashion living on chain or living on these types of markets — may ultimately be able to be cured in the same way. So it's neither all bad nor good, but for now it's a great source of incremental useful information. It's a good conditional prior. All of us on this call in some way, shape or form live in a Bayesian intellectual and investing framework. And if you can give us another high-alpha conditional prior, we'll take it. So thanks Paul and Mark.

Austin：参数化保险的死角 — Basis风险

Austin: I'll pile in though to say I think the parametric stuff is a severe dead end. As somebody who's probably traded maybe more ILS than almost anybody in the world over the past two decades, which is to say — you have two very severe problems in parametric markets as you think about building out that market, that has caused them not to take off.

Number one is your basis to what your actual exposure as an insurer is. On the front end of the contract, I owe people economic losses for things that have happened. On the back end of the contract, I have a parametric trigger. And all too often they move in the same direction, which puts me towards bankruptcy, not away from it. I will have missed on the parametric trigger and lost a shitload of money, or the storm will miss some location but it'll have hit some parametric gate, so I kind of made money for no reason. It starts being a very weird thing.

This leads to a regulatory overhang where they don't give you full reinsurance credit for the parametric cover — which is why they don't want to buy it. If you look at the balance sheet of like an Allstate, or Prudential if we want to think about life markets, they're trying to get as close to risk distribution as possible. We do a bunch of business on the front end, we have to have some level of legal risk retention, but we want to offload as much of the rest out the back as cheaply as possible as we can. If you look at Pru's balance sheet, by the way, they are offloading vastly more risk than they hold on to nowadays. And when you don't get full reserve credit for offloading through parametric markets, it's just incredibly inefficient. So the prices that you're willing to pay are nowhere near a market-clearing price. So you just don't use it.

Where I think parametrics are useful is more going to be — and Gordon, you may have alluded to this — like local disruption type events. I don't think it's going to be useful in insurance markets, because this whole framing of economic losses and exclusions and principal-agent problems and fraud are really what drives all of that. And the parameter is like number eight on my list of things that I'm worried about there.

Gordon：这也解释了Duffy vs Lana

Gordon: Yeah, it's a stop-gap. I think you're right, and I think it actually speaks to the Terry Duffy and Lana problem. You've got pugilistic dinosaurs and very lithe, nimble ballerinas, and they each have their own view of the world. Terry Duffy would say that the regulatory framework to which he must uphold himself is the same as the one that the insurers would say, "Hey look, parametric's a great idea, I can't use it because I don't get full offset." And the prediction market people would go, "That's because your regs suck, and I can't work with those. We're here to solve the future problems of finance."

And that may be part of the gap that those folks are trying to solve, both in the insurance space but also trying to think of how you reconcile — and as you say, both cases it's going to be the insureds who are seeking coverage. In this case, of course, it's going to be the client, the directional position person who wants to come in and get that. And they're going to say, "Okay, maybe I like the products that appear on Terry Duffy's CME in various shapes or form, or maybe I really like Polymarket, Kalshi, or maybe I pick and choose. Some are good for some risk mitigation situations and some are not."

And I think as a portfolio manager, Chris, you probably could relate to that as well as anyone.

Chris：颗粒度更细的价格发现

Chris: As you think of the utility of prediction markets, there's a few things to consider.

Number one, the information can be invaluable if there's sufficient liquidity. The paradox of prediction markets is that they're these micro-mini markets. And oftentimes these micro-mini markets, which is where the value is — there's just not enough liquidity. So it's hard to find truth.

I do think you're going to eventually see pretty amazing markets form where you're betting on parts of the company. So then rather than just reading an earnings statement and coming up with a recommendation, buy or sell — if you're an analyst, you'll be able to (and these markets are already forming, guys) — you'll be able to look at certain parts of like sales in the Southwest, or number of phones units sold. You'll be able to bet on them and you'll get much closer to truth. Again, the value's deriving from the data.

Then of course any good derivatives markets, you have hedgers and you have speculators — those are defined terms. We're starting to see the emergence of some hedging. There's the classic story of the bar owner who's betting for/against the Knicks so that they can hedge the drinks that they're going to give everyone for free. That will start spreading, provided there's enough liquidity in the market that you can actually put on a hedge.

And then the last thing is speculation. Speculation is a very important part of markets for those of us who study them. It creates liquidity, and there's plenty of speculation to go around. My daughter, who thinks that she's smarter than any market, will tell you that.

四、20美分的Frontier模型与AI的新地缘政治

Austin: I want to get to a last item so that Ram has his chance to take the once-per-show mandated shot at Sam Altman.

Ram: Oh, here we go. Nothing burger. Nothing burger.

Austin: Which is the 20-cent Frontier model. So there was a mystery model released called 0xAI or 0x Alpha, depending on how you want to look at it, which appeared on OpenRouter — quote, "a frontier model built for efficient coding, sustained agentic work in real world production use."

A lot of people have been speculating it's from ZI and the GLM family of models. There are a couple of things that led to that potential conclusion within the architecture of the model. Some of the other models evaluating it were guessing that that was the case. But rather than talking just about the hunt, let's talk about something important here.

This is the top open-weight coding model. It scored a 28.3 on Terminal Bench 30. By the way — Fable is 33.7, GPT 5.6, Soul is 34.6. So we're talking a pretty goddamn powerful model. And then it's going to be priced apparently at a tenth of the frontier per-token rates.

Coin Bureau said: "A mysterious new AI model reportedly beating Claude, Fable 5, and GPT 5.6 Soul at coding, and nobody knows who built it." They said the model designers "have the capacity for 100 trillion tokens per day" — decent amount of compute. And Bloomberg is saying the US-China AI gap chart is getting obliterated, noting that Kimmy K3 is also close to Fable and 70% cheaper per task.

Ram：可能是Poolside

Austin: Ram, I want to lob this ball over to you first because I know you've been thinking about AI economics for a while. What do you make of the speed at which open-weight models are coming and the economics of them when they're getting this close to or better than the frontier models?

Ram: Yeah, capitalism and competition is wonderful. Consumers win. Small business adoption on-ramps — customers are now at 42% and growing. This is all wonderful news.

I have a theory on who this could be — this model. Nvidia, it was announced today, is investing $6 billion into a company which is America-based. It's called Poolside. They're investing at a $12 billion valuation — sorry, they're investing a billion dollars at a pre-money of a $12 billion valuation. So this could be an American open-weight model. Maybe this article was timed with the release of that model on OpenRouter. That's my hypothesis.

I was at Anthropic headquarters last week — a friend who I called a member of technical staff. You know, it's impressive what they're doing. I think their margins will come in better than most people think. When they drop their S-1, I expect it'll be a market-defining event. People are going to look at: are they subsidizing users? Or are their gross margins attractive without the need for subsidy? I think it'll be more of the latter.

This is not a bubble. It's a real story. You're going to see continued investment. The question is: in the midterms, will politicians continue to press utility companies and press data center firms? Or will that drive up data center cancellation rates, which would be very counterproductive for American progress?

Austin：模型公司如网景，电力才是瓶颈

Austin: Yeah, I think — one, your point about the ultimate winner here being consumers is almost certainly correct.

It's interesting to see with the AI build-out how much of a parallel there has been so far to the original internet build-out — which is to say we've gone through things like: where is the value going to accrue, what companies are going to have these problems, who is developing these frontier solutions, and then rapidly destroying everything and trying again and destroying everything and trying again as we get better and better very quickly. I will remind everybody almost nobody is still using Netscape or AOL — and yet at the time those were paragons of the market in some ways.

So I think you're right that the ultimate value goes to consumers. What is very interesting to me here is that whether you're a call-it open-weights or closed-weights model person, and how you think about the economics there, the bottleneck is going to be compute and power. Those are structural areas. And we're seeing a lot of pushback against that.

Gordon and Chris, I'm curious what either of you are making of this sort of schizophrenia in the market — of the market being very excited about the model companies while everybody is trying to kill every data center known to man.

Gordon：北美电力的可行性问号

Gordon: Yeah, well I was just going to say — look, I think Poolside is a great speculative projection. Clearly, Jensen Huang was out in his first ex-post not long ago talking about the merits of open source. And people have trumpeted this. Open source has a great track record — but not always the king of the hill. Linux, many people cite surely.

As someone who for my own econometric research and quantitative insights do sometimes use open-weight models — the stuff is great. I mean, what can you say? Monopolies oftentimes have a shelf life. Monopolies on LLM like we see out there — they look like monopoly-type pricing. So it stands to reason that at least in some use cases, the king of the hill may be dethroned.

But the big picture, as you say, is consumer wins on token pricing most likely at least in the short term. But the big picture long-term is power — really kind of the binding constraint of human productivity expansion.

I often ask this question tongue-and-cheek: is the compute industry and data center industry going to look like the Bitcoin mining industry? Because when I was at Genesis making markets and trying to convince miners in 2021 and 2022 to collar their production, and they're telling me that they had three or four cent power from now until the end of time, I usually just laugh.

The question now is: how viable is the massive buildup of North American compute going to really be? Or if you are a frontiersman, should you be calling up Serdar Berdimuhamedow in the independent free unaligned Republic of Turkmenistan, who will sell you power at 1 cent from now until as long as he shall live? He may live 100 years from now. And is that a place that you should really be thinking about diversifying compute? I don't know, because I'm not in that business.

But I do look at the paradigm of guys who swore up and down that North America was an economically viable place for Bitcoin mining. And then it became: it was economically viable as long as you had an ERCOT contract. And then it was: well, it's economically viable because it can fund data center business that runs at much higher and more distributionally stable IRR.

These are questions that are going to need to be asked — just where do you source the power for your compute, and is the political establishment going to permit that? And therefore, the question I always like to ask is: how do you hedge that? And that's probably a subject for another podcast.

Chris：AI行业需要讲更好的故事

Chris: Prediction markets. Look, it's very rare that Republicans and Democrats agree on things, and when you're starting to see them beginning to agree that data centers are going to be a major issue as we go into the elections, and it seems to be that they're starting to align a little bit — that's not good news for the AI industry.

The good news is I think they started to wake up and they realized that they're going to have to really work on their narrative. They're going to really have to work on explaining the value that they're here to bring through these data centers. The whole NIMBY discussion is very much in effect. But believe you me, this is going to be a defining election for the AI industry. And I really really hope that they are able to tell a better story about the utility that they're bringing.

To the extent they've gone too far and the data centers are maybe not built in a way that you want them in your backyard, maybe they need to adjust their approach. But I think the entire industry is going to be under increased political pressure. But as crypto people, we know what that's like, guys. So maybe we can give them a couple of ideas.

Austin：反AI叙事的信任缺口

Austin: I mean to some extent — if you look at sort of the grab bag of reasons people have for opposing AI, most of them are factually incorrect about data centers. Like the water usage arguments are just wrong. Some of the job arguments are just wrong.

I think what we really have here is just a factual, like, narrative structure problem for the data centers. Because let's be totally honest: nobody trusts big tech. Especially when the pitch of a lot of the AI companies has been, "We're going to destroy all your jobs, and then as a side effect our machine god is going to rule over your society, but totally trust us, this is fine." It's not surprising to me that a lot of people are like, "We don't want these things around."

Ram：中国85%好感度 vs 美国35%

Ram: I'll challenge you. Tell me — people don't like social media. People like Amazon. They like usage of their Google services which they get for free. They consume Netflix. They enjoy their Tesla. So Americans do like technology.

The issue is the leadership of these frontier lab models are scaremongering Americans about mass unemployment. The perception of AI in China has an 85% favorable rating. In the US, it's 35%. Now we've only seen the criticism of the AI data center. So these are just utilities. You know utility — sewage systems, utility. No one complains about NIMBY that someone is upgrading the sewage in the backyard. They're utility. Intelligence on demand is utility.

All these utilities confer benefits. It's not going to be hard for people to combat these once you're in the election debate — talk about his daughter who is cured of a disease or cancer, see these innovations, and again, small business using this. So they're going to see through this. I don't think it's a winning argument. I think it's actually a very weak argument.

And to the earlier point, you've got firms like Andreessen spending $200 million in pack — pro-AI PACs, that rivals Fairshake, by the way, in the last election. A lot of this criticism against AI and the wealth tax is actually a political move because they've seen Silicon Valley lean right. And so they're trying to attack that at the knees. Let's do a wealth tax. Let's control AI because we want to preserve political power.

Austin：不只是信任，还是"呆子的复仇"

Austin: So I will say, I think — having been in a meeting or two just to see what these are like — I agree with you: people hate social media, they hate AI. I think some of them just don't have trust with the big tech companies, because I'll counter you on Google — I've had a lot of people criticize them for surveillance. Ram, I do think it's a trust issue on all these things.

I also think it's to some extent like a revenge of the nerds kind of thing. By which I mean: you've hollowed out rural communities. You've been unrepentant about it. You don't understand the human cost. And you've just acted like everything's a number in a spreadsheet. It's not surprising to me people are pissed with you and just kind of want to poke you in the eye with the stick.

But I think we need to figure it out because — to channel Chris here before we have to go — there are national security implications to this as well. And I think it's important that the US has these capabilities.

收尾

Since we're out of time, I'll say thanks again for joining us for this episode of Bits and Bips. We'll be back in one week to discuss more about how the worlds of crypto and macro are colliding. Until then everyone, thank you for watching and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips.

Just remember, nothing we say here is investment advice, and please check unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips for more disclosures.

Hey hey hey.

## 一、被忽视的"波动率虹吸"：Bessant如何把国债市场的病灶变成比特币的养料
大部分人在讨论Bessant的长债回购时，纠结的是"这算不算QE"、"4亿够不够"。但节目里Gordon透露了一个更隐秘的机制——**波动率的跨资产传染**。国债市场的坏胆固醇（bad cholesterol：on-the-run/off-the-run错位、swap spread异常、TIPS的蝴蝶失衡）正在系统性地把"方差风险溢价"推向右尾。
这里有个反直觉的对称性：**利率的波动率下沉在零附近（有下界），而向上无界，其对数正态分布的右尾在被重新定价；比特币的波动率结构正好相反——价格下方接近历史底部十分位，右尾同样在被重新定价。** 换句话说，国债市场的"晕船"和比特币的"起飞"共享同一个数学骨架——skewness在往同一个方向漂移，只不过一个是灾难信号，一个是狂欢信号。
这其实揭示了一个更深的模式：**当一个庞大的、被视为"无风险"的市场开始定价尾部风险时，它释放出的方差不会消失，而是会寻找那些天然"喜欢波动"的资产作为宿主**。比特币在这个循环里，扮演的不是"数字黄金"，而是**波动

item.title: [Latent Space] ⏭️ Forward Deployed: Voice AI on what works in 2026
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"时间悖论"：语音AI是编码智能体的祖先

最反直觉的发现藏在Vron的一句话里："voice AI has been one generation ahead of coding agents"。我们习惯认为编码智能体是AI前沿——它们操作代码库、调用工具、管理上下文。但实际上，语音AI早在两年前就在10,000 tokens的窗口里解决了"compaction"问题，而这正是Claude Code、Cursor今天才开始头疼的事。

这里有个令人震惊的时间反转：语音领域因为被迫使用小模型（延迟约束）+ 高频对话（turn多），反而被逼出了整个AI Agent工程学的原型方法论。约束不是限制，而是加速器——就像早期嵌入式工程师因为内存受限，反而发明了后来整个操作系统调度理论的基础。

如果这个规律成立，那么下一个"编码智能体的未来"，可能正藏在今天某个被硬件约束折磨的边缘领域——比如机器人语音控制、卫星通信AI、或车载智能体。去看被约束折磨的人在做什么，那就是三年后主流的样子。

二、"填充词"揭示的深层真相：不完美才是可信度的凭证

Retail的工程师提到一个奇怪现象：零填充词的语音agent反而显得更僵硬。人类"嗯"、"我看看"、"稍等一下"这些语气词，原本被视为要消除的杂音，现在却成为可信度锚点。

这里藏着一个跨领域连接——认知语言学中的"disfluency理论"：Fox Tree等人的研究早已证明，"um"和"uh"实际上是听者认知加工的路标，标记"新信息即将到来"或"我需要修正表达"。语音AI意外地重新发现了人类几万年演化出的对话机制。

更深的洞见是：在AI时代，"完美"正在变成一种反信号。 就像Photoshop过度美化的图片让人本能怀疑，"零延迟零错误"的AI反而触发恐怖谷。未来的AI产品设计可能会走向一种反常识方向——故意植入不完美，就像高端威士忌会保留少量杂质来证明真实性。这与LLM生成文字里越来越多"其实"、"某种程度上"这类hedging词汇的现象，可能是同一种进化。

三、隐藏的产业规律：语音AI是"分布式认知"的实验田，比编码Agent更接近未来

播客里提到一个几乎所有人都会漏掉的关键点：Sudarshan说他们的speech-to-speech模型追求的是"边听边想"的异步架构——因为人脑就是这样运作的。而当前的cascaded pipeline本质上是同步walkie-talkie模式。

这里有一个惊人的跨领域映射：这不就是CPU从单核同步到多核异步流水线的历史重演吗？1990年代的处理器架构革命——分支预测、乱序执行、推测执行——现在正在语音AI里以另一种形式复活。Baroon那句"if you love computer architecture 20 years ago"不是玩笑，是精确的预言。

但真正意外的观察是："outbound电话一接通就被挂断" 这个现象。人们不是拒绝AI，而是拒绝被单方面调用的AI。这暗示未来AI产品的核心竞争力不在于"更像人"，而在于"社会契约的合法性"——你有没有权利在此刻打断我。这个原则未来会扩散到通知系统、日程AI、甚至AI代理的所有主动行为设计中。

最后的暗线：voice AI公司现在都在做hybrid架构（部分speech-to-speech + 部分cascaded），这与其说是技术选择，不如说是认知劳动分工的具象化——autopilot负责快系统，cascaded负责慢系统。这就是Kahneman《快与慢》在硅片上的实现。当AI架构开始镜像人类认知结构，我们其实正在见证工程学向神经科学的收敛。

Yeah, the answer I got was that the CEO had already made a ton of money and he just really wants to play around basically. So I guess he can do whatever he wants.

系统 Prompt 设计：单一大 Prompt vs 工作流分节点

Um, cool. Um, so is it standard practice for in this like cascaded pipeline for you to just give just have one giant like system prompt that you're giving the LLM on these are all the rules for how you should be responding? um or is it more of a um like a workflow approach? How do you guys think about that? What's the standard best practice right now?

So I think it highly depends upon the use case and also the size of your prompt, right? So I think I have a counter approach to Baroon in in terms of that like usually in inbound I find you know you you're usually having dedicated lines and you know specifically where the workflows are going to go right and so in these cases if you know a little bit more about and you can predict where the conversation's going to go then you can have a more of a node or graph builder kind of approach

but if you don't know what's going to happen typically I think in outbound yes there is a dedicated like message but what the caller says back you never know because they could just be frustrated they could be angry or they could be I don't know like annoyed and in that case when they're erratic when a person's erratic you never know so having it in a way that is like all in one one prompt allows you to have an more like a central brain in terms of I can pick up components from my prompt that may not have been in a dedicated flow but actually can be utilized iz to enhance the response.

And then on top of that, you have to think of your knowledge base and knowledge the things at your at your expense, right? Like in a inbound flow, maybe you know exactly when you need to pull a specific part of your knowledge. So you don't need to extract every single piece of context, right? Whether it's your websites and documents, but sometimes in outbound, you should utilize all that information to get a better response. then you will rely more on cosign similarity and stuff to make sure that hopefully your retrieval is good enough to respond to them.

情境化 Prompt 的演变

I think from my perspective um the limiting factor has been and and will continue to be although it's getting a lot better over time just uh to you know some of the earlier points made uh the ability for these uh frontier LLMs to be able to take a massive wall of text and not just read the first three lines and the last three lines but actually be able to properly uh reason and like localize themselves into you know we are halfway through this procedure and these things have already happened and these things haven't happened yet and these things are true and these things are false about this situation and so therefore like this is the one thing that I should be really zooming in on right now right

um so from our perspective I think um we kind of take an approach that depends on the customer um but we do within our execution engine have the ability to um make some of these rules or prompts or guidelines more situational so that we can you know check if these are uh relevant right now before we even uh include include them or or uh uh don't include them in the system prompt. And so that was our solution that was especially relevant, you know, like 7 months ago when the LLMs really were just like consistently skipping step 4 A1.

Um but we have found over time now that uh sometimes the reliability of deciding when these things are relevant or not is actually worse than just giving all of it to the model because the models have improved a lot since that time. And so now we're going back, I think, swinging a little bit back towards just give the model everything and more or less it will figure it out. Um, but at the end of the day, you know, with nondeterministic systems, it really just ends up being customer by customer. uh we have to really understand their use cases and at the end of the day just build it and then test it a whole bunch of times and then use LLM as a judge to tell us you know did it work was it reliable or do we need to add a little bit more um pre-processing and and context optimization ahead of time in order to make it reliable. So the the real answer is most likely always just test and find out and then test again and then find out again and you know it goes on forever.

延迟、填充词与"人味"

I'm assuming that yeah maybe the models are able to handle those edge cases now like just in a giant prompt but that probably also increases latency. So first could you talk about like what is a good latency look like for a voice agent and is that even true that yeah the models are getting better but they also require more time and so for the end user that's actually a bad thing.

Yeah that is a really good question. I mean I I think the definition of what like benchmarking latency stats look like that are good have uh changed a lot and um expectations are you know getting better and better and better from our customers.

Overall, I think it it is also important to mention that um as much as fillers and contextual fillers is something that uh we don't like to hear just as a noun, um it is normal for in normal conversation for humans to say a few words while they're thinking. And so we've actually found that when we have zero contextual fillers, sometimes it actually feels more rigid than when we don't. And so we tend to find that uh having the the right amount of fillers that um kick in when you know we are experiencing some sort of latency because of some very large prompt or some very complex thing that the model is thinking through uh most commonly you know running a tool call where our customer's API becomes the bottleneck and we're waiting you know 5 seconds for something to come back.

Um being able to say hey just give me a sec uh looking at that. Okay, cool. Here's here's your answer, right? There's actually nothing wrong with that. Uh when we've when we've tested with our customers, um obviously the the limiting factor in that case then becomes how good are your fillers and how natural do they sound. Um and so that's been a place where we've invested a lot of time as well to say how do we create an execution engine where we really don't need fillers, but in those moments where we do, they're really good.

Um, so that's at least my take, but again, I know folks have probably a lot of opinions here about latency and and how to find that trade-off because in my opinion, I honestly think that that's the hardest problem to solve in voice deployments is just that trade-off that's always going to be there of like performance versus um stability and reliability in in general. So,

Offloading 与 Multi-Agent 架构

um, yeah, I agree with all of that. Some of the ways that we think about it in Vappy, uh, is offloading, uh, some of that instruction. So break it down. Uh sometimes you don't really need um that you know 10 15 step workflow in the in the prompt.

Uh one example I can talk about is um this uh collections uh use case. Um we do allow users to capture um businesses to capture credit card information. Uh but not every call is uh about that. Some people already have a payment method maybe added or that. So uh one way of doing that offloading into a uh specialized agent uh so we can start thinking about multi-agents and there are many architecture and patterns in there um is to constrain the uh instructions that you give it to to that particular moment of the conversation and once that achieves its goal it can go back to that u more free form approach which has loaded like uh your longer uh context.

Something we're also been uh experimenting lately um and it's more about the guar space is um to uh your point where you can have uh think about it as a waterfall you can actually stream to multiple places. So what if you have uh streaming down to a a small language model which can uh do inference in a very little time. So think about classifiers to maybe collect the intent um while the pipeline is still maybe adding a filler word as well to keep a consistent experience but uh kicking off a background process that is still intelligent still um thinking. So those are still things that we'd like to invest a little bit more research on. Um so yeah constantly investing on that.

成本考量：不只是延迟

Sure. I think of one thing that we haven't also factored in in terms of the latency uh tradeoff is cost right now that you're putting such a big large prompt into your your LLM. You have to think about those calls where many people just hang up and predominantly calls just hang up 10 seconds into the call. Right now you're having to pay for all those tokens to just get inputed in. So that like Stephen mentioned splitting out your prompt, you are also playing to that strength of lower latency and lower cost.

Benchmarks、Evals 与自托管小模型的兴起

I'll speak just to the benchmarks. So we publish u turnbased ST benchmarks, LLM benchmarks and TDS benchmarks. The whole point of that is that as I think today Neumatron 3.5 launched and there's already an ASR um benchmark out did very well the Nvidia one.

So um the idea there is that all our tooling is open source. So with the HTT benchmarks, the TDS benchmarks and the LLM benchmarks all the turns are actually open. So you can run it against any new model that comes out. Uh you can look run it locally. you can look at the outputs from from our graphs and compare that to what you're getting on your infrastructure if you're self-hosting or you know elsewhere.

Um so that's one important aspect to like uh consider if you know what your turns will look like you can just update or you know just download our benchmarks update the turns and see how that like goes for your own flows. Uh usually for the LLM stuff, it's really useful because you can throw out the ST and the TTS and just run the LLM inference loops to like check against uh a customer.

So yeah, I think eval are really important. Um, and if you have like a like while talking to customers, if you can evaluate like what type of conversations or like what type of workflow they're going to have, like those are real direct inputs into like what you can directly start testing even though you're not live with them or even they've not shown any intent. Uh, so I think that's where like the sees and the forward deployed engineers can actually come to for like you we all have cloud running in the background, right? So you can just say here's what we had a discussion like can you build an eval like based on our eval suit like can you like just run a smoke test with the conversation information that we already have and that helps a lot I think.

Yeah, just just adding to that like we are seeing so we while we focus on models we also have all the model sort of orchestrated on our platform. So you could build a voice agent on smallest. Um we are seeing a lot of customers who just pair our models with our own like small language model. It's called electron. fine-tune one of those to make it work for realtime voice use cases and see a lot of folks using that with better knowledge basis memory etc over GB 40 4.1 you know the popular realtime models

um just a from a cost perspective it's lower b from latency perspective it's like way lower u and then just more reliable I think I'm not sure if everyone faces this but like um open AI APIs spike and in um you have no control on those latencies. Um with if you sort of have a self-hosted model um you could scale up scale down based on your requirement. So that's one thing we are seeing a lot with our customers.

item.description:
## 一、被忽视的"时间悖论"：语音AI是编码智能体的祖先
最反直觉的发现藏在Vron的一句话里："voice AI has been one generation ahead of coding agents"。我们习惯认为编码智能体是AI前沿——它们操作代码库、调用工具、管理上下文。但实际上，**语音AI早在两年前就在10,000 tokens的窗口里解决了"compaction"问题**，而这正是Claude Code、Cursor今天才开始头疼的事。
这里有个令人震惊的**时间反转**：语音领域因为**被迫使用小模型（延迟约束）+ 高频对话（turn多）**，反而被逼出了整个AI Agent工程学的原型方法论。**约束不是限制，而是加速器**——就像早期嵌入式工程师因为内存受限，反而发明了后来整个操作系统调度理论的基础。
如果这个规律成立，那么下一个"编码智能体的未来"，可能正藏在今天某个被硬件约束折磨的边缘领域——比如机器人语音控制、卫星通信AI、或车载智能体。**去看被约束折磨的人在做什么，那就是三年后主流的样子。**
