item.title: [GoldRepublic Global] John Butler: Gold And Chinese Bonds Replacing US Treasuries?
item.dc:creator: GoldRepublic Global
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：这不是"QE"，而是"债务的期限套利"——美国正在把自己变成一家投行

大多数评论把 Bessant 的长债回购简单等同于 QE，但 John Butler 点破了一个更让人不安的真相：这是用短债融资来回购长债——不是印钞扩表，而是"缩短负债久期"。这个动作在结构上和 2008 年之前雷曼、贝尔斯登所做的期限错配套利惊人地一致：借短、买长、赚利差、维持流动性幻觉。

换句话说，美国财政部正在把自己资产负债表投行化。这个洞察真正让人后背发凉的地方在于：投行倒下的方式从来不是资不抵债，而是短端融资突然拒绝滚动。当整个联邦债务的加权期限被系统性缩短，美国就把自己暴露在了"日频再融资风险"之下——这是雷曼式的脆弱性，只不过发生在主权层面。

跨领域连接：Rollover（1981 电影）× 中国黄金 × 期权定价理论

Butler 提到那部 1981 年的 Hollywood 电影《Rollover》——但他没有明说的深层类比是期权定价。

他关于中国 10 年期国债收益率为何异常低的解释，本质上是一个隐含期权价值论证：投资者愿意放弃 3% 的票息，是因为他们在为一个"未来可能宣布债券以黄金兑付"的看涨期权定价。这就把"中国国债 vs 美债"从一个利差交易，重构成了一个波动率交易——你不是在赌利率，你在赌货币体制变革的概率。

这个视角有个更疯狂的推论：中国国债收益率越低，反而说明市场对"金本位重启"的隐含概率定价越高。传统宏观分析师会把低收益率读作"通缩预期"或"经济疲弱"，但如果 Butler 的框架成立，那么中国央行的最优策略恰恰是允许收益率保持低位——因为这是市场在无声地为它想要的叙事投票。收益率就是选票。

隐藏的系统性真相：美国经济"欧洲化"是黄金货币化的真正引擎

Butler 说了一句几乎没人展开的话："美国经济现在看起来更像欧洲经济"——税负接近、福利体系接近、劳动参与率下降。这句话表面平淡，但拆开来看是一颗深水炸弹。

布雷顿森林体系之所以能把美元推上王座，不是因为黄金，而是因为美国当时是全球唯一的"结构性增长溢价"来源。美元的储备地位本质上是一张"押注美国经济动能"的股权凭证。当美国的经济结构收敛到欧洲水平时，美元丧失的不是购买力，而是"股权溢价"——它从一只成长股变成了一只价值股，然后是一只债务重组股。

这里的意外连接是：黄金的复兴与其说是货币现象，不如说是"去股权化"现象。当没有任何一个主权经济体能提供结构性增长溢价（美国欧洲化、中国老龄化、欧洲长期停滞、日本已经躺平），全球资本被迫回到唯一不需要增长故事支撑的资产——一种以"不产生现金流"为最大美德的资产。黄金的多头逻辑，最终是对"增长时代终结"的对冲，而不是对通胀的对冲。

一个额外的"啊哈"：日本的债务反而是它的护城河

传统叙事把日本 250% 的债务/GDP 视为定时炸弹。Butler 反手指出：日本欠的是自己，而且它同时是美债最大的外国持有人。这意味着日本可以通过减持美债来"偿还"自己的国内债务——它拥有一个别国没有的杠杆：用别人的负债去对冲自己的负债。

这就把"日本干预日元 = 抛售美债"这个动作重新定义了。它不是被动的救火，而是主动的资产负债表重构。日本每一次干预，都是在悄悄用美国的信用来赎回自己。这个动作可以持续很多年——而美国对此几乎无还手之力，因为反制手段（比如冻结日本的美债持仓）会立刻摧毁美元的储备资产地位。

日本手里握着一把美国不敢让它使用、也不敢从它手里夺走的核武器。

📝 转录文本

John Butler：黄金与中国债券会取代美国国债吗？

开场：主持人引言

Alex Adrenov： The dollar is not distressed at the moment, but these Treasury market actions are wartime actions and they could lead, combined with the oil shock such as the 70s, they could lead to a run on the dollar. That's the recipe that I see here.

You could argue that alongside the shifting demand for dollars vis-à-vis gold, you're seeing a shift in the demand function for Chinese debt. Even though it's not fully integrated into the global financial system, various ways to get exposure to Chinese debt are becoming more attractive vis-à-vis the US treasuries.

There have been rumors for years that at some point China would feel it had accumulated sufficient gold reserves to announce — at some point when convenient, when they thought it served the national interest — that Chinese bonds would henceforth be redeemable in gold. The successor to the dollar will be a gold-backed currency. And that is yet another step along the road of full-on gold remonetization at the international level.

Welcome back to the Microscopic Podcast. My name is Alex Adrenov. I'm your host. And today I have the pleasure and the honor to welcome back my friend John Butler.

John Butler： Alexi, say hello.

Alex： So last time we spoke, John was in South Africa. We had this retreat for a week. We had amazing content, amazing backdrop, some activities, and we discussed a lot of very important topics. So I also urge the listeners and the viewers to have a look at those sessions. We had, I think, four roundtable sessions, one-on-one interviews, and a lot of what we actually discussed back then is more relevant than ever now.

I would say today is Friday, 21st of August, to put things into perspective. Markets are shifting not on a daily basis, on an hourly basis. I notice especially the past days — we will cover important topics as the elephant in the room, obviously the sovereign debt crisis, starting with Japan and the bond market, the Treasury market now in the US with heavy interventions and all that.

So let's start with this and also then see what the implications are on a more global level, but also more precisely in gold and silver and other assets.

一、30 年期美债收益率与 Bessant 的干预

Alex： So let me first start with this question, John. What is there to understand with what we're witnessing now with the 30-year yields? So the long end of the yield curve for the treasuries in the US is getting higher. Scott Bessant tried to intervene with a few of the repurchases of the long end. We've seen actually that this, within the day, reverted to its level. So help us understand what is happening here.

John： Wow. Well, you could argue a bit of monetary history is happening here. I believe this is a big deal. And I'm not alone, by the way. Many people think this is a big deal.

Last week, we saw the US jointly intervene with Japan to intervene in the yen–dollar exchange rate, euro–yen exchange rate. You could argue the ulterior motive there was to prevent Japan selling even more Treasury bonds than they otherwise would have done.

And now you're seeing the United States Secretary Bessant announced that he's going to be buying back even more long-dated treasuries than previously planned. Now, of course, if you're going to buy back long-dated treasuries, you need to finance that somehow. So how do you finance it? Well, you finance it with short-dated debt.

So the US has made a decision now to try and prevent foreign countries selling treasuries and to sell more short-dated debt to buy back long-dated treasuries. Why? Because the United States appears to believe — and there's good reason for this — that the Treasury market needs this support to prevent yields rising, because if yields rise, that's going to kill the economy, and they're desperate to keep the economy going.

We have elections coming up. We have a war to finance. We have a huge deficit we're already running. This is desperation disguised as policy. I think that's the simplest way to explain it.

二、收益率曲线的数学：为什么"操纵一段就会扭曲全局"

Alex： So if we now look at the long end of the curve, and it seems like that there's also — if we look at the steepening, there's not per se a steepening. It's rather flat if we compare the spread between the 10-year, the 30-year, the 2-year — I mean, if you go across the whole board of the treasuries — and the problem seems to be that the long end is not high enough. It's not necessarily that it's already high, but it's not high enough compared to all the shorter-term treasuries. What is the underlying problem?

John： Well, keep in mind that the Treasury's existing program was to buy back everything from 10 years on out at a regular rate. Now, they're saying they're going to buy it at an even faster rate, but again, 10 years on out. So other factors equal, that's going to flatten the curve a bit as you get farther out.

Now, you mentioned the 2-year yield. The thing is, there is a relationship at the long end of the curve and the short end of the curve which is kind of mathematical. It has to do with the arbitrage opportunities that are available to bond traders when they choose to play the curve, arbitrage the curve. A change in the slope and shape of one part of the curve will affect other parts of the curve indirectly. It's bond math, if you want to call it that.

So the normal relationship across the entire curve breaks down when even one part of the curve is being manipulated. The manipulation does not only impact that one part of the curve.

And in fact, back in 2002, I wrote a lengthy paper on precisely this topic, because the Fed Chairman at the time — sorry, Fed Governor at the time — Ben Bernanke, before he became chairman, wrote a paper detailing ways in which the Federal Reserve might go about manipulating the Treasury curve if they felt they needed to do so for extreme reasons. And this was something he talked about. And so I wrote a paper on the back of that which drew out the bond maths. It's a little bit technical, but the point is: the moment you start manipulating the yield curve in one area, other areas have to adjust, and it means the curve won't look normal, as it were.

三、这是 QE 吗？技术上不是，效果上差不多

Alex： There's a lot of commentators — obviously if you go on social media and especially on X, so formerly Twitter — there's always chatter about what this is and interpreted in different ways. And one of the things I saw recurringly is that this is a form of QE, that the Treasury buybacks are sort of cle— but it seems to be quite different, isn't it?

John： It is and it isn't. You could argue in its general macroeconomic effects, it has a similar impact on the Treasury market, and by extension everything that trades off the Treasury market — such as the mortgage market, other forms of borrowing, and economic activity which is financed with those forms of borrowing.

However, technically you're right, because QE in a simple sense is simply taking debt onto the central bank balance sheet. And here you're shifting debt from the long end of the curve to the short end of the curve. So technically in a narrow way, yes, they're different, but in terms of their broad macroeconomic effects, they're not terribly different.

The reality is that the Treasury in this case, with the support of the Fed — we can't leave the Fed out of this. And actually it's intriguing that Warsh, the new chairman, has just showed up and these events are happening. It makes me think that Warsh was already aware that this was part of the plan before he showed up. But who knows?

Anyway, this is designed to protect the Treasury market. It's designed to protect the economy, but those can only buy time — the same way QE can only buy time. And it makes you wonder what will happen after the elections. It makes you wonder what will happen assuming the Iran war eventually gets settled somehow. You can't continue doing things like this and not undermine the dollar dramatically and possibly permanently.

四、历史对照：二战、1970s、1987、1994、2008

Alex： Now, I would say it would be also interesting — and your student history as well — to kind of look back on when did we have a similar setup with higher yields. This was pre-2008 already the case. It was the case also the early 2000s, before, in the '90s. How does this compare then if we look at all the major times or periods — in the 1970s, the bond sell-off of 1987, or even 1994, and even 2008. How would you then plot the different settings or circumstances with what we have today, and how is this time different?

John： Well, it's interesting you point out those historical episodes because today contains elements of several of them.

二战与 1954 年前的收益率封顶

Let's go back to the Second World War. It was decided during the Second World War that the best way to finance — in the US — the best way to finance the war effort was to cap Treasury yields at 2.5%, and to have a huge PR campaign to encourage households to fund the war with so-called war bonds. So you tried to find a new investor base for the Treasury market, yet you were also capping yields. And so there was this big patriotic PR effort to try to get every household to at least buy some of these so-called war bonds. But you didn't allow yields to rise to a level that would naturally clear the market.

And that continues until 1954. That is, this cap on Treasury yields is not removed until 1954. And by that time, President Eisenhower had made a lot of progress in reducing the deficit. And in fact, President Eisenhower will be the last US president to oversee a federal surplus — budget surplus — as opposed to chronic deficits the way we've seen in modern times.

1970s 的石油冲击与 Volcker

Okay. You mentioned the 1970s. Yes, we had the oil shocks in the 1970s. We're getting one of those again today. They were hugely stagflationary, but eventually Paul Volcker decided — that is, Fed Chairman Paul Volcker decided — that that had to come to an end. He raised short rates to around 20%. Long rates went up to — oh, I forget exactly where they peaked out — low teens, I believe. And that was very, very damaging to the US economy.

But what it did do is it helped to shore up support in the dollar, because in the late 1970s there was a run on the dollar. Gold the gold price was soaring, the silver price was soaring, the dollar was falling versus multiple other major currencies. And indeed, that was such a big deal that Hollywood made a big-budget film about it called Rollover. If you've never watched Rollover, you should watch the film.

战时行动 + 石油冲击 = 美元挤兑的配方

So here you have a situation where the dollar is not distressed at the moment, but these Treasury market actions are wartime actions. They are reminiscent of wartime actions, and they could lead — combined with the oil shock such as the 70s — they could lead to a run on the dollar. That's the recipe that I see here. It doesn't necessarily unfold tomorrow, this week, this month, but that's the mix we're looking at based on history.

五、插曲：《Rollover》电影里的 Jane Fonda

Alex： All right. So another question is: who is Jane Fonda in all this?

John： Yes, she starred in the film. Again, this is a big-budget Hollywood film — Rollover — starring Kris Kristofferson, Jane Fonda, and Hume Cronyn. And Hume Cronyn's character is brilliant. He's this old financier. He knows everybody. He's hugely connected. And he's confident that his actions behind the scenes will manipulate financial markets in a way that will maintain stability. And he constantly reassures others: "Don't worry, just let me get on with it. Everything will be fine." He literally says that in the film — "everything will be fine."

Well, by the end of the film, everything is not fine. Global financial markets blow up, the dollar collapses, gold soars. I'm not saying that is exactly what's going to play out in the real world this time around. But that film is a fantastic example of just how fragile confidence can be, of just how fickle financial markets can be. And investors who are interested in these developments, and who want to watch something entertaining one evening that they might actually learn a thing or two from, should watch Rollover. It's great.

六、实体经济：私营部门被"挤出"了吗？

Alex： I mean, in this case we're not talking about, obviously — well, conspiracy of crashing the Western system by foreign investors like you described in the Rollover movie. But there is things at hand in terms of the sphere of influence that China has on the monetary system as a whole. We can cover this on the second part of this interview.

But here I would like to still focus on also the state of the economy in the US, because those higher yields are also a higher borrowing cost for pretty much anyone. And we're not talking about just corporates, we're talking about also consumers, we're talking about also the real estate market and housing. So where is the rollover here? I mean, sorry for the pun here, but—

John： No, that's fine. That's fine. Look, there's no free lunch in economics, and when you intervene in the bond market to try and lower borrowing costs for the government, that doesn't necessarily easily transmit through to the private sector. And in fact, some economists argue that what ends up happening is you effectively crowd out private sector borrowing by subsidizing public sector borrowing.

And that may keep government spending going. It may allow government finances to not deteriorate quite as quickly, but that doesn't necessarily support private sector economic activity. I mean, it might at the margins, but the idea that you get full pass-through is not necessarily the case.

令人震惊的劳动力数据

And in fact, when you look at the private sector economy in the US, it hasn't been doing well for a while. And I looked at some economic data recently which I actually found rather shocking.

If you look at, for example, the labor market over the past year, the US workforce has declined by 1 million workers — more than 1 million — more than 1 million workers over the past year. That's a large decline. You don't normally see that outside of recessions.

Now, the official data does not say the US is in recession. They say the US is growing — not very strongly, but it's growing. But the labor market data suggests that the US in fact is in recession. We've also seen some very weak retail sales data recently, which normally you would associate with very weak, if not outright recessionary, conditions.

So the US economy is perhaps not doing as well as people previously thought. And in fact, I believe that a lot of economic data fails to capture what is really happening in the economy during periods of inflation, because measuring inflation is difficult. It can be quite subjective. And ever since COVID came out back in the early 2020s, we've seen these waves of inflation rolling through. And now, of course, we're getting a wave of inflation rolling through due to high energy and other commodity prices, partly if not entirely as a result of the most recent Gulf war.

So I'd be skeptical of a lot of economic statistics, especially when they don't line up. When they don't line up with one another, you have to wonder what's going on. And my take, when I look at these inconsistencies as it were in the data, is that the US economy is not doing particularly well. This attempt by Treasury Secretary Bessant to suppress long-dated Treasury yields may help the government, but I'm not sure it's going to help the broader economy.

七、为什么这一次的收益率格外危险？

Alex： I mean, if we then look at what those yields were already happening in the past — right, it's not that we haven't seen those yields before, and you've mentioned that there were different episodes, different circumstances — but what specifically makes them potentially destabilizing now?

John： Well, the fact that the US debt-to-GDP ratio is historically very, very high. It's even high with respect to World War II. And the US economy is fundamentally not as dynamic as it used to be. That is, the tax burden is far higher. The workforce as a portion of the overall population is far lower. You've had a lot of structural changes in the economy that make it more difficult for the US to service its debt.

美国经济已经"欧洲化"

And I mean not to be mean — I mean, I live in Great Britain and the same is true in Great Britain and continental Europe — but the fact is, the US economy looks much more like the continental European economy or the British economy than it used to. It used to have a structurally lower tax burden. It doesn't really anymore when you add in state and local taxes along with federal. It used to have a smaller welfare state. It's still smaller, but not dramatically smaller than what you find in much of Europe and Great Britain.

And so the US economy is not quite the dynamic, free-market, entrepreneurial economy it once was. Still more so, but the difference is negligible now.

And so I don't believe that the US is in a good position to retain investor confidence as the debt burden — the federal debt burden — continues to rise and rise and rise as a result of this war, as a result of an economy that is weaker than it might appear on the surface. And so I do believe that Treasury Secretary Bessant is sort of playing with fire a bit with these manipulation shenanigans.

八、40 亿美元回购在 12 小时内蒸发：接下来怎么办？

Alex： We've seen — and that's how I started the conversation — that this $4 billion of buyback operation just evaporated within 12 hours. I mean, that was pretty useless, one could say. And the question is: what will be the next actions undertaken by the Treasury but also by the Fed? Is there anything that they can coordinate to achieve their goals?

John： Well, as I suggested earlier, it's probably the case they are already coordinating, if not officially.

Now, policy makers, economic officials, always like to get markets to do their work for them. They like to speak and get the markets to react in the way they want. Sometimes they actually have to transact, which is what we saw with the yen intervention and what we're seeing with the increase in Treasury buybacks. But you want small actions to have big effects.

What you don't want to happen is to need to go in with big actions, because that's when you really start to burn through whatever credibility you still have left, and that's when markets really test you. That's what happened in 1992 when Secretary Bessant and others broke the sterling peg to the Deutschmark. Right? That's what they were doing. They were forcing the UK to go in big, and they blew up the peg. And they made — I believe the rumor at the time was they made roughly $1 billion in a single day when that peg broke in 1992.

Policy makers never like to be in that position. But the problem is this: it's a slippery slope. You start by talking, then you start with little tweaks and actions. But if those do not generate the desired effect, you can either just give up and stop. But economic officials don't tend to just give up and stop. These are people in power, after all. So you double down. You get more aggressive. The actions become bigger. You grab a bigger hammer. You pull a bigger lever.

The problem is that if there's not something fundamentally supportive, fundamentally improved by those actions in the real economy, ultimately it's not going to work. It will ultimately fail. It might buy time, but it will only buy time. It might get you through the midterm elections, but after that, who knows what will happen. This is a very, very, very dangerous road in terms of the credibility of US economic policy generally, and specifically the demand for dollars in the international monetary system.

九、日本：最大海外债主，正在失控？

Alex： I mean, there's also things that you could argue that market mechanisms are going to be making the job of Scott Bessant and Kevin Warsh extremely difficult. And the trigger which Japan was in a way — we could talk about all the other factors obviously, but Japan is arguably one of the most important factors.

John： Yes.

Alex： It seems that also the Bank of Japan is losing control of their yield curve. I mean, the 2-year has broken the trend line. They went from zero in January 2024 to 1.7 now, and it was negative for all those years before. And not only is the yield rising that high, but the Bank of Japan owns 54% of those outstanding Japanese bonds, and the Japanese debt-to-GDP is about 250%.

And in a lot of conversation I had in the past, there's always talk of Japanification of economies — that Japan is always a bit the frontrunner of, so to say, what we can expect in more developed economies post-industrialization, where this is where we see a glimpse of the future. Obviously there's a lot of other factors. The demographics is also very important. But where can we — at least in the case of Japan — expect things to go, even though now they've set up the FIMA repo operations that allow the Bank of Japan to transfer US bonds to the Federal Reserve and so on? What can we expect now, and how can this maybe turn into a huge door into the US Treasury market in a way?

John： Well, Japan is the largest foreign holder of US debt by a large margin — very large. The Japanese historically have had a very high savings rate. A lot of that savings has been invested in dollar assets. And so the cumulative foreign asset portfolio in Japan is enormous, and the bulk of it is dollars.

日本的独特之处：欠自己 vs. 欠外国人

The funny thing about Japan is, however, is that yes, they have a huge debt, but they owe their debt to themselves. They don't owe it to foreigners, and they hold a huge amount of foreign debt. So the Japanese are in this unique position where they can actually fund a significant portion of their own debt just by dissaving and selling out of their accumulated foreign debt. And that's always an option. And every time they intervene in the foreign exchange market, that could be part of that sort of policy. It doesn't need to be a one-off. They could do it for years, many years, and help to pay off their own accumulated debt.

And so Japan is in this position which is somewhat unique. And comparing the US debt — which is externally financed largely — to the Japanese debt, which is not, is not a like-for-like comparison. That's apples and oranges. The US does not owe its debt to itself. It owes a lot of its debt to foreigners.

And so in Japan's case, a weaker yen does not automatically help to reduce their accumulated debt burden. And in fact, if they were to use their foreign asset pile to help reduce their domestic debt, the yen would strengthen.

Whereas in the US's case, the debt burden, if it needs to be financed, could be financed through a weaker dollar. And that is always a temptation for the United States to follow that policy. And indeed, what we've seen recently — again, the increased purchases of treasuries — is a possible step in that direction.

So Japan and the US are similar in some ways, different in others. But the takeaway, the important one, is that the yen is less undermined by a rising Japanese debt burden, domestic debt burden, than the US dollar is undermined by a rising debt burden that is externally financed. Those are the — that's where these trends diverge.

十、黄金、白银与"需求函数的阶跃变化"

Alex： Let's maybe also put things also a bit together, also in terms of the impact it has on assets. We've seen gold, silver rise in the last days after — I would say quite a — yeah, a half a year of consolidation or downward trend. But here the key difference here is that they rise while real yields are also rising, and this hugely is not the natural mechanism that these assets — and also including risk assets like Bitcoin for example — do tend to actually behave. So how do you decipher this, and what does this mean? Obviously, we've talked a lot about this, but more explicitly.

John： Yes. Well, you point out something which I think is extremely important and which in fact I write about in my book and sometimes my other writings on Substack and elsewhere.

There is a relationship, a very good relationship, between real yields and currencies — in the case of the dollar specifically, real yields in dollars and the US dollar. And you can look at that versus other currencies in relative terms, or you can look at it versus gold, and which is what we're doing here.

阶跃变化：黄金需求函数的历次跃迁

That relationship is observable, but it goes through step changes, discontinuous step changes, now and again when you get some sort of shock to the system. And there are several good examples of that. You had one in the early 2000s. You had one in 2008–2009. You had one when the Ukraine war broke out. And arguably you're getting another one now.

What is happening? What's happening is you're seeing a shift in the demand function for gold vis-à-vis dollars. A qualitative shift: for any given level of real rates, investors want a larger gold balance versus dollars for some qualitative reason.

In this case, you could argue it's because people sense that US policy is fundamentally changing as a result of these events we've been discussing — interventions, manipulations, and so on. In the early 2000s, Ben Bernanke among others was talking about very extreme Fed policies. In 2008–2009, of course, we had the global financial crisis. The Ukraine war breaking out was a big deal — all the sanctions, weaponization of the dollar escalated. And now we have the US starting to act very aggressively to manipulate US financial markets.

So there you have it. I think that's the best explanation. You're seeing yet another shift in the demand function for gold vis-à-vis the dollar. And that is something that could propel the gold price — the dollar gold price — to all-time highs, because these previous ones have done the same. When you get these demand function shifts, they tend to result in a new all-time high dollar price for gold.

Alex： And it's funny because I mean, I actually would tend to — if I understood you correctly — saying that an addition in real yields would tend to be compensated by a bigger amount of gold, is something that I would say is the opposite usually, right? Especially when we talk about the long term of the yield curve here, the treasuries. Usually what you see is that investors who like to be compensated with high yields, and then park their savings — whatever hedge or whatever you want to call this — into those long-dated Treasury bonds. But here it's the opposite, and it signals, as you I think mentioned, the fiscal and the monetary risk, which is a totally different regime change, right?

I mean, it's also the fact that we've ended the bull market in bonds overall. It's been six years that we have one of the worst-performing bond markets in a generation. And arguably, so we see it in balances of central banks all around the world — with central banks adding gold more than ever, thousand tons on average per year since 2020, and becoming also the reserve asset compared to any US bonds.

十一、黄金重新货币化的长路

Alex： So what does it say now about this new regime we are in, and how far can this go? Because if we are expected to go back to the 60% dominance that gold used to have in its balance sheet in the 60s, then where does gold go in that sense?

John： Well, clearly the market clearing price for gold in any currency is going to be a lot higher if we go back to that — that is the road we're on. You know, we won't get there tomorrow. Who knows? Maybe there's a crisis tomorrow, but we probably won't get there tomorrow. But that's the road we're on.

Now, I argue in my book that the road we're on is not only that the gold share of assets, official and unofficial — not just central banks, but other investors — that the gold share of assets is going to increase very dramatically over the coming years. I go so far as to argue that as the gold share of assets grows, ultimately countries will begin to use those gold assets to settle external trade imbalances. And that is a form of de facto monetization of gold. So my book argues that that's where we're going. It doesn't argue we get there tomorrow, but that is the road we're on.

You can only manipulate the US financial markets so much, suppress yields, intervene in foreign exchange markets, whatever it is. You can only do that so much. You can only weaponize the dollar so much. You can only play fast and loose with market confidence so much, before the price of gold rises sufficiently that the balance sheet value of gold vis-à-vis dollars around the world becomes so much larger that it becomes literally just more convenient to use your accumulated gold balances to settle external trade than to use the residual dollar balance, which has shrunk so much it no longer is able to as easily settle those imbalances.

I believe that's the road we're on. And I do believe there is some sort of tipping point out there when all of a sudden you'll start to see this gold remonetization occurring not just between two countries, but between 20 or more. The BRICS might do it as a group, for example. They've talked about it, and some argue they've got behind-the-scenes plans to remonetize gold. I have no privileged knowledge of that, but it makes logical sense if you want to have freedom of action from what has become a manipulated, weaponized dollar.

So I do believe that's the road we're on. It does imply a far higher gold price. You and I have discussed this before — you're talking in the tens of thousands, in my opinion, based on the Bretton Woods equivalents of gold balances on balance sheets, official and unofficial. I do believe that's where we're going, even if we're not going to get there tomorrow.

十二、中国：低收益率 + 大量买金 = 一个隐藏的看涨期权？

Alex： And so now I would like to combine all the topics in one, and this is maybe like the last topic I would like to discuss with you, John, and which is the fact that China's 10-year government bond yields has been falling while the country has actually been importing exceptional amount of gold, in addition to the PBOC adding to their gold reserves officially. With, of course, this whole talk about how much the Bank of China really has, the Central Bank of China. So how would you then interpret first the falling 10-year government bond yields in China?

John： Yeah, I've been thinking about that, because the gap you're seeing now between China's borrowing costs and those in other major economies, including the United States, is historically very, very large. And so it makes you wonder what the hell's going on here.

Is the Chinese economy collapsing, for example? Is China heading into outright deflation, for example? That seems unlikely to me, based on the fact that China remains a very, very large net energy importer and importer of other commodities too. So the idea that this is about inflation expectations or deflation expectations, I think, is probably not the case.

Okay, so is the economy imploding? Is it just a flight to quality? Again, China has struggled — the economy has struggled over the past few years compared to the prior couple of decades — but has it struggled to the point where you would expect the bond market to implode like that? I don't think that's true. And in fact, I've been in touch with some people recently who have been travelling around China, and they say that there are not clear signs of economic distress anywhere they go. That's just anecdotal, but for what it's worth.

一个大胆的假说：黄金可赎回的中国债券

So what's going on here? You could argue — and this is a bit of a stretch, but I will offer this as a possibility — you could argue that alongside the shifting demand for dollars vis-à-vis gold, you're seeing a shift in the demand function for Chinese debt. That is, there may be a realization domestically in China, possibly in other countries, that given what the US Treasury is now doing, given how desperate they are, given how expensive this war is becoming and so on and so forth, that Chinese debt — even though it's not fully fungible, even though it's not fully integrated into the global financial system — that various ways to get exposure to Chinese debt are becoming more attractive vis-à-vis the US treasuries. That's a possible explanation here.

And I'll go one step further now. And this is way out there, but bear with me. There have been rumors for years that at some point China would feel it had accumulated sufficient gold reserves to announce — at some point when convenient, when they thought it served the national interest — to announce that Chinese bonds would henceforth be redeemable in gold on demand. That is, you could choose — you could just roll them over and redeem them in renminbi and reinvest, or you could take delivery in gold.

That rumor's been around for a while. And if anyone thought, "Gee, I have a choice now. I can get a US Treasury yielding 5% that's not backed by gold, or I can get Chinese paper yielding 2% that is backed by gold" — tough choice, isn't it?

十三、Alasdair Macleod 的思路：人民币的国际化必须挂钩黄金

Alex： I had this conversation also with someone you're very familiar with, I think — Alasdair Macleod — who was saying that the internationalization (sorry if I stumble on this word) of the yuan would be only achieved through the pegging of gold, or at least linked to gold. And we've entertained, I think, this scenario as well, with also through the different — let's say — gold hubs that they would, or vaults, SGE vaults, that they would set up in different parts of the world. So far, there's only been the one that we know of in Hong Kong that is outside of mainland China — well, Hong Kong is now part of China, but — and then the one in Saudi Arabia. But what are your thoughts on this? I saw you want to say something about it.

John： Yes, absolutely. Look, I write about this in my book. Basically, I make the point that the only reason why the US dollar remains the world's preeminent reserve currency is a legacy of Bretton Woods. The US economy is much smaller than it used to be. The US share of global trade is much smaller than it used to be. Confidence in the dollar is much lower than it used to be. The dollar didn't used to be weaponized to the degree it is today through sanctions and so on. And so really the only reason why the dollar retains the status it has is a legacy issue. That is, the world hasn't found a way to move on.

So how do you move on? Well, that's the problem, right? No other currency can just step up and say "we're better," right? We talked about Japan — I mean, Japan does have, you know, problems, right? They have this huge debt. But again, they owe it to themselves. But they have this huge debt. They have demographic issues. The euro, as we know, the euro area has issues. They have internal debt issues. The ECB actively intervenes to try and subsidize relatively weak sovereign borrowers within the euro area, something which could at some point run out of road.

So there's no other currency that can step up — unless there's a currency backed by gold. And then it is qualitatively superior, qualitatively more credible, qualitatively a better store of value.

And if China is in a position to do that — and I'm not claiming they are, I'm not an expert. I don't know what, you know, exactly how much gold China has. No one does. I don't know exactly what China's monetary plans are. No one does. Well, some do, I guess, but certainly I don't. But Alasdair is correct. If China do want to internationalize the yuan, if they do want to become the new reserve currency, or at least one that is at least able to rival the dollar if not completely surpass it, they need to back their currency with gold. That to me is obvious.

The successor to the dollar will be a gold-backed currency. And that is yet another step along the road of full-on gold remonetization at the international level, as I discuss extensively in my book. Right? I really — I've believed for many years that's where we're going. I've never known — and no one does know — exactly how that's going to play out. I've gone through many different scenarios. This one may be the most plausible of those.

十四、中国债券收益率与黄金进口的耦合关系

Alex： So now if we tie it back to the initial question I asked, was about the relationship between the Chinese bond yields and the import. And here this is a generalization, because there's obviously the dissociation between general import into the country of China and what the PBOC is adding to its balance sheet in terms of gold reserves. Could we say that if, let's say, the bond yields begin rising again, that this relationship with the import — or at least on the balance sheet perspective for the PBOC — of addition of gold reserves would then wane? Or is there like another angle to that, or is that a false observation?

John： Well, in a way what you're pointing out, Alexi, is that is how financial markets work. That is, if bonds are more attractive than gold, you own bonds. If gold's more attractive than bonds, you own gold. And interest rates move up and down to reflect that relationship. I mean, that would be a normal relationship. So as Chinese bond yields go down, they're less attractive, everyone will want to accumulate more gold, in which case yields have to go back up again.

And I think the best way to understand — again, possibly, again this is possibly — I'm speculating here — why Chinese bond yields are so much lower than those in the US and elsewhere, is because of this perceived future possibility that in fact this is going to become a gold-backed instrument. So you receive a bit of yield in the meantime, and you have this implied optionality that you get to redeem in gold down the road. And I mean, again, I'm speculating here, but maybe some of that's going on.

十五、德意志银行、德国的两难与人民币清算

Alex： And so there's another question I want to ask you, and since you've been — oh, a director at, if I'm not mistaken, at Deutsche Bank — you might also have maybe some perspective or at least know, let's say, a bit more background information about the way Deutsche Bank operates. But it was about the fact that Deutsche Bank has become the first non-Chinese European bank that has been authorized to clear renminbi transactions in Europe, if I'm not mistaken. But even though — well, the bank is German — the government, Germany's government itself says it wants to de-risk from China. So it's quite the opposite signal here.

What do you make of, first, that it became a clearing renminbi bank in Europe, and the fact that it might entail other things that we've just discussed now previously about the ambitions of the internationalization — I have really a problem with this word today?

John： Look, I lived in Germany for years, and I believe that Germany's instincts politically have in recent decades been to try and maintain good relations with all major countries — Russia, China, and so on. That situation has become very, very complicated as a result of the Ukraine war, and the current governing coalition in Germany clearly believe that they need to be on the side of NATO, the US, and against Russia, which by implication of course means that they cannot be particularly friendly towards China, because everyone knows that China is a huge consumer of Iranian oil exports as well as Russian energy exports.

So Germany's really in a bind, and really conflicted. If you were to take a survey of major German business executives, including Deutsche Bank, and ask them, "Would you prefer to be able to remain neutral in these conflicts and just do business and just make money and just import cheap Russian energy, and get Deutschland AG, or Germany Inc. in English, up and running again?" — I think a sizable majority would say yes, absolutely. Let's just get on with it. But the government, as it's currently constructed, for whatever reason, is acting against those interests.

That won't last. In my opinion, that won't last. And I don't know exactly how long it takes for Germany to go back to business. But it will happen, in my opinion. So the fact that Deutsche Bank is trying to build a future relationship with China, a special relationship with China, does not surprise me at all. I would expect, discreetly behind closed doors, most large German companies are retaining warm relations with the Chinese Communist Party government, and Chinese companies with whom they've worked in the past and would like to work in the future. They are doing everything they can to keep relations cordial, and they are patiently waiting for these conflicts to end.

And when they end, these German executives will get back to work, and hopefully that will be a tremendous benefit to the German economy. I certainly hope so. But that's my best explanation for what's going on.

Alex： One could say this could be also the path for building renminbi reserves, renminbi trade invoicing, or even eventually the gold-linked settlement that we've mentioned earlier on.

John： Oh, certainly. I mean, look, Germany does not have a modern history of being a major financial center. I mean, don't get me wrong, Frankfurt, obviously is an important financial center for Germany itself. But with the exception of the ECB just happening to reside there as a result of treaty convention, it's not disproportionately important.

That could change. And certainly Deutsche Bank would like to see Germany have disproportionate financial influence in the future. And so again, I think their motives are quite clear, and those might conflict with the current government, but there's only so much the current government can do to stop them behaving in that way.

十六、人民币的资本管制与"最后一段路"

Alex： Now if we look at the renminbi in general, there's also the capital control and the limited convertibility constraint that also plays a role, right? If it's—

John： Yes. Look, as I mentioned earlier — right, as it stands today, as it stands today — the infrastructure is not fully in place. It's not. But you've got to the point where, again, if China is confident that they have sufficient gold reserves to back the currency, and if they're confident that they have sufficient international support for a gold-backed bond market denominated in renminbi, the remaining steps that would need to be taken to properly internationalize the currency and make it a reserve currency to compete with the dollar — there aren't that many. There aren't that many. The gold backing is the hard part. And that part may be more or less done now.

And keep in mind, China remains a large net exporter. So the gold backing is really a liquidity mechanism. That is, they don't actually need to be able to provide the gold externally, because they're the ones exporting. So they'll just keep accumulating more gold. But you need — you'll still need the gold for liquidity purposes. That is, as a bond matures, you still need to pay off the bond holders, right? So you need enough for that liquidity management. But presumably the structure of the Chinese economy will remain such that it remains a net exporter for some future period of time — not forever perhaps, but for some period of time, given the structure of the global economy as it stands today.

So once they cross that line, then these final infrastructure steps — you know, payment systems, settlement conventions, confidence building — there's not a whole lot more to do, in my opinion.

结束语

Alex： All right. Well, it's, I guess, time will tell, and we'll see how those things develop. And obviously we will keep on talking about those topics in our future interviews.

John, thanks for your precious time. You also write, as you mentioned in our conversation, you have regular newsletter reports on Substack that you write. You are also on X, I think. And is there anything else you would like to share with the viewers and listeners?

John： Well, just — I mean, thank you for everyone's attention. Look, I've been thinking and researching and writing about these topics for many years now since the early 2000s. I've hardly got everything right, but it's been exciting to see things develop as they have, and to try and stay as on top of it as possible, and I continue to do so.

So anyone who is interested in these topics and would like my unique perspective as someone who's worked as a managing director at major financial institutions on both sides of the Atlantic, and yet who went a bit off-piste some years ago — yes, please please go to my Substack, theamphora.substack.com. That's probably the best place to learn about and become familiar with my work.

Alex： And you're also the author of The Golden Revolution. We talked about this — your book — as well in Cape Town. I urge all viewers and listeners to also have a look at this interview, which is more of, let's say, your foundational thinking and thesis about all this, which you spilled over obviously in this interview as well.

Thanks again, John.

John： Thank you, Alexi. My pleasure.

Hey hey hey.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一个反直觉的观察：这不是"QE"，而是"债务的期限套利"——美国正在把自己变成一家投行
大多数评论把 Bessant 的长债回购简单等同于 QE，但 John Butler 点破了一个更让人不安的真相：**这是用短债融资来回购长债**——不是印钞扩表，而是"缩短负债久期"。这个动作在结构上和 2008 年之前雷曼、贝尔斯登所做的**期限错配套利**惊人地一致：借短、买长、赚利差、维持流动性幻觉。
换句话说，美国财政部正在把自己**资产负债表投行化**。这个洞察真正让人后背发凉的地方在于：投行倒下的方式从来不是资不抵债，而是**短端融资突然拒绝滚动**。当整个联邦债务的加权期限被系统性缩短，美国就把自己暴露在了"日频再融资风险"之下——这是雷曼式的脆弱性，只不过发生在主权层面。
## 跨领域连接：Rollover（1981 电影）× 中国黄金 × 期权定价理论
Butler 提到那部 1981 年的 Hollywood 电影《Rollover》——但他没有明说的深层类比是**期权定价**。
他关于中国 10 年期国债收益率为何异常低的解释，本质上是一个隐含期权价值论证：*

item.title: [Business of Sport] Vik Banerjee on The First Season of New Ownership, Big Sponsors, & What Comes Next
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一场被伪装成"体育联赛"的风险投资实验

表面上，Vik 谈的是板球联赛"The Hundred"的第一个新赛季。但如果把耳朵贴近他的措辞，你会听到一个更陌生的声音——这其实是一场用"体育 IP"作为标的物的种子轮融资仪式。

100 多个买家竞投 8 支队伍、"venue + investor"的相亲式配对会议、最后一轮拍卖定价、5 亿英镑分配给英格兰板球生态——这些不是传统体育联盟的语言，而是 YC Demo Day 的语言。ECB 不像在办联赛，更像在做一个 "体育资产孵化器"：中央先用 5 年建立最小可行产品（MVP），达到"因成功而触及天花板"的临界点，再把 8 个"子公司"拆出去独立融资，让每支队伍在下一阶段各自跑增长。

这里有一个让人意外的观察：Vik 反复强调"我们没有印度球员，但除此之外都有了"——听起来是限制，其实是结构性护城河。IPL 靠垄断印度男球员保住了金字塔尖；The Hundred 恰恰因为"抢不到 IPL 球员"，才被迫把资源、叙事、球员体验、女子板球溢价全部拉高到最大值。限制反过来成了产品定义。这和 Netflix 早年因带宽不足被迫做剧集算法推荐、后来变成核心壁垒，是同一种逆向进化。

女子板球被"藏"在双打包里的隐形革命

大多数体育联盟推动性别平权靠的是宣言、赞助商 KPI、政治正确的仪式性投入。The Hundred 做了一件在结构上无法被回退的事：把男女比赛物理绑定成一张票、一天一场的"双头赛"。

Vik 顺口一句话暴露了这个设计的真正杀伤力——"如果我们改成 T20，每场多 20 球，一天下来就多出接近两小时；带孩子的家庭 9 点就得走，女子比赛的时段就会被牺牲。"

翻译一下：100 球制不是为了让比赛更"现代"，而是为了在时间预算里给女子比赛留出不能被商业逻辑侵蚀的位置。这是一种典型的"制约设计"（Constraint-Based Design）——把伦理选择编码进物理规则，让后来的商人即使想牺牲女子板球也做不到，因为那会打碎整个产品架构。

跨领域看，这和建筑师 Christopher Alexander 的"模式语言"如出一辙：真正的公平不是靠道德说服，而是靠让不公平在结构上"跑不通"。也很像瑞典把育儿假强制切分给父亲——不是鼓励，是让"不休"变得比"休"更麻烦。

100 球 vs T20：一场关于"感知复杂度"的心理战

所有质疑者都在问同一个问题："这跟 T20 差 5 个球，为什么不直接改成 T20？"

Vik 的答案表面是市场调研（"英国观众的三大障碍是时间、复杂度、感知"），但更深的答案藏在他没明说的地方——"100 球"是一个心理定价锚。

T20 = "又一种版本的板球"，观众会自动调用旧脑回路：规则、术语、要坐 3.5 小时。 100 球 = "一种新东西"，观众被迫放下预设。

这是行为经济学里 "类别重命名" 的经典操作：Uber 不是"出租车 App"，Airbnb 不是"民宿"，Peloton 不是"卖健身车"。当一个产品能被塞进旧类别，它就永远逃不出旧类别的价格上限和期待上限。

The Hundred 的核心创新其实不在球场上，而在感知层——它需要在观众心里被归类为"新事物"，才能吸引那 40% 从不看板球的家庭。5 个球的差异不是竞技规则，是一道认知防火墙。

有意思的是，Vik 自己也承认："对我 6 岁的儿子来说，这就是 T20 少一个球。"——他知道这件事在竞技层面无关紧要。真正重要的是它对不看板球的人来说"看起来不一样"。整个联赛的成立，建立在一个精心设计的"外行错觉"之上。这不是欺骗，这是产品设计的最高级形式。

📝 转录文本

开场：第六个赛季，也是第一个赛季

Vik: We've just come off the back of our sixth season and in many respects also our first season.

Host: And you went to every game.

Vik: I did. My wife tells me I have a job that lasts one month, so you might as well turn up. I don't know of any others that's gone through — the level of change that we've gone through is unprecedented. In that first round, we had over 100 people that put in bids and put in interest for teams. So very much boyed by that.

Host: Over 100.

Vik: Yeah. Yeah. We've got incredibly proud and humbled of the investors that we've got. Four from the IPL, four from NFL, Premier League, NASCAR. We've got tech giants, we've got all sorts of different experiences and knowledge now in that melting pot.

Host: Since we chatted 2 years ago, you've had 500 million in essence now distributed to the English game.

Vik: I think it's generational change for the sport. In my humble opinion, I think we have now set ourselves apart from the Chasing Pack with the IPL being kind of out there.

Host: Everyone just goes, "It's going to be a 2020 competition soon." Why is it not?

Vik: Why is it — Go on.

Host: Exclusive business. Fascinating.

欢迎回归 & 赛季回顾

Host: Vic, good afternoon. Welcome back.

Vik: Thank you very much. Great to be here.

Host: Back in the seat.

Vik: It's been — feels like a long time, but I'm glad to be here.

Host: We were just reminiscing. Was that a couple of years? I think — and a lot's changed. A lot has happened. Last time, as I said, I think you were just kind of in the process of getting some of the deals done for the teams, and this year was the first year we actually saw a lot of those changes happen. Um, I guess I can't really start anywhere else other than — go on, tell us how was it?

Vik: It was a lot of fun. It feels like a lifetime ago when we were doing those deals and in many ways it was. Um, but yeah, we've just come off the back of our sixth season and in many respects also our first season. And it was — yeah, it's been a lot of fun. The new owners and the new structures have bedded in really well and most importantly we've had a really good season of cricket both on the men's and the women's side. It's been brilliant. We've been helped by the weather. But it's been phenomenal.

Host: There — one one game that was affected by rain at all.

Vik: One game in Manchester, one women's game was affected by rain. The rest of it was blue skies everywhere.

Host: That's extraordinary, isn't it?

Vik: I mean you can't — you can't when it comes in.

Host: And you went to every game?

Vik: I did. I went to every day. My wife tells me I have a job that lasts one month, so you might as well turn up. But no, I think I look — I think it's important. It's such a brilliant tournament and for someone like me to have the privilege to lead it, to then to be there to be able to engage with the playing side but also the operational team that put in so much work behind the scenes to get the games to what they are, get the events and the venues and the broadcast to where they are. But also — what I like to do in Norm is just sit in the stands and sit around the stands for a little bit and just kind of get a feel for what's happening and what people are saying. So, it's a real privilege to do our jobs and so I enjoy it.

作为普通观众的体验与外界评价

Host: Well, look, I — you know, I sent you a message and said I'd love to do this because for anyone that does tune in — really they — I'm a fan, right? I've been to a few games. Thank you.

Vik: Thank you.

Host: And I love it as an experience. I think it's been really good. I think it's been really fresh and the atmospheres that I've been in as a standard like punter sitting in the seats, you know, it's been really cool and something that I think cricket has desperately needed in this country for a long time.

There is also the other side of it where newspaper headlines and people — you know, the people that know their cricket — will come and all the time comment or say to me, "Oh, well, you know, I don't like it. This isn't for me. Attendances are down." All of this. You're always going to get that in sport and you got to be open to it. But I thought this was a really perfect time to actually have a look at this from the development perspective because when we did have the chat, it was — you were positioning something which had had a few years of really good, should we say, establishment, but that was the major time you were taking this from centrally owned and controlled and operated to — does this really have value to people outside of it? And that could have backfired massively on you. People could have said no, sorry, don't see the value, don't find the assets attractive.

So from this year, what really changed? Give people an understanding of why this was kind of like iteration one almost all over again.

从"中央运营"到"八队独立"的结构性转变

Vik: So yeah, it was a strange brand — so for the first five years the 100 had been run entirely centrally. And what that means is the initial team names and brands were all controlled centrally. For a fan buying a ticket to any of the games, was all sold and issued centrally. For all of the kind of player contracting we did at the ECB, for hiring the security guards — everything from start to end was all done centrally from one office at Lords.

And that was great and, as to your — use your word — establishment, it established the tournament and it did great things and it had done some wonderful things in its five years that it had done and a lot of credit to a lot of people for that. But we just felt that, almost because of its success, it had hit a ceiling of what could be done with a small number of people based out of St. John's Wood. How do you take what it had done and build on it and go to the next level?

So that's where the investors came in. That's where the kind of the operational change with the teams came in.

Host: And that was in the plan from day one.

Vik: That was always the plan. That was always the vision when we went to market: okay, if we can't do it, then who can? Who are the very best people in the world at fan engagement, at digital and data, at commercial growth, at cricket? And so on and so forth. And if you can get them round a metaphorical board table all looking at the hundred going, "Well, here's how I can help. Here's how I can improve. Here's an idea." Then some magic is bound to happen. I don't know what that is, and some of it we've seen, some of it will come in years to come, but something will happen.

And so that was always the plan when we went out to seek the investment. We've absolutely got that in my opinion. We've got incredibly proud and humbled of the investors that we've got. Four from the IPL, four from other sports. We've got NFL. We've got the Premier League. We've got NASCAR. We've got the tech giants. We've got all sorts of different experiences and knowledge now in that melting pot.

What then happened this year in terms of the amount of change is massive. So you go from that all being run centrally to effectively now the league being run similarly to the NFL or other leagues of our nature, where the teams themselves are responsible for their ticket sales. They're responsible for their branding. They're responsible for their commercial sponsorship. We at the center effectively do a few things. We govern the league. So a lot of the regulations and that governance side sits with us. We work with broadcasters and help the broadcasters display our tournament in the best possible light. And then we have our own commercial deals that we work with.

And then what happens effectively is the central revenues get distributed 80/20. So each team gets what turn out to be 10%. We keep 20% which then gets redistributed into the sport.

8 支队 = 16 个新关系的运营挑战

Host: Okay. And therefore the challenges — if you're going into this season to overcome — were from an operational perspective having eight individual businesses really running and making sure that all of those different parts of those businesses could function to ensure that the business maintained its — what power, I guess.

Vik: It was huge. I mean I don't know of any others that's gone through — the level of change that we've gone through is unprecedented. Because it's not just eight, it's kind of 16. Because this time last year, October — actually last year, some into December — the teams were signing their own deals. So you've got the venue like an Oval or Surrey signing a deal with Reliance — two very successful organizations in their own right. They were coming together to create a partnership. That partnership was them figuring each other out and, at the same time as doing that, they were — that we were — figuring out a relationship with them as a team, as my London.

And so to go from that and then go, okay, now by the way, you've got to find sponsors. You've now got to sell tickets to your home games. You've got to create a brand and start to build an affinity and a fandom in your own kind of location and do that eight times over. So effectively 16 times over — was huge.

And hopefully not really massive for a fan, if that makes sense. I would hope that a fan would be able to buy a ticket with their family, come and watch and just enjoy the experience. But behind the scenes there is a huge amount of change that's gone on there.

上座率：数字、亮点与不足

Host: Okay. So, attendance — something that was brought up immediately.

Vik: Yeah.

Host: I will say, some people talking about it from a positive perspective — I was at the oval for that opening game.

Vik: Yeah.

Host: With you — and I saw it in all its glory, to the extent where over 20,000 people for the men's game, over 10,000 for the women's, I think. The concourses were alive. It was great, right? It was a really good atmosphere. Then you see other matches which didn't have as good attendance. The total stats — you had over half a million I think throughout the —

Vik: About 550,000 total, yeah.

Host: But not as many as you did last year.

Vik: Correct.

Host: Stick beat for people, right? How have you looked at attendance internally from that success perspective and where you really wanted to be?

Vik: Yeah, look, given the change that we talked about, I'm very happy with where we are. To get 550,000 tickets sold I think is a real positive. It's a real positive for cricket to get that number. Importantly as well, the demographics were there — to your point — I challenge anyone to walk around any of the concourses and not have a smile on their face because there are kids everywhere having a great time. So — I think we had 40%, just over, of our attendees were families with kids and that's brilliant. That's brilliant for the sport.

So given that, I really happy with the attendances. Yes, look, we hold our hands up — we're not perfect. We haven't achieved a sellout at every game. That's obviously the aim. And there were games and lessons learned where we want to improve next year. But I think having had this year, I think next year will be even bigger still and even more positive. We'll keep going with our demographics. We're still all about growth. We're still all about families. And so it'll be bigger and better next year.

Host: Do you think that the fact it didn't follow a major test series does play a part? I saw that referenced by a number of people.

Vik: Um, without getting too technical — there's effectively — the 100 shifts year-on-year, so some years it is after a major five-match men's test series (so the men's Ashes or an India series) and then the hundreds a bit later in August. In other years, like it was this year, we have a New Zealand series and a Pakistan series and we slot in the middle. The ticket sales historically have always been much higher after the Ashes or after an India series. Couple of reasons. It's a bit later so you have more time to sell those tickets. But cricket rises and cricket sells other cricket. You think next year with the Ashes coming up and the opportunity hopefully that England have to do well off the back of that, we will sell tickets and that will really help. So for an even year when we're slightly earlier, I believe we were thereabouts as the highest year ever of ticket sales — which again comes back to my point that we're really happy with where we are, but places to improve next year.

拓宽板球观众群：家庭、女性、儿童

Host: Yeah. Colin Graves when he came on talked about a core reason for the hundred being to not just recycle the — let's say — 1 million people that engage with cricket in this country, which is what we'd seen historically for many years. I.e. if there was a new short form tournament, it would still be the same people that would be engaging with maybe the test format or the 4-day game. The aim of the 100 from day one was to do something different to that and bring people that didn't have that history, that association with cricket, into the ground.

Now, you mentioned those stats — I did have a look at it, and from my side, it's massively influential in developing what Colin said about that — because if 22% of tickets were to junior fans under 16, 40% of families, 28% for women, they're not coming necessarily to lots of other forms of cricket.

Vik: Our purpose is simple. We have to throw cricket's doors open to as many people as possible. And that can be — look, if you're a — you know, so I play for Gloucester. There are people there that follow the county championship. They're very welcome. Absolutely. But equally welcome and accessible needs to be for those that are maybe a sports fan but have never tried cricket before or find cricket a bit daunting. We've got to bring children in because they're the lifeblood in generations to come. They're those that are going to be playing it. They're going to be watching it. They're going to be buying tickets. So bringing them into the sport is huge. So that is our aim. That is what we've set out — almost a simple purpose right from the very start. And that DNA runs through everything we try and do as a tour.

沟通挑战与真诚性

Host: How do you reflect on your communication? Do you think you speak about it in the best way possible when you talk about the things and the ways you can develop? And I'm not pinning this on any form of communication that I think hasn't been good — you know, how you communicate with an audience, how you try and capture them, how you try and deal with the negativity that's around something, how you quell the fears of emotion in sport — which, you know, we said before we came on is obviously the driver of so much about the best things of sport, but it can also be a big problem. You being able to communicate to this potential audience in the right way is going to be a huge part of you filling those stadiums that aren't necessarily full, of making those people feel included in something that is new and — let's be honest, right — maybe threatening or challenging to the sport that they love.

Vik: Yeah. Look, I think you can always improve how you do things. I think what we have tried to be very clear on is a core set of principles — what we're about and what we're trying to do. And I think then if you put at the heart of that some high quality cricket. So the product — what you see on the field — is unbelievable, and that is impressive, you know, in the final Ciphert smashing it to all parts of the ground. My dad was there and my son was there. My dad's watched cricket for his whole entire life. He was really impressed with that, as was my 8-year-old who just enjoyed balls flying everywhere and fireworks going off.

And so if that product stays really positive and high quality, then our role is to be authentic in how we talk about the sport and who we're trying to talk to. I think this year one of the things that we've learned is that with eight or nine teams and us, we can do that better in terms of how we coordinate amongst ourselves. But I would like to think that hopefully you have an authenticity in what we're trying to do. We are always going to receive some criticism. We take that on board. We do listen to it. We look at it and see if there are things that we can improve off the back of it, because we don't want to exclude anyone. That's the opposite of what we're trying to do. We want everyone, as I say, regardless of your affinity already to the sport, to feel like actually the hundred is something I really enjoy and want to come and see.

破纪录的上座率 & 伦敦 vs 全国

Host: Record attendances this year. You had a few. Right. They were — you had, am I right in saying three? I think. Yeah.

Vik: Three in — you had one in Wales which was a record for them. But you also had three record attendances — total number, as in most people through the gate. Is that — Yes. For a women's game at Lords, and the third one I believe was the Oval, but I may have got that wrong.

Host: Yeah. Do you have a London versus the rest of the country challenge? The experiences I've had — and this is all I can base it on — have all been in London. So I'm very conscious of that, and me saying this is great. But it does also strike me that it is perfectly tailored for London.

Vik: I think there are differences and I think that's what we have to be alive to, and part of the reason for doing the JV, if you like, and having the county involved in each of the teams, is that you are then able to have that deep-rooted connection and knowledge of the local area. And I think what I've learned through this last year is that is a hugely important — and I won't call it a challenge. I just think there is a difference with the fan base in Birmingham as there is in Cardiff as there is in South London. I don't think one is good or bad or more attuned or less attuned. But those that have done well this year — and you mentioned Welsh Fire — they've done brilliantly this year. Their fandom numbers, their digital numbers, their attendances — like you say, they sold out on a Saturday, they had great crowds in on a Monday night. It was unbelievable. But what they did fantastically was lean into the fact that they are the Welsh Fire and lean into that aspect of the local audience, the local fan base, and that was driven through the Glan team that know that area.

So I think that's important, and that will increasingly be important going forward — that as a tournament we have teams that are rooted in the local geography, and a competition we are rooted in the England and Wales kind of foundation of one of our tenants.

品牌重塑 vs 保留身份

Host: So what were the discussions, if you were privy to them, on the branding elements? Because you had four teams that rebranded, let's say, and four that maintained their original identity. When there's the rebrand, you've been working for 5 years to establish something from scratch, which is incredibly hard in sport. Now you're, as you said, kind of going again — any associations that may have been established now have to develop or change again. How did you deal with those challenges?

Vik: I think the teams have done a great job. You can completely understand why teams would want to do that, especially when you have a global portfolio and brands that you can therefore use to your advantage to bring fans in from around the world. But those that did rebrand were aware that they had work to do and have done brilliantly. From the Manchester and Leeds teams that were giving away shirts, from my London that had the shirt exchange — so if you had an Oval Invincible shirt, you could swap that in — I thought they've done a great job, in one year.

It was fascinating to see the amount of Manchester Super Giant shirts or the Sunrisers Leeds shirts not at the cricket grounds. So you'd be wandering around Leeds, you would run around Manchester. Interestingly as well, you'd see them at away games — which I think that's the first time, and it's anecdotal, but the first time I've really noticed that you would go to the Oval and see yellow for Trent Rockets, or you'd go to Birmingham and see the orange of Sunrisers and so on and so forth.

So I think they've all taken it upon themselves in different ways, aware of the challenge to establish that brand over the coming years. It will take time. It's not an overnight thing, but we've had a really good start.

面对头条与"深度球迷"的漫长养成

Host: What do you think about the headlines? Because I've seen a few and it — I was quite interested to see what people meant by it, where you said you've had these core identities and rules that you've lived to for the competition today. I saw one looking at it going — well, the specific headline was: "The hundred's costly makeover still leaves English cricket playing a waiting game." I.e. what they were saying is we're still trying to understand what this actually is. Is that fair? Because I didn't feel immediately when I read that. I was like, well, I kind of know I think what it is.

Vik: I look — I think the core tenets that I mentioned and you referenced there is: it's always been about growth, new fans coming into the sport, establishing ourselves as this unmissable event of the summer that is designed to throw doors open. And that's what we've been about. Then you add on top of that it's around the gender parity and the men's and women's on one club, two teams, equal footing. And that DNA runs throughout, and has done, through that.

What we now need to do to go to the next level is to deepen fandom of the eight teams. I understand and appreciate the feedback of previous years, and probably still to this date: fans are coming because it's a great day out at the 100. We are now only starting to build a — "I'm coming because I'm a My London fan" or "I'm a Sunrisers Leeds fan." And that is the next step that we need to do to become where we want, to achieve our objectives. But that's not an overnight thing. That's years in the making to get to that point. I have no doubt we'll get there, but you can't just flick a switch and say "you're a deep-rooted Birmingham Phoenix fan, and that's it, that's who you are." That will take time.

商业升级：赞助商与投资人的网络效应

Host: Yeah. Commercially, to me, it looked like a real level up. And I mean that just purely as like the breadth of associations that you seem to have now part of this year. You had — I mean, well, you had Barclays, you had Soen, Sketchers, Vitality, DP World all on front of shirts. That's a huge part of developing value in emerging sports, but it's also a huge part in now creating more value, driving better business. And I would imagine the new ownership that you have being able to add some form of value and bring their networks and experiences into the —

Vik: Exactly. And you'd hope it's a bit of a virtuous cycle, right? Host: And can you just quickly explain to those that may not know how the distribution worked? Because you only have eight teams, but as you said, there are previously — you know, there are 18 counties.

And what it ended up being is that if you were a host venue of the 100, then there's £18 million there and thereabouts. If you're a non-host, there's about £26 million that you had. Host: Yeah. Exactly.

Vik: So the bids that came in were for individual teams, and we had some firms that were like, "I've got eight teams. Here are eight bids." Others were, "No, that is my team. That's the only one bid I'll have." Okay. We then, because of the JV, we then went to the venue. So take Notts for example, Trent Rockets, and said, "Look, here are the bids that have come in for you."

We reviewed paper bids and then it was October, November — it was about a month where we organized meetings. So on one side of the table was a venue, other side was a potential investor. I would give my vision for Trent Rockets and where I see it going. They would do the same. And you'd have these matchmaking sessions that were half a day to a day long. And off the end of it, we'd then work with the venue to go, "Okay, let's narrow those down."

You'd then have another round of bids and then — the final round was an auction. And at that point between us and the venue, the venue had to pick at least two, so you'd have some competitive tension. And they would say, "Well, we're happy with that. Any of those would be fine." It is shorter. We're able to present it in a very different way, we're able to present it in a way that pulls it apart from the Blast and those sorts of things. Jude Bellingham 与年轻观众

Host: No, completely. And seeing young people engage with it, I'd imagine, is a huge part of it because obviously they are the audience now, everyone's trying to capture. Seeing Jude Bellingham come in — you know, it's so easy now for names just to turn up at sports events and just to be associated, and everyone questions whether it's genuine, whether it's real, whether they want to be there, whether there's some other reason. But I think, you know, as anyone that was there, as we saw, he actually really wants to be there. He's part of an ownership group. It's not just, "Oh, okay, you know, I'll put a bit of money."

Vik: It's brilliantly authentic. It's great. It doesn't seem to be, but I'm pretty sure it's not just a bit of money and there you go. He was there all day. He seemed to really enjoy his cricket. He enjoyed spending some time with the Phoenix players — which is great, and it's great for our competition to have someone like that involved in it, is unbelievable.

目标、北极星与故事

Host: Okay. So we've had five years, we've now had the first year of brand new. Looking ahead, how do you set your targets? Do you go year by year? Do you go, we would like to be here in five years time? What does success for this really look like?

Vik: I think success in the long term is huge. Really exciting. The ceiling is now very very high from a sports product full stop. And therefore to your point around how you set it, you then will set our target with the ambition and the passion of the teams that we've now got around that table — very high, five, ten years down the line. Okay. Well, to get there, the first step we need to do is X, and then we need to do Y, and you go step by step, but you have a north star that means that we are in that sporting calendar, an unmissable part of that sporting calendar in August. And so yeah, hugely exciting.

Host: If sport is all now stories, right? Is that the story you're really trying to tell?

Vik: I think — yeah. Well, people engage with stories. They engage with human stories. And I hope that fans can engage with the human side of the competition. We're going to sit here on a Business of Sport podcast and talk about the business. But the story that I'd hope they'd like to see is Phoebe Litchfield's superb batting, or Tim David's amazing catch, or Ciphert winning the game for the Manchester Super Giants. Those are the stories that I'd like to live and be in people's memories for a while to come. There'll inevitably be a lot of challenges ahead. There'll be ups and downs throughout that. But to your point, we have a great product. We have a great set of investors. And we've got people up and down the country that are passionate about what we've got, that want to try and improve it on a day-by-day basis. So yeah, an exciting time ahead.

Host: Awesome. All right. Now I will shut up. Thank you so much for coming back in. It's great. And congratulations to you and all the team putting it together. I think it's been really cool to watch it grow.

Vik: Oh, brilliant. Thank you very much.

## 一场被伪装成"体育联赛"的风险投资实验
表面上，Vik 谈的是板球联赛"The Hundred"的第一个新赛季。但如果把耳朵贴近他的措辞，你会听到一个更陌生的声音——**这其实是一场用"体育 IP"作为标的物的种子轮融资仪式**。
100 多个买家竞投 8 支队伍、"venue + investor"的相亲式配对会议、最后一轮拍卖定价、5 亿英镑分配给英格兰板球生态——这些不是传统体育联盟的语言，而是 YC Demo Day 的语言。ECB 不像在办联赛，更像在做一个 **"体育资产孵化器"**：中央先用 5 年建立最小可行产品（MVP），达到"因成功而触及天花板"的临界点，再把 8 个"子公司"拆出去独立融资，让每支队伍在下一阶段各自跑增长。
