item.title: [a16z] The Evolution of Computers & Abdication of Reasoning
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的相变：这一次抽象跃迁，方向反了

Steven 与 Ben 争论的核心其实是一个隐藏的相位反转——过去七十年的每一次抽象上移（晶体管→逻辑门→OS→应用→平台），人始终"在机器之上"下达指令，机器只负责执行。但 LLM 是历史上第一次让人"退到机器之下"——你不再规定端状态，你祈祷一个模型给你端状态。Ben 反复说的 "abdication of logic" 不是又一层抽象，而是抽象堆栈的方向倒转。

这里有个让人意外的观察：四色定理其实在 1976 年就已经完成了同样的"退位"——那不是一个人类能理解的证明，而是让计算机穷举 1936 种构型的 200 页黑箱结论。数学界当年也吵过一模一样的问题（"这算证明吗？"）。也就是说，"推理外包"并不是 AI 时代的独创，只是从边缘学科的一次事件，变成了所有认知工作的默认基础设施。这才是真正惊人的地方。

二、数学家为什么最兴奋？——一个反直觉的"存在主义分层"

被 AI 冲击最狠的群体，反而最兴奋。Ben 半开玩笑地抛出一个残忍的诊断："如果一件事被解决你反而抑郁，说明这件事本身可能不值得做。" 这句话表面刻薄，但它揭示了一个跨领域的普适规律——

任何长期缺乏经济外部性的智力活动，会把"过程"内化为"目的"。禅宗僧侣画沙曼陀罗、学院派研究后现代文学、加密圈研究拜占庭容错——这些活动的价值一部分（有时是大部分）来自"从事该活动的人的自我意义"。而癌症研究、材料科学、蛋白质折叠这类有明确外部端状态的领域，AI 帮忙推进只会让人狂喜。

由此可以做一个大胆的预测式判断：未来五年，AI 冲击带来的"存在危机烈度"，将是一个学科"内部意义 / 外部效用"比值的精确函数。你甚至可以用这个比值给学科排序，谁最痛苦，谁最快乐——这比"哪些工作会被替代"是一个更根本、也更预测力的问题。

三、资本-工程的百年反转：一个被大多数人忽略的康德拉季耶夫波

Ben 讲的这个数字最震撼："20 年前给 10 个人 10 亿美金，他们不知道该怎么花；今天给 20 个人 10 亿美金，他们能有效地用掉。"

这不是一句金句，这是行业物理定律的翻转。让我把它往回推，你会看到一个精确的三段式循环：

  • 1945–1985：资本约束（你首先得买得起一台机器）
  • 1985–2023：工程约束（Brooks 定律主宰，加人不减速，只增速）
  • 2023– ：资本约束（模型训练、GPU、数据中心，钱直接换算成能力）

这是同一维度上四十年后的镜像回归。跨领域看，这几乎精确对应能源行业的历史节律：铁路时代（资本）→ 内燃机时代（工程/工艺）→ 核电与超大规模电网时代（资本）。当一个行业进入"用钱买物理约束"的阶段，赢家标准就从'谁最聪明'变成'谁最能募资 + 最能配置资本 + 最能承担系统性风险'。

一个几乎没人明说的推论：既然行业物理反转了，风险投资的"精益创业"叙事（Eric Ries）在 AI 底层就彻底失效了，而"胖创业"（Ben Horowitz 的老论调）意外地重新成为默认路径。更微妙的是——这一次不是选择，而是必需。你不下注 200 亿美金去训练下一代模型，就没有下一代模型可谈。这也是为什么 Google 要走债券脱表、微软要给内部产品"限令牌"——巨头第一次尝到了"资本不够用"的味道，而这恰恰是过去四十年他们从未体会过的痛。

四、被埋在最后的洞见：AI 解决了分发问题

Ben 顺口提到但没展开的一句话，我认为是整期最被低估的洞见："AI 一并解决了分发问题——因为对 token 和 GPU 的需求是无限的，你可以把营销当作纯粹的资本投入。"

翻译一下：过去创业公司死于分发（distribution），不是死于产品。Clayton Christensen 的颠覆理论之所以成立，一半是因为大公司的销售渠道无法被撬动。而现在，Cursor / Anthropic / OpenAI 的火箭式增长，本质上是用无限的推理需求 + 无限的资本 = 无限的漏斗顶端——历史上第一次，一家 100 人公司能和微软在分发上正面对撞。

这才是真正颠覆'创新者的窘境'的东西。不是模型能力，不是团队规模，而是分发经济学的物理变化。老巨头擅长的所有护城河（销售、渠道、合作伙伴生态、政企关系），突然被一个"你想要多少 token 就买多少 token"的粗暴逻辑绕过了。这才是 Microsoft 焦虑的真正原因——不是 OpenAI 更聪明，而是它可以在没有销售队伍的情况下达到分发规模。

📝 转录文本

冷开场：三段主题预告

Ben: Right now, if I give 20 people a billion dollars, they can actually use it usefully. We've kind of moved the industry from like this engineering bound problem to a capital problem. That's fundamentally very different.

Steven: Math is very much a leading edge indicator of what the market might be interested in. Why? Some people will walk in and say the foundations to AGI and to reasoning is going to be math, but like that doesn't tell you anything about reality. For me, it's still in the domain of like it's really good at playing a game.

Ben: The startups don't aim straight at the incumbents and the incumbents just don't pay attention. Microsoft is worried way more about what Amazon and Google are doing than anyone in a startup space. Everybody who's from a big company in Silicon Valley, you always think, "Oh my god, we're just going to crush all of these little companies." And then you realize they never get crushed. And I think this is why we're seeing such meteoric roasts of the cursors, the anthropics, and the open AIs. Although capital is scarce and it's hard to get and all of these other things, once you get it...

一、开场与议题引入：AI 解题黎曼猜想

Host: First off, thanks for both of you making time to be here. That's great.

Um, Jared Ser tweeted a few days ago something along the lines of how he told Claude to try to solve the Riemann hypothesis and to try harder, and I don't know if there was actually any progress made, but it's part of the larger conversation around, hey, it seems like there's some accomplishments that are being made. How do we make sense of this in terms of what is actually happening and what does it mean for math?

Ben: I'm gonna let Steve go.

Steven: Oh, well, I'm no mathematician at all, but I think it's just an important moment because it sort of divides the world into two groups—the groups that are just very very excited that like, oh my god, these things are being solved. It doesn't matter if you understand them. Actually nobody understands—the universe of people who understand what these things are is very small. And then there are the people who are just like, oh, it's fake, it's going to put people out of jobs, no one's going to know the future of where these fields go.

And the most interesting thing about it is the group that's most excited are mostly the mathematicians. And so that actually confuses everybody, because if you're of the school of people who are like "it's going to put people out of work and we're going to all get dumber, and it's, you know, the dawn of idiocracy because computers are doing all of our work," you're confused that the people who are impacted most by this level of AI are the most excited.

Host: Yeah. Yeah.

Steven: And I think that itself is shining a light on this moment that we're in right now.

二、数学突破的经济学检验

Ben: You know, you're talking to two systems guys, two product guys. We're like—to have the same caveat—there's some things we're actually both very expert on. This is not one of them. So I'm going to, kind of from the peanut gallery, I've got two comments.

One of them is: I view economic utility to be a very important measure when you're talking about AI. So I was trying to think—there's a lot of hours been trying to solve some math thing, right? But if you sum up the entire posttock salaries of all the people that have been working over the years on these problems, it's probably not very much. And so part of me is saying, it's great that there's these capabilities. I'm not sure that the fact they've been longstanding is that much of an indication, because there hasn't been a huge economic incentive in order to solve them. Now that doesn't mean it's not hard or whatever. It's just—I don't think we have that validation of "this unlocks some deluge of economic value."

And the second one is: it's kind of not surprising to me that AI is very good at solving an almost purely axiomatic domain that requires knowing a whole bunch of different things and putting the solutions together from very disparate spaces. Because often, really—I've been reading, like everybody else has been obsessively—they're like, "Oh, I came up with the solution." It's like, yeah, the solution was pretty straightforward. It just borrowed from a bit of math that I didn't know.

And so I think if there's a meta-learning here, the meta-learning is: there is a set of problems that probably require you being too broad for most humans or most education, and it's going to solve those. It's clearly very good at solving axiomatic systems. But I don't think it provides a strong indication of "is this solving things that the market hasn't been able to solve," because there really hasn't been a market around these. And so I think that's the best question for us to answer. So very exciting, seems kind of reasonable and understandable, not sure what the longer term implications are.

Steven: I do think that there's something interesting—that math is very much a leading edge indicator of what the market might be interested in. Why? I remember when I was in school, there was some big thing that someone at AT&T invented—a new algorithmic, a new program for doing linear algebra, a new way to solve linear, which is super important right now in the AI world. But his big thing was, "Well, now we can just calculate the United Airlines flight map in like three hours less time than we could last week."

Host: Right. But let's dig into—

Ben: So, it's just not clear to me that the problems being solved are those that are roadblocks to existingly economically useful tasks. And if they were, it's not clear to me that they wouldn't have been solved. A posttock that's been ruminating on a problem, getting paid $30K a year for five years—it's very different than "the market has decided that this is the one thing to unlock." And maybe they're there, maybe these problems being solved are the key problems to unlocking some big economically productive use case. I just haven't seen that yet. So for me that's the next thing I'm looking for.

I don't even know what 12-dimensional spaces or what that means. So I'm completely with you on—I don't even know what problems are in 12-dimensional space. Like, are you very skinny? Are you very tiny? I'm really confused by that.

And maybe I'm wrong here, but for me it's still in the domain of "it's really good at playing a game." Like, this is the best Starcraft player ever, which is cool and very powerful, but I have a hard time connecting that with (a) maybe the reason we didn't have them before is because there just wasn't an economic need, and (b) how does that actually map?

So listen, there's a huge range of these things. We get pitches all the time. Some people will walk in and say, "The foundations to AGI and to reasoning is going to be math. And once you do that, you'll be able to answer every question because the universe is based on some fundamental mathematical principles. And once you understand that, you understand everything." And then there's other people, candidly, that walk in the door and they're just like, "Listen, that's great, but that doesn't tell you anything about reality." And so I think there's more work to do, and this isn't just about getting better at math.

三、数学家的兴奋与存在主义焦虑

Steven: I do think what's interesting is that part of the reason mathematicians are very excited about it is because they work a certain way. If you work in history, there's basically no abstraction in history. There's just a bunch of facts, and then people develop these models that you can think of almost as force diagrams that explain war or famine or whatever. Whereas mathematicians and mathematics have this super long historic arc of layering on abstractions after abstractions—and don't worry, we'll get to OSI in a minute—but this idea that a bunch of math all of a sudden becomes a new level of abstraction—

Ben: Is it true that they're so—I've found that it's mixed. I found that some are very excited and some are in an existential crisis. The ones who are excited basically say, "Listen, it solves 20% of my job—the 20% I didn't like anyway. So this allows me to explore a new frontier that's very important."

And what I've always wondered is—is that a function of the type of problem being solved? Like, I just can't imagine, if AI came and solved cancer, whatever, someone that works on cancer would be like, "Oh, I'm so existentially depressed." This is amazing! But whereas on the other hand—"Oh, we solved this math problem, oh I'm so depressed we solved the math problem." Like, maybe literally the entire utility of that problem was keeping somebody employed to solve the problem.

Steven: Or just writing articles in the back like "another attempt, and here's where I went wrong." So let me offer it this way—

Ben: There's nothing on the other side of the solution. And so we're depressed because now, whatever, this useless activity is gone. Let me stop—no, I mean too cynical on this thing. I love math.

Steven: I think we caught you being a little cynical, but not really. But more that it's just—let me take a side of it this way. Looking at the history of computer science, because I had to take this class which I looked at all the course catalogs for a bunch of schools—you don't have to take it anymore. That was like discrete math basically.

Ben: Yeah. Yeah. And like, or algorithmic complexity theory, which was a required class for a very long time. And now—do you remember concrete mathematics from Donald Knuth?

Steven: I didn't. You're a Stanford guy, I'm not. My state school, my state school we didn't have that. But that's a Cornell joke for us Cornellians. But my class, I got taught by one of the luminaries in the field of algorithms—ironically a Stanford PhD—John Hopcroft, of course, who invented, for the people who are pragmatic ICs, two-three trees and a bunch of stuff as his thesis at Stanford. That's a legend.

But John was our professor in all this crap, and we had to learn all this P equals NP stuff. And I remember, this is the four-color—

Ben: This is the four-color—

Steven: —proven by computers.

Ben: No, ex—but that's where I'm going. You just buried the lead.

四、四色定理：算力驱动的证明先例

Steven: Yeah, but so those of you that don't know—we had to take a whole course in college on that, basically boiled down to this problem. And the interesting thing is why: it was because the theoreticians had postulated that if you can solve this problem in non-exponential time, in polynomial time, then you could solve all these other problems like the traveling salesperson problem, and all these other problems much much faster—which mattered because all of our computers were just so compute-bound. So if you were the AT&T people that gave, you know, "here's our node of 6,000 switches, how do you route optimally?" You'd be like, "Well, we don't have enough. That's like two years of running the simulation to solve this."

And so it turns out that one of the interesting things was they proved the four-color theorem.

Ben: Yeah.

Steven: But they did it—which, by the way, I mean, just—the four-color theorem says for any 2D planar map, you can color it, you can use only four colors such that no two adjacent areas have the same color, right? And you only need four colors, you'll never need five colors. And we learned it just so people—like, you kids know—that's literally how we learned it, and we could all repeat it like that. It's this very weird imprint over this problem.

And so what sort of happened was, no one ever arrived at basically what you could think of as a proof that looked like calculus. Instead what they did is they actually proved that the number of potential solutions was finite.

Ben: Have you actually seen the proof?

Steven: Yeah. Yeah. 200 pages of combinations. But they basically proved there's a finite number of them, and then they just computed all of them and said, "Look, it's only four colors." And so it's this sort of bankshot proof, but it was only possible because of compute.

Ben: And to your point, that was actually very very useful in the practical applications.

Steven: Right. And certainly as a topology person, setting strong bounds and things like that. So actually I see—I think that to me was just a really good lesson in when you have a new level of abstraction that says this is a whole class of problems that can be solved, you can then build tools working at that level of abstraction, and everybody doesn't have to start from "okay, what's the two-three tree representation of what we're doing?"

五、模拟、物理与数学的经济距离

Ben: So listen—it's hard not to get philosophical when you're talking about AI. So I'm gonna get philosophical and you can tell me to shut up, but I just can't—like, you kind of do. So this math thing seems to me a little different, because it kind of begs the following question, which is: will math ever be representative of physical phenomenon? Right? Has anybody ever taken a bunch of equations and actually predicted something physical? I don't know the answer to that.

So I worked on these large simulation codes, and these large simulation codes are actually trying to compute physical phenomenon like the explosion of a star, or what would happen to an airplane in a wind simulator. But all of those, even though they're just calculating these large differential equations, they were all based on empirical results.

Steven: Yeah. Like literally the equations of state for the—

Ben: Well, they were models—they were just, we could measure temperature in these places.

Steven: That's exactly right, so it was all based on empirical equations of state.

Ben: And so I've always wondered—is simulation computationally irreducible, and so you actually have to run the simulation? In that case it's not clear to me to what extent AI helps. I know people are trying to solve this problem with AI, but I don't know if these math answers have any impact on that type of stuff. Right? So maybe there's some separate algorithmic domain to your point where they do—or, you know, maybe like modeling or logistics—but when it comes to "will this star explode, will this building stand up," like the actual simulation, I think these things are pretty disjoint.

And then I read a lot of these discourses on the math solutions, and there are these claims where "if it can solve all math, you can predict anything." And I just think that's a huge logical leap, which is not clear to me is obviously true. Or that there's any indication it's true at all.

六、工具的历史：算盘、计算尺与 Curta

Steven: So the way—one way that I might talk about that (again, this is so out of my league on the actual math)—

Ben: Two systems people.

Steven: I'm good. But I'm compelled. I'm inherently a tools person, and so I kind of get this part of it—which is that what's happened is that AI might not be the next tool to solve math problems at some scale that matters, but it might lead to the development of a new kind, a new level of model.

And so I brought props to show this off. So of course this is the original math tool. And so before something like this, this is one of these real ones from like Beijing market—

Ben: Well, you know, the ones they tell tourists in French.

Steven: But I'm very proud of that because I negotiated it down to like seven cents. But that became a level of abstraction, and all of a sudden you just had this basic math thing. And then you just fast forward a whole bunch. I brought this because it's just so freaking cool. It is—so this, everybody knows what slide rules are.

Ben: Yeah. Nobody knows how to use them.

Steven: This is called a Curta, which is an Austrian—basically it's a round slide rule. It's like a coffee grinder or a pepper mill, and you have all these ways you set the numbers on the side and then you turn it one way to add, another way to subtract.

Ben: Whoa. Wait, is that used for like multi-number arithmetic, or is it used for stuff like logarithms?

Steven: No, it's only arithmetic. Well, I think—but of course it depends on how you use it. It's from the mid 20th century, I think. My uncle brought this back from the war. But what's incredible is this is like 600 pieces of machined metal inside this. It would cost like $50,000 to make one now.

Ben: Do you know how to use it?

Steven: I actually did, but I'm not going to try to do it. For prepping for this, so I wouldn't be a complete—just go look what I have. I actually went through the trouble of learning how to use it, although it's been sitting on my shelf for years.

七、计算器争议与"变化 vs 基线"

Steven: But it's the interesting thing is, then all of a sudden a whole new level of problems get solved.

Ben: Wait, so you're saying the new model is the new calculator or the new graphing calculator? I actually remember when—remember the TI-85?

Steven: Oh, of course. Yeah.

Ben: I remember that came out. All of the math teachers had this crisis. They're like, "You know, we used to give you a piece of paper. We plot the XY equation. Now they could do it on the calculator and they can solve equations, and our field is dead."

Steven: But what's interesting is this is why it's so important to AI today. Those people didn't complain about when calculus came out, because calculus was a baseline to them. And what it is—there's this notion that people react to change more than they react to the baseline of where they all started. And so much of the concerns—I literally got a TI-35—the first calculators in schools. The only advanced math they did—they had a percent key and factorial, which we didn't even know what it was, and you could do like 59 factorial, and that was the max that you could display. And I went to college and the classes were "no calculators allowed."

Ben: My whole life I've been on the cusp of allowed and not allowed for everybody. I mean, I was there for the graphing calculator. You literally have a blue book, just to show all of your work, just to show that you weren't plugging it into the graph.

Steven: See, I missed the graph, which most of us were like actually writing video games in the back and could care less about its ability to write math.

Ben: Absolutely.

Ben: But read Exile, the Steve Jobs and Exile book. Because you can really get a sense for building up. In fact, of course, NeXT was famously—it took the code from Mach at Carnegie Mellon and started from there. We couldn't have done it from scratch completely. But this whole idea of just how important it is to think through the domain specific and how you disrupt people—

There was an old joke at Harvard Business School when Clay was still with us, which was: "It's weird that they teach disruption as a theory in the business school when really it should just be a fact in the physics department."

Steven: And I love that. I was there in '98 when he was writing the book and the paper and everything. That's when I was teaching.

Ben: That's nice.

Steven: And I really used to be—of course, there's a lore with everybody who's from a big company in Silicon Valley. When you arrive, like I did, the theory is always like, you always think, "oh my god, we're just going to crush all of these little companies." You always think that when you're at the big company. And then you realize they never get crushed.

Ben: And that—Ben always makes this point, like they just—and Mark does in his movie—it was AWS actually put out of business.

Steven: Right, right, exactly. And because the startups don't aim straight at the incumbents, and the incumbents just don't pay attention. The incumbents are only interested in what the other incumbents are doing. Microsoft is worried way more about what Amazon and Google are doing than anyone in a startup space. But the elements of disruption that matter are the cultural ones of being a big company, and those are constant. Those are the laws of physics, and so you can't change those. You can't change scorecards, you can't change field sales and go-to-market and compensation and org structures and legacy and customers, because the way you behave if you have 500,000 customers you're serving, there's a bunch of stuff you just can't do that. You're just stuck.

And that is really the essence of disruption. And that's why we're at a magic moment where it's not just that the culture is there like it always is, but the startup ecosystem—it's a reflection of what happened during cloud, which was: a whole bunch of stuff that you needed—again, it's this abstraction layer. If you're a startup like you were, you don't have to go build a data center and build your own egress and call AT&T and do all of that stuff. Now you're up and running in the first hours of your first dinner.

Ben: But the thing with cloud—I actually think you actually articulated it very well and I actually use this because this is great. Like the thing with cloud is nobody thought they could put AWS out of business.

Steven: Right.

Ben: You just kind of accepted the oligopoly and you built on top of it. And the question is: will they kill us in our little pipsqueak corner?

Steven: The answer was—will they just add you for free, or for some price could match or whatever?

Ben: I actually think—and that's always been the question, "will Microsoft do the app?" Right. But now these companies are actually taking on the incumbents. And you make this great point, which—I had thought about it this way—but computing has been defined by these very complex large engineering efforts, building a chip, building a system.

Steven: What's that—The Age of the New Machine or—

Ben: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. The Soul—well, the Soul—

Steven: The Soul of a New Machine. Yeah. Beautiful book, right? Talked about how hard it was to build these—you know, these Jack systems, building an operating system. Even in the cloud, like Jeff Dean in that era of people were building these distributed clusters, and they're the first time that people could figure out how to do that. Once you had that, that was a massive advantage. So these were these massive engineering efforts that no startup could do. And now for these models, it really is just capital access. And so it's a very different laws of physics where, like, if you can amass the capital, you can do something.

I mean, Google is Google. They have all the data, they have all the intelligence, and their models are getting trounced.

Ben: Yeah, by OpenAI and by Anthropic. And it just goes—

Steven: Because of the cultural element.

Ben: I think that people on the outside underestimate it until you've lived the cultural element of trying to—

Steven: I'll bet it's cultural. It's not a typical engineering problem, like they're very good at, because they've out-executed—like GCP is fantastic. That's engineering after. And then also I bet it's probably hard to free up that much capital for one of these companies, honestly.

Ben: Well, all the big companies—you can tell from their earnings calls how consternated they've been over the capital. You know, you have Google doing their bond deal to move it off balance sheet basically in some weird way. You had the rumors of, I don't remember which company, the rumors of, "well, they're rationing the tokens so that they go to the enterprise customers and not to the internal products, and so the internal products are AI starved." And of course, none of their competitors to those products are starved.

I've learned to really appreciate the—I mean, look, I fought and fought and fought to not be disrupted by the mobile platforms, by ARM basically. And Intel just didn't care. I came down here, I sat across the table from all the Intel leadership, and I pulled out the first Surface and I said, "Here's our new computer." And they got very excited, and then they were like, "But what's in here?" I said, "Well, it's an ARM chip."

Steven: Oh, wow.

Ben: And the fact I even brought one into the building—it was very very tough. And they just never felt that that was going to—that was like a chip used in a printer, and also they looked at me like, "we're ARM licensees, we knew all"—and I'm like, "but it's the power, it's the graphics, it's the always-connected, all of this stuff." And the culture was—they do Moore's law at Intel—and just like with Google, they do hyperscale. So if AI moves on device—

Steven: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Of course. Like that's not what they do.

Ben: Yeah. And with Microsoft, they were squeezed. They're squeezed now. And I think you raise super interesting points about the opportunity though for startups with this capital inversion kind of thing.

Steven: Go raise capital and go after the—

Ben: Well, and it's not just—it's like you're also saying, "we're actually not going to question you if you're trying to raise that capital." Like, we're not going to look at you like you're crazy. And you just look at the raises that are happening right now, and these companies have been quite successful as a result.

十五、模型作为 200 亿美元数字艺术品：能力预测的失效

Host: The last thing—when Vinod Khosla came in and we had him on the podcast, he was sort of—he thought LLMs were a great achievement but he was bearish on their ability to invent new discoveries, particularly like scientific breakthroughs or things like that. And I'm curious if you think the math progress is consistent with that, or what is your latest thinking on sort of the limitations of the current model architecture versus, like, well, we need more—

Ben: So here's kind of my new view, which is: I think we know exactly how these things work. You put a bunch of data in them, they're stuck to that data, they can only do distribution stuff, and they can move along that manifold in a perfectly Bayesian way. So, okay, so we can say these words. And then the question is: okay, but what are the implications of that? What problems can it solve?

I think it's just so hard for a human being to reason about a digital artifact—in this case the model—that was built with $5 billion. So in the history of humanity, we've never created a single digital artifact that had that many flops and that much data in it. So on one hand, we know exactly how it works from a mechanic standpoint. On the other hand, that is so much data and that is so much compute, maybe all of that stuff's already in there and it can solve anything that you want.

And so the conversation has moved from "how do these things work?" We know. Can it do out-of-distribution stuff? No. Does—is there transfer learning? Probably not. Is the singularity here? Probably not. I think most people kind of agree—we're not in fast takeoff, we're stuck to it being in distribution, we haven't closed—we all agree about that. But what I don't think anybody knows is: okay, but you're still putting tens of billions of dollars in that thing. What's it capable of now? And if you consider this meta-economic machinery, which means the ability from Anthropic to raise lots of money, then pour all of that money into this thing to create this super powerful thing—I don't think any of us can predict what that means and where that goes.

And so it's a different conversation, but the question is the same. It's like, will that be able to cure cancer? Maybe. But if you put $20 billion into something, maybe it can cure cancer effectively. And that's where I think the discourse has evolved, and where it is now. And I honestly have decided that I cannot predict what an artifact worth that was—that you used $20 billion to create—is capable of.

Steven: Look, I think it's just so important. It's important for people who are deep in watching everything that's new to admit that they can't predict. And I think that's great, because it turns out I wrote 58 memos on what the internet was going to be, and I was wrong on a lot of them by far.

Ben: But even this one is a little different. This is like—I take $20 billion and I put it into a model, right? And then you and I look at that model, and we can do whatever we want. I don't think we can comprehend what that even means. It's so many flops and so much data. Like, I don't know what that's capable of.

Steven: I think we are—I think that that's really true. And on biomedicine in particular—look, the other half of my household is a research doctor who uses AI. We have a Spark at home, and she's loaded—

Ben: Like a ton?

Steven: Like a Sun Spark. No, no. Nvidia Spark.

Ben: Oh, yeah. No, no, no. Not with a C or with a K. Oh, yeah.

Steven: Not a Scott McNealy Spark. A relic.

Ben: No, no.

Steven: And it's all AI. She does brain stuff and surgical brain stuff. All AI. And it's so interesting to see, because what it really can do is—it sees the patterns that you can't, that only experience could tell somebody. But if there's 10,000 papers on a topic that's part of her model, then it's just finding the patterns that no one has. And that's a pretty basic AI capability at this point, but it's actually opening up solutions or problems or research directions and things like that.

I will say, just for the—this is not magic to discover drugs, because the hard part of drugs has always been candidates—not candidate. It's always been efficacy and safety. The candidates have, since the 80s, been able to develop more than we could test. It's human patients and it's very very very hard.

Ben: Can I just tell you something that I got wrong on this? So I love the question that you asked, which is: how has our thinking evolved on whether these things—their capabilities in generality—

I was responding to this Bostrom notion of recursive self-improvement fast takeoff. You create one of these things, you step back, and it takes over the world, right? And so I kind of poo-poohed that, because that's clearly not what's happening. And I think most people—a lot of people agree that that's the case. Right?

But here's what I got wrong. What I got wrong is: I did not know that we could effectively just continue to pour money in this. Like, the scaling laws are holding. And I don't know what it means to—let's say we do a $100 billion training run to have this thing that you're putting $100 billion in. And then that money comes from this meta-economic machinery that may be able—want to solve whatever they may want to solve—cancer, but they may also want to create a weapon, who knows. And so this concentration of this many resources in a useful way, I think is very new. I don't think we understand the implications. I think you could reasonably argue that that's very dangerous if you kind of apply that $100 billion in the wrong way.

So I think that's kind of where this conversation needs to evolve to. So less the FOOM, and more the: what does it mean to be able to concentrate resources?

Steven: Which also was in all—I mean, this is—you're basically talking about exponential growth. And this is just exponential in dollars. And we all know none of us can model exponential very well.

Ben: Yeah, we've never been able to do that. Like, complex engineering projects—you were not tackling one problem with a lot of money—or just kind of building this machine.

Steven: Well, you're right. You're 100% right, and I completely agree. But I remember just sitting in meeting after meeting at Intel saying, "we have 5 gigahertz, we have this many gigahertz, this many transistors," and literally nobody knows what we're going to do with them all.

Ben: No, no, you're building the machinery. I'm saying, in this case, if you're like, "I want to exhaustively explore every protein combination," right? We can just turn that into a money problem.

Steven: Yes. Got it.

Ben: A very strange—

Steven: Which is a great way to say it. That we can take previously infinite problems and apply capital, and it becomes finite.

Ben: Just makes it a capital problem and not an engineering problem. Yeah. Which is just a very different laws of physics.

Steven: Yeah. Yeah.

Host: Let's wrap on that, because it's 2:30. This has been a great episode. Thank you guys.

Steven & Ben: Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、被忽略的相变：这一次抽象跃迁，方向反了
Steven 与 Ben 争论的核心其实是一个隐藏的**相位反转**——过去七十年的每一次抽象上移（晶体管→逻辑门→OS→应用→平台），人始终"在机器之上"下达指令，机器只负责执行。但 LLM 是历史上第一次让人"退到机器之下"——你不再规定端状态，你祈祷一个模型给你端状态。Ben 反复说的 "abdication of logic" 不是又一层抽象，而是**抽象堆栈的方向倒转**。
这里有个让人意外的观察：**四色定理其实在 1976 年就已经完成了同样的"退位"**——那不是一个人类能理解的证明，而是让计算机穷举 1936 种构型的 200 页黑箱结论。数学界当年也吵过一模一样的问题（"这算证明吗？"）。也就是说，"推理外包"并不是 AI 时代的独创，只是**从边缘学科的一次事件，变成了所有认知工作的默认基础设施**。这才是真正惊人的地方。
## 二、数学家为什么最兴奋？——一个反直觉的"存在主义分层"
被 AI 冲击最狠的群体，反而最兴奋。Ben 半开玩笑地抛出一个残忍的诊断：**"如果一件事被解决你反而抑郁，说明这件事本

item.title: [Sequoia Capital] Parallel’s Parag Agrawal: Building a New Web for AI Agents
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：Parag 正在把"惰性"重新定义为价值来源

大多数人把"人类的懒惰"视为产品设计要克服的障碍——自动补全、下拉推荐、SEO 摘要页，都是在补偿人类不愿多打三个字的懒。但 Parag 把这一层惰性翻转成了商业洞见：那些"预 AI slop"页面之所以存在，不是因为它们劣质，而是因为它们完成了一项被低估的信息劳动——从 300 页的 10-K 中挑出了 20 个应该"above the fold"的关键事实。

真正令人意外的地方在于：Parallel 的差异化，不是"消灭 slop"，而是把 SEO 页面对人类做的那种"预压缩"，改由 agent 在实时推理阶段完成。SEO 内容农场其实是"人类版的语义压缩层"，而 Parallel 是在做"agent 版的语义压缩层"。这两者本质上是同一个岗位，只是雇主换了。

二、跨领域连接：Shapley 值 × 二价拍卖 × 神经网络特征归因——一个统一的"贡献计价学"

Parag 提到 Shapley 值时，把三个看似毫无关系的领域悄悄缝合到了一起：

  • 合作博弈论（1953 年 Lloyd Shapley 用于分配联盟收益）
  • 广告拍卖机制设计（Vickrey 二价拍卖，激励真实出价）
  • 机器学习可解释性（SHAP 值做特征重要性归因）

这三者其实是同一个数学骨架在不同物理层的投影。Parag 真正在做的事情，是把"神经网络里如何决定一个特征贡献了多少"这套方法论，搬到了"互联网内容生态里如何决定一个网页贡献了多少美元"的分配问题上。

惊人的推论：如果这套体系成立，网页会从"内容资产"变成"神经网络的特征通道"——网页的价值不再由 PageRank（连接拓扑）决定，而是由边际替代成本（去掉它，agent 需要多花多少 compute 才能达到同等质量）决定。这是从 Google 时代的"关系图价值论"到 AI 时代的"消融实验价值论"的哲学跃迁。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：Parallel 在赌一个"倒转的康威定律"

传统康威定律说：软件架构会复制组织架构。但 Parag 描述的第三阶段——"web 从 pull 转向 push"——暗含一个更深的反转：未来组织的架构，会复制 agent 的调度架构。

注意他那句几乎被一带而过的话："如果今天能做的事、还有 GPU 可用，就直接做了。那明天做什么？明天做由某个信号触发的响应式工作。"

这句话在预言一个静默的转折点："计划性工作"这个人类文明的核心组织形态正在消失。过去 200 年，MBA、甘特图、OKR、季度规划，全都建立在"资源稀缺 → 必须提前分配"的前提上。当 compute 变成边际零成本、agent 随时待命，"计划"就从必需品变成了摩擦成本。剩下的只有两类工作：立刻能做的（就做了）、被外部事件触发的（等信号）。

跨领域连接来了：这与生物学里的免疫系统结构惊人一致——B 细胞不做规划，它们只是海量并行地待机，等待抗原信号出现就克隆扩增。Parallel 想建的"web 变化 feed → 触发 agent 工作"，本质上是在给互联网装一套免疫系统式的响应架构。

而这也解释了为什么公司名从 Shapley 改成了 Parallel——不只是"并行计算"的意思，而是两个平行宇宙的分岔：一个是给人类惰性优化过的 web（SEO、autocomplete、above-the-fold），另一个是给 agent 完整性优化过的 web（authoritative source、结构化 excerpt、Shapley 计价）。而真正的洞察是：这两个 web 不会合并，它们会彼此喂养、共同进化——就像 DNA 的两条链。

📝 转录文本

开场：Parallel 的核心观点

Our view at Parallel is that human click data is a bug, and agent doing work with search should rely on agent feedback, not human feedback. We believe that these models are really good at compressing information, and we can benefit from a lot of the research that have gone into building models and apply it to search indexing and ranking.

And so you can now make many, many arguments — and that's the arguments we made back then — that actually now it's way more tractable as a problem because of the existence of agents, not just as in technology, but as a distinct customer.

主持人介绍

Sonia: Parag, thank you so much for joining us today. Uh, we're delighted to have you on the show. For those who don't know, Parag — of Twitter CEO fame — was CEO of Twitter um before selling it to Elon. Uh, and is now back on the founder arc.

Um, you founded a company called Parallel Web Systems, which is scaling up Agentic Search uh for the Agentic Web. Um, we're very excited to have you here today to talk about the future of search and the future of the internet.

So, let's get started. What's Parallel?

Parag: Thank you, Sonia, for having me. Thanks, Andrew, for joining us. I'm really excited about this conversation.

At Parallel, we're building uh a bunch of technology in order to allow agents to search and use the web. So just like humans forever have figured out how to use browsers and search engines and clicking and browsing around the web to access information, uh agents need to do the same things.

We started Parallel with the bet that agents would do it a thousand x more than humans ever have. And as a result, we need to reinvent the technology that can power search for agents, but also the business models that go alongside it. And that's what we're doing at Parallel.

从 Twitter 到 Parallel：需要遗忘的经验

Sonia: Okay, I want to go back into what makes human and agent search so different. But before we get there, you've told us that, you know, you're unlearning a lot of the lessons that you learned from running Twitter as you build Parallel. Why is that?

Parag: Listen, when I was at Twitter in leadership roles, Twitter was a post-product-market-fit, extraordinarily scaled business where your feedback loops were from the hundreds of millions of customers using the product for 30-plus minutes every day. Right?

In that world, you operate differently than a pre-product-market-fit company based on the premise that in a few years a new customer is going to show up on the internet, and let's go build technology for the not-yet-here customer that we are all learning every day and every week.

Sonia: Fantastic. Okay, let's talk about Parallel.

Andrew 登场

Andrew: I have a question actually. Can I jump in?

Sonia: No, no, you cannot, Andrew.

Andrew: I'm Andrew. I didn't get an introduction, but I'm also happy to be an inaugural guest on the Training Data podcast.

Sonia: Andrew is making his podcast debut on Training Data. We are honored to have you finally here.

Andrew: Thank you.

什么是网页搜索？先讲清楚基础问题

Um, I feel like all of us in Silicon Valley have a very surface-level idea of search. Like, what is search? Like, the job to be done is, you know, getting the answer — makes sense. But we all know there's crawling, and there's an index, and there's ranking. But maybe let's take a big step back and explain: what is the problem of web search, be it for a human or an agent? And then we can dive into the differences.

Parag: Um, the problem of web search — and we all know it and experience it. When we want to find something and we do not know where it is on the web, we go to a search engine like Google, and the search engine then hopefully surfaces the answer to us in the most convenient of locations. That's the base problem.

Now, in order to do this, what is the search engine doing? The search engine is going and crawling the web, which is finding every URL that's out there, trying to read it, trying to organize that information in what might be called an index. So that by having all of this stuff in memory in one location, you don't have to — once the query comes in, you don't have to spend time loading up pages because you already have them. You've already done pre-processing to organize them.

And then when the query does come in, you quickly understand the query. You find the most relevant results. And then there are many, many — because you're essentially taking hundreds of billions of pages and narrowing it down to what, five or ten, or ideally one, in terms of what someone is looking for right now. So you go through these multiple stages of retrieval and ranking in order to surface the most relevant result.

So that's the broad problem. One way to think about it is it's a billion-to-billion matching problem. Right? So you have hundreds of billions of pages and hundreds of billions of queries over time, and you need to figure out how to match-make across these two.

为什么一家初创公司敢挑战 Google 和 Bing 的地盘？

Andrew: That sounds like an enormously expensive infrastructure challenge. And I think for the longest time basically only Google and Bing had, you know, done full webscale crawls and indices. Why did you think about you, as a young company, could go off and tackle that problem? It seems like a problem of the giants.

Parag: So it is expensive in the long term. So what's actually interesting is that when I was starting the company three years ago, you could imagine a world where — one, some of the reasons it was difficult for others to compete which was not having access to great feedback in terms of "is this a better search result than this?"

To collect that feedback at scale, there was a problem around human ratings, there's a problem around click data — you need to access those. Now it is of course expensive to crawl the entire web and index it.

Uh but as you think about what agents and the large models that we now have access to have enabled: the ratings data can be now created by experts way more cheaply. Our view at Parallel is that human click data is a bug. An agent doing work with search should rely on agent feedback, not human feedback. We believe that these models are really good at compressing information, and we can benefit from a lot of the research that have gone into building models and apply it to search indexing and ranking.

And so you can now make many, many arguments — and that's the arguments we made back then — that actually now it's way more tractable as a problem because of the existence of agents, not just as in technology, but as a distinct customer.

And then we figured out a way to go about building this business which did not require us to go spend all of the money on infrastructure upfront before we could service a customer. Right? So if you can paint a path of incrementally being able to build an increasingly larger and more sophisticated index over time as you solve problems for more and more customers — that's the insight that actually convinced me that this was a viable problem for us to take on.

冷启动策略：先做 Search Agent，再做 Search Engine

Sonia: And how do you make that happen? Because I imagine this is one of those things where customers want full coverage day one. So how do you go about making that happen?

Parag: When we first launched the product, right, we did not launch a search product first. We launched a search agent product first.

Our search agent could go essentially crawl the web after a query arrived. So if you're doing deep research, you have patience to the extent of a minute. And we've had products which sometimes take — do — 10 minutes of research. That's a lot of time to be able to crawl a lot of pages, if only you have enough of a map to know what to prioritize crawling. Right?

So you can make up for shortcomings like index — oftentimes you can think of it as a latency optimization. So if you give up on that dimension, if you're competing with humans — that's why our search agents were competing with the alternative being outsourcing to humans to curate amazing data. Right?

So we said, it seems like humans sitting on search engines are far way easier to compete with than a search engine on day zero. So by building a product that was a search agent to do real work on top of web data, we were able to incrementally go build our index.

早期用户案例

Andrew: Were there some examples of what people built with your search agents?

Parag: In the very early days, there were search agents being built with us for doing some kinds of insurance underwriting workflows and claims processing workflows. People in uh sales were doing all kinds of sales data enrichment. People in finance uh who would previously and historically go to build a model, collect data by sending it overnight to a set of humans who would curate data that would feed into a modeling exercise they would do — would start using us to do that instead.

And so we were going initially after replacing where there was outsourced human work on top of web data, in order essentially to collect evals to run agents to figure out what search for agents should look like in the first place with empirical use cases instead of theoretical evals.

Andrew: I see — you're trading off the crawl for inference-time compute effectively.

Parallel 是 Neo-lab 吗？

Sonia: You guys were started before the term "Neo-lab" came into existence, and you have, you know, a "Web Systems" product, but you also have like a bunch of AI people. From the outside, before we met for the first time, like it wasn't obvious to me how much of a web systems company or an AI company that you've built. The more time we spent together, the more clear it's like — by some definitions this is a Neo-lab.

Do you want to talk about like where the research side of what you're doing comes in, not just the like infrastructure and system side of what you're doing?

Parag: So we don't categorize ourselves as a Neo-lab.

Sonia: Well, of course you would not.

Parag: Shapley values is this very theoretical mathematical concept. It is used — SHAP values — in feature importances for those who are ML folks here.

Let's say the three of us collaborate on something, and the whole is bigger than the sum of parts uh in that moment. The theoretical question is: okay, how do I divide up this sort of bigger pie that we created by collaboration, so all three of us have incentive to collaborate. Right?

Shapley 值的局限与工程近似

Now, that sounds amazing, right? Like, you could — if you're co-founders, you could figure out how to divide equity. Unfortunately, it's not that useful.

It's not that useful because in order to compute Shapley value, you need to simulate worlds where some subset of the two of us collaborated but the third one doesn't, and play out those realities to then impute back to today in terms of how we should divide the pie. Which in practice you can't do most places.

Right? In ML models, when you do feature importances, you kind of can — you can hold a feature back, run your model, and see how well it did.

In web search, we can run simulations of "if we did not have access to this URL or this domain or this collection of them, how would the agent perform?" We can — if you're good at evals, if you're good at assessing quality — you can build that data by running various scenarios, collect a bunch of this data, and then you can train models to —

Parag: When I incorporated — I'm telling you, I was obsessing about everything to do with the problem space. So while knowing that — first, "Shapley" is a terrible name for a B2B product — it was not going to be the long-term name.

So we incorporated as Shapley Inc. for lack of a better word, and Shapley.ai happened to be available. Shapley.com is a parked-porn domain. So it was not going to be a name. I went around not talking about my company as Shapley, and my badges at all events used to call it "NCO" or "stealth company."

So it took us almost 6-8 months to figure out what the real name of the company will be. We ended up at Parallel, in part because — like, one, at the time we're doing a lot more in parallel; and two, we started visualizing this sort of a parallel web built for AIs and how its properties are different, and this metaphor that when you publish, you're now thinking — as we all are now — of two audiences.

"Okay, I'm going to create a page. I know humans will read it. What should it look like to them? And then how should I make sure that agents can read it too?" So it feels like you're dual-publishing to two audiences. And so we had this like — this parallel web for agents will emerge. And so that's why we started liking "Parallel."

Sonia: Love it.

Agent 作为文档的主要读者

Andrew: I actually was thinking about this recently with the um, you know, things like earnings transcripts. Right? Like, I feel very confident that more people are consuming earnings transcripts through agents than are actually — certainly listening to the audio, and honestly probably even reading the transcript itself. So there are these like very high-value portions of the web that have flipped already to being agent-first, and obviously the communication has not yet flipped.

Um, but I think if I were a public company CEO today and I was doing an earnings report, I would make very clear that the thing that I'm saying will be transcribed and interpreted correctly by the agents, not just by the people listening. Theoretically.

Parag: Yeah. Same for us when we're publishing docs for our APIs. Like —

Andrew: Yeah.

Parag: It's like — our customers are building AI solutions. They are using AI to do it. It's their agents reading our docs and code in our SDKs. It's not humans fumbling around docs pages for the most part. So in fact, for us the primary audience is an agent, and that's how we test our docs.

Sonia: A parallel web for agents. It's very cool.

未来三阶段：从工具调用到 Web 主动推送

Um, maybe close us out. Just give us a snapshot of where Parallel is today, and if everything that you hope to build comes true, what does Parallel look like, what does the world look like, what's your role in it?

Parag: I think of three levels in this journey.

Level 1：Web 作为工具

Level one is: people are building simple agents that use the web more as like a tool — like a web search tool — because it's familiar, because the first set of agents we built, to your point, was just like model and give it the same tools. Because these models have been trained to use all the tools humans have been used to, and let them do work.

By and large, if you think of like most work — it's there today, of inference, it's there today.

Level 2：多智能体系统

We have now started seeing some subset of customers who are in this world where they're building more sophisticated multi-agent systems, which use sub-agents and have agents wake each other up or orchestrate uh in interesting ways.

Right? People are seeing that as sub-agents — most familiar one is sub-agents with coding agent harnesses — but we see a lot more of that. Like, if you're building an AI scientist, uh, some of those systems are very interesting, very sophisticated, very long-running, and like — just throw large amounts of compute and data at a really hard problem.

Level 3：Web 从 Pull 转向 Push

Uh, and I think the third layer for the web specifically is: the web goes from pull to push.

So today, by and large across the first two modalities I described, either an agent is calling a tool or a sub-agent, but it is telling it a request saying "go find this for me right now."

And I think where we will end up in a couple of years is: a variety of use cases will be the web — "Parallel, call me if this happens, so that my agent can do some work or a human can do some work."

So I use this line with my team all the time, which is like: imagine agents are everywhere and they can do a lot of things. Right? If there is something you can do today and it's worth doing, and we still have GPUs available, we'll just go do it. Right? Like, we won't be like "oh, let's just do this tomorrow for the sake of it." If it can be done today, do it.

So what will we do tomorrow? We will do tomorrow work in response to something that circles through — either another agent's work, or something changes in the world as visible in satellite imagery, or some customer commentary that happens, some agent finishing some compute, a human having a new insight — to trigger work.

But there are going to be a few feeds like this which will drive new agentic work tomorrow. And one of those feeds is going to be everything that changed on the web. Which is really exciting for me, because then you're framing not a point-in-time need — a long-term "here is what is actionable for me. If something like this happens, as evidenced by all of the information on the web that is changing all the time, call me." Right? And then I'll run my agent on it.

And so we get to then allocate compute onto the entire web all the time on behalf of all the customers, and that's really exciting.

结尾

Sonia: That's awesome. Really ambitious vision. You're clearly extremely passionate about this, and exciting to see you building. Thank you so much for joining us today, Parag. And thank you for joining us, Andrew.

Parag: You're very welcome, Sonia. Thanks.

Sonia: Thank you, Andrew, for your debut.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：Parag 正在把"惰性"重新定义为价值来源
大多数人把"人类的懒惰"视为产品设计要克服的障碍——自动补全、下拉推荐、SEO 摘要页，都是在补偿人类不愿多打三个字的懒。但 Parag 把这一层惰性**翻转成了商业洞见**：那些"预 AI slop"页面之所以存在，不是因为它们劣质，而是因为它们完成了一项被低估的信息劳动——**从 300 页的 10-K 中挑出了 20 个应该"above the fold"的关键事实**。
真正令人意外的地方在于：Parallel 的差异化，不是"消灭 slop"，而是**把 SEO 页面对人类做的那种"预压缩"，改由 agent 在实时推理阶段完成**。SEO 内容农场其实是"人类版的语义压缩层"，而 Parallel 是在做"agent 版的语义压缩层"。这两者本质上是同一个岗位，只是雇主换了。
## 二、跨领域连接：Shapley 值 × 二价拍卖 × 神经网络特征归因——一个统一的"贡献计价学"
Parag 提到 Shapley 值时，把三个看似毫无关系的领域悄悄缝合到了一起：
- **合作博弈论**（195

item.title: [Invest Like The Best] Ex-NVIDIA Engineer: Why AI Is About to Get 1000x Cheaper
item.dc:creator: Invest Like The Best
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的洞察：延迟的消失，不是通过加速，而是通过"提前"

大多数人以为"更便宜的 token"和"更快的响应"是同一场战争的两条战线。Neil 却做了一个近乎哲学性的切割——"最好的延迟就是没有延迟"。这不是工程口号，而是一次范式颠覆：

传统 GPU 优化的整个话语体系（NVLink、tensor parallelism、低延迟推理）都建立在一个隐含前提上——人在等。而 Neil 说：让人别等了。让机器在你睡觉时工作，让答案在你打开手机前就已生成。

这里藏着一个让人后背发凉的推论：当"等"消失，人类就不再是系统的瓶颈。你不再管理你的同事每 5 分钟一次，你一周检查一次。人类的"注意力带宽"从生产资料变成了产品的采样接口。整个 GPU 架构、数据中心设计、能源结构，都可以围绕"人不在场"重新推倒重建。

二、跨领域连接：Sal Research 其实是"电力系统 + 快递物流 + 边缘银行"的混合体

Neil 一次次强调"scavenger strategy"（拾荒者战略），但真正的隐喻不是拾荒——是电网调度加FedEx 分拨中心再叠加影子银行的资产错配：

  • 电网侧：他愿意接受 95% 甚至 80% 的数据中心可用性。这在传统 IT 是死刑判决，但在电力行业，这就是"可中断负荷"（interruptible load）的经典客户——用可靠性换电价。他把太阳能、风能这些电力公司的"垃圾电"（intermittent power）变成了自己的核心资产。
  • 物流侧：pipeline() 里那个"公交车 vs 私家车"的比喻不是随口说的。他做的其实是 UPS 的 hub-and-spoke 网络，只不过运的是 token。长距离的 async agent 就是集装箱船——不追求速度，追求单位成本。
  • 金融侧：这才是最微妙的。他在做期限错配套利——买 spot 市场的短期算力（波动大、便宜），卖长期稳定的 API 服务（可预测、溢价）。这跟一家投行的资金池管理没有本质区别。硅谷从没有一家"AI 公司"这样想过自己。

啊哈时刻：Sal Research 的护城河不在 CUDA，不在模型，而在它对"不确定性"的定价能力。谁能忍受最多的抖动、最多的中断、最多的"非标"，谁就能拿到别人拿不到的供给。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：Transformer 的"原罪"暴露了整个 AI 产业的错位

Neil 顺口说了一句可能是全场最重的话——"Transformer 的原罪，是把一个极度内存受限的层（attention），紧贴着一个极度计算受限的层（MLP）"。

这句话炸开来看：

我们目前所有的芯片竞赛——Cerebrus 拼 SRAM 带宽，Nvidia 堆 HBM 容量，Grock 押 SRAM 密度——本质上都是在为一个架构缺陷买单。一个统一的 chip 永远做不好两件相反的事，于是我们造出越来越贵、越来越异构的硬件来强行匹配一个 2017 年设计出来的软件结构。

跨领域看：这就像19 世纪铁路的轨距之争——一旦标准锁定，整个基础设施围绕它演化，即使更好的方案出现也难以切换。Transformer 就是 AI 的"轨距"。真正的百倍降本，很可能不来自 Neil 的所有软硬件优化，而来自架构层面的一次"废轨换轨"。

而这里最惊人的暗示是：Neil 在下一个双重赌注。表面上他赌的是"背景 agent 会取代聊天机器人"，深层他赌的是"Transformer 的架构错位会持续足够长的时间，让他建立起以异构硬件套利为核心的商业模式"。如果某个新架构（Mamba 类、diffusion LLM、或还没被命名的东西）真的把 attention 和 MLP 的失衡解决了——他所有的护城河都会同时贬值。

这就是这个行业最有意思的悖论：一个鼓吹"abundance"的人，商业上却在押注"scarcity 会以特定形式持续存在"。他不是要终结稀缺，他是要成为管理稀缺的那个人。

📝 转录文本

开场：让 token 尽可能便宜

Neil：My job is to make the tokens as cheap as humanly possible. I will achieve that and I will do it through every layer in the stack available to me. I love the supply side levers. I will use every chip. I'll use every source of power and I will use every piece of land in the United States that's, you know, suitable for this.

We still treat the agent as a person that is expensive to consult and you should ask them when you have a hard question. That's not the way to think about intelligence. It's incredible that the machine can think and we should try to get that into as many hands as as many people as possible.

一、Sal Research 是什么：一座 token 工厂

主持人：I think it's important early in these conversations to just say the thing — literally what you're building and what it does today. So maybe just orient us there with a brief description like literally what the system is that you're building and why it should exist.

Neil：Sal research is a token factory. We have an API where anyone can send us requests where they can use large language models, open source large language models for any task they want. We will serve those tokens to them at a price that is unbeatable in the market.

We also support their ability to build agents on top of this. We host what we call sandboxes, which are long-running agent virtual machines hosted in the cloud that are designed for agents that run for hours, days, or weeks.

主持人：So you should think about you as a peer company to others that serve different kinds of inference. You're serving one specific kind of inference and your goal is to be the absolute cheapest provider and enabler of a certain kind of use of intelligence.

Neil：Exactly. The theme of our company is abundance. We want to deliver this new commodity of intelligence to as many people as possible at a cost that is sustainable for almost every industry. We think that whenever you make something 10 times cheaper, it's a new product category, and we aspire to do that for tokens. We think it's so profound that the machine can think, and now our job is to make as many machines as possible in the world work towards thinking.

二、Token 成本还是最终单位吗？

主持人：So if you think about the theme of the day being token costs — is token cost the right way to think about this? Is there some other way you'd put it?

Neil：To start with, absolutely. Token cost today — my north star is I want to have the lowest cost per token in the industry and do that by a mile.

I don't think tokens are the final unit of work or intelligence, but they are what we use today, and so it's very straightforward. After tokens, you start to move more towards outcomes, which is a vague direction. You can imagine, for example, today when you consume tokens through an agent, you don't actually control how many tokens the agent reasons for. It can reason for a certain amount of time or it can call a certain number of tools.

Increasingly, I think we will have agents do some unit of work — take as many shots on goal as they can — and however many tokens they use to get there is going to be kind of a dependent variable depending on the task. So you think about agents that self-administer a token budget, as opposed to a company setting a budget for how many tokens engineers can spend per month.

三、机会窗口：开源与"长时程 agent"的兴起

主持人：Why is there an opportunity that you can tackle? It seems like the entire world is oriented around more/better/faster/cheaper tokens. What was the unique opening that you saw?

Neil：There's two things that are tailwinds for our company.

One is the rise of open source. I had to talk about that first. We are starting to see an increasing number of our customers and the broader market care about owning intelligence. They want to have control — sovereignty — over the thing that they depend on. That created a much more robust market for customized models or even just these vanilla open source models that no one can ever take away from you. You always have the weights. You always have the right to deploy them however you like.

In that world there's been a reasonably robust market for the past couple years serving these models at large scale. The challenge is all those companies — you could take your pick, Baseten, Fireworks, Together — they all focus on low latency inference, and they were pulled in that direction by one very important customer: Cursor.

I think that that was the right choice about a year ago, and as of six months ago, it started to look like maybe low latency wasn't the only thing you wanted from an agent. You wanted more persistence, more long-horizon tasks. And now, it's to me very obvious that the future of agentic inference is long-horizon tasks. You're going to run the machine for hours or days at a time. It doesn't matter if it spits out tokens at 100 tokens per second. Maybe 10 is just fine. That comes with corresponding advantages and efficiency.

四、"最好的延迟就是没有延迟"

主持人：Why are you so confident in that? To me it seems like I want everything as fast as possible.

Neil：When you're waiting on it, you absolutely deserve the fastest answer possible. My trick is I don't want you to be waiting on it. I want it to be proactive. I want it to be in the background.

One way to say it is: the best latency is no latency at all. When you wake up in the morning, the work's already been done overnight — you didn't even have to ask for it. That's the dream. We're not quite there yet.

But more importantly, the more you're in the loop as you prompt agents and wait for a response, in fact you're the bottleneck in having the agent do more or less work. What we'd like is the agent to operate on more human time scales. You don't manage your colleagues every 5 minutes. You ask them to do a high-level task and you come back and check in maybe every day, but more likely once a week. That to me is the future of human–agent collaboration: more like human time scales.

主持人：Say more about the early indications that this is happening and therefore you should be building this company.

Neil：The first and most important thing is the idea of test-time compute scaling — the idea that you can give an agent more time and it will give you a better answer. That was theorized about 2 years ago now, but it wasn't really something that we could actually bet on until, I would say, late last year with Opus 4.5. Opus 4.5 was the first agent that was at all suitable for longer-horizon tasks, and it was pretty mediocre when it first came out. But you look at the more recent models and what we've done on open source as well, and you see that agents are capable of running for an hour at a time. I wouldn't say it's days, but definitely an hour is quite suitable today.

Just seeing that average turn or task length get longer and longer — it doesn't take many points to draw out the exponential and see that agents are worth running for longer periods.

五、后台 agent 会吃掉多少市场？

主持人：What do you think will be the market share of long-running agents in 3 years or something like this?

Neil：I love this market because it's unbounded. There's no human in the loop. So you can consume as many tokens as you like in the background — versus human attention span. If you tell me to consume 10x as many tokens at Codex or at Claude Code, I'm actually not sure if I can anymore. I'm already in a loop and locked in coding for most of the day that I'm at the laptop.

What is unbounded is how many tokens can be consumed in the background or proactively. Long-term, I think we're going to end this year at maybe 50/50 background and real-time workloads, but I see this going to 90/10 in favor of background.

主持人：What are your favorite examples of something that gets accomplished much better as a background task than as a human-in-the-loop task?

Neil：Most deep research — most questions where you want to have a definitive answer over not 100 sources, not a thousand sources, but 10,000 sources or more. If you want to build an authoritative index of information — for example, one of our customers, Parallel Web Systems, seeks to do this. They want to build an index over the whole internet and monitor the internet in real time for changes. That is the kind of crazy exabyte-scale task that you need a very different scale of intelligence to achieve.

Deep research is a top category for us, and then increasingly we see cybersecurity following this direction. Yes, there's so much code you can generate, but there's exponentially more ways to break that same code than it is to generate that code. There are some great customers out there who are working very hard to find agents that can break any piece of software and proactively patch them.

When Fable first came out, or Mythos first came out, basically there was this push in the cybersecurity community to run Fable against every line of code we've ever written and look for bugs in 20 different ways — meaning you're looking for memory errors, business logic errors, network vulnerabilities, all these things. These are all things that you would write specialized agents for. You wouldn't just have Fable look at the source code once, you'd have it actually set up environments where you can pen-test these applications.

At some point, people started to make this joke that security has become proof of work. When you want secure software, it's really a question of how many dollars did you spend on Anthropic's APIs trying to break into your software. That is the best indication for how secure it is, because that's the best tool in the world.

Increasingly, we found that the frontier of intelligence here is quite jagged. It's not the case that Fable finds a superset of all bugs in software. You would find some bugs with a very small model that you don't find with the large model. You'd find some bugs with Haiku that you would find with Fable and vice versa. So it encouraged this very diverse approach to sampling and trying to build cybersecurity agents that break software autonomously such that you can patch them.

六、放飞想象：主动式智能与"任何可验证问题"

主持人：If you were to get speculative and imaginative about the sorts of things that long-running, very cheap agents can enable — new product categories that this sort of inference will unlock — dream a little bit about what that might enable.

Neil：For individual users, what I'm excited about most is this idea of proactive intelligent agents. You can imagine Siri that is running in the background all the time to understand all the emails you received in a day, all the text messages you receive in a day, and has a much more encyclopedic view of your life and how to be helpful in that life.

Right now there's still point solutions, and so you end up doing a lot of prompting. Siri is not very proactive. That's something we can fix with abundant inference. If you trust the machine enough that it's reliable and also trustworthy — as in private — you might even imagine the machine can understand how you interact with it and proactively surface your next action whenever you open your phone. Can we build a good model of what you're going to do next? My estimation is yes, we totally can. And the key to that is incredibly cheap intelligence. You have to be willing to spend tokens without any promise of return. That's the unlock.

The long-lens view to take on this is that we have a form of intelligence that can tackle any verifiable problem. Any verifiable problem means most software. It means a lot of formal math proofs and similar. And it could also mean scientific discovery. These are all relatively verifiable problems. And all those things currently have a dollar cost attached to them — essentially a hidden one. It's like: how many tokens could you possibly harness to make this work?

We have actually started to bring within view a dollar cost for these long-horizon tasks that is reasonable. It's not millions, it's thousands, and maybe it could be hundreds or even tens of dollars in the near future to have a definitive answer to any scientific question, to any research problem.

[广告插播：Ramp / WorkOS / Felix by Rogo]

主持人：And so if we dream about that future, we then become limited just by the questions that people can ask.

Neil：Pretty much the questions we can ask. The models are on the cusp of basically taking even a high-level question and chasing it down every possible follow-up — you can have the model essentially take that on its own. And the question is: what is your token budget? And we will solve the token budget problem.

主持人：What about non-verifiable tasks?

Neil：I put basically the entire category of human taste into that category. We have not solved human taste yet, and I don't know that it fundamentally can be. I'm excited to be surprised here, but we are focused on very quantitative problems. We leave the quality of writing, the beauty of art, to people.

七、软件层：追求"光速"的 Nvidia 精神

主持人：Now, let's talk about the very clever stack of solutions that you hope to build to have this giant token factory. I think you think about this in terms of software, hardware, and power. Talk through what your master plan is.

Neil：We always have to start with software. Where is the opportunity on today's chips with today's data centers to improve efficiency? The first thing we did was we tried to build the entire LLM software stack around peak GPU efficiency — meaning we're using Nvidia GPUs, we wanted to squeeze out more tokens from the same chip than anyone else in the world.

That starts with the lowest level of programming: kernels. It's actually my background. I spent my whole professional life working on GPUs and kernels. Nvidia was my first job while I was in college, and I got to see how the tensor cores got to earn their right to be on the chip. This is back in 2016.

主持人：Just describe what that means for the layperson.

Neil：Tensor core is a specialized unit on the GPU that accelerates matrix multiplication. Simple as that.

主持人：And why is matrix multiplication so important?

Neil：I cannot say that there is a divine truth of the universe that explains why matrix multiplies seem to be the atomic unit of computation. But one way I've heard it described to me is: well, it's a really succinct way to mix two blocks of numbers together and have them interact in some interesting way. It is really convenient that linear algebra turns out to be a very compact representation of arbitrary relationships in data.

Nvidia 的 tensor core 起源

Nvidia — great graphics company, obviously has had market share dominance in GPUs and gaming graphics for quite some time. Starting in the mid-2010s, they started these skunkworks projects to make the graphics processor more suitable for machine learning tasks that they were tracking.

I remember reading some of the lab notebooks of some of my managers when I was at Nvidia. They would visit these small ML conferences like ICML or NeurIPS at the time and they would just take note of these papers: "Oh, this deep learning thing seems to be catching on, and what's really interesting is that these grad students are using gaming Nvidia GPUs in order to train their large models. We should double click on this and figure out what's going on here."

By 2015–2016, at least Jensen had the conviction to double down on: "Hey, this usage of our chips is only going to grow. Let's start allocating more and more precious silicon die area to this capability that seems to be emerging. Let's put the first version of tensor cores on the chip."

So we're talking about taking this gaming chip which is designed for painting pixels on a screen and adapting it to do matrix multiplies. It was early, and you would be competing against the graphics teams essentially when you ask for more silicon area. In any chip company, there's always competition for that. It is something that the designers guard so carefully — you don't ever want to invest in the wrong technology because that's opportunity cost.

We fought tooth and nail and got just a tiny bit of die area — maybe like 5–10% — for the first generation of these chips to get some amount of acceleration for basic convolutions, which were the fundamental operation for computer vision models in the day.

Then we had a software team that was trying to squeeze all the performance we could out of the chip. On that software team — which is where I worked — that's what actually taught me the most about the ethos that Nvidia has around what they call "speed of light". They always chase the speed of light for any piece of hardware that they make. It is so ingrained in every engineer's mind that if the machine can do it, we're going to push the machine to the frontier until it does what we think it can do.

主持人：And the speed of light is the edge of what's possible.

Neil：Exactly. If we think the chip can run at this frequency and produce this many multiplies per cycle, we're going to get there. We're going to break every bottleneck and get to that peak level of performance. To this day, I tell all my engineers: we're chasing 100% speed of light. I don't care about relative numbers versus the competition. I only care about absolute numbers.

八、Nvidia 文化：吝啬到连牛奶都要 AA

主持人：Before we leave that chapter of your time at Nvidia, anything else beyond that cultural touch point that really changed the way you think about things?

Neil：I have a ton of stories about Nvidia. One of my favorites is that on the tenure side, a lot of people I worked with in Nvidia in 2015–2016 are still there today. That company has incredible retention, and these are the best engineers, frankly on the silicon side at least, I've worked with in my whole career. They're extremely motivated and passionate. They've believed in parallel computing as a concept through its various incarnations and have loved seeing the chip evolve. This is their life's work.

They're also a very frugal company. Nvidia and all the Silicon Valley companies after 2008 had some cutbacks in perks — so, no free lunch. Nvidia took it one step further. There was no free milk in the fridge. So if you wanted to drink coffee at Nvidia and you wanted some milk, you actually had to chip in a dollar every month to the "milk club," and the milk club would stock Costco milk in the fridge. I remember that distinctly. We don't do that at Sal, but it's a frugality that permeates the company.

九、吞吐 vs 延迟：GPU 世界的根本取舍

主持人：So coming out of that time, you get this experience of what it's like to develop more efficient usage of the underlying hardware through software. Link that to today's environment.

Neil：The GPU is fundamentally a throughput machine. The GPU is happiest when you give it a lot of work to do and let it chew through that work at peak utilization of its compute units. But that's actually not the way that we've taken AI in the last couple years. We've really pushed AI to be an interactive chatbot tool — the most common form of AI usage today.

In that world, you care a lot about spitting answers out to the person at the keyboard as quickly as possible. It's very difficult to put the GPU in its happy path of being fully compute-utilized when you're trying to spit out tokens quickly. There's a fundamental trade-off on the GPU between being throughput-oriented or latency-optimized, and everyone has chosen latency optimization because the shape of usage was chatbot-oriented.

I believe that's the most profound change we're going to see in the next year. We're going to move away from chatbots to more proactive or background agents. And in that world, it makes a lot more sense to build a stack around throughput.

主持人：Can you explain technically why the trade-off between throughput and latency is unbreakable?

Neil：It's quite foundational in almost every system. There's always a trade-off between getting a small amount of data through the system as quickly as possible and leaving buffer room for that, or trying to run "narrow and fast" vs "wide and slow." That's a classic trade-off in all computer science.

For GPU specifically, there's one thing to focus on: the concept of batching. We want to group many users' work together into a batch that we can run all at once on the GPU. That's the parallel processing of the GPU. The thing is, you're doing net more work when you run a large batch of compute together. So you might be filling all the units, but every step along the way as you carry a batch of work through the GPU, there's more work to be done. Any individual token or user's request in that batch is going to spend a longer time on the GPU being carried with other people's traffic.

Maybe the way to say it is: if you want to get downtown in SF, you can take the bus or you can take a private car. The private car is going to have its own direct path — as the crow flies, or using exactly the roads that you want from point A to B. A bus has to serve many more people and it fundamentally has to do something that works for everyone. So it takes a slower path and it stops and waits for other people to get on and off. The bus versus car analogy is pretty accurate.

主持人：Step one for what you're trying to do is create the best possible bus on top of Nvidia GPUs.

Neil：That's exactly right. It means we explore things like different parallelism schemes. With Nvidia GPUs, one of the things that they've really innovated on is the NVLink interconnect between GPUs. The NVLink system is so good that if you have a large matrix multiply, you can actually cut that matrix multiply in half and shard it across two or more — up to eight — Nvidia GPUs and have them all work on pieces of that larger matrix multiply and reduce their results together at the end.

This is a great way to cut the minimum latency of an operation. Each GPU is now doing 1/8 as much work, therefore it can finish faster — but not eight times faster. It's sublinear scaling. You'll use eight times more hardware, but you'll get maybe 4–5× the speed, not 8×. This is because of communication overhead, and because every GPU is a little bit less efficient working on a smaller tile of work than a larger tile.

It's the only way to speed up if you want the minimum latency possible. But it is not the choice I would make. I would prefer to use a different parallelism scheme — expert parallelism or pipeline parallelism — and we may do interesting things to overlap and hide the communication latency in a way that you would have less ability to do for a low-latency server.

主持人：So is the right way to think about NVLink as a technology which improves latency performance?

Neil：Yes, and only latency performance. NVLink is mandatory, I would say, for low-latency inference. So Nvidia is excellent at low-latency inference. And I'm telling you that we don't really care that much about low-latency inference. So where does that leave us?

I'm not holding my breath for other companies broadly to figure out NVLink quickly. It's a challenging technology to figure out. It's hard to scale, hard to productionize. So if I have some other vendor's chip and it is good at the foundational compute components — it can still do matrix multiplies really well, it just can't communicate those results across its peers quickly — well, maybe there's room for that other chip in my stack as a really good compute-per-dollar option.

That's what I actually optimize for in most cases: how many flops does this chip have, and how much is it going to cost me per hour to own and operate. There are other chips that definitely rank higher than Nvidia on flops per dollar, but they may not have as much interconnect. So it's my job to figure out what parallelism scheme I'm going to use that's going to make this chip suitable for inference. It's not going to be tensor parallelism — Nvidia is basically mandatory for that. But other techniques may work well for me.

十、Cerebras、Groq 与"SRAM vs DRAM"的物理学
