## 二、Khabib无意间透露了一个被现代人系统性遗忘的哲学：**肉体的痛苦是治理能力的先决条件**
注意他说了一句极其古怪的话——"2000年前，这样的人可以轻易统治整座城市"。这句话乍听是即兴发挥，但其实是整段访谈里最锋利的一刀。
他在暗示：**古代精英选拔的底层逻辑是"通过身体苦难验证决策资格"**——罗马将军、蒙古大汗、日本武士、斯巴达执政

item.title: [Latent Space] Simulating Humanity: from Generative Agents to 8 Billion Digital Twins — Joon Sung Park, Simile AI
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"逆莫拉维克悖论"：为什么"变笨"比"变聪明"难得多

June 反复强调一个反直觉的技术定位——Simile 的模型必须"as dumb as I am"（和我一样蠢）。这是一个几乎被整个 AI 行业遗漏的洞察：前沿模型（GPT、Claude）是在 Mercor 之类平台上用职业程序员、科学家的顶级推理数据训练出来的"超理性机器"，它们越强，越无法模拟一个真实的人在星期二晚上点披萨时的懒惰、偏见和情绪化。

这其实是莫拉维克悖论的镜像版：机器人做不了三岁小孩的动作，同理，超理性 LLM 也无法犯正常人那种"明知会后悔却还是点了甜筒"的错误。整个行业都在往"更聪明"的方向 scale，而 Simile 在悄悄地朝反方向做 scaling law——这是当前 AI 版图里唯一朝"人类愚蠢"方向扩张的严肃项目。

二、隐藏的产业依赖链：所有"个人助理"公司都在暗中押注 Simile 成功

June 提到那个"第二名"的时间机器候选——个性化 agent。他随口一句话透露了一个巨大的战略判断：没有精确的人类模型，就不可能有真正的个人助理。凤梨披萨的例子看似小，但推论惊人——ChatGPT Memory、Claude 的 markdown 用户文件、所有 AI wearable、每一个"AI copilot"，本质上都在用穷人版的行为建模来临时对付这个问题。

跨领域连接：这就像 1960 年代操作系统对编译器的依赖——你以为你在造应用，其实你在等一个更底层的抽象成熟。如果 Simile 的"行为基础模型"真的做出来了，它会变成一个所有 consumer AI 都必须付费调用的"人类物理引擎"，就像 GPU 之于图形、Stripe 之于支付。这是一个还没被 VC 定价的、隐藏的 platform layer。

三、社会科学的复现危机，意外地为 AI 造出了完美语料库

最让人拍案的伏笔藏在 OSF（Open Science Foundation）那一段。社会科学界过去十年因为 p-hacking 陷入"复现危机"，逼出了"预注册研究"制度——研究者必须在做实验之前公开假设。这个为了拯救科学严谨性的补丁，居然无意中为 AI 造出了地球上最干净的"因果机制"训练集：数万个高质量 RCT，带假设、带干预、带反事实。

这里的跨领域讽刺极其精彩：社会科学的失败催生了 AI 的解药。它类比于中世纪炼金术士为化学准备了纯度极高的试剂——他们本意不是这个，但历史选择了这份副产品。

四、painter/fractal 隐喻背后的深层世界观

June 的画家背景不是简历彩蛋，而是他整个技术哲学的密码。他说"最好的画从不完美，它只突出关键本质"——这解释了为什么 Simile 不追求预测未来（那是股票模型的活），而追求揭示走向未来的每一步。这正是 Asimov《基业》中心理史学的核心：不是"帝国会崩溃"，而是"把科学家流放到 Terminus"这种反直觉的具体步骤。

跨领域的意外连接：Schelling 1971 年那个红点蓝点的隔离模型，其实就是最早的 Generative Agents 论文——两者相隔 52 年，用同一个方法（简单规则 + 涌现）研究同一个东西（人类群体行为），只是从"红点"升级到了"有 markdown 记忆的 LLM"。而 Schelling 靠这个拿了诺奖。June 在悄悄告诉你他要什么。

五、被低估的观察：Facebook > LinkedIn 的数据学

被问到"如果只能拿一个平台数据"时他选 Facebook——不是 Twitter，不是 LinkedIn。理由是"人在 LinkedIn 戴着职业面具、在 Twitter 演一个人设、只有 Facebook 是 default state"。这直接对应社会学家 Goffman 的戏剧论自我呈现理论：数据的价值和"表演成分"成反比。

这句话对整个 AI 数据行业是个重击：Reddit、X、GitHub 这些被高价采购的"高质量语料"其实是表演性最强的，而真正有价值的"基态人类"数据反而被 Meta 独占且从未真正对齐外部。下一个真正的 data moat 也许不在文本质量，而在"表演系数最低"的语料上。

📝 转录文本

开场：8 billion digital twins 的愿景

Joon: Can we create a simulation of 8 billion people living on earth? I think that's quite interesting and that really is the vision. And once you get to that kind of state, the kind of questions that you can help answer for the society also start to change. From my perspective, for me it's questions like: can we help solve climate change?

If you look at climate change as a problem space, this is what social scientists would often call the "wicked problems" problem — where you have many actors with competing incentives trying to make a very complex coordination decision. Can simulation help us solve that?

主持人开场白

Before we get into today's episode, I just have a small message for listeners. Thank you. We would not be able to bring you the AI engineering, science, and entertainment content that you so clearly want if you didn't choose to also click in and tune into our content.

We've been approached by sponsors on an almost daily basis. But fortunately, enough of you actually subscribe to us to keep all this sustainable without ads, and we want to keep it that way. But I just have one favor to ask all of you: the single most powerful, completely free thing you can do is to click that subscribe button. It's the only thing I'll ever ask of you. And it means absolutely everything to me and my team that works so hard to bring the Inspace to you each and every week. If you do it, I promise you we'll never stop working to make the show even better.

Now, let's get into it. Today, we have Joon in the podcast. Excited to kick this one off. Very exciting company.

个人成长故事：从韩国到画家再到研究者

Host: I want to kick off and ask you the question — talk us through the story of your life. How have you gotten here?

Joon: Yeah, for sure. Really excited to be here. A story of my life… So I was born in Korea, and I lived there for a good 11 years or so. Then my family moved to Boston when I was 11. My parents were doctors — they were basically going through their post-doctoral studies. My dad was a surgeon, so he was doing his sabbatical years actually at the Boston Children's Hospital.

So I grew up there, not too close to tech actually. I was very much like a music, artsy, painting kind of guy. I actually got into painting a little bit later in high school, but that's what I used to do. And then I grew up mostly in the East Coast after Korea. So I lived a good number of years in New Hampshire, and then I went to college in Pennsylvania.

I got into more of this tech scene in college. So I was originally trained to be an artist. I actually thought that would be my professional career. It wasn't a hobby — it was actually like "hey, let's make a living out of this." And then gradually I got really interested in this idea that the greatest artist often creates their own medium, and the best medium that we had available today was actually in computation. So I decided to go deeper into that. And one thing led to another, and obviously we can go deeper into this, but I decided that research was something that gradually I got interested in. And here I am.

Generative Agents 论文的诞生

Host: So there's obviously a lot that you packed into the research component. You had one of the best papers of 2023 — the generative agents paper commonly known as the Smallville paper. Feel free to call back to anything else that you mentioned, but most people would have heard of you from this. Do you have any statistics of how many people have read it? Arxiv gives you something, right?

Joon: Yeah, it's a good question. How many people have read it? I'm actually not sure. I know that we do keep track of the number of citations, which is going up quite fast, but the readership…

Host: Google Scholar has 72,000. It made a bigger hit — it was a pretty instrumental paper. It was one that got cited so many times. It is frequently when people ask "what is the best paper of the year, best paper you've read recently" — it's this one.

Host 2: I thought the memory component was pretty underrated — a very good early memory system. But yeah, one of the biggest papers.

Joon: Yeah, yeah. So maybe I can talk a little bit about how this particular paper came together.

When I got into research it was back in 2020 when I started my PhD program at Stanford. That was the year we were about to get GPT-3.5, GPT-3 to be available. So we already had GPT-2, and you could sense that there's this new class of models that was just becoming available in the market. The team got very intrigued, and the general consensus was: well, is this model actually going to be useful for anything? It's really strange that these models are not trained to do any particular task. But we decided to take a bet.

So a large group of scholars at Stanford — and it was actually led by one of my co-founders Percy Liang — came together…

Host: …who coined "foundation models."

Joon: …who coined the term foundation model. We wrote this paper called "Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models," and during that process, the thing that I started to think deeply about was: here is a model that is fundamentally new in our ecosystem. The reason why this was new was — again — it wasn't trained to do anything in particular. Its premise was it could do anything and everything. It was like a stem cell, if you were to take a biology analogy.

I got really interested in this idea that: if we were to really think about what the killer applications of this particular technology would be, what would that be? Many of my colleagues were using this for simpler classification, simple generation. Interesting that these models can do that, but from an interaction perspective, not that interesting. We've known how to do that for many decades.

What we came down to was: these models are actually trained on this very broad data from the web — these are human behavioral data. It's social media, Wikipedia, all these kinds of data. So if you poke at the right angle, you could see human behavior that would just pop out — that's actually quite realistic. And we've never seen that before.

The "Time Machine" 思想实验

So that got us really interested. The exercise that we decided to do — this is something that we, this particular group of colleagues that I have, myself, Michael Bernstein, Percy Liang, who ended up becoming my co-founder at Simile — we sat down and we played this game that we call the "time machine game." Imagine we were to get on a time machine and fast-forward 10 years and look back: what would have been the single application that would have mattered, that would be the most interesting and inspiring?

Well, we thought: what if we can just recreate the world that we live in? I mean, it's really hard to get more ambitious than that. Like, let's just create a world. And that's where we started. Initially we had this paper that was a precursor to the generative agents paper called Social Simulacra.

Host: Before you go further — were there other candidates for the most ambitious thing in the time machine exercise? What was number two or number three, if you remember?

Joon: Okay. So there is a close second that we were considering, which basically ended up becoming more of these automation tools — but especially the vision around really personalized agents that actually do things for you.

Host: That's also happening.

Joon: It's also happening. But it was sort of interesting for us, in that the reason why we decided to go with the idea of simulation… one, I was a huge science fiction nerd, and this idea of creating simulation, I was personally really just fascinated. I love the idea. It's really cool to see a game town like this and just see these agents live in it.

But at the same time, my bet was: if you were to create a really amazing personal assistant out of this technology, what you actually need first is an amazing model of your users. For instance, I told the model "hey, can you go buy late dinner for me," and it orders Hawaiian pizza, and I do not like pineapples on my pizza — then it totally failed. The way for it to not make that mistake is only by having a deep understanding of who I am. I gave a very simple and dumb example here, but you can imagine how this core understanding of people is instrumental.

This is how, for instance, if we have our family, closest friend, they have a good mental model of who we are — that's the basis of our social connection. So our bet also was: this technology around simulation, creating accurate representation of people, ought to precede the more complex agents that would automate the world that we live in. So that was the bet.

That was a very close second, and I'm still very much fascinated by it. I think there's a lot of interesting work going around. My hot take actually here though is: I don't think we've actually seen a true personal assistant that's actually useful in ways that meet the ambition of that particular line of work. I think there are early applications that are obviously interesting, and if you talk to even ChatGPT nowadays or Claude, they obviously know a lot about us. So a lot of the generation it's doing, I do think it's much more tailored. But I think the ambition is quite large in that field, and I don't think we quite have all the right ingredients just yet.

个人助理的差距：从 markdown 到真正的人类模型

Host: So OpenAI, Claude — all these clients, personal agents — what do you want to see from them that they don't currently have?

Joon: I do think it's slowly getting there, but I generally want them to have a much deeper understanding of the person. Right now you look at the models — OpenAI, Claude — what it's basically leveraging is basically a markdown file. And I think it's quite clever.

If you look at the generative agents paper, this actually was the same intuition that we had. Initially, when we were creating the memory architecture for the generative agents — this is like back in 2022, so we didn't really quite have the idea of agentive architecture or the term "agent" — but the intuition that we shared with some of the work that's coming out today was: we initially thought, well, do we want to make the memory into let's say a knowledge graph? Do we want to train a bespoke model? All these kinds of things.

And what we decided to do was: no, no, just forget about all this. These language models are actually quite good at modeling text and understanding and reasoning about text. So just put everything in a markdown file or text file. You're done. I thought that was quite interesting that we could do that, and there's a lot of strength in doing that.

But also there is limitation. It's the way you retrieve and make sense of data that's extremely large — it takes a lot of work. So I think that technology is getting better. I also do however think there are certain things you just cannot shape just by prompting the model. So to some degree you do need to touch the parameters of the model itself. There are these kinds of work that I do think do need to happen, and obviously it is happening. The question is how far can we take it, how do we source data, and how do you also create an ecosystem where the people are continuously feeding data to this model so it's learning about them.

何时需要训练模型 vs 提示模型

Host: What's the intuition between why you need to do it in the model?

Joon: My intuition behind when do you train or even post-train a model versus just prompt a model is: if the model has to learn the underlying physics of the world that it's operating in — so it has to learn new social physics. The places where it doesn't have to train: it already has the physics. We trust the physics. It already has the base statistics, but it's just trying to react to an environment. Then I think you can just prompt your way into getting the actions out of it.

I don't think the model has yet — at least the models that are out in the open have yet — learned the complete mapping of social physics of humanity. And this actually is one of the core theses of Simile. One of the core reasons why that is the case is: if you look at the data that the model was trained on, these models were trained on the web data — whatever was available on the web. These are really interesting datasets, but they are fundamentally the self-exposed attitudinal data, with some behavioral data sprinkled around here and there. And it has yet to learn really deep behavioral nature of people — not just what people say they do online, but what they actually do in real life.

This is actually what I would consider to be the "dark knowledge" of humanity that we haven't quite captured. And it's these kinds of data that would also need to get factored into the model creation.

三类数据：Interview / Observational / RCT

Host: You call it "behavior foundation model." There's a good one-liner there, but outside of that — what type of data do you need? What are you changing on the model level? How do you go about actually building a behavior foundation model?

Joon: We think about data in three buckets.

Bucket 1 — Interview data. For instance, qualitative rich qualitative data is interesting. It's not behavioral, but we would literally ask people "hey, tell me the story of your life."

Host: Yeah, that's what we're doing here.

Joon: Exactly. The question that you all asked at the beginning of this interview literally is the question we also ask — and obviously we ask our participants to go a little bit deeper than how far I went. Maybe I can actually give more of my life story in lieu of this.

But the reason why that data is interesting is: by learning about this very long-tail information about people, you actually get a lot of texture around this model, like this person as a model. So even understanding their childhood memory or their trauma, their first love, these kinds of things — quite informative in ways that's really hard to predict. So that's one.

Bucket 2 — Observational behavioral data. These might actually be transaction data, or these might be data that you can get by scraping the web. You can imagine why these datasets would be interesting: they give you the base statistics of people's behavior.

Bucket 3 — Cause and mechanism data (the "why"). The last category of data — I personally think perhaps the most important — is the data that basically describes the cause and mechanism, the whys of people. Some of this is covered by the interview data, the qualitative, because people talk about why they made certain decisions. But really where you get to see the most behavioral aspect of this actually is in randomized control trials (RCTs).

Imagine you basically have the same setup but you have a few different variables that you're trying to tweak. Can you actually get realistic human behavior out of it? "Imagine you had this particular option. Imagine you're even trying to choose whether you're going to drink coffee or not. The day you drank coffee versus the day you didn't drink coffee — does your behavior change?" That's a dataset that describes a cause or mechanism.

This actually is quite important in modeling people. The reason why: oftentimes when people come to us — or not just to us but the reason why people are interested in simulation — actually isn't because they want to predict the future. If you're trying to win against the stock market, predicting the future is interesting. But most decision-makers, what they want to know is: how can we shape the future?

It doesn't really help you to hear that your sales is going to tank in two quarters. They're just going to say, "wow, that sucks." What they want to know is: what do we need to do now to avoid that future? That's cause–mechanism. And this is also very hard data to come by, because the world is our ground truth, but it happens once. So in a very controlled setup where everything is equal except for one variable, this kind of dataset almost rarely happens. So it's both hard to come by but also quite important if you're trying to model human behavior.

如何获取行为数据：虚拟实验室

Host: The behavior, I think, is the hardest dataset to acquire. What is out there, what is possible? Because — you're not going to know a lot of details about my life. I don't even have data for myself on… I want to analyze my own health or habits and I just don't log everything. So how can you have that data?

Joon: So we actually run a lot of randomized control trials.

Host: Yeah. But you put people in the lab, they watch them sleep or what?

Joon: We do actually care a lot about the consent process. So people know that we invite them to be a member of this community, to both share data and also have themselves represented in different forms. But we bring a lot of people to the lab, or virtual lab, where we design experiments that would actually pose them real behavioral decisions.

Often in these kinds of experimental setups, what makes the difference between what is attitudinal versus behavioral is: if the stake in your decision is real, that's ultimately what makes it behavioral. In these kinds of setups, we are inspired by our colleagues in social sciences, psychology and so forth. When they run studies, the kinds of techniques they utilize — imagine there's an online store that you're inviting people to come by, and whatever they purchase in this experiment, they actually get that item delivered. These are the kinds of things that make the stakes real.

So we run a lot of these experiments, and we also partner with firms. Right now we also have customers who are quite excited to at least give us a glimpse of the kinds of behaviors that their users exhibit, so we can get a little bit deeper understanding of how people behave in these different platforms.

客户是谁 & 使用流程

Host: I think on the customer side, they have a lot of data about their users — who has bought, the action data. Can you walk us through an example of what does someone come to you for? What questions would they want solved? Do you customize a model for them? Do you have something off the shelf?

Joon: Today, when people leverage our models, it's often to better understand the population of their interest. So usually the start of the relationship: we basically come together and hear about what population they want us to model. If you're a CPG company that's selling to all of the US, it might be fairly straightforward — you want to model the gen pop of the US. But at the same time, if there's a vertical or a market that they're trying to go into — imagine they want to better understand, let's say, people in their 20s and 30s living in California — that's a much more specific population.

So we hear about this population, we go recruit these people with consent and with incentives, we basically collect some of their data and create a model of these people. And then what our product allows you to do is basically query them.

It can take as input a filter — a description of the population you want to talk to — and an environment. Environment can literally be a survey question, behavioral experiments, A/B testing. Oftentimes the core use cases are things like concept testing to start with. But also people sometimes want to do focus groups, or one of the sort of fun use cases we also serve is even modeling things like the earnings call for public companies. So these are the use cases we often start with.

Host: Concept testing — is that an established term? I've never heard of it.

Joon: Yeah. It basically has to do with… they have let's say different messaging, different products, different ideas.

Host: It's like a marketing exercise. Got it. Politics?

Joon: We do have a strategic partnership with Gallup, and of course Gallup is deep in policy space. Right now we have not worked deeply with politics like that area just yet.

Host: I'm curious if there is demand.

Joon: I think there's certainly demand. But we are very much mindful of how this technology gets adopted and the societal impact we'll end up having. I do see politics as an area where a company has to be particularly thoughtful about the way they operate and make impact. So this is where we also want to make sure that we form enough of a guardrail and perspective on how to leverage this technology before we go on to serve markets like politics.

The West Wing 例子 & 灵敏度问题

Host: I'll give people an example. One of my favorite shows is The West Wing. One of the key storylines: the president has multiple sclerosis, but they need to figure out how to disclose it. So they run a poll with a fake governor and ask people to respond on the poll, and they try to make decisions based on the results of that poll on how well they'll be received. I'm like, well, I think those kinds of counterfactual things — I would actually use a simulation for this if I could trust it.

Joon: For sure. In that show, how did it go?

Host: In that show, it basically was a foregone conclusion. They were like, "we know it's bad. We just don't know how bad." And then the poll came back — "it's really bad." And then they just did it anyway.

Joon: Part of it is: it's a show, right? So you're maximizing drama.

Host: How bad could it be? Oh, it's horrible. And to some extent I think that is part of the challenge of being a customer of yours — which is that if I roughly know what the effect is going to be, do I need you? What sensitivity of effect do I need in order to make a decision? For example, my approval rating is 50%, and this negative news item comes out and it drops to 30. If it drops to 20, if it drops to 40 — do I care? No. I know it drops. It's negative. So when do I care about simulations?

Joon: Well, so there are a couple of things.

One: every day, developers, designers, policymakers, marketers — they create assets, new products — and turns out many of the decisions in hindsight are sort of obvious. "Yes, of course this is bad." But we still run those studies because understanding the magnitude and understanding how acute something is is actually quite difficult. Even if we feel like "of course, this makes sense" — I mean, this is the reason why we make so many mistakes. Every time somebody goes online and says something that has huge backlash, you look at that and go "what an idiot." However, it's tough. That's one.

Simulation ≠ Prediction：Foundation series & psychohistory

There's also another aspect here, which is: this is the reason why simulation is actually different from prediction. In the ideal-case scenario, what simulation is trying to show is each step of the way — each step that we need to take to get to a certain outcome. In the most advanced simulations, sometimes the next step that we're suggesting might actually be quite counterintuitive.

The analogy I sometimes give — as I mentioned, I'm a huge fan of science fiction — I don't know how many of the audience members have read things like the Foundation series.

Host: We've mentioned psychohistory a number of times.

Joon: Okay, fantastic. I might actually be talking to the right crew. If you read the Foundation series, literally the first act is: there's a group of scientists who have found out that the Galactic Empire is going to collapse, and we're going to have 30,000 years of unrest. They basically run psychohistory, the simulator that tries to teach them: okay, how can we keep this unrest to a thousand years? And they plan this out. And the first step of that plan is to get the scientists who say "okay, this is coming" exiled into this random place in the galaxy.

Host: Terminus.

Joon: Exactly. And that's so counterintuitive. What a strange move — that you literally sent the group of scientists who was raising voice around the potential collapse of the Galactic Empire into nowhere. How is that the right first move? Well, it turns out in this particular simulation that actually was the move.

It's these kinds of things. The reason why these kinds of reasoning are possible is because you're showing the step function — each step that results in a particular outcome. So really what simulation allows you to do in its highest form is: you give it not a problem or question like "what would people answer to the survey" — that's not what we do. What we tell it is: "here is a goal that we have." In the context of Foundation: we want to keep the unrest to a thousand years. What is the path we need to take now to get to that particular future? That's what simulation allows you to do.

Translating that into a real market: imagine you're an automobile company, and you're about to release an EV, and you're trying to understand how do we market EV to make sure that our stock price goes up. But what if the answer comes down that — well, you can market your EV in XYZ way, but that might change people's perception around the cars that's not EV and actually make your overall sales go down? Not very intuitive. Especially if all you're trying to optimize is EV sales and that's the only thing you're tracking, then that might actually result in a completely wrong solution — or at least a different solution than what you would have expected, whether it's right or wrong.

Host: Yeah, that's the power of simulation.

For listeners, we covered a similar topic with ML Parin from Shopify where they are working on SimGym. I don't know if he ever talked to you about it. It's very similar — the goal is increase conversion, but the journey is very unusual. 如何验证 simulation 是 grounded 的？The 1000-agent paper

Host: You had a good quote at the start about this as well — it's not about people wanting to know the outcome. It's about how they can change it. But I want to take it back to: how do we know this is grounded? How do you run evals? How do you test that simulations come through?

Basically, if I was to do the same thing that you described with, say, your favorite LLM — Opus, GPT-5 — have some agent to map out these things, how different are the answers we would get if I give it the same goal, the same objective? You have some interesting stuff on your site that actually points to how you run evals. I think that's one of the big concerns that people have. They're like, "LLMs hallucinate — you're just hallucinating layer after layer."

Joon: The way we do this — and this is actually the paper we worked on after the generative agents paper — that really became, at least for Simile and also the field of simulation and synthetic panels, the foundation.

Host: Yeah, this is the paper "Generative Simulations of a Thousand People."

Joon: Here's what we've done for this paper. We actually brought a thousand people that's representatively sampled from the US to a virtual lab. What we basically did was: we spent two hours collecting fairly wide-ranging data. In this particular study, we focused a lot on this interview data, whose script was taken from a project called American Voices Project, and then we would also pair it with a lot of behavioral data and so forth — whatever we can collect within two hours.

Then we would actually send these people away for a couple of weeks, and during that time I would use this data to create their digital twins. And I would bring the human participants back after two weeks and have them complete a battery of surveys, experiments, behavior studies — the list includes things like behavior economic games, the Big Five personality test, General Social Survey. We would also run the randomized control trials that were published on PNAS. And we would have their digital twins predict how the source individuals would have acted in these studies and surveys.

This is where we basically could replicate people's behaviors and attitudes 85% as accurately as people would replicate their own. So that actually was the first paper that gave this validated result that we can actually model individuals in an accurate way.

Host: For listeners who are not seeing the YouTube — the headline figure is 85% accuracy, which is a big improvement over all the other methods that you showed.

前沿模型 vs Simile：为什么"太聪明"是问题

Joon: But the part that was actually particularly striking to us, especially as we improved this technology even further, was: the generative AI models like ChatGPT, Claude that's coming out — it does give you the right foundation, however what they do not consider is the true attitudinal and behavioral aspect of people, especially in the population that you care about.

What these models are really really good at today is: they're trying to basically become the super-rational objective machines. So you go get their data from places like Mercor Scale, you talk to professional programmers, scientists, to create models that's amazing at reasoning. That's what they do.

Simile actually doesn't care about any of this. The models we're talking about here — what we're trying to create are models that are as dumb as I am. If I make those mistakes, the model has to make the same kind of mistake.

Host: Oh, that's very hard.

Joon: That's very hard. You're solving Moravec's paradox.

Host: That's exactly it.

Joon: And this is actually a completely different kind of data and training objective. This is also where we actually see quite a bit of discrepancy in the performance in human behavior prediction between the frontier models and simulating being created in the space. In some cases the model performance of frontier models goes all the way down to 20–30%, especially if you go into that more niche population on topics that our customers would actually care about. On more gen-pop it might be around 50 to 60%. So it's not very robust — you wouldn't want to make your decision off of these kinds of findings. If you can bring that up to 85%, that is ultimately what people end up getting very excited about.

The OSF Paper：用 RCT 后训练模型

Host: Do we want to keep going on the paper route?

Joon: Yeah, for sure. So the last one was sort of an interesting one. This paper was the follow-up paper to the thousand agents paper, where the idea was: now can we augment the models even further and actually post-train a model based on a lot of randomized control trials?

The data is always the most interesting part of modeling in many ways. The data we got here — there's this platform called Open Science Foundation. Some of the audience might be familiar with this. Especially in the social sciences over the past 5 years or so, there has been this concern around replicability of studies. It's a bit of a crisis the scientists acknowledged: where we rerun the study and we don't actually see the same finding. It's tough.

The reason why that was often the case: there's basically the survival bias, where the papers that get published often need to maintain what we call the p-value of less than 0.05 in the experiments that we ran. That basically suggests that there's only 5% chance that the results we saw is a false positive. But the tricky part was: all the papers that were not published — and there's still a 5% chance that whatever we publish is actually totally just randomly generated. There's 5% chance that "hey, this effect is not real, but it just happened to be real because of the sampling bias."

Because of that, what scientists started to do was pre-register their studies. Before running an experiment, they would go to this platform and say "here is the data, here is the population we're collecting, and here's the hypothesis" — and they would just say "here is our hypothesis, this is what we believe" — and you cannot retroactively change those hypotheses. This is what actually gives us more scientific statistical confidence that whatever effect you ended up seeing is actually true.

So that ended up creating this really interesting platform where there's one platform that now contains tens of thousands of real-world experiments and hypotheses, and a lot of these are actually really high quality, professionally designed behavior studies and randomized control trials. So we actually got the data and the studies from this platform and basically used that to make a point. Obviously this particular model is not something we're serving commercially because this was a part of the open science. But this particular dataset helped us make a point: by collecting a lot of these well-designed randomized control trials, we can make significant improvement in a model's capability to predict human behaviors. So that's what this paper was about.

个体级 vs 群体级建模

Joon: So this particular model actually was trained… the data we actually had at the level of individuals, but this particular model actually was trained… we experimented with both. And this is actually what we end up doing at Simile: we always train two distinct models. One is what we call the population-level model. The other is what we call the individual-level model. Both actually take very similar input, which is the description of a sub-population or individual and a stimuli.

In this particular work, we've done the same here. The results we are reporting are much more geared towards individuals because we do actually think that is the harder task in many ways.

模型没抓到的"人味儿"：走路上班

Joon: It's less "what can we solve" and more about what biases or mistakes do people make that models miss.

For instance — when I was at Stanford I lived in Palo Alto, so it's about, I would say, a 40-minute walk from the campus. You ask the model "okay, let's go home, what can I do?" So that actually I think is fundamentally what we're trying to model — what is fundamentally human might not be the most efficient thing to do, might not be the "right" thing to do, but things that make us who we are.

Simulation 的 scaling laws & 终极愿景：8 billion people

Host: I want to talk about scaling simulations. So what can't we simulate? What can we simulate? And how does scaling affect this? How big are the models? What if we go from an 8B, to a couple hundred million, to 100 billion parameters, to trillion? Do we get any interesting emergence at a certain scale? Any learnings from that?

Joon: What we are seeing is: at Simile, we do post-train our own model. The thing that we're actually seeing is the early glimpse of scaling law in simulations — the more data about humans and more compute you ingest, you actually start to get predictive and predictable gains of the model performance in simulating and predicting people.

Host: We need a scaling.

Joon: Whenever you find it, it's a beautiful thing. We're starting to see the glimpse of it, which is quite exciting.

But if you talk about the ambition of simulation as a whole, it's not merely about building a model. It's about building a model, then creating the agents that become the individuals in a much larger ecosystem. So you're basically creating this multi-agent simulation. Down the line you want these multi-agent simulations to also live in a very rich environment.

What we are really trying to get to at that point is: hey, can we actually — let's do the time machine game again — 5 years, 10 years into the future, can we create a simulation of 8 billion people living on Earth? I think that's quite interesting, and that really is the vision.

Once you get to that kind of state, the kind of questions that you can help answer for the society also start to change. From my perspective, the answers are fundamentally about emergence — the emerging behavior of society and large groups of people. So for instance, the kind of questions that I get excited by — maybe this is a bit… I have my academic side of me — for me it's questions like: can we help solve climate change?

If you look at climate change as a problem space, this is what social scientists would often call the "wicked problems" problem, where you have many actors with competing incentives trying to make a very complex coordination decision — very difficult to really solve in real life, which is also the reason why we couldn't solve it. Can simulation help us solve that?

Another one is: can we actually understand the signals for a collapsing democracy? Or can we uncover the origin story of the monetary system? These are societal questions that we never really had a good way of answering. If we can create simulations of our society, you have to believe that these are the kinds of problems that we can solve. So that's really the ambition of this field.

I also think — yes, I think there's a Nobel Prize to be won there, which wouldn't be surprising. And I think there's some amazing societal impact that we can have to help people make better decisions.

Host: Nobel Prize in economics.

Joon: In economics.

Thomas Schelling & 隔离模型：agent-based modeling 的原点

Joon: One of the scholars that I was deeply inspired by when I was coming into the space of simulation actually is the scholar named Thomas Schelling. Schelling Point.

The canonical example of the work that he's done was: he was one of the creators of agent-based modeling. This was like in the 1970s and '80s — very early days — but this was truly one of the first exemplars of simulations. And one of the canonical models from that time — of course many of these simulations are trying to tackle the societal problems most relevant for their era — was called the model of segregation. Racial segregation was a big topic that we cared about.

What they've done was they created this grid world where they had red dots and blue dots — and these dots, back in the day, they were the agents — and they had a simple rule that governed their behavior. If a certain percentage of your neighbors are of a different color, and if that goes above a certain threshold, then you move to a new location at random.

One of the striking findings of this agent-based model was: for the longest time people thought that segregation within society was caused by explicit and overt racism. But if you look at this model, people's preference towards living with people of the same color — that preference can be very minute, but the very small difference actually causes the society to segregate completely over time.

This was very counterintuitive for a lot of people. And this particular work ended up informing housing policies — mixed-income housing, for instance, got really inspired by this kind of work. And Thomas Schelling ends up winning the Nobel Prize for having laid the groundwork for very early versions of simulations.

The opportunity that I do see here in more scientific terms is: agent-based models for the longest time had impact in the 1980s, '90s, to some extent early 2000s, but it has now sort of gotten forgotten by the community a little bit. Because as you can imagine, red dots and blue dots is not really a rich description of people. But with the emergence of things like generative AI, and in particular generative agents, we do have an opportunity to create these kinds of agent-based models that are high-fidelity enough to help us make really complex decisions. And that's the opportunity that I see. If that naturally works, then yes — that is the kind of work that will result in a Nobel Prize.

Host: For what it's worth — I grew up in Singapore. 80% of Singapore is in public housing, and public housing has enforced racial quotas for exactly that reason. Which is really interesting.

成本、可复用性、面板规模

Host: Okay. So we talk about scaling, we talk about all these sort of agent possible applications. I'm scared about the cost. Let's just keep it to the US — not 8 billion people. But how much does it cost to model so many hundreds of millions of people?

Joon: Oftentimes today, obviously we don't start at that scale — this stage of the industry and simulation as technology — but we can actually get to our users extremely rich and meaningful insights even by modeling thousands, tens of thousands of people. Today what we do is: every week we are collecting data on the scale of tens of thousands of people with data, and we actually have panel partnerships that gets us to tens of millions of people globally. So that's what we do today.

Host: And just as a side note: once you've collected one person for one study, can you reuse that same person for all the subsequent studies?

Joon: That's exactly right. The beauty of this model and these agents is the fact that they are domain-agnostic. What you're really trying to understand is what is the fundamental nature of these people, what's their social physics.

Obviously there are a lot about people that does change over time — like even things like "how many times have you been to CVS in the past week" — obviously that will change. But there's so many traits about people that are also known to never change, like your risk tolerance doesn't really change over time. It's very consistent. So it's these kinds of things that we're trying to [capture].

The scale we are operating at is right now hundreds — or tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands — and in many of the core use cases that we are deployed in, this is more than enough population to cover those. Really at that point what you care about is less the number of people, but more: do you have the right sub-population of interest covered? This is also the reason why people want a larger sample — it's not because they actually want stronger statistical guarantees, it's more that: can they actually filter down to any population of their interest?

However, you can also imagine in 10 years, if we truly believe that compute is going to scale, that we'll have much more availability for compute, and our ambition for simulation is also going to scale accordingly. There's definitely a reason for us to create an entire data center worth of simulations. My hunch here is: I do think in the next some number of years, we will start creating simulations that will actually cost as much as training a foundation model. But perhaps it's going to be so valuable to the society that it would be a no-brainer.

I mean, right now even today, we are training a bunch of new foundation models just so we can say we trained one, and we spend tens of millions. But if we can create a simulation at the level of society that would actually solve climate change, I would run that today. I would raise the money right now just to run that.

In that way, ultimately what drives us is the impact.

Does the simulation we provide have a real impact in people's decision-making in ways that progress our society forward? If the answer is yes, then — I mean, that has to be great business. And we see that in numbers, and we do care deeply about that upside story. But that's the higher bit.

Part of your work — there's a very famous book called Working. I don't know if you've been referred to it before. It's very famous, to the point of having a Wikipedia page — about this kind of really in-depth understanding and interview of people about their lives, which seems mundane but is told in a very compelling way. 1970s as well.

Joon: Okay. It was an amazing decade.

十年展望：UBI 作为可仿真的社会问题

Host: Before the closing question — you said that you started with a similar question, right? If we do that now, 10 years down — what can we simulate? What would you simulate if you've made significant progress? Are there any questions outside of the ones that we brought up? Anything that you think is most impactful — any 10-year vision?

Joon: In many ways, as I mentioned, I am somebody who is very much impact-driven. So what would actually inspire me is: I would want to ask 10 years later, what would actually be the most important societal question that we as a society have to ask? I would love to tackle that. Like for instance — do we need UBI? That could be an interesting one.

Host: Ooh, has anyone done that?

Joon: Well, I mean, you know, we're thinking about it.

Host: Can I get access? OpenAI — this is like just trivia now — OpenAI, I think Sam Altman actually funded a study on this in Africa, and the answer was no.

Joon: The answer was no. But was it something about the implementation?

Host: Yeah. But this is the thing.

Joon: See, when Sam Altman funded this particular [study], he spent $14 million — quite a bit. But this is the thing. This is the reason why you want to run a simulation. You spend 5 years, $40 million on this one study and have one finding. But if you can run simulation many, many times instantly, then that's the value.

Host: I feel like that one you could have done in a simulation. If you can do the housing study, you can do the UBI one. I mean, come on.

Joon: I think sometimes people will spend the money because they want to verify what you think. Sometimes you just want to — is it actually right? Like, you got to test it.

收尾问题：我们是否活在 simulation 里？

Host: Okay, closing question: what are the chances we are in a simulation right now?

Joon: It's a fun question, and at some point I just answer "yeah, we're definitely in a simulation." But what I do feel however is: whether we are in a simulation or not — I don't think that makes our experience any less real. And I think that's fundamentally what I believe in. Maybe we live in a simulation, maybe not. But…

Host: It's real to us.

Joon: Yeah. For me, I don't really care.

Host: Yeah. Unless you die and you wake up in like the level higher.

Joon: That would be interesting.

Host: I feel like you wouldn't care. Once you die, then you find out you like—

Joon: I worry about it when I die.

Host: I think the other thing that I — okay, so I like the mathematical answer to this, which is: the sheer number of possibilities that you are in a simulation far outweigh the sheer number of possibilities that you're not.

Joon: Yes.

Host: Except for the simplest answer, which is: it is computationally very expensive to have you be a civilization. Okay, great — you've been very generous with your time. Congrats on all your success. I met you just after your Smallville paper and had no idea that you could build such an enormous company. And then now you're like "well, it's a hundred-billion-dollar market, but that's just where we're starting." So this is very exciting.

Joon: $100 billion market was not the TAM — that was only part. If you're thinking too small… I do believe that. My final note here might be — again, I love science fiction. You look at any advanced civilization in science fictions: there's two twin-pillar technology. One's AGI in some form, and the other is simulation. So I think the market's pretty big here.

公司介绍 & 招聘

Host: Tell us about the company. You guys just raised a lot. You're half a research lab, half a company. I guess you're hiring. Where are you based?

Joon: Yeah, so we're based in Mission Rock — not too far away from where we are right now. So we're in SF. But we're also bi-coastal. So we have our team — I would say our headquarters is in SF, and we have a lot of our technical talent in SF, and we do have a smaller office that just opened up in New York.

We are as a company an interesting one, in that today obviously there are AI neo-labs, and then there are AI product companies. Simile truly is both. This is a company that was founded by four co-founders: myself, Michael Bernstein, Percy Liang, Ellen. Michael, Percy and I are all researchers. Of course, Michael was one of the co-authors of the ImageNet — kickstarter of the AI revolution back in 2013 — has been instrumental in human-centered AI. Percy coined the term "foundation model" and obviously is one of the greats of the AI researchers today. And Ellen is my business counterpart, where she lands all the fastest-growing AI-native companies from her C to AMV.

But we have this DNA at the company where the vision of the technology that we're creating is continuously developing — where we are getting people who were basically my labmates. We are right now about 60 or so people, 15%, almost 20% of the company population actually are just my labmates from my previous lab. And it's actually quite fun because many of them then had gone on to OpenAI, Google Gemini and these places. And so it's been a few years since we really got together and had a chance to work together, but now they're coming back and really building out this vision that I find to be quite exciting. And that excitement is shared.

So there is that motion at Simile where we are a group of researchers trying to do something that no one is working on that we find to be the most impactful potentially. But at the same time, this is again technology that can make impact today. So we have an amazing group of engineers, product people and designers who are sitting here with us, basically trying to imagine what does it look like to help people understand what simulation can do, and make real world decisions with this — having both, and then deploying it to some of the largest customers in the world today. It feels quite unique.

Host: Yeah, it's very compelling. One part of it was this is the call to action — like, who are you hiring? You've done part of it, which is you've got a very talented group. Who are you hiring? What roles?

Joon: So honestly at this point we are hiring a small section. We are always excited to bring on amazing research talent — so if you're interested in working with our labmates, we're always welcoming of amazing researchers. But also we hire amazing engineers, and some of whom I respect the most. Many of them actually come from places where we have personal connections with. Many of the members are from Figma, Notion, Harvey and so forth. But also more broadly from the companies that we as a team heavily admired. So engineers both on the product side, infra side — we're all looking for those hires.

Host: Well, lots of people I think you make a really good case. So thanks, and we'll see you in the simulation.

Joon: Amazing. See you all there.

## 一、被忽视的"逆莫拉维克悖论"：为什么"变笨"比"变聪明"难得多
June 反复强调一个反直觉的技术定位——Simile 的模型必须"as dumb as I am"（和我一样蠢）。这是一个几乎被整个 AI 行业遗漏的洞察：前沿模型（GPT、Claude）是在 Mercor 之类平台上用职业程序员、科学家的顶级推理数据训练出来的"超理性机器"，它们越强，越无法模拟一个真实的人在星期二晚上点披萨时的懒惰、偏见和情绪化。
这其实是**莫拉维克悖论的镜像版**：机器人做不了三岁小孩的动作，同理，超理性 LLM 也无法犯正常人那种"明知会后悔却还是点了甜筒"的错误。整个行业都在往"更聪明"的方向 scale，而 Simile 在悄悄地朝反方向做 scaling law——**这是当前 AI 版图里唯一朝"人类愚蠢"方向扩张的严肃项目**。
## 二、隐藏的产业依赖链：所有"个人助理"公司都在暗中押注 Simile 成功
June 提到那个"第二名"的时间机器候选——个性化 agent。他随口一句话透露了一个巨大的战略判断：**没有精确的人类模型，就不可能有真正的个人助理**。凤梨

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on the meaning of life and the nature of good and evil | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最出人意料的观察：巴萨—皇马时刻是他整套神学的微缩镜像

对话结尾那段关于足球的闲聊，看似轻松插曲，实则是整场访谈中最精妙的结构性回响。

Khabib 说："没有巴萨，就没有皇马。"——这句话表面在谈足球，实际上完美复刻了他前面所讲的整套形而上学：

  • 七十年的现世 vs 永恒的来世
  • 好的一面 vs 坏的一面（"我们都有 the good side and the bad side"）
  • 手中的财富 vs 心中的财富
  • 信者与不信者

他的思维底层运行着一个"对立必要性原理"（Principle of Necessary Rivalry）——万物的意义都来自它的对立面。一个连球队都要用"没有对手就不成立"来理解的人，当然会用"没有审判日就没有真实道德"来理解人生。他不是在讲两件事，他是在讲同一件事的两个层次。这是一种极其一致的世界观，一致到连闲聊都在无意识地重复它。

二、跨领域连接：Khabib 无意中描述了"名人版的 LLM 幻觉"

他说了一句极其惊人的话："Sometimes people even start believing in a fake version of themselves."（有些人甚至开始相信自己虚构出来的那个版本。）

这不是道德警句，这是一个认知科学 + AI 对齐领域正在苦苦研究的问题：

  • 心理学称之为 self-narrative confabulation（自我叙事虚构）——人会把自己精心筛选后展示的形象反过来当作真实自我。
  • AI 领域称之为 model self-hallucination——大模型被大量关于自己的文本训练后，会生成关于"自己是谁"的错误陈述。
  • 名人在社交媒体只发精修照片，与 LLM 只输出高置信度回答，是同一种失真机制：输出被过度筛选 → 训练数据被污染 → 自我模型偏离真实。

Khabib 的解决方案（"try to stay on the honest path... to show my true self"）在技术语言里就叫保持训练数据与推理输出的分布一致。一个从未接触 AI 论文的摔跤手，用宗教语言精确描述了当代最前沿的对齐问题。

三、被忽视的翻转：他把"宗教约束权力"讲成了 AI 安全问题

启蒙运动以来的主流叙事是：宗教是对人性自由的束缚，去魅化让人类得以自我实现。

但 Khabib 悄悄做了一个逆向论证，而且逻辑严密到令人不安：

有钱 + 有名 + 有权 + 不相信有审判 = "like a nuclear bomb"

请注意这个论证的结构——它不是在说"没有信仰就会做坏事"。它说的是：当一个人的能力（power）远超其可被追责的机制（accountability）时，系统就会失稳。

这在其他领域早已被反复验证： - 公司治理：为什么需要 SEC、独立董事、审计——因为 CEO 的权力必须与外部追责匹配。 - 博弈论：无限次博弈中合作才可能，一次性博弈中背叛占优——"审判日"其实是把一次性博弈转化为无限次博弈的技术手段。 - AI 安全：一个能力极强但没有内在价值对齐的系统 = 灾难。这与 Khabib 的"核弹比喻"是同一个方程式。

换句话说，Khabib 提供的不是一个宗教劝勉，而是一个关于任何智能体（人类、企业、AI）能力—约束比失衡时的系统性风险模型。这大概是他自己都没意识到的深度。

一个额外的"啊哈"时刻

他反复用时间比例论证人生意义——70 年 vs 2000 年 vs 永恒。这个论证的结构在现代思想里有一个惊人的世俗对应物：长期主义（longtermism）——Nick Bostrom、William MacAskill 用几乎相同的算术推理主张"我们应该为一万年后的人类负责"。

一位达吉斯坦穆斯林摔跤手和牛津的效果利他主义哲学家们，用完全相同的数学直觉，得出了两套截然不同却结构对称的伦理系统。这提示我们："时间尺度"本身可能是伦理学一个被严重低估的自变量——你把时间轴拉多长，决定了你能看见什么样的善恶。

📝 转录文本

一、七十年与两千年：一个关于时间的算术

So my advice would be: read, and find within yourself the strength to come closer to one God, and seek to understand why we were sent here in the first place.

Today, you and me, we're almost the same age. So let's just think about this. For example, my grandfather on my mother's side passed away in 2003. Now it's 2026. He's been lying in the grave for 23 years. And then there was his grandfather, or let's say his great-grandfather, who also died and has been in the grave for over a hundred years, roughly speaking.

But what about people who died two thousand years ago? They've been in the grave for two thousand years. What's next? It's a good question, isn't it? They've just been in the grave all this time, and that's it. So what was the purpose of their life? A person has been in the grave for two thousand years, but maybe lived for seventy years. Roughly speaking, let's say one hundred. They lived for one hundred years and have been in the grave for two thousand. So what matters more — those one hundred years, or these two thousand years?

二、信者与不信者的分界线

And what happens after those two thousand years end? People believe different things — whether there is a day of judgment or not. That's where the difference lies between a believer and a non-believer.

After everyone is resurrected, there will be the day of judgment. There will be judgment, and after that, people will enter eternity. Eternity compared to eternity — what are two thousand years? They're nothing. And we live for, let's say, seventy years. And many people choose those seventy years over eternal life.

And if a person understands that these seventy years they have here — roughly speaking, seventy or eighty years — are meant to be used to prepare for what comes after, so that when the day of judgment arrives, and after that judgment they can live forever, not in hell, but in heaven — if that becomes their ultimate goal, then they will strive to do good deeds because they will fear the day of judgment. And that's really what life is about: preparing yourself for the day of judgment.

— Lex: That's true. To truly understand life and its deeper meaning, you have to think about eternity. Only then can you really understand your role.

三、约束之必要：那颗"核弹"的比喻

— Khabib: Actually, it can keep a person away from evil. From evil — and it can stop them from treating other people badly. It can hold a person back.

But if you don't have that understanding, if a person lives completely convinced that there's nothing after death, what's there to stop him from doing evil? Just like that. What do you think?

And on top of that, an even more dangerous combination: you become powerful, wealthy, and you become famous. What now? Suddenly every door is open to you. Just imagine a person like that. And on top of all that, he doesn't believe in the day of judgment. He doesn't believe he'll be held accountable for his actions. That's, you know, it's like a nuclear bomb. He can end up causing harm to people everywhere.

But if you know that for everything you have here, you'll eventually have to answer — that there will be a day of judgment and that you'll be called to account, and if you fail that test, you'll burn in hell forever — that'll make you rein yourself in a little. You'll have to take that into consideration. You'll have to tighten things up a little. You'll begin to understand that you're not nearly as important as the image you've created of yourself in your own mind. You start becoming more, as Americans say, down to earth. You become more grounded. You're not flying, you're walking on the ground.

四、手中的钱，心中的钱

— Lex: You once put it beautifully — you can allow money and fame to stay in your hand, but not in your heart. You've still got many years ahead of you, but you're already an example of someone who's become famous, made money, and remained the same person.

— Khabib: If money stays in your hands and not in your heart, that's a good thing. But the moment it gets into a person's heart, it corrupts them. Once it's there, it's very difficult to pull it out of your heart.

If you have wealth in your hands and use it properly — for good causes, for the right purposes, for people in need, for your family, relatives, friends, people from your hometown — that's a good thing. But as soon as that wealth gets into your heart, it becomes very difficult to share it with others. And this is a very dangerous place for a person to end up.

And I'm sorry, but as a believer, I believe that most people in hell will be wealthy.

五、成长中的人，未曾改变的核心

— Lex: One of the reasons millions of people find you so interesting to watch is that you're constantly growing. First, you were a great fighter. Now you're becoming a leader. Your wisdom just keeps increasing. You're evolving as a person, but still the core values remain. It's good to see — inspiring for people. Money and fame haven't changed you. You're just growing as a human being, as you always have.

— Khabib: I hope it's in the right direction. It's just — the thing is, people only see the good. They don't see the bad. And we all have the good side and the bad side. Everyone, sadly.

And especially when it comes to celebrities, we only show the best side of ourselves. Even when you post photos, you only post the good ones, the pictures where you look your best. So I hope that the way people see me, as you pointed out, is the way I really am, because it's difficult to judge yourself objectively. You're always biased when it comes to yourself. That's how it is.

We tend to think highly of ourselves, right? You can't really see yourself objectively. We hide our flaws and put our best qualities on display. Sometimes people even start believing in a fake version of themselves.

For me, I try to stay on the honest path throughout my life — to remain true to who I really am and to show my true self to people. Maybe not everyone agrees with my behavior, my opinions, my worldview, or my attitudes towards sports, religion, and other things. Not everyone shares my views. Not everyone is a fan of mine. There are people who, let's say, see me very differently.

So I'm just… I've tried, I continue to try to be who I am. That's all. And I hope that my ending will be a good one, too. Well, you know — at least that's my hope.

六、一个轻松的收尾：巴萨与皇马

— Lex: You've stayed the same, but you've also grown. I mean, today you even managed to say something nice about Barça. So see, that's progress. Yeah. Well done.

— Khabib: Come on, without Barcelona, there wouldn't be Real Madrid. If the Spanish league didn't have either Real Madrid or Barcelona, it just wouldn't be the same. They've been competing against each other for how many years? One hundred twenty. It's hard to imagine Barcelona and Real Madrid without each other, and so is the Spanish league without that rivalry. It's impossible to imagine.

So yeah, we have to give you some credit — but Real Madrid is the royal club. Come on. It's the best. You know?

— Lex: And thanks to both of them, we've been able to enjoy truly incredible football for so many years.

— Khabib: For so many years, yeah.

七、告别

— Lex: Um, Khabib, brother, I don't even have the words to explain how honored I am that you're here talking with me today and showing me so much warmth. There's no way to fully express what you mean to millions of your fans around the world, including me. Thank you so much for everything. Thank you for this conversation.

— Khabib: Thank you. Thank you very much, Lex.

观看原视频 →
