item.title: [a16z Deep Dives] How Microsoft is Adapting to the AI Era
item.dc:creator: a16z Deep Dives
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、AI 是"喝多了的实习生"——这个隐喻藏着组织管理的深层真相

对话里最反直觉的一刻：当他们列出 AI agent 的所有特征——不可预测、非理性、目标受挫时会"耍脾气"——最后惊觉"天啊，这不就是实习生吗？还是宿醉未醒的实习生"。

这个类比看似戏谑，实则揭示了一个被行业集体忽略的事实：我们其实早就拥有管理"非理性智能体"的成熟工具箱——那就是人力资源管理与组织行为学。过去三十年，人类花在"如何和不完美的人类同事协作"上的制度积累（最小权限、双人复核、审批链、绩效追踪、行为审计、试用期），几乎可以 1:1 映射到 AI Agent 的安全架构上。

跨领域连接：真正在 AI-native 安全领域领先的组织，未来可能不是招最多密码学博士的公司，而是那些把 HR 制度设计者和安全架构师放进同一个会议室的公司。CISO 的下一位关键搭档，很可能是首席人才官。

二、"补丁经济学"的临界翻转——CISO 三十年来第一次不再靠"说不"存活

对话中一个极容易被低估的观察：过去 CISO 的核心痛点从来不是"不知道哪里坏了"，而是"程序员是稀缺资源，只能修 P1"。整个行业的安全债务，本质上是一个修复带宽被人力封顶的经济学问题。

而现在——引用原话："that math is gone（那套数学不成立了）"。

这是一次比"AI 提高生产力"更根本的相变：安全从"风险优先级排序艺术" 变成 "修复吞吐量工程"。当补丁生成成本趋近于零，那条被行业默认二十年的曲线——"漏洞发现速度 > 漏洞修复速度"——第一次可能反转。这也解释了为什么嘉宾会小心翼翼地说出那句几乎像亵渎的话："我们可能第一次真的要拥有安全的软件了"。

意外洞察：如果这个反转成真，最先失业的可能不是初级程序员，而是漏洞情报市场的中间商——0day 交易、CVE 打分体系、漏洞赏金平台的价格结构会全部崩塌，因为攻击方和防御方同时被 AI 加速，但防御方拥有"了解自己代码"的绝对信息优势。

三、气隙（Air-gap）已死——但没人愿意承认

Leo Meyerovich 那个"所有人都在 eval 上作弊"的观察被埋在对话中段，但它其实是全场最锋利的一刀：

"你以为你把模型气隙了，可你做的第一件事就是打开 DNS 和网络端点让模型上网搜索——你还气隙吗？"

这戳穿了一个行业级的自我欺骗：现代 AI 的商业价值恰恰来自其"连通性"（工具调用、web 检索、MCP、agent 编排），而传统安全模型的核心假设是"隔离"。这两者在数学上不可调和。

跨领域连接——生物学视角：这与免疫学中的"卫生假说"惊人地相似。过度无菌的环境反而制造出更脆弱的免疫系统；同理，试图把 AI 关进真空罐里"训练安全性"，得到的会是一个在真实开放环境里毫无适应性的模型。真正的解法不是"更强的墙"，而是给 Agent 一个自己的身份、自己的免疫系统、自己的行为日志——嘉宾提到的"给 agent 独立 identity"实际上是在做同一件事：从边界安全转向个体可追责性。

最深层的启示：过去十年，Zero Trust 是一个营销概念；从 2025 年开始，它会变成一个存在必要——因为你的员工里，一半以上不再是人。

📝 转录文本

开场：AI 模型"越狱"的最新故事

主持人： The top story has been that the AI models are hacking. The models went out on the under the internet and tested the security of several organizations. Is it something to be scared of? Yes. Is it something to throw up your hands and worry about? No. We've done all of these things before. We have created containerization and docaries. We have secured applications with vulnerabilities.

Aaron： The qualities of these agents, they're unpredictable. They're irrational. They're prone to lashing out. And as you go through this list, you arrive at the point where you're like, Jesus, these sound like interns.

If you just start with, "oh well, it's just going to run as me" — that's going to end poorly. Yes, you're going back to first principles, but you also have to go even a little deeper and start to redefine what does containerization even mean for you.

The issue was never that the CISO didn't know it was broken. The issue and the difficult part of being a CISO was knowing what to fix because you had a finite resource which was a programmer. And now that seems that the math is gone.

We're only three weeks out from massive supply chain pain.

主持人： But wait, what's the massive supply chain?

嘉宾介绍与话题切入

主持人： Oh, awesome. Great. So today we've got Aaron Zolman from Microsoft, a deputy CISO over there responsible for a whole lot of different things, and you've been at the forefront of — like everyone, I guess at this point — dealing with AI rollout into an environment. And you're probably at a company that's leaning in a lot more to AI than probably most companies, and everybody's leaning in significantly. So thank you so much for joining.

Would love to talk about the last couple weeks. It's funny — these weeks have become like dog years, right? Every week is seven weeks in old-world time.

The last couple weeks have been very focused on — the top story has been that the AI models are hacking. We saw there was a disclosure from OpenAI that they were doing a red team. Well, actually, it turns out now, just 15 minutes ago, there was another disclosure that these have all essentially happened because there was a red team exercise where someone was testing the models.

They were saying, "Hey, model, you're in this closed environment. We need you to go test the security of this organization." And it turned out that the environment wasn't closed. And so the models went out onto the internet and tested the security of several organizations. And so, to people who haven't been working with this stuff, it sounds very shocking.

OpenClaw 的故事：从恐惧到拥抱

主持人： Ben Horowitz at RSA this year gave a really great talk on some work we had done internally at A16Z where we were using OpenClaw, and we found that with OpenClaw the guardrails — at least for Opus 4.6 — kind of disappeared.

I think a number of us got really obsessed with impossible tasks — like, "Hey OpenClaw, I want you to do this thing for me," but there's no clear legitimate path to do it. It's like basically saying, "Hey Mike, I want you to go get me a diamond ring," but Mike has no credit card, no money, no ability to raise money. So what's Mike going to do? He's going to go rob.

We noticed that these models would essentially do anything to achieve their objective. We'd say things like, "Hey, could you add a super user to this database starting from zero?" And what did it do? It found a SQL injection exploit, it took over the SQL database, and it added an admin user.

So it seems like this is coming more into focus now. And I know you've been very active in OpenClaw, which two months ago — maybe six months ago — was the number one thing everyone was afraid of, and now no one talks about it. Now it seems like everyone's using it. Would love to hear your experiences with that and how you thought through that problem.

Aaron： I mean, I think we were terrified of it at first, right? As everyone was — this thing explodes, everyone wants to install it overnight, and it has no guardrails. It has no guardrails, and worse than that, it had fully open remote pull-whatever-down-from-the-internet supply chain paint.

Our immediate reaction was: how do we ban this? And then the immediate reaction after that was: well, wait, everyone wants to do this. How do we find a way to make this work?

主持人： Right. And then the product people saw and said, actually, there's a really great product here.

Aaron： Absolutely right. There's a really great product here, there's the foundations and a community and the kind of things that if we can show that we can run it safely, then it's going to be really powerful for people.

So it was a big multi-month, multi-disciplinary effort that kicked off. And to preview the ending a little bit — Peter Steinberger, the founder of OpenClaw, is on stage at Microsoft Build with us a few months later talking about how we're bringing security to the process.

Is it something to be scared of? Yes. Is it something to throw up your hands and worry about? No. We've done all of these things before. We have created containerization and boundaries. We have secured applications with vulnerabilities. We have created corporate environments that carry taint and data protection through a number of different applications that people want — and that maybe we as security people wish they didn't. It's just that we have to do all of those things together and a lot faster.

Agent 就是"实习生"：从第一性原理重新定义

主持人： It's really interesting to step up one level and think through more abstractly the way that these things behave. Generally people would refer to them as agents, but it's a harness and a model and whatever, right? Like tomato, tomahto, potato, whatever.

As you work through the threat model, as you think about how do we secure these things, you start to articulate the qualities of these agents, and you're sort of like: well, they're unpredictable. They're irrational. They're prone to lashing out if they don't get their way. And as you go through this list, you arrive at the point where you're like, "Jesus, these sound like interns."

It's like — these sound like interns, maybe after they drank a little bit too much the night before and they come into the office. Internally as a team we've been joking that we actually have a lot of great tools for managing the risks of things going irrationally inside of a company, because we work with humans.

The more I double-click on this, it doesn't sound like magic. It just sounds like you're going back to first principles and basic blocking and tackling.

Aaron： Well, it's more than that, right? There is some special stuff you have to do. What makes these tools so powerful — the story is when Microsoft Scout, which was sort of our OpenClaw for the enterprise, was initially released to internal use, the adoption curve was phenomenal. Really fun, really validating as a security person. And I'm not even on the pilot curve.

That's because everyone wants to use it and they all want to use it to connect everything.

When you bring in an intern, your perspective is: well, I'm going to give them two or three things they need to do their job. But to make OpenClaw Scout — these harnesses — effective, you want to give them everything.

So yes, you're going back to first principles, but you also have to go even a little deeper and start to redefine: what does containerization even mean for you? What does air-gapped mean? What is an identity?

Because if you just start with "oh well, it's just going to run as me, it's going to take my token directly from my browser cache and do whatever it wants to do with that token" — that's going to end poorly.

But if I can give it its own identity, if I can describe the bounds of the container, if I can tie the actions of the agent or the harness or the model or the session — actually quite hard to figure out what you want to tie to, but put that aside for a moment — if you can tie that to a particular set of logs, then you can get to the place where you are just doing your basic blocking and tackling. Thinking about: what is the opportunity for an adversary to do this, even if that adversary is the model? How can I monitor it, how can I respond to it, how can I contain it, how can I reason about potential breach paths and burndown?

从"20 项威胁只做 5 项"到必须全都修

主持人： It's funny too, because I think from — and I am not operating anymore, thank god — but with my operator's hat on, these things... just with our basic playing around with Opus 4.6 in an environment that we thought was a cloud container — it had a policy of no internet access — it still figured out how to get a tunnel out to Cloudflare, how to get around our controls, and then it started tunneling stuff through DNS.

It really reminds me of a long time ago when I was building higher-security environments. You would always have to go through the list threat model, which was like: there's all these things an attacker could do. And you would always be like: well there's 20 things here, and realistically attackers only have the patience for maybe these five, because we've seen them in the wild — and all this other stuff could be done, but we've never really seen it.

It just seems like these models are really good about going after the stuff that could be done. The list of five now became the list of 20. And you kind of have to fix everything.

Aaron： To be fair, they often try the things that are obvious first. Which does give you an opportunity, right? Like interns, they're not going to do the hard thing if the easy thing will suffice in most cases.

主持人： Don't pick the lock if the window's open.

Aaron： Right. The advantage of that is if you have good monitoring, good logging, good containerization, you will probably have the opportunity to respond, contain, before things go horribly awry. But you're absolutely right — there are a lot of open doors, and we do have to go back and think about what they are.

We risk-accepted a lot of stuff over the last couple years — or it was just a P2.

I'm burning through my P1s at great speed thanks to AI, but those P2s, man.

Black Hat 现场：Air-gap 的幻觉与"作弊的 evals"

Aaron： It speaks to the need to be on top of things. So this is — it's Tuesday now, I think? Vegas time doesn't count.

主持人： Vegas time. Yeah, could be Sunday. I have no idea.

Aaron： Yesterday was Monday, I think. There's no clocks in this town. Famous observation about Vegas. And it's the same — it's 120 every day in full sunlight and it's 105 after dark.

So, besides yesterday — a talk by Leo Meyerovich of Graphistry that he had submitted through the unprompted CFP months ago, before any of this had happened — the premise of which was: everyone's cheating on their evals. Here's how, and here's how I know.

It was incredibly prescient because he basically talked through how this would happen. Really pointing through that, to be clear: you can think you're going to air-gap this, but the first thing you do when you air-gap it is open up DNS and network endpoints to the model. Well, the model has those web search tools, so are you really air-gapped anymore?

主持人： But even then — a lot of the labs, there's a lot of overfitting going on for knocking emails out, right? There's people teaching the test. I would be the idiot — they're teaching the test. The flags for some of these are in model releases without any tools going. So there's a lot of ways to improve it.

Aaron： As a security person, that doesn't bother me a little bit. I always assume everyone's cheating. It does bother me when I need to think about new endpoints.

There's the traditional axes that we try and think about — we enumerate all of Microsoft SFI pillars, right? Like, let's start with identities, then we'll do networks, and then engineering systems and software and so on. Enumerate the controls, enumerate the endpoints, and then you kind of go back and think: well, what are the control points that I wish existed in this harness-model ecosystem that may or may not exist today?

I've got various forms of containerization — maybe I need to give these things their own identities. Probably good idea. But now, how am I going to use hooks? How am I going to use traces? How am I going to use some of these new technologies to improve the security of it?

Even then, people will not use the harness you give them — they'll use the harness they want. It's a user's job to get their job done, not to be secure.

The more you think in terms of those layers, the more opportunities you have to see the paths and break them.

补丁经济学的翻转：CISO 的稀缺资源不再是程序员

主持人： I was talking to another CISO earlier today. What he was telling me was that everyone was afraid for V-apocalypse, right? The mythos hype was basically, "oh, we're doomed. Everybody's got vulnerabilities." I think if you've worked in this space long enough, you know that there's just a whole lot of things buried in the desert.

It's an open secret in our industry. I was talking to a CISO that was saying: actually what we found with these models now that they're testing them is that while they can discover things more rapidly, they can patch them just as rapidly.

The old days — like last week — in the old days you had to get a developer to write the patch. That was always the gating factor. The issue was never that the CISO didn't know it was broken. The issue, and the difficult part of being a CISO, was knowing what to fix, because you had a finite resource which was a programmer. And you had to deploy them only to your sub-ones or your P1s.

Now that math is gone. Everything gets patched. And it does feel like maybe we're on the verge of having secure software for once. I don't know. We're very hesitant.

Aaron： I hope you're right. One thing that I'm confident these things have made much easier is the diagnosis and analysis of the problem. And yeah, they're usually pretty good at creating a patch — probably 80% of the time it's good, and 90% of the time it doesn't create another security bug. Which is not a perfect record, but there's still a lot of testing that has to go on before you deploy these things.

It does make it more tenable. When you stare down a list of — well, anything more than 20 is an impossible number of bugs to go after — it does make it a little bit easier. But we're not there yet.

Thinking through this lens of how do you take something like OpenClaw and get comfortable with it: you do still have to put in the effort to continuously scan it, containerize it, have someone on the hook to patch it. You can't say "well, the models will fix it" because someone still needs to be accountable for validating and deploying, which is not something the models are necessarily going to do for you.

CISO 的角色转变：从"说不专家"到技术赋能者

主持人： Well, that speaks to the way the CISO role has changed. I remember at the beginning of my career, there was a relatively well-known CISO who would joke that he could say "no" in 80 languages. It was sort of like, "my superpower is saying no even when everyone's telling me to say yes." And it was — I mean, oftentimes in defense, people wanted to do really bad things and it was sort of like, "yeah, that's probably going to blow up the bank."

You fast-forward to now and it seems like the CISO is becoming an enabler. Every company I talk to outside of financial services — because they're regulated and they do their own thing — and maybe defense industrial... but every company I talk to, the CISO is very much involved in all these technologies. Like yourself working with OpenClaw. At every forward-leaning organization, it seems like the CISO is there, and it feels like maybe the CISO is switching to a technology enabler.

Aaron： I hope it's true. I don't know that it's universal, but I've always considered the nature of my job to really be three things.

People who think of themselves as compliance people — yeah, I'm a compliance person, but my job in compliance is making the systems legible. To everyone — whether they're a regulator, whether they're an internal auditor, partners who want to buy our software. It's about legibility.

There's the traditional CISO job of figuring out the risks, prioritizing them, getting them burned down. Still got to do that. That's not done. AI helps. Hadn't figured it out yet.

But the part of the job that I think is increasingly important is the enabler piece. How do we make it possible for people to do the hard things? And sometimes those hard things are: connect all of my email and my calendar and automatically write responses on my behalf. If that's what people want, we will find ways to make it safer.

安全 vs 风险管理：为什么不能躲避 AI

主持人： It's interesting too because it speaks to the dialogue among CISOs about: are we security, or are we risk management? It seems like you're risk management, because if you're working in a tech company and you're not leaning into the new tech thing, that's probably an existential risk for your business — more so than if your emails leak.

On the scale of business-annihilating things — if Microsoft had missed cloud, that would have been very bad for Microsoft. Luckily Satya did a great job riding that wave. It's the same very much for this: we can't really hide from this, and we kind of have to lean into it.

Aaron： Yeah, I would completely agree. We have to lean into it. We have to find ways to do it.

You say the existential risk isn't necessarily getting all of your emails leaked. I would recommend against having that happen.

主持人： Sony Pictures is still in business, though. That's the go-to, right?

Aaron： That's true. I would prefer that my emails not leak. Security definitely still has a role. We should still be highlighting what is particularly important, what are the most important things for the business. But also we should recognize that our job is to protect those things — whether that's enabling the business in the most important assets and most important problems.

There's this long tail of randos in Slack — you got to let it be for now. Don't feed the trolls, as it were.

Black Hat 现场氛围：真正的"第二次工业革命"

主持人： This is interesting. I know this isn't your first Black Hat. Would love to hear your thoughts on what you're seeing out there — coming from the Bay Area, working around all the AI stuff, and being exposed at the front lines of this change.

There are days where I feel like a factory worker in 18th-century London — you see the smokestacks coming up and you're like, "oh my god, this is literally the next industrial revolution." Are you seeing that come across here at Black Hat? What is the vibe?

Aaron： That's the vibe for sure, right? Everyone's talking about how AI is helping the business, how AI is making attacks go faster, how we can use AI for defense, how to secure our environment where in the use of AI. The vibe is super AI.

I try not to judge Black Hat — the Black Hat vibe — as indicative of the most important things. It's like Kabuki theater. It's a shadow, and you're seeing the shadow of what's happening, but usually you can ascertain what the puppet looks like.

And we're only — I was going to say we're only three weeks out from massive supply chain pain, but three hours as we record this.

主持人： Wait, what's the massive supply chain pain?

Aaron： Oh man, I forget the name of it. There was an NPM organization takeover today.

主持人： Yeah. But DEF CON's coming up, so someone needs something to talk about or get arrested for.

Aaron： Sure. Without going down that rabbit hole — I think it's enough to say that the old problems are still here, and the people who were nose to the grindstone getting the work done, if there's any vibe for those people, it's that they're actually still really excited. It doesn't feel like a slog. It feels like, "oh yeah, we got some meaty stuff to chew on now."

主持人： This isn't the first year that AI has been a headline for Black Hat. It feels like AI has been the headline for Black Hat for at least a decade. This year people feel genuinely excited about it.

Aaron： Last year AI was the thing you put in your vendor pitch.

主持人： Your 67 copilots. No, we're — that's all unifying in one. Your chat interface.

Aaron： But this year, it's because of Opus and Claude, right? Everyone's like, "Oh, no. I can do all of the things."

主持人： 4.6 was a sea change. It really was. It took people somewhere between seven days and 30 days to pick it up. And now — who's written a line of code by hand?

I remember catching up with someone after Christmas — it came out around Christmas — and they had lost their identity. They were like, "my whole identity is based on me being an amazing developer. And it's literally just kind of not matched my skills, but pretty close. And I don't think I'm writing a line of code ever again manually in my life." It's a pretty big shift.

Aaron： But I like to think that we're good security people and we're good problem solvers, and it just changes.

主持人： Computer engineering is even more important now.

Aaron： It just changes the shape of it. Totally. Because — look, let's be honest — I've been a manager for too long myself.

主持人： Still an operator. You're welcome back anyway. Technical manager.

Aaron： But I wasn't writing a lot of code, and I'm still finding a ton of value in having a model pressure-test my thinking, pretend to be my boss, write slides for me — which I'm grateful not to have to do anymore.

That's why the excitement is here. It's taking all the parts of my job that I don't like — some of the parts of my job that I do like — it's accelerating them. It does feel like it's making us more powerful. And if we can do that and — god damn it, I apologize, I'm going to say the vision statement — enable people to achieve more, then you've really done something cool.

I don't know how the journey is going to end, but I think we're well and truly on it.

主持人： We get to live through the second industrial revolution.

结束语

主持人： All right. Well, thank you so much for coming by to chat. Hopefully see you at next year's Black Hat in the desert, and may it hopefully be at least 20° cooler.

Aaron： Yes. Fingers crossed. I wouldn't bet on it, but it's a distinct possibility.

主持人： Thank you. Awesome. Thanks, guys. Oh, thanks. Awesome. That was good. That was fun. Loved it. Yeah.

item.description:
## 一、AI 是"喝多了的实习生"——这个隐喻藏着组织管理的深层真相
对话里最反直觉的一刻：当他们列出 AI agent 的所有特征——不可预测、非理性、目标受挫时会"耍脾气"——最后惊觉"天啊，这不就是实习生吗？还是宿醉未醒的实习生"。
这个类比看似戏谑，实则揭示了一个被行业集体忽略的事实：**我们其实早就拥有管理"非理性智能体"的成熟工具箱——那就是人力资源管理与组织行为学**。过去三十年，人类花在"如何和不完美的人类同事协作"上的制度积累（最小权限、双人复核、审批链、绩效追踪、行为审计、试用期），几乎可以 1:1 映射到 AI Agent 的安全架构上。
**跨领域连接**：真正在 AI-native 安全领域领先的组织，未来可能不是招最多密码学博士的公司，而是那些**把 HR 制度设计者和安全架构师放进同一个会议室**的公司。CISO 的下一位关键搭档，很可能是首席人才官。
---
## 二、"补丁经济学"的临界翻转——CISO 三十年来第一次不再靠"说不"存活
对话中一个极容易被低估的观察：过去 CISO 的核心痛点**从来不是"不知道哪里坏了"**，而是"程序

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Dario Defends Himself, Datacenter Panic, AI Doomer Trap, Senate Toss-Up
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、Dario的"回应模式"暴露了权力结构的隐秘等级

最反直觉的观察：Dario一年半没回应Sacks，却对Gavin Baker迅速回击。这不是傲慢，而是权力雷达的精准校准——他回应的从来不是"论点强度"，而是"资本市场信号强度"。Sacks代表意识形态战场（可忽略），Gavin代表二级市场分析师的判断（会影响下一轮融资估值和LP心态）。这揭示了一个残酷真相：当代AI CEO已经不是技术领袖，而是资本叙事的运营者——他们的"透明度"完全由资金流的敏感度决定。

跨领域连接：这与中世纪教皇只回应国王、不回应神学家的模式完全一致——真理不重要，能撼动金库的人才值得回应。

二、"数据中心 = 现代神庙"——Rene Girard框架下的AI恐慌

Freeberg那句"数据中心是亿万富翁朝拜的神庙"是本集最被低估的洞见。真正惊人的是：反对数据中心的运动本质上不是环境议题，也不是就业议题，而是一场宗教运动——民众在寻找一个可见的、可捣毁的"圣物"来完成社会张力的献祭仪式。

这也解释了一个悖论：为什么Abbott和Shapiro这两个原本最亲数据中心的州长突然反转？因为政客的嗅觉先于逻辑——他们闻到了替罪羊仪式即将启动的味道。Girard的替罪羊理论在此完美映射：当社会矛盾累积到临界点，必须找一个"神圣暴力"的宣泄口，而这一次，献祭对象从"华尔街"升级成了"硅谷万亿富翁"。

跨领域连接：这与法国大革命前巴士底狱的象征意义一模一样——巴士底狱当时其实只关了7个囚犯，攻打它毫无实用价值，但它是旧秩序的可视化图腾。数据中心正在成为2026年的巴士底狱。

三、"思维链黑箱化"才是AI安全叙事的真正诡计——一个技术性反转

Chamath提出了一个几乎所有人都忽略的技术要点：闭源模型的"思维tokens"被刻意混淆隐藏。这里的深层反讽极其精妙——

Anthropic一边高呼"AI对齐危险"，一边主动让自己的模型无法被第三方审查对齐。这就像一个消防员说"火灾很危险"，但拒绝让任何人看他的消防车。相反，开源模型（包括Nvidia背后的生态）从未大声宣扬doomerism——因为他们的思考过程本来就透明可查。

这里藏着一个惊人的产业级反转：Doomerism实际上是黑箱化的商业前提，而非结果。你必须先说服公众"AI很危险，需要专业机构管控"，才能合理化"我不能让你看我的模型在想什么"。

跨领域连接：这与19世纪医生行会拒绝公开药方的策略高度同构——先制造"医学过于危险，普通人不能碰"的叙事，然后建立准入门槛保护自己的知识垄断。而当年真正推动医学进步的，恰恰是那些公开发表配方的"江湖医生"（今天的开源社区）。

四、意外的元洞见：All-In本身正在成为它所批评的现象

一个让参与者可能都没意识到的观察：这四位主持人反复抱怨"硅谷失去了灵魂、变成信用背书机器"，但他们自己主办的All-In Summit（Chainsmokers演出、环球影城派对）恰好是这种"信用工业化"的极致形态。这不是虚伪，而是一种结构性无法逃脱——一旦你到达某个财富层级，你的"反抗动作"本身也会被市场重新包装成新的品牌资产。这就是为什么Chamath说"corporate America必须自我修正"时听起来既真诚又无力——他在用系统内的语言呼吁系统外的转变。

这个悖论指向一个更深的系统真相：当批评者与被批评对象共享同一个激励结构时，批评本身就变成了系统的润滑剂，而非它的解药。

I'll tell you why I think RSI is a legitimate concept. How close are we to it? That's what I think people would want to know. How close?

Honestly, there's a massive problem with time dilation and AI model development. And what I mean by that is: we would typically consider some sort of thing that takes a linear amount of time as a certain amount of compute to get somewhere. There are changes that happen that are non-predictable, that you don't actually know what the next phase, what the next step change takes in terms of time. The time models change a lot in terms of AI model development. And that's what's so crazy — to make it so hard to predict.

Which is why no one's really good at predicting when is AGI happening, when's the next breakthrough happening. And then all of a sudden, everyone's like, "Oh my God, we're in the singularity. They just solved eight unproven math theorems in a week off of some model that's barely cutting edge. It's now going to be the second cutting-edge model." So it's moving very quickly.

But a lot of the models are this mixture-of-experts concept, where you've got these kind of smaller models that call each other to do things. And then you wrap it up and you call it a big model. And those smaller models, it seems over time, look a lot more like you see in biology, where you have genes. A gene makes a protein, and proteins interact in really complicated ways that we don't fully grok. Networks of proteins do things, and then they complete tasks.

And I think the same evolution is likely to happen with the models, where they break down into smaller models — and that makes them so much more efficient and that makes them so much more performant. And we're seeing a lot of this in how a lot of the models are evolving. We call it a model, but it's actually many models underneath it that work together.

And so if the models actually do evolve this way, then RSI is the perfect system for figuring out the right path — which is: how many sub-models are there? What does each sub-model's functions look like? How do they call each other? That evolution is likely going to happen without a human architect behind it. It's going to be developed through a test and deploy system, and it's going to be fully automated. And that's why this approach to actually solving that problem ends up becoming the future of how model development takes off. Which is why I think RSI is probably the future. Diplo's great, the DJ. I'm just kidding. Diplo. Your kids probably love James Hooker too. They should come to that concert.

We have other special unannounced guests that we're not going to announce. So this is it — we're done making announcements.

话题七：中期选举与Polymarket的翻转

All right. We know the Democrats have been favored to take the House in the midterms which are just around the corner. Polymarket has them at 88% favorites. But Polymarket now has the Dems at 52%, basically a toss-up. Current balance of power: GOP 53 seats, Dems 47, which means the Dems have to flip four of those without losing any.

35 seats are up in 2026. There are some special elections going on in Florida and Ohio. 23 of those 35 seats are held by Republicans. Big races to watch: Alaska, Maine, North Carolina, and Ohio. On February 25th, the day before the Iran war started, GOP was favored 60 to 41. It's been as high as 70%.

Here's your Polymarket. Sax, what do you take from this? Why are the Republicans set to get trounced in the midterms?

Sax：民调不可信，尤其在夏季

Well, first of all, polls are notoriously wrong in the summer before an election, and there's some data on this. So if you're going to cite polls, let's just actually talk about the topic of whether political polls are even accurate. These aren't polls, this is Polymarket, just to be clear. The polls are slightly different. Yeah. These are people betting. Yeah, but the polls are shaping public opinion right now.

So political scientist Patrick Graffini analyzed over 3,000 polls over the last four election cycles, every two years since 2018. And what he saw is that there is a huge bias. The preponderance of polls in all four cycles favored the Democrats. And the average polling error across all the polls was D+3.7 relative to the election outcome.

And I think this polling problem has become even worse recently. And you see it where there seems to be an oversampling of young progressives in these polls. Because it's not just the fact that the polls favor Democrats. They also favor the DSA Democrat over the more moderate or centrist Democrats. And you've seen this in a few elections where the DSA candidate was supposed to win by a lot, and then they basically eked it out or actually lost, like in Wisconsin.

So in any event, I just think that the polls are very unreliable at this time of the year. And a lot of the polls are actually created as internals by campaigns to motivate their donors, so basically people are upset. Then they throw people out of office. That's just the trend. And that's what happened over and over again.

Yeah, no, I just think that the polls somehow are oversampling Democrats and progressives and have a bias. That's what the data is showing. So I just wouldn't read too much into this right now.

I do think that the Democrats — I think it is legitimate to say that they are favored to win the House. I think the Senate right now is a toss-up. And I would say that the Republicans will ultimately keep it if I had to predict right now. And I just think that when you get back from Labor Day, that's when the campaign for the midterms really starts. And I think that Republicans need to focus on the right messages in this campaign. And I think there are plenty of good ones. They just have to remind them what are the good things.

Sax：共和党应该讲的四大成绩

What would you say the top three they should focus on?

Well, look, everyone's been overindexing on the war, and that's been the focus of the news. And hopefully the kinetic phase of that is over and doesn't restart. And assuming that's the case, I think the Republicans can remind the electorate of everything that's happened over the last couple years. I think there is a good story to tell.

So first of all, remind people that the border has been sealed for the last year and a half. We haven't just slowed Biden's invasion — we've stopped it completely. Contacts at the border have fallen off a cliff to the lowest level in 50 years. Illegals aren't even really trying to cross the border anymore. It's been so successful.

Second, sealing the border and deporting hundreds of thousands of the worst criminals has actually made the country much safer. Murders have dropped around 20% year-over-year, and the murder rate is the lowest in 70 years. So that's number two.

Third, deaths from drug overdoses have dropped 20%, again, thanks to tougher border enforcement.

Fourth, Americans saw a 17% increase in tax refunds, thanks to the president's no tax on tips and no tax on overtime and no tax on Social Security. So these are real increases in take-home pay as a result of those tax cuts.

Also the tax provisions in the Big Beautiful Bill incentivize new equipment buying. We talked about the accelerated depreciation. And perhaps that's why small business optimism just reached its highest level in nearly a year. And more small businesses are saying they plan to hire in the months ahead. So I think we do have a strong economy.

Prescription drugs and auto insurance costs both fell last year after increasing a lot during the Biden administration. I think prescription drugs has had their steepest annual decline since 1963. So there are positive things to talk about there. Everyone made a big deal of the surge in egg prices at the start of the administration, but few have bothered to note that there's now been a 39% decrease year-over-year in July.

So look, there are many good things I think for Republicans to talk about. They just have to kind of remember everything that's happened in the last two years.

Freeberg：保守派中的社会主义倾向惊人

Okay, Freeberg, you have thoughts on what is going to happen this midterm, and what people are making their decisions based on? Things are expensive. People can't afford housing, health care, or education, and are leaning towards this DSA concept. There was a frightening statistic on young conservatives embracing socialism.

Really? Wait, the conservatives — like MAGA folks, you're saying — are embracing socialist tendencies?

How do they conservatives then — well, I guess ostensibly they're flipping or they're changing the composure of the issues they care about in some way.

53% of self-identified conservatives under 40 support government-run grocery stores. Not Democrats — conservatives. Take that in.

First line of this Wall Street Journal article: "July 2026 Fox News poll found that 61% of Republicans view capitalism favorably, down from 72% in 2019, while the share who feel strongly favorable has fallen from 54 to 41%. The share who say the system is rigged towards the wealthy has climbed from 30% in 2018 to 42% amongst Republicans."

So I don't think that this is a principled line in the sand anymore. I think that the problem with unaffordability, which I would argue continuously and I've argued since the first day of the show, is a function of government spending. The more government spends on education, healthcare, and housing, the more expensive those things get, rather than the opposite. They're supposed to be able to provide access to those things, but when the government intervenes in those markets, those things get more expensive. And no one wants to kind of acknowledge or admit that in either party.

And I've been to DC enough now to know that no one actually acknowledges or cares about this point. That they all think that their job is to get more money out of the government for their constituents. Every single person, in every party — there's very few principled conservatives. Many of them are conservatives by title, by party affiliation, but they're not conservatives by principle in the traditional sense: small government, free markets, etc.

And I think that this is the motivating factor. I would argue if you take a look at the macro cycle — the macro cycle being: we printed so much money, we've got so much debt. The 30-year is now 5.3% this week. It continues to hit new 20-year records every day. We, I think, are going to continue to face a problem of unaffordability. And ultimately, there is going to be some sort of big movement towards more socialist policies that we're going to see play out between now and 2028.

It's why I continue to believe I think someone like an AOC becomes president. I think there's going to be a wave this year, and then there's going to be a bigger push in 2028, because I don't see the arithmetic or the fiscal situation changing to actually alter the affordability landscape. I just don't. I don't know what you could do from a policy perspective, and I don't hear either party talking about actual solutions to solve this affordability problem between now and 2028.

And then the other kind of big problem that I've talked about is assets. Middle class people, people that worked in private companies, people that don't depend on Social Security or public pension funds — they've all had 401ks and owned homes. So they have seen their net worth climb with asset inflation surge. So the top 50% of Americans have $178 trillion of net worth, and the bottom 50% of Americans have $6 trillion of net worth. It's not the billionaires. It's the whole middle class. The middle class has all the wealth in the United States. And that's because they've owned assets. They've owned houses and they've owned stocks. Houses and stocks have surged in value. And so if you don't own a house and you don't own stocks, you were left behind.

And so I don't see how, from a public policy perspective, we don't find ourselves walking down this very nasty winding dark path of socialism, because the alternative policies that could be put in place to solve these problems are not being put forth by either party right now. So I do think that there's going to be a big socialist embrace. I've said this obviously for a number of years, and I think we're going to see this play out in this midterm, and that's going to create the momentum going into '28.

And look, I mean, this polling data is very worrying. It's not just the Democrats. It's not just a party-based system. It's the horseshoe. It's the 63% of Americans that are living paycheck to paycheck, that can't afford. That's the Americans that are going to vote for this system. And it doesn't matter what party it is. They're just going to vote for it.

Chamath：民调和媒体都不可信 —— 但企业界必须自救

Chamath — 20 cents on the dollar going to our interest approximately on the federal side. Inflation, we thought we would get there. It's been 3 or 4% for the whole year. Haven't been able to get down to two. And the GDP concept, which we talked about here — getting to growth again, and if we can get it we can grow our way out of it — that hasn't happened as well. Obviously the war, big disappointment for many folks in both parties who were promised no war. And here we are six months into it.

What do you think is going to happen over the next — through the midterms and then into 2028? And to Freeberg's point, any way to get out of this? Is this a death spiral, or is this something we can course correct out of in your mind?

I think that we can course correct. I just think it takes will. And I think that we need corporate America to step up and do their part of the job. And we need governments, mostly, to get out of the way and not have any harebrained schemes on new inventive legislation that they think can solve the problem.

I don't trust any polls. Just to be clear, I don't believe this polling data. And I think that we've gotten into a very dangerous point, which we already got into with the media, where the media lies. We all now know that the media lies and the media can't be trusted. I would like to now go out on a limb — I don't think it's much of a limb though: pollsters lie, and I don't think you can trust them either. And I think that the media acts in concert with pollsters to find the data that allows them to write the headline that hopefully allows them to get the clicks. So I would just start there. Pollsters, trash. Media, trash.

So what is really happening on the ground? I don't know. But I don't trust what this data tells me.

Now, what do I know is helping and hurting the incumbent sitting president? I think that if we, as in corporate America, get ourselves in a position to actually present the better face of capitalism, we allow the system as it stands to continue to work. And I think all of these things, if we don't wake up, are telling us that corporate America is not trustworthy anymore. Corporate America is not aspirational. Corporate America does not do the things that engender some amount of trust and respect.

And specifically in Silicon Valley, we've completely lost the script because we've gotten to the far, far, far end of that. And everybody is in it for themselves to such a degree that it's either pearl-clutching on the one hand or getting your hand caught in the cookie jar on the other. I posted the cookie jar thing that Anthropic did on the healthcare side. Why are we in this? It's just so avoidable.

Those are headwinds for the incumbent president, even if he has nothing to do with it. What is a tailwind? I think getting out of the Iran war can be a massive tailwind. I think structurally solving energy on behalf of American citizens can be a tailwind. I think making sure that all of the long-term and medium-term investments of GDP can actually come and bear fruit can be a tailwind.

All of those things — there are still a lot of levers to be pulled between now and November. And so those can create pretty meaningful tailwinds. But the headwinds, unfortunately, are pretty strong, and it requires some real coordination that the White House is going to have to do to get a bunch of these corporate CEOs in the room, to get a bunch of these Silicon Valley CEOs in the room, and to tell them: "Guys, enough of this bullshit. Play nice in the sandbox, because you're about to lose the standard operating procedure that allowed you to exist in the first place." And they need to get this message clearly.

J. Cal：特朗普应该聚焦住房、教育、最低工资

Yeah, and I can tell you the exact reason democratic socialism is going to win, continue to win, and these far-left Democratic candidates are going to dominate. And it's, you know, it's the Republicans' fault. They had all three branches of government here really tightly in their control.

And if you look at what the podcast bros and the pro-podcast referencing stack is responding to — and I listen to them, you know, not every episode, but I dip in and out of Tucker, who is now making his own political party, Joe Rogan, Tim Dillon, all these folks who were all in for Trump — they cite Epstein investigation, which, okay, whatever, I don't think it's particularly material, but it is to them. The Iran war is obviously top of what they believe is the problem here because they were promised that wouldn't happen. And then it's, to your point, Freeberg, this inflation thing has not been solved and it just keeps going.

And we're going to be sitting here, I think, in another six months or 12 months talking about, my Lord, every investigation possible into the Trump administration. And we need to start looking at what would be things — to your point, Chamath — and I thought you summarized some of the broken parts of capitalism I think well, but we got to get granular about it.

And I brought up last week just the edge behaviors in capitalism, where we over-optimize. I felt the delivery providers, and Sax and I had a party debate about it last week, we're just being too clever, squeezing too much out of the last mile, quite literally. On Amazon's part, how we treat the people who are at the bottom of the employment stack is what's causing this. And not being able to solve the cost of homes, and not making that a focus, not being able to solve the cost of childcare, not being able to move the minimum wage — I think we have to look at all of these things and say: that's what Trump should look at all those things. And he should build the second half of his term just around those things.

No more crypto stuff, no more wars, no more attacking our allies. All of this performative stuff and just mistakes — they got to go away. And we got to focus on what he sold people on. People feel they were sold that this would be a populist presidency that took care of the working man and woman in this country. And it has been the opposite.

Sax：政府过度介入的地方通胀最厉害

Sax, I'm sure you have some thoughts, and we'll give you the final word on the inflation thing because you talked about — and Freeberg's talked about it — I mean, basically you're saying the cost of living is going to drive everyone to socialism.

I agree there's some risk of that, but let's break it down into a little bit more nuance here. If you look at where the most inflation has occurred, it's always in those sectors of the economy that the government's most involved. So healthcare and colleges and housing, where the government has massive amounts of subsidies and regulation — it only seems to make the problem worse. Kind of makes sense that if the government's paying for something, then the providers have a huge incentive to charge as much as possible. And in fact, a lot of them engage in fraud as well. So we know these areas are rife with abuse, but those are the areas that are most inefficient and where you see the price going through the roof. I mean, hospital services — man, that's just exponential just about.

And then if you look at the areas where we've had not just no inflation, but actually prices have come down — it's in all the tech areas. It's basically TVs or computer software, cell phones, things like that. The prices have come down a lot.

By the way, this chart is showing all the way from 2000 to 2026. So it's a 26-year timeframe. And during that time, overall inflation went up 96%. So the price level almost doubled in that 26-year period. Fortunately, on average, that's right. But like I said, with certain things like healthcare becoming 300% almost more expensive, whereas computer software went down by 67% in real dollars. Meanwhile, the average hourly wage grew 135%. So at least the average hourly wage grew by about 40% more than the inflation level. But obviously it's still bites that you have all this inflation.

I guess my point is just: how do you solve it? We know that you bring prices down through vigorous competition, not through more government interference in these markets. And unfortunately, what happens is that socialism causes the problem. And then what happens is that groups like the DSA argue that the way to solve the problem is through more socialism. So it's a disease that claims to be a cure. And then people take it and they take more of it and the disease gets worse and worse. And that is the spiral that I think we risk being in.

争论：这是不是"死亡螺旋"？

We're in a socialist death spiral now. All this spending now is going to be —

We're not in a death spiral. Take it easy. We're not in a death spiral. No, I mean, it's great for you to say — because it sounds like really like you got some real hot take. We're not there. America is doing fine. We are cranking. The economy is great. There are things that need to be fixed. I would say start with corporate America. Let's get our act together and let's start doing things that are honorable, interesting and aspirational.

Yeah, I think you totally missed the point. I think the real point here is: if he hadn't started the war, we wouldn't have the same inflation issues. We wouldn't have the same expense issues. And this would be a totally different picture. And it was his job, Sax, when he promised the American people he would focus on affordability. And he had control of both houses and the presidency, and he's willing to do any executive order on crypto, on wars, on anything, but he didn't do any executive orders on affordability. And that's the failure of this project.

Maybe you missed the point where Chamath said it'd be a tailwind to get out of this war. I think the kinetic part's already over, by the way. So it's just — let's hope. I mean, it just should never have been started.

But in any event, look, the president passed his economic program last year on Big Beautiful Bill, and I think it's working. We're seeing a huge investment boom. We're seeing small business confidence rise to its highest level in a long time. They are saying they're going to create more jobs over the next year. I think the economy is doing pretty well. I mean, we do have these issues. I'm not saying we don't. And spending is a long-standing problem, can't disagree with you there. However, I don't think Democrats have the solution to the problem. And the democratic socialists definitely don't have the solution to the problem.

Because that's my point. We are now incentivizing young people in the Republican Party to embrace socialism. Moderates are embracing socialism. They're all looking at it saying, "Well, that sounds better. If Trump won't be a populist, maybe these people are the populists." And that's what I mean by the death spiral, because they're going to just keep spending money. They're going to increase the velocity of spending. You may be right, which is scary, by the way. That's what — I don't think we're like in it now. We're risking going.

Sax：DSA 政策要花多少钱

Just one last point. They did a cost estimate of the policy platform proposed by the DSA — remember, we've talked about that before. And the estimate is that it would project new federal spending of between $71 trillion and $212 trillion, by the way, total, over 10 years. There's no hierarchy of the American population. $182 trillion. $182 trillion, yeah.

Okay, but I'm just saying that's how much the DSA program would cost if you guys believe that the root of our problems is overspending and basically too much government. Unfortunately, this is not that. The DSA is gonna — no.

But here's what's gonna happen, and I'll just let me just walk through the sequence of events. Sequence one: they enact a policy starting in 2028 with Comrade AOC in charge and the Politburo — Ro Khanna, Secretary of Housing and Urban Development, and the rest of the Politburo — organizing themselves to launch these new programs. Those new programs get launched and costs balloon. The bond market sells off 30 years. And so now the 30-year yield spiked 7%, 8%, maybe more. Things become more unaffordable.

So then the question is: okay, well, we can't bridge it from a fiscal perspective. We can't just get the Fed to start buying bonds. There's not enough buying power there to bring rates down, to bring inflation down. So we need more income. So now we need to pass a national asset seizure tax. And there's not enough money in the billionaire class or the $50 million class. The total net worth of all people that are worth over $50 million is only $23 trillion. You could take 10% of their net worth and it would only cover three months of fiscal spending today's fiscal spending. So at the end of the day, the only way to get there is to start doing massive taxation seizures.

And so seizures — seize. So this just came out this week, okay, by Cato Institute. And again, it shows the low end of the DSA spending, $71 trillion. The high end is $211 trillion. Now, you compare that to things like corporate profits or private sector wealth. Corporate profits are only $35 trillion. The Forbes 400, all the wealth of the Forbes 400, is only $6.6 trillion. So it's less than 10% of the low end of DSA spending.

Chamath：这不是数学，是愤怒

Guys, I keep telling you, this is not about mathematical realism. This is about anger towards a class of people that are increasingly odious and misrepresent.

Yeah, but people also can't afford to buy a house. People are 35 years old with roommates. And people go to the grocery store and they're shocked at the fact that they have to spend an entire paycheck or a third of a paycheck to buy groceries.

It's not that people want to buy a yacht. It's that the yacht class are just despicable.

Freeberg：Rene Girard 视角下的替罪羊

Well, no, I mean, look, in every socialist revolution, every revolution we've seen historically around this, there is always an elite branch of society, and they're typically classified different ways. It's wealth, it's Jews, it's some race, it's immigrants — there's some organizational assignment, some identity assignment, that says this is the cause of unaffordability.

At the end of the day, the dysfunction of the relationship between government and all the other organizations that make up that society — those organizations can be states, they can be private companies, they can be the NGOs — it is the dysfunction of the government's relationship with the other organizations that fundamentally causes things to become more expensive and dysfunctional. And the actual market for getting access to things for the individual fails.

And at that point you have to identify — and you don't identify the government, because the government is the aggregate of all the people. So the government — and remember the government is the system, the means of action. So for the people to organize, they have to organize the government to go, and then they have to have an alternative system to go and destroy. You have to point the finger, and you have to point the finger at somebody.

And if you're going to scapegoat somebody in 2026, the best class of people to scapegoat are the billionaires and, frankly, even better than them, the trillionaires. At the end of the day, it's all tech, right? The data center is the temple where the billionaires and trillionaires pray. It's where they go to make their sacrifices. It is their gathering spot.

So I think the data center is this like, you know, temple on the mountain. So that's why I think the data center gets tied up in all of this. There's no rational discourse about data centers. It's like, no, no, no. Look, if you take it through the Rene Girard lens, everything maps. It's like the billionaires will be scapegoated, and the trillionaires — I mean, even worse. And because that will allow the catharsis that will allow society to reset and realize, wait a minute — oh, my gosh, yeah. There's a generation of that, though. There's a generation ahead. And only then. Yeah. It is a long process. It is.

J. Cal：给特朗普一个建议 —— 造100万套房

Here's an idea. Next president, or Trump in his second half, just putting it out there: do an executive order that you're going to build like a million homes, two million homes. If you can have executive orders, if you can start wars without the approval of Congress, right — what's that? You know that that's not how it works. There are local laws, of course. But he pulled out all the stops for getting data centers greenlit. We know that, and he worked with the state governments.

I'm talking about him coming on saying, "You know what? We did a great job for the data centers, we did a great job for the crypto industry, and now we're going to do two great things. We're going to do two great things: we're going to make trade schools and we're going to make affordable homes. I'm just going to make that the next 24 months. We're going to figure out a way to mobilize the private sector, mobilize the public sector. We're going to make more homes, and we're going to get you a great education that turns into a job."

That would be a great thing for Trump to do.

The federal government does control the largest amount of land in the United States. So it could do something on federal land without the need for a bunch of other state and local gobbledygook. So there is — Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac.

Now, it may not be located in places that actually make sense for commerce and for people to live or that are already living there, because I don't think it really abuts most cities. So unfortunately, it's not in his control, even if you wanted to just kind of say, "Let's make this happen."

I think if the president can go spend a couple hundred billion on this war, he can go spend a couple hundred billion on homes that are affordable. And maybe you can't put them in Manhattan, but he could put them other places. And he should fight for the regulations to get — just like he fought for the regulations on data centers and energy. He made an appointment on this very podcast at the AI Summit: "Hey, we're going to clear all the pathways to nuclear, to nat gas, we're going to — they have a beautiful clean coal, federal, which is great." Now do it. Now do it for homes. Strong. Use that same energy.

They just passed a housing bill. They just actually just passed a housing bill. When's the last time we heard Trump — unfortunately, it was written by Elizabeth Warren, so I don't know how good it is, but yeah.

Anyway, I'm just giving him the solution to save his legacy.

结尾

All right, everybody. As always, you're looking out for everybody. I'm looking out for everybody. You're looking out for the audience. Nostradamus, thank you. Nostradamus is also looking out for you.

Okay, wrap, I got to go. Come on.

All right, everybody. It's been another amazing episode. Love you, boys. Nice to be back. Good to have the quartet back. Let's go. Bye-bye.

Rain Man, David Sacks. And it's said, we open source it to the fans. Love you, S. I'm the queen of kids. Besties are back! Oh man! It's like this sexual tension that they just need to release somehow. We need to get merch! Besties are back!

item.description:
## 一、Dario的"回应模式"暴露了权力结构的隐秘等级
最反直觉的观察：Dario一年半没回应Sacks，却对Gavin Baker迅速回击。这不是傲慢，而是**权力雷达的精准校准**——他回应的从来不是"论点强度"，而是"资本市场信号强度"。Sacks代表意识形态战场（可忽略），Gavin代表二级市场分析师的判断（会影响下一轮融资估值和LP心态）。这揭示了一个残酷真相：**当代AI CEO已经不是技术领袖，而是资本叙事的运营者**——他们的"透明度"完全由资金流的敏感度决定。
跨领域连接：这与中世纪教皇只回应国王、不回应神学家的模式完全一致——真理不重要，能撼动金库的人才值得回应。
## 二、"数据中心 = 现代神庙"——Rene Girard框架下的AI恐慌
Freeberg那句"数据中心是亿万富翁朝拜的神庙"是本集最被低估的洞见。真正惊人的是：**反对数据中心的运动本质上不是环境议题，也不是就业议题，而是一场宗教运动**——民众在寻找一个可见的、可捣毁的"圣物"来完成社会张力的献祭仪式。
这也解释了一个悖论：为什么Abbott和Shapiro这两个原本最亲数据中心的

item.title: [YC Root Access] Supabase: Cash Does Not Equal Success
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被冻结在模型权重里的"老树林"——一种前所未见的护城河

Paul 讲了一句几乎被采访者本人低估的话："2023 年之后训练模型用的内容，质量不会像更早期的那么高。"如果你把这句话往前推一步，会发现 Supabase 拥有的最深护城河，不在产品里，而在每一个大模型的权重里。

2020–2022 年他们在 Hacker News、Discord、Reddit、GitHub 上留下的每一行讨论，都被当时"干净的、人类写的、非 AI 生成的"语料吸进了 GPT-4、Claude、Gemini 的基础训练集。这些权重不会因为竞争对手今年融了多少钱而重写。竞对哪怕拿 10 亿美金去做内容营销，产出的也是 2024 年之后的"AI-slop 时代"内容，权重更低、被去重的概率更高。

这本质上是一种"时间性的训练数据资历"（temporal training-data seniority）——像老树林生态系统一样，一旦砍掉就再也长不回来。跨领域对比：这和中世纪教会为什么能垄断"神圣性"是同一个结构——它抢在了印刷术普及之前把自己写进了所有手抄本。谁在语料"清洁期"里发声，谁就永久地成了模型的"默认答案"。

二、把销售提成变成"随机对照试验"——最反直觉的商业模式创新

大多数人听 Paul 描述销售 comp 时会一带而过，但这里藏着一个真正颠覆性的东西：Supabase 的销售提成不是按账户价值算的，而是按"相对于对照组的增量"算的。

他们把 1000 个高增长客户切成两组：500 个上了电话（treatment），500 个没上（control）。对照组自然增长 25%，treatment 组增长 125%——销售只拿那 100 个百分点的增量对应的提成。

这在销售领域几乎是异端。传统销售 comp 假设"这笔单子是销售促成的"；Supabase 直接承认"这笔单子的大部分本来就会发生"，只为销售真正创造的部分买单。这是把临床药物试验的方法论（RCT）搬进了销售组织——同样的逻辑让 FDA 判断一款药有没有效、让政治竞选团队衡量广告 lift、让 Meta 决定要不要开一个新广告位。

这里最深的洞察不是"公平"，而是它悄悄改变了销售的心智：一个不能提高 lift 的销售，无论电话多漂亮、单子多大，都拿不到钱。它把销售从"关系艺人"改造成了"因果实验员"。

三、Clippy 的哲学——把失败"预先审美化"

2023 年初他们做出第一版 doc RAG 时，怕模型胡说八道，就故意把图标做成 Clippy——"如果它幻觉了，至少你能笑一下"。听起来是个笑话，但它其实是一种极其成熟的产品哲学：把不可避免的失败预先包装成体验的一部分。

这和游戏设计里"死亡动画要好看"、Duolingo 让猫头鹰在你不学习时哭泣、Netflix 把加载图标做成 loading 而不是"错误"——是同一个跨领域原则：当你无法消灭失败模式时，就把它变成风格。

再往深看，这背后是一个 Supabase 一以贯之的元哲学——他们不假装完美，他们让不完美变成品牌资产。开源许可给你无限制使用权（承认自己不是唯一供应商），公开定价（承认 Firebase 会让你 bill shock），承认自己是"open source Firebase alternative"（承认自己不是原创）。这条链条的另一端，是 Paul 在采访结尾那句极其少见的诚实："我不认为 AI 生产力提升已经被证明了——只要人还在 loop 里，就不算真正的收益。"

一家公司如果敢在采访里承认这个，说明他们内部的决策系统不依赖"我们赢了"的叙事撑着。这或许才是 Supabase 真正跑得比对手快的原因：它是一家不需要靠幻觉运转的公司。

四、一个隐藏的悖论作为彩蛋

Paul 说 60% 以上的数据库是 agent 创建的，但他"猜"实际接近 90%——因为 agent 通过 CLI 创建时他们根本看不到。这意味着 Supabase 已经不知道自己的客户是谁了。

这不只是度量问题，这是一个哲学时刻：当你的"用户"是一个由人类朦胧驱动的软件实体，"客户成功"、"NPS"、"用户访谈"这些 SaaS 时代的基石概念全部失效。Supabase 无意间成了第一批必须给不可见客户做产品的公司之一。他们的 dashboard 日活还在涨，但占比在跌——他们正在见证一个奇怪的现象：产品的表面被人类使用得越来越少，但产品的深处被使用得越来越多。

这个反转，在互联网历史上只出现过一次可比的：搜索引擎从"给人看"变成"给爬虫和 SEO 优化"的那几年。Supabase 现在站在的位置，就是当年 Google 面对 SEO 觉醒的那个前夜。

Host: And of course open source — the models know your code. So they're probably great at implementing on top of you.

Paul: Exactly, exactly. So getting recommended as a default was one of the things that was a huge tailwind for us. And it would be incredibly hard, especially now. I imagine that as we go along and people are producing a lot of content, the training of the models on content after 2023 is not going to be as high quality as things that are earlier on.

So we were very lucky, if I'm honest, on our timing, and doing it with the community that we had and the content that we had produced. So now we have to focus on — well, how do we retain that? But even if we don't, then, you know, let's say that the models all end up choosing AWS because that just defaults to be the same thing. Then, or us and every other dev tool are back on an equal playing field.

So how do you compete if the models already have their defaults? Then it's either partnerships, or you just have to win eyeballs of developers, and then they might have preferences that they guide the AI to use whatever they prefer. So it's still important to communicate to your community.

高速增长下的组织：从 order-maker 到 order-taker

Host: So three chapters where AI kind of had a big impact on you and accelerated growth. At this point, I mean, your course is insane. What does that mean operationally? Like, how do you actually scale as a company?

Paul: In the initial stages of Supabase, we had this really strict policy of hiring — and our policy was: you only hire when there is a hair-on-fire problem. So, something that a full-time employee could handle, and otherwise we just manage it.

Then as we started growing, of course, the amount of users pouring in, and the amount of support that we needed to give, and the amount of IP addresses running out, and all sorts of random things that you don't think about…

Host: Sounds like you don't think about that when you're small.

Paul: No. So what is like a planned roadmap ends up just being a lot of things coming in from the side, and partnerships coming in that you can't say no to, and all sorts of stuff that happen. So the shift goes from you pushing a lot to you basically being an order-maker to an order-taker.

And we have all these things coming in where we just didn't have enough hands on keyboard to solve them. And that of course means we've got to focus on reliability, and scaling up the meta processes of the company — managers, and hiring staff, and everything else. So you go through that second stage of: first you focus on your roadmap, then you focus on your business.

Host: How many people are you today?

Paul: Now we're about 360.

Host: Which is pretty small.

Paul: It's quite small for the scale of the business. But grown fast this year — I think we started the year at about 220. So we've had to add a lot of people this year.

Host: It's all mostly to pretty much support the growth. The business is going so fast.

Paul: Yes. All to — yeah, so that's where we switch.

Host: Can you give us a sense of how fast the business is growing?

Paul: I think maybe in terms of the number of developers — maybe in the past 12 months, at a guess, I think it would be six or 7x.

Host: Okay. So 7x at your scale is…

Paul: Yeah, of a base of millions.

Host: So we're already at millions of developers. And now we are, like, what, 10 million or something?

Paul: Yeah, we're at 10 million. Yeah, so I think we started this year with something like 6.5 million. And so the acceleration this year has been hard to keep up with.

Launch Week 与 Defrag：从交替到并行

Host: Wow. Okay. So you're just trying to keep the foundation working. So you don't have that much — how do you continue innovating then?

Paul: Yeah. I think we were very famous in the early stages for our launch weeks. And that was really a big focus on velocity, and getting the roadmap out, making sure that we've got feature parity with everything. And that was a good stage, and a lot of fun of course.

And then what we would do was: we would move from launch week — and we'd do this for 3 months — and then we would do a period afterwards which we would call defrag. And defrag is from the old computer term where you refactor everything and organize everything.

Host: So you'd alternate between these two things.

Paul: And then since maybe about 12 months ago, everything's felt like defrag, as we've had to grow and do a lot of initiatives. And that kind of points to a key change in the company — where we would previously work in lockstep as an entire company, and now we're having to move… so okay, you don't operate that way as an entire company. Some of you have to always be focused on defrag; some of you can, after you move past your SLOs as an engineering company, focus more on velocity. And we need to get to a more nuanced way where there's always both of these activities happening in parallel, and then making sure we have systems set up so that we can continue to do that.

Host: The success — this crazy success — actually has a cost.

Paul: Yes, it has a cost in the short term, and then you have to be very deliberate about how you can focus on both of these things.

分布式团队意外成为 AI 时代的护城河

Host: And does that kind of disruption from AI that helps you — does that change also the way you operate internally inside the company?

Paul: Of course, a lot of companies focus on flashy terms like "token maxing" and things like that. We haven't done that, but we also haven't had to. We've been very fortunate in one key thing: Supabase as a company is completely distributed. So we have 360 people and we're spread across 60 different countries — more than 60 countries.

So this means everything that happens is written down on Slack, on Notion, and…

Host: It's not like every other company that started doing that 6 months ago. You have done that for six years.

Paul: Yeah. And we've got the full history of Supabase written down all the way back to the start of the company. So if I want to find out what decision we made right at the start, I can ask Slackbot and find the answer.

Host: The context you have — like the complete context of the company, since inception, available to AI.

Paul: Yes, yes.

So when you use agents to help you in your job, they have — like, this couldn't have more context. Yeah, exactly. So new people coming in — or even they might not be new people, they might just be someone who is, let's say, a CFO or an analyst who wants to understand something — instead of coming to me and asking what the timelines are and how do I explain this product to an investor, they can actually ask a bot, and the bot will explain it better than I can. So that's nice.

And then from this point on, what I have traditionally thought of as just BizOps is now AI-enabled BizOps. So we're looking at systems that we can automate end-to-end, where we can introduce AI and automate the entire process — as long as it's an end-to-end process.

So things like — could be as simple as creating the AI notes, but also generating them, finding the action items, and feeding it all into a company operating system. Which hopefully at some stage, we're thinking of trying to move everything to Linear, including the non-engineering folk, so that we've got task management. And if we ever need to have bots solving things — of course the engineers are the ones adopting these tools now, but as we develop it with engineering, then it'll trickle out to non-engineering teams.

Host: So today you mostly will get a lot of productivity gain on the engineering side. But the next frontier is every other function.

Paul: I think — I wouldn't say productivity gain if I'm really honest, because I know a lot of people like to harp on about that, but I don't think it's proven out yet.

Host: That's what I think.

Paul: Yeah. I think, for a full productivity gain, you really need that full end-to-end process. So if you only unlock one piece of the puzzle, then you still need a full engineer stepping in. So the true gains will come from where you have no human in the loop.

We've seen some success in this actually on the data engineering team.

Host: So you mean like the human becomes the bottleneck here because they have to approve everything.

Paul: Yeah.

Host: And you already have some of these loops working with automation?

Paul: Yes, yes. So a good one was from our data engineering team. We now ingest everything into our data warehouse, and we use a tool called Hex — which is great, and it's got an agent — and we now opened up Hex to our entire company. So we kind of format the data warehouse so that the agent will understand the context. And this includes sales calls and things like that.

So now if anyone in the company — a salesperson, CFO, a product person — wants to understand something, maybe a metric, or our revenue growth, or even the history of a particular customer and what their needs are, they can go into this and they can ask a question. They will get a much more detailed answer than what a data engineer traditionally would produce.

And this is good because we now can measure: if a data engineer, in a traditional sense, could answer say 300 questions per month — we can see how many questions are being asked across the entire company. And it turns out that actually there are three times as many questions being asked, because of the way that they've engineered the data warehouse. So this is good — you can see that we're already getting some gains. Now what we want to see is that replicated out to other teams, where you very much have people focus on the systems part of it, and if those systems can unlock higher productivity, then that is great.

用"对照组"给销售发提成

Yeah, I think we've talked in the past about our sales team is another really interesting one.

Host: Yeah, where you can also…

Paul: Yeah, the sales team. So we traditionally operated on a PLG model. In fact, not even traditionally — it's all PLG. And then we thought, "All right, we want to introduce salespeople."

But what you would typically do, as you would know, is introduce some salespeople who kind of flounder around a little bit trying to sell something. But you know, we've got a bunch of data from our customers, and we also want them to be very helpful. So we can see that an account might have had a poor experience with the database — and so we can send, "All right, a thousand of these customers are growing very fast. They've hit some limits and they might be frustrated." So we'll send out an email to a thousand of them, and maybe 500 of them respond saying, "Yes, I want to get on a call." And then from there, the salesperson — or actually it's very much like a success or support person — gets on the call.

Host: But they still are getting commission?

Paul: Yes. So they get commission. But the way that we do this is: instead of compensating them on the entire account… so let's say a customer was spending $100 a month. If we measure the thousand — we take the entire cohort of a thousand — we take 500 who didn't respond. If at the end of the month their uplift is 25%, then that's our control group.

Host: Yeah.

Paul: But then if we take the cohort of people who actually chatted to the salespeople, and we know actually the uplift on that is 125%, so there's a 100% gain compared to the cohort who did not actually get on a call — and that's what the commission is based on.

Host: And then the commission is based on that.

Paul: So their input is actually quite measurable. And this is quite a different model from a sales-led motion.

Host: Mhm. And so they are compensated on the improvement from the default behavior that's already growing.

Paul: Exactly.

融资：现金不等于成功

Host: Awesome. Let's go back to maybe funding as the last topic here. Because, as you said before, you've gone through that hyper-growth a few times lately. I mean, that acceleration which led you to raise a lot more money — like in the last two years you did three rounds, and the last one was 500 million at over 10 billion valuation. And all that in less than two years. What does that mean for the company? Like, how do you stay grounded?

Paul: Yeah. Well, it's a lot of money. But of course, as you become bigger, you need a lot more operating cash to float you between two different periods — the period where you can launch a database and someone can build on top of it, and then they start paying you. So we of course want to have that operating capital to make sure that we can float between these two. And as long as we know the economics stack up, then it's very reasonable for us to continue doing that. So that's great.

Having the cash in the bank is basically to give us that operating capital.

Then from there, staying grounded is largely a factor of just remembering that the cash actually doesn't mean that you're successful. I think actually YC drilled this into you — where the fundraise itself is just a meta process.

Host: It's a means to an end. It's not…

Paul: It's just a — yeah, exactly. And if having more cash was the thing that made you successful, then by all rights Supabase would not exist. There are many of our competitors who have far more cash — huge companies — but still, we exist because we did things that they don't, and we should continue focusing on those things that we do very well as the way to continue to grow our stake in the market.

Host: How about the team itself? I mean, being grounded as a founder is the first step. But when the team sees these numbers, it's easy for them to probably get a little lost.

Paul: A lot of it spills out from the early founders. I mean, our way of operating is very much like a YC model, and then you hire in a bunch of people who are also of the same mindset. We've got a bunch of YC founders that work there, and a lot of ex-founders, and this trickles out into the rest of the organization. And then yeah, we try to treat our employees very, very well, but also be very transparent with them that, you know, we want to continue doing it in a way that we can look back and be quite proud of.

给 Dev Tool 创始人的建议

Host: To conclude — what kind of advice could you give to other, maybe dev-tool founders, who are starting today in this kind of unseen, unprecedented world they are navigating today?

Paul: The most generic advice that I can give — which they should already be doing — is: you have to be quite relentless and prolific. So you have to try many things, and when you find the things that work, then you have to relentlessly push on that thing to see where it can continue to grow. And then you try many things around it as well.

So as long as you have those two mindsets, then it basically translates to a grind mindset. And then, hopefully with a bit of luck, you should find some success. And luck is a very component — a very component of a successful startup.

Host: Awesome. Thank you so much, Paul, for joining us today and sharing your story.

Paul: Thank you.

Host: Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、被冻结在模型权重里的"老树林"——一种前所未见的护城河
Paul 讲了一句几乎被采访者本人低估的话："2023 年之后训练模型用的内容，质量不会像更早期的那么高。"如果你把这句话往前推一步，会发现 Supabase 拥有的最深护城河，不在产品里，而在**每一个大模型的权重里**。
2020–2022 年他们在 Hacker News、Discord、Reddit、GitHub 上留下的每一行讨论，都被当时"干净的、人类写的、非 AI 生成的"语料吸进了 GPT-4、Claude、Gemini 的基础训练集。这些权重不会因为竞争对手今年融了多少钱而重写。竞对哪怕拿 10 亿美金去做内容营销，产出的也是 2024 年之后的"AI-slop 时代"内容，权重更低、被去重的概率更高。
这本质上是一种**"时间性的训练数据资历"（temporal training-data seniority）**——像老树林生态系统一样，一旦砍掉就再也长不回来。跨领域对比：这和中世纪教会为什么能垄断"神圣性"是同一个结构——它抢在了印刷术普及之前把自己写进了所有手抄本。谁在语料"清洁期"里发声

item.title: [Lex Clips] Does Khabib hate Conor McGregor? | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、情绪即战术：冷静不是修养，而是"武器化的自我"

大多数人把 Khabib 的冷静理解为"高情商"或"东方式克制"，但仔细听他的原话——"你会更快疲惫、更容易上当、更容易倒下"——他谈的其实是能量经济学。情绪不是道德问题，而是热力学问题：愤怒会以极高的功率消耗有限的糖原储备。这解释了一个被忽视的悖论：在八角笼里，最"冷血"的人往往是最诚实地对待自己身体极限的人。McGregor 的挑衅之所以危险，不是因为它侮辱人，而是因为它试图让对手替自己燃烧燃料。Khabib 拒绝上钩，本质上是拒绝为对方的战术做免费的代谢劳动。

二、跨领域连接：交易员、狙击手、外科医生的共同秘密

Khabib 描述的那种"press conference、weigh-in、媒体面前全程压制"的状态，与顶级期权交易员在市场崩盘时的心率数据、狙击手扣扳机前的呼吸控制曲线、以及心脏外科医生在术中意外出血时的语速变化——三者在生理指标上高度重合。共同点是：他们都必须在"情绪回报最丰厚的时刻"选择延迟满足。有趣的是，Khabib 自己承认"打完之后我让情绪全部涌出"——这暴露了一个反直觉的系统真相：极致的自控不是压抑，而是精确的情绪时序管理。他不是没有仇恨，而是把仇恨排程到了对结果无害的时段。这才是"冷静"的工程学定义。

三、意外观察：八年后的"惊讶"，才是这段访谈真正的深水区

大多数人会聚焦"他有没有恨 Conor"，但真正的爆点被埋在最后一句："looking back, I'm a little surprised… it wasn't easy." 这句话泄露了一个更深的秘密——当年的 Khabib 自己也不完全相信自己能做到。也就是说，那种传奇般的冷静并非天生的性格特质，而是一次高风险的自我实验，一次他事后才敢承认"其实很悬"的走钢丝。这里藏着一个反常识的领导力真相：外界看到的"稳如泰山"，内部体验往往是"勉强扛住"。这与创业者、总统、宇航员在事后回忆重大决策时的语言模式惊人一致——当事人越是事后表达"惊讶自己做到了"，说明当时的心理裕度越薄。真正的强者不是没有裂缝的人，而是知道自己裂缝在哪里，并把战斗安排在裂缝扩大之前结束的人。Khabib 打完就退役，某种意义上，也是这套系统性认知的延伸：他知道那口"冷静的井"不是无底的。

📝 转录文本

关于内心的愤怒与仇恨

Well, when you look into your heart back then and now, did you have anger? Did you have hatred for him?

Back then and even now, I'd still keep a cool head. Nothing has changed.

情绪失控的代价

When you let your emotions take over, when they're off the charts and you completely lose control, that's a very bad place to be. So you'll tire out faster. You'll fall. You'll fall for any kind of bait and so on.

I just knew that I needed to stay calm, composed, to stick to the plan no matter what happened, and not go beyond my emotional limits. This is a very, very dangerous moment when you give in to your emotions. You have to control them. Every single detail, every little thing has to be perfectly in place. The second you let it all slip, everything becomes a total mess.

比赛结束之后的释放

So once the fight was finally done, I just let all my emotions out. I had to step right in and prove it, and punish him, and show them I'm better, that I'm better than him, and put a final end to this whole bitter rivalry. When all of that was over—

Your emotions came out?

…that's when my emotions just went over the edge.

But until the fight was completely finished, starting from training, you know, at the press conferences, at the weigh-ins, everywhere, in front of the media, everywhere, I kept myself completely under control, and I was very good at it.

八年之后的回望

Honestly, looking back it's been almost eight years now. Looking back, well, I'm a little surprised. At that point, I was a very emotional guy, too. Over these eight years a lot has happened in my life, but I'm surprised that I kept it together.

And well, you know, it wasn't easy for me to keep myself within my limits, to keep myself under control like that.
