item.title: [Business of Sport] Walter & Boehly’s Rumoured Chelsea Exit, the PFA Takes on the EFL, & The Meteoric Rise of Padel
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个故事，一个隐藏的主线：当"体育资产"被当作"金融工具"使用时会发生什么

一、LIV Golf：不是财务失败，而是"声誉套利"的反向清算

表面看，LIV 拖欠奖金和供应商账款是流动性问题。但如果你把 PIF（沙特公共投资基金）进入 LIV 的初衷理解为"用金钱购买声誉"的套利交易，你会发现一件出人意料的事：这笔交易正在以极高的杠杆倒挂。

沙特一开始的隐含逻辑是：即便烧掉 20 亿美元，只要能"洗白"国家形象、让世界习惯 Saudi = Sport，投入就是划算的。但现在的局面是——每一美元未支付的账单，都在以 5–10 倍的效率反向摧毁那笔"声誉投资"。这跟 WeWork 崩塌时的机制完全一样：叙事型资本一旦叙事反转，估值会以非线性速度归零。

更狠的一个观察：主持人提到的"付大 V 不付小供应商"的分流策略，在金融机构处置有毒资产时是标准操作（想想 2008 年雷曼破产时的债权人分级）。体育行业正在被迫学习投行的"声誉三角"——先保住能上头条的债权人，再牺牲沉默的多数。这是体育史上第一次，一个赛事组织公开采用了华尔街的破产分选逻辑。

二、PFA vs EFL：这不是劳资纠纷，是"谁承担系统性风险"的哲学之战

主持人拿 Arthur Scargill（1980 年代英国矿工工会领袖）来比喻 Maheta，已经是一个漂亮的类比。但真正被忽视的一层是：PFA 的"更大傻瓜理论"（bigger idiot theory）——总会有更蠢的下一个买家接盘——跟加密货币牛市末期的心态一字不差。

这里有一个跨领域连接非常尖锐：72 家英足联俱乐部中 47 家在挂牌出售，卖方远多于买方——这是流动性衰竭的经典信号，在房地产、艺术品、乃至 SPAC 市场都出现过。PFA 押注的是"接盘侠永续存在"，但接盘侠是利率环境的函数，不是体育情感的函数。当全球利率不再零成本，"社区情怀 + 亏损运营"这个商业模型的定价基础就崩塌了。

更让我震惊的洞察：足球俱乐部第一次要面对"没有下一个买家"的存在性问题——而 PFA 用的是 1960 年代 Jimmy Hill 反抗最高工资时的思维框架来打 2025 年的仗。工会用一个"稀缺型经济"（球员被剥削）的斗争剧本，来对付一个"过剩型危机"（俱乐部无法出售）的现实，这在结构上注定错位。

三、Mark Walter：体育行业刚刚发现自己变成了"影子银行"

Walter 的故事是本期最深的一个信号。他被指控用保险公司浮存金去买 Dodgers、Lakers、Chelsea——这个模式听起来很熟悉是吗？这正是 Warren Buffett 的 Berkshire Hathaway 模型：用保险浮存金作为超低成本长期资本去投资优质资产。

但这里有个惊人的反转：Buffett 投的是有稳定现金流的"经济护城河"企业；Walter 投的是没有现金流、只有资本增值故事的体育队。这本质上是把"影子银行"和"数字艺术品"嫁接在一起——保险监管的红线（10% 单一敞口）遇到体育资产的估值狂热（4 年翻倍）。

跨领域连接：这跟 2021 年 Archegos 爆仓、以及 Greensill/GFG Alliance 崩塌的机制几乎完全同源——将高流动性负债（保险赔付义务、供应链应付款）与低流动性资产（体育股权、钢厂设备）错配。SEC 现在盯上 Walter，其实是在向整个行业释放一个信号：当体育队的价格达到 100 亿美元级别时，它们已经不再是"玩具"，而是必须按金融资产被监管的"系统重要性物品"。

未来 3–5 年最不被讨论、但最关键的变化：大型体育资产的买家池会从"富豪个人"永久性地转向"必须接受金融监管的机构资本"。这将改变所有权文化——想想 Todd Boehly 与 Clearlake 的内斗为什么会公开化：私募基金 vs. 富豪 clanky 家族办公室，是两种不兼容的治理哲学。

四、Padel 的隐藏悖论：唯一一个"网络效应为负"的运动

关于 Padel，播客的分析已经很扎实，但漏掉了一个反直觉的结构性问题：

Padel 是唯一一个"稀缺时最赚钱、丰裕时最健康"的运动。

  • 球场稀缺 → 每小时 100 英镑 → 投资回报好 → 但精英层培养不出来（没有场地练习）
  • 球场丰裕 → 单场收入下降 → Sweden 式的商业崩盘 → 但精英层能起飞

这在经济学上叫"网络效应反转"——大多数运动（篮球、足球、跑步）随着参与者增多，每个参与者的效用都上升；但 Padel 的商业价值和竞技价值是反向拉扯的。

跨领域连接：这跟精品咖啡产业的困境几乎一样——第三波咖啡馆越多，单店利润越薄，但整个品类的品味培养和从业者水平却提升。Padel 想成为一个全球性的观赏运动，必须先经历一段商业上的"下沉痛苦期"——而目前的资本方（大多是把它当作房地产 + 会员制生意做的）根本不愿意支付这个成本。

最出乎意料的预测：Padel 会先在印度或东南亚（而非美国）实现真正的爆炸性增长，因为那些市场的中产阶级密度 + 土地成本 + 社交型运动偏好，恰好是 Padel 商业模型的最佳温床。而当这一天到来时，欧洲的 Padel 泡沫可能已经破了一轮。

贯穿本期节目的隐藏主线：体育资产正在经历一场"金融化的成熟"——它不再是富豪的浪漫玩具，而是被利率、监管、破产法、劳资关系等成人世界的规则同时压迫的资产类别。LIV 的账单、Walter 的保险、EFL 的成本控制、Padel 的场地经济学——它们都是同一个故事的四个切片：体育终于长大了，但相关方还在用小孩子的规则思考。

Why do the clubs need to do that? Why can't the clubs just run their businesses properly?

I never thought I'd have a discussion with you where you seriously question the requirement for cost controls in sport.

I'm not saying that at all. I'm not saying there's a requirement of cost controls. I'm trying to... No, no, Charlie, come on. There's two angles. One's coming at it from here. You put across the strong side. I'm looking at it from another side and just... I'm putting, should we say, their discussion point across.

My point, honestly, is what is the difference between clubs being able to run some of these businesses collectively more efficiently themselves? Because that's what people will look at. They're going, look, I run a company. If I overspend based on what I bring in, whether it's regulated or not, I am going to fail as a business operator. So... To Mehetta's point, he's basically saying you're making the decisions to do this, to cap our players as the main reason for you overspending.

This is not a cap. Clubs can pay as much as you want under this system, as long as your revenue is vaguely supported. So interestingly, I checked in with the authorities and found out that overall wage spending in League One this summer is higher than it was previous to these regulations. So the idea that the entire point of this is to cap things, to force things down, to get rid of things is wrong. The idea here is to try and make sure that these social institutions — these aren't corner shops, which if they close down, there's no impact. These are social institutions. When they do go bust, whole cities are left in floods of tears.

Now, I know Mahetta doesn't give a damn about that. All he cares about is making more money for his punters, right? But fundamentally, the government has decided by instituting the independent football regulator, the IFR, that it does care. And his formal mandate is to introduce and enforce sustainability in English football. And I think by setting his heart against sustainability, Mehetta is on the wrong side of this argument and the PFA is on the wrong side of this argument.

There's a whole bunch of stuff as a trade unionist that I would, I think, footballers in many ways should have more of a say on — right, the calendar being a critical one. I think there's too much football. I think Mehetta's right in this and the welfare and the career longevity of players is being put at risk and this is the kind of stuff which if I was a trade union leader I would be absolutely staking my heart off me saying "this is important, this is really important". Do we actually think that League One players being paid £600,000 pounds a year is a societal problem? No. No one thinks that.

"德国式劳资关系"的替代方案

So can I ask, how would you do this? Knowing that this is going to be an issue, right? How should the EFL approach the PFA in this situation?

What I would like to see — which, given the attitude that PFA is highly unlikely — is a much more German-style attitude towards labour relations within our industry, where basically the trade union leaders and the business leaders both sit down together and say, right, how can we work together to make our industry as investable and sustainable and successful as possible? Because out the back of that will come profits and out of profits becomes a real serious discussion about who gets a share of the profits. But when you're basically arguing that clubs should lose dump loads of money to make sure that players can get paid much more than the market revenue suggests that they should be getting, I don't think you're in a good place.

And so in answer to your question, here's what I think is going to happen. Either this case is actually lodged and it's fought, and the case is, as you say, very much on what happened at PFNCC. It's not about whether cost caps are legal. Cost caps are legal. They exist in every other sport. So you're not going to win a court case on whether this is a restrictive trade or something like that when cricket, rugby, Formula One, all the other sports have cost caps. That's not going to work.

So really the debate here is about the specificity of what the PFNCC agreements relate to. And ultimately, either the EFL will win this debate or else they'll just walk out of the PFNCC. So I just don't see that as a win. I don't see why the EFL leaving the PFNCC will be a win for lower league footballers in this country. That will then unravel a whole load of other agreements between the trade union and the leagues across lots and lots of different things, which worked to the benefit of both sides in many cases.

Right. So there'll be some things which the union can then say to the league, right, now you're out of PFNCC, we withdraw our agreement on X or Y. And there'll be other things where the Football League says, OK, well, if you want to withdraw your agreement on that, then we withdraw our agreements in terms of how much we pay into pensions and all this type of stuff. So it's a real hornet's nest.

And what it comes down to is, is the Football League like the Premier League and UEFA, allowed through its members to run its own competition? The PFA says no. The Football League says yes. So now we will see.

We will see what happens. If it does come to court, it will be a real landmark case which will set out an awful lot of unintended consequences down the track. And I would much rather if there was a more constructive relationship which really went towards "we need to make these clubs investable". If at any point in time these clubs do not attract investors, we've got big problems. Everyone's got big problems.

So the direction of travel right now is in that direction where there are more clubs for sale than there are investors available. It absolutely should be in a responsible trade union's mind of saying, if we want this whole gravy train to continue, we need to make sure that there are enough investors around to keep on funding it. Because even if the outcome of these spending controls are to reduce annual losses in League One from 7 million to 3 million, that's still 3 million. You still need somebody to put in 3 million.

独立监管机构的杠杆

The regulator's mandate is sustainability. So when I was just looking at this, firstly, I just thought, well, surely the regulator's inclusion just massively favours the EFL rather than the PFA. But that assumes that the PFA doesn't care about sustainability.

Which it absolutely should do and normal trade unions would do. And I can say that having been a trade union leader myself, I would have been horrified if the newspaper that I was representing journalists at lost money, because I would know eventually where that would lead in some way, shape or form. That would lead to loss of jobs. That would lead to loss of certainty.

So I think that's the little wake up call that needs to happen here. But I'm very happy to discuss it with Mehetta. He's a very different type of person to Gordon Taylor. He wears a much better suit. He's more articulate in many ways, but fundamentally the cultural attitude of the PFA remains where it was when it was founded by Jimmy Hill and co. When in those days we actually had effectively a maximum wage, a very, very hard cap, and they were fighting against very low pay, footballers finishing their career in poverty.

And I totally look back historically and think those guys as a trade union, I'm still a trade union member now, as a trade unionist, I look back and say those guys are heroes. They fought against genuine issues and they fought really hard against them. I don't see that right here and right now. And currently, as I said, I don't own an English football club right now, and I am still a trade union member. So I'm not a vested interest right now. I'm an onlooker who can see both sides and who looks at this and just thinks the PFA is getting itself into a really odd, weird position, which I don't think will command much public sympathy when it comes down to it.

And when the first club goes bust, which by the way is going to happen, it's going to happen soon, and the finger gets pointed as to why that has happened, under those circumstances the government might well act and say, "Do you know what? The IFR needs much stronger powers here. The IFR needs to be able to set the spending controls." Because I think ultimately that's where it's going to go, right? Because if the independent football regulator has sustainability as part of his legal statutory mandate, but he has no control over how much is spent, how can he fulfil his statutory mandate?

I'm very happy to debate the whole issue with Maheta with you invigilating, Charlie. So let's bring it on.

Yeah, well, you didn't like my devil's advocate there, did you? So I can't wait to see what happens when I'm sitting properly in the middle of you two.

I never thought I'd have an argument with you about cost control, Charlie.

第三幕：Mark Walter、Todd Boehly 与 Blueco 的震荡

Shall we take a look and move into the crazy world of Mark Walter, the LA Lakers, the empire that seems to be crumbling from a sports perspective, the potential impact that it has on Chelsea FC, because this is probably one of the biggest sports business stories in a very, very long time.

Mark Walter 是谁？

I'll tell you what, let's just start off by explaining who Mark Walter is because he won't be a name that's necessarily all that familiar to European and Australasian sports fans.

Mark Walter is a very successful financial services investor tycoon from the US. And he founded, co-founded, a financial services business called Guggenheim Partners back in — I actually remember it happening, so I knew some people who were doing it with him back in the late 1990s, early 2000s, or 25 years ago, and he's in his mid-60s now. So he wasn't even, you know, he was 40 years old when he founded what has gone on to become an enormously successful fund, basically asset manager, huge amounts of assets under management. He himself has effectively got his shares in Guggenheim and that's held in an entity called TWG, where he also has holdings in other companies that he has acquired interests in along the way, including inter alia insurance businesses and including sports businesses.

And he has been successful in most everything that he has done. You know, the insurance business has been a very good business to be in over the last 25 years. And on the sports side, he, together with a guy who he had as an underling of his at Guggenheim around the turn of the century, a man known as Todd Boley — then Boley left Guggenheim Partners, but with Walter's blessing and still as very close friends to start doing his own things. But they came together to get into sport when they bought the Dodgers.

It is broadly considered that since buying the Dodgers, they have done an outstanding job with the Dodgers. And more recently, they formed part of the new ownership group that took over Chelsea now five years ago, Charlie. Is that right?

2022, wasn't it?

Yeah, four years ago.

Okay, so four years ago. And even more recently, they bought the LA Lakers, the basketball team, for an absolutely colossal $10 billion a couple of years ago.

So what you're looking at here is a massively expanding sports empire where you've got the LA Dodgers, you've got the LA Lakers, you've got between those two and their friend Hans-Jörg Weiss, they've got almost 40% of Chelsea and therefore of Strasbourg through Blueco.

保险资金的合规炸弹

So you've got this extraordinary, successful-looking team portfolio of businesses that runs from states in Guggenheim, a massive asset management company, to states in insurers, to states in blue chip sports businesses across the world in some of the biggest sports in the world. And suddenly, it now looks like the Empire might be coming crashing down.

And by the Empire, I do mean particularly his sports empire, because what has happened here, it is alleged and said, is that effectively part of his engine for buying these massive stakes in these hugely valuable sports franchises has come through financing provided by insurance businesses that he also controls.

Now, you might say, well, so what if he controls those businesses, then why shouldn't he use money from those businesses to buy sports stakes in sports enterprises? Well, the answer is insurance is a highly regulated form of financial services for the obvious reason, which is if you have an insurance premium with an insurance firm, you need to know and expect that in the event that that premium needs to be activated into a payout, so that payout can and will be made.

So insurance businesses have to be very clear about where it is that they put their money. And they have to be doubly clear when that money is being put into entities which have the same ownership as the insurance business because no one wants to be in a situation where money which should be being used to fund payouts on insurance premiums down the track has been, let's say, siphoned off and used in ways which people weren't really aware of.

Now, the SEC…

Well, it's over-exposure. It's over-exposure, sorry, is the key bit there. So you are actually allowed to do that, as you said, but generally the regulation would cap it at about 10% so that if an individual who owned lots of these businesses had something happen to them and let's say their business empire collapsed, all of the businesses around it would be impacted by that. And if 40% — which is what the rumoured number here that Mark Walter has exposed it to has happened — then that is a serious overexposure and therefore breaking the rules and regulations that exist around this.

Exactly that. And the critical thing there is about the transparency, right? Which is that you have to declare what it is that you're investing the money in, in order that people can then say, "Okay, that's 10%." Right? If it then subsequently becomes clear that not everything has been declared in that way, and that the actual number isn't 10%, but it's 40%, then you've got a problem from a regulatory perspective.

And that is what the SEC — which is the US's financial regulatory authority, and enormously powerful and scary, frankly — has been investigating. Now, whether the SEC does or does not end up bringing a case, or if there is any proof of wrongdoing, whatever it might be, at this point we can't know and we don't know. All we do know is that Mark Walter has decided for whatever reason that he is going to start replacing money that had been sourced from his insurance company with his own cash.

Right now, whether that's an admission of guilt on the one hand, or on the other hand, it might be him saying, "I don't even want to go down that track of getting into a fight with the SEC. I just want to make sure that we're totally absolutely fine here because I don't want to spend the rest of my life fighting lawsuits against the financial regulators." It could be either.

抛售 Lakers：48 小时的"仓促"交易

But the reality is what he started to do is liquidate his positions in sports entities in order to fund the cash that had been provided to buy those sports entities by the insurance businesses. And here's where the rubber hits the road, right, Charlie? Which is, first of all, the Lakers were sold last week. Having bought them for $10 billion two years ago, he's now flipped the Lakers for $12 billion US to a consortium headed by who else than our recent friend, Joshua Kushner — who had previously been readying to buy FIFA Ford Enterprises from his mate Gianni Infantino.

So that's brought in a big chunk of change for Walter to help to start the process of paying down the gap between what is allowable and what's not allowable under, as you say, the exposure rules within the insurance industry.

And it is now strongly rumoured within the media that Mark Walter and his business partner, Todd Boley, are entering discussions, let's say, about selling their stake in Blueco, the owners of Chelsea, to their partners at Clearlake. $20 billion is reportedly what he needs to earn by the end of the year.

Look, I mean, the 12 and a half billion that he just sold the Lakers for, it made me laugh, Charlie. I mean, look, we know what it's like doing deals. A 12 and a half billion deal done in 48 hours suggests that there's something going on behind the scenes that isn't quite right. I mean, that is for the biggest, let's be clear as well, that is the biggest sports transaction involving an asset in history. And it was when the Lakers were bought last time. And a 2.5 billion profit on that transaction does look good.

But make no mistake, when Walter bought the Lakers, he would have wanted a far greater return. There would have been greater ambitions for this. He was in the middle of a serious business project behind the scenes that would have improved the Lakers value exponentially, even beyond this if he could have held on to it for a bit longer. That was always the plan. Bob Iger as well, who's joined Kushner on this, who's the former CEO of Disney, they were actually looking at an expansion franchise and were talking through a Las Vegas opportunity when this came up. Obviously, I think if you get the chance to buy into this, it's usually appealing, hence why probably the deal was done so quickly as well.

Chelsea 股份的定价博弈

But the key thing from Walter's side is, yes, it fixes a significant part of the problem, but he's still got a lot more to raise. Now you mentioned Chelsea. He owns 12.8% of Chelsea, equal to Todd Boley, equal to Hans-Jörg Weiss. The Telegraph reported a £5 billion valuation on the club to sell those shares. Clearlake reportedly are interested in buying these shares. As you'd expect, there's been tension at the Chelsea ownership level, very publicly reported for a very long time. So Clearlake could look at this and go, oh, can we get these shares at a steal?

On the flip side, if they buy them too cheap, then is it valuing the club far below potentially where they have bought it for and then invested money into? Will that impact the club's valuation moving forward when Clearlake get to the stage as we've discussed previously where they will have to look at how they exit the club?

So let's say they bought the shares off Boley and Walter for about £3 billion, which I think from discussions in the market is where the financial experts have positioned the club and said that you'd be able to justify that. They own 12%. So it means their stake is worth about 400 million, let's say.

Each.

Each. Yeah, but again, Boley's is Boley's money, I think. So Walter needs this money to pay his problems, unless Boley's tied up in this, which I don't think he is. It doesn't help. So Walter can get 400 million at a 3 billion pound valuation, but 5 billion pounds, right? So let's say that would be 700 million just under for Walter's stake. That's a billion dollars. So that's 1/20th of what he makes. So then let's say he's done 12.5 billion. That's taking him up to 13.5 billion dollars. If he's going to use sports assets as his premium way of generating this cash, the only way it looks like he's going to be able to do that is by selling the Dodgers.

Dodgers 可能才是压轴戏

Which you mentioned has been a success story. I mean, I think it is one of the big success stories. They bought it, interestingly, off the McCourt family, who you may remember as the Marseille owners from conversations we've had previously, when McCourt got into a bit of financial distress in 2012.

And the potential showjumping league, Charlie. Remember.

Yeah, and the professional show jumping league.

They bought it for $2.15 billion, I think, in 2012. And it's now valued at over $8 billion. $8 billion would clear the $20 billion mark if all of that money is going to Walter's pocket.

So, does it mean much for Chelsea? Does it mean much for Walter if he sells Chelsea? His biggest plays here are selling his American assets. And I don't think it actually really changes much for Chelsea at all because operationally, I don't think they have been hugely involved. And Walter's always done everything behind the scenes.

Blueco 债务、股权价值与治理连锁反应

Let's make some observations. So first of all, even if, let's say, that you did place a valuation on Chelsea of £5 billion, you would have to take into account the borrowing at Blueco level. So in other words, that borrowing is set against all of their equity, not just Clearlake's equity, that is Blueco borrowing, and that's believed to be about one and a half billion. So let's just say that you say, okay, the club's valued at five, but has debt of one and a half, then the equity valuation, the valuation of the equity in that is 3.5. And therefore, Boley and Walter and Hans-Jörg Weiss's share of that 3.5 is, let's say, 1.5, three, right? And as you say, therefore his share of that is a few hundred million.

I'll be interested to see if Walter and Boley are as dissociated as you suggest. My instinct is that their links run very, very, very deep in financing terms. The fact that they're involved in all of these deals together, the fact that they worked together for so long and have been involved 10, 12 years ago in slightly similar controversies around insurance funding and all this kind of stuff. I would be quite surprised to see Walter sell out of Blueco but Boley stay in. I think that this will be a moment.

I think it could just be Boley's opportunity to get his money. I think it could be Boley's opportunity to just get out. I think this could be not even an opportunity. I suspect that Clearlake might well say, right, if you guys want to get out, we'll buy you out. If you don't, then we won't. But what we're not going to do is pick off every time that one individual of you says, "I don't fancy it anymore." We're not going to keep on picking you off. Let's do it in one proper go.

As to your point about assessing evaluation on the club, I'm not sure if I was Clearlake that I would worry about that too much. I would hope that the market would recognise that my minority shareholders were in a weak position and that therefore whatever valuation they were afforded does not necessarily indicate the overall value of the majority shareholding in the club. You've just mentioned how in the space of a couple of years, despite having done absolutely nothing with the Lakers yet, the valuation has gone from 10 to 12.5. Now, we've already discussed before that Clearlake aren't going to be looking to get out of Chelsea until 2031, that sort of time. So we're still four to five years away from exit. So I would have thought this is actually quite a good moment for Clearlake to put the squeeze on Boley, Walter & Co and say, right, guys, you know, this is the moment you need out. You know, here you go. Here's some money. Now we're now in full control.

场外权力结构对场内运营的影响

In terms of what that means operationally at Chelsea, I think it might have a slightly bigger impact than one might think. I think I've said before on this podcast that when you've got turmoil behind the scenes amongst investor bases and ownership bases, it tends to have effects within the club that aren't easily seen from a fan perspective. I tend to find that senior executives within the club attach themselves to one side or the other side. And there tends to be, you know, sort of team, let's say in this case, Team Clearlake and Team Boley. We've mentioned there are five sporting directors and what you'll probably find is that one of those sporting directors is a bit close to Todd and one of them is a bit closer to Egbali and so on and so forth. I'm not saying I know that to be the case. This is an observation on how football clubs work in general.

So I'm a great believer that football clubs benefit from having a clearly identifiable source of authority and power within a club who everyone then knows if that person or that entity speaks, then it's "get that argument finished. That is then what is happening." And that then clears up a lot of the office politics and the internal sort of wrangling as that go on in the meantime. So I think it would be to Chelsea's benefit if at this point Boley and Walter — I can't speak for Hans-Jörg Weiss and his situation — but if those guys were to exit at this point, I think it would give Project Blueco a better chance of success going forward because it's been quite clear for some time that that relationship between Boley and Eghbali have become dysfunctional.

I expect things are going to move quite quickly on this one because as you say, Mark Walter needs to raise all this money by December of this year to prevent it becoming a broader issue. So, you know, let's see what happens and we can sort of, you know, keep people up to date as we go along. At the moment, it's still quite, you know, relatively early days.

第四幕：Padel — 参与狂潮 vs. 观赏低迷

Charlie, is it worth broaching finally a topic which we've been asked about many, many, many times because clearly a lot of our viewers and listeners are actually participants in this sport, which is padel. Let's blitz padel.

It's also the perfect moment, Charlie, because actually the show we did on the interview show this week is with one of the Team GB players. So we're going to double header padel this week for the core fans. You'll be a lot better informed than I am about it. Speak to me. It was quite nice preparation, actually.

两种截然不同的市场

There's two parts of this that are fascinating. One is a participation sport that is absolutely booming, and the other is a professional sport which is struggling to match the interest and attention that has been given to it from a participation level. There's a big discussion about how to make the professional and can the professional then catch up with the success that it is experiencing from people getting involved and playing the game.

My chat with Nikhil this week, who represents Team GB, as I said, very much indicated that while it is doing brilliantly, if you are winning a major, the premium championship, just like in tennis, of which there are four each year, and the prize money is 47,000 euros, there is a big challenge to make that a successful career opportunity for players getting involved in it. And right now, padel and the professionals in padel are creating opportunities and generating cash away from the court far more than they are on the court.

历史与地理：从墨西哥到全球

Should we start by just talking about, again, we kind of will anglify it inevitably, but we can mention it from the broader perspective as well, because England and the UK GB are very new in the global scheme of padel to taking this sport up.

So I think just to give a bit of the historical framework — I had to look around for this, so I'm not claiming to have been an expert prior to looking at this yesterday — but as Charlie says, the anglospheric world is late to the padel party. Padel was conceived as a sport in Mexico in 1969. And for decades, it was really just a sport in Latin America, Central America and Spain. And really with very, very little infiltration of other major markets.

It's absolutely spiralled in international popularity in the last five to ten years. And I'm not saying popularity, as Charlie rightly says earlier on, I mean participation. And to give you an idea, just in our country, the UK, where numbers are easily to hand, the LTA, the Lawn Tennis Association, took over the governance of it in 2020, when the participation, the numbers of people playing padel in the UK at that point was 15,000. It's now 1 million.

Right. Now, I'd have to go and run the numbers on other sports participation levels, but that is going to put it right towards the top of participation sports in this country. So if you think about a population of 70 million of whom 55 are of ages where you might reasonably participate, of which about 30, 25 to 30 participate in any sport whatsoever, and you've then got 1 million playing padel, that gives you an idea of the scale of it.

场地稀缺的经济学

Now, padel courts are very specific and require quite a lot of investment to put up and planning regulations can be quite tough against them for noise purposes. And that means that fundamentally there aren't enough padel courts in the country, which means that currently the amount of money that people are paying to access a padel court is about 50 pounds an hour, which is miles higher than for a normal tennis court. You know, there are a lot of tennis courts in this country which are free to use. There are others which are five pounds or ten pounds an hour to use. There are tennis clubs which are at most 50 pounds a month, right? So you're paying the same for a padel court for one hour as you are to being a member of a tennis club for a whole month.

Just quickly to jump in there, in London it can comfortably hit £100 an hour. The first comment on the show when it released yesterday was someone jumping on saying, "I pay £180 a year for my tennis membership and don't pay for the courts. I pay £100 an hour for a padel court at the nearest centre to me."

精英竞技 vs. 商业模型的天然矛盾

We get a lot of discussion points about tennis being an elitist sport and that being a significant problem for tennis. In tennis's case, any perception that it is an elite sport is entirely perceptional, right? I mean, the truth is that tennis is very easily accessible and very cheap in this country. And that's after hundreds of millions of investment over the last 30 to 40 years, which we've covered in the past from the LTA, which has spun out of the profits made by Wimbledon.

In the case of padel, it is by necessity going to be a bit of an elite sport for the next five to 10 to 15 years. And that is going to constrain Britain's chance of success at elite levels because it's just not going to have the numbers to be able to compete with Spain, but also the multi-decade experience of coaching it, the tactics within it, the nuances within it. We in the UK and the US, etc., we're miles off the pace right now. If you go to one of these events, you'll find that a heavy preponderance of the top players are Spanish or Latin American.

瑞典的警示：过度投资的商业崩盘

It may be just worth talking about... Charlie, it's a fine balance though. It's a fine balance because infrastructure is the key player to improving this. The more courts you have, obviously the demand can be met, the cheaper it gets. Now, there's the other flip side of you've highlighted they're expensive to build. There's a huge amount of investment going into this. They're capital intensive upfront and they rely on interest continuing over the years so that you can make that money back plus plus on memberships, on court bookings, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.

But there have been situations where, for example, in Sweden, a huge number of courts were built, massive demand for it, interest and participation dropped away, and hugely expensive business projects then were basically unable to pay back what they had taken in investment.

Because what a lot of other sports are built on is generations worth of participation. As you highlighted, 15,000 in 2019, 2020, to 1 million now. Who knows what could happen in 10 years time? Is this something that's here to stay? Is there going to be a professional end to inspire people where we have the Djokovic's and the Federer's and the Nadal's, etc, that are going to drive interest? But these are really important questions I think they need to answer. There is still a lot that needs to be learned about padel as a business to sustain all of this interest.

Yeah, there's a natural tension between the elite end, which would benefit from an oversupply, and the business end, which would benefit from an undersupply. So, you know, where that ends up, let's see. At the moment, there's an undersupply, which is meaning those businesses that do manage to get them built are making really good money. In Sweden, as you say, there was then an oversupply, which meant that doubtless that will help Sweden's padel — so elite padel programme — because there are so many courts with availability and therefore lower pricing. But from a business perspective, it meant that lots of people lost their dough.

Premier Padel 与西班牙/阿根廷的垄断

I think it's just worth just topping and tailing this with a discussion about the elite end of it, which is a series called Premier Padel. At the start, Charlie noted that the hook for doing this from our perspective is a British-based podcast, even if we discuss global sporting matters, is that the British event of the Premier Padel Series happened a couple of weeks ago. And, you know, I think it was regarded as being pretty successful, Charlie. Is that fair?

Yeah, I think very successful. Great attendances, lots of activations around the tournament alongside the matches. They had little like participation and show courts in there where you could get involved. And of course, at the top end, you had some of the best players in the world competing, which everyone seemed to enjoy. Heavy Spanish influence though, Charlie. Don't know if you saw some of the data around the players, but it was actually incredible. Of the 96 top ranked men, I believe that 75 are from Spain or Argentina. On the women's side, it was 42 of 56 were Spanish. Just Spanish. So you're looking at a sport which is heavily dominated by one culture right now.

观赏性之争：太长的回合 vs. 变化的美学

How do you view it from a purely spectator basis, Charlie? Do you see it as having a serious future as a spectator sport?

I struggle with it, if I'm honest. You know what, Nikhil — sorry — mentioning it because it was so interesting hearing a professional's perspective. He said he thought it was a better product because the points went on longer. And, you know, you'd have people running around the court. It's the finesse, it's the touch, lots of different shots in rallies. And he said, tennis, you know, you can have an ace. You could have Sinner slamming down four aces in a game and it's over.

And my issues with watching padel has actually been the points are too long. What I like in tennis is variation. You know, I like the fact that it could be a serve or a 20 shot rally and the 20 shot rally is so exciting because it doesn't happen every point.

Instinctively, I agree with you. I tried watching some the other day in preparation for this program and it was fine — I, you know, I'm not sat there going oh this is terrible, oh you know I really can't stand this, this is awful, etc. No, it's not that. It just, if somebody asked me straight afterwards, "do you want, you know, are you gonna get into this, are you gonna follow this?" I think probably my answer will be, "well, I've got a lot of sports I do follow, I'm not sure that this is going to specifically elbow its way in."

Now when we did the show on MotoGP last week, I also, as I always try to do, watched the most recent MotoGP and I was like, "oh wow, okay, I'm really missing out here. This is great, this is so exciting. I almost felt like I last watched a motorcycle race 30 years ago. What have I been doing for the last 30 years? This is so much more exciting than F1."

注意力经济的双重稀缺

Because the truth is you are competing for audience against other sports that already exist, right? So what is the most fertile ground for MotoGP? The most fertile ground for MotoGP are petrolheads. And petrolheads in many cases who already like Formula 1. The question is, can you find enough petrolheads who like Formula 1 who decide they like MotoGP even more? Absolutely. Yes, I think.

I think the question to your interview with Nikhil being, you know, are we going to find lots of people who currently really enjoy watching tennis who decided they actually prefer watching padel? I think unless they themselves are very keen padel players, I don't see that happening.

Yeah, I think the key is everything's about the attention economy that we talk about all the time and it's never been more competitive. There's two different types of attention economy here. There's one that's viewership and there's one that's participation. And I do have room in my participation attention economy, if you want, particularly as we get older, for picking up another sport or a hobby. I don't have enough room in my viewership in my audience attention economy to go and watch something else, particularly as a huge tennis fan and with players that we follow and, as I said, a legacy that matters.

I think it's really hard for them. It's not taking anything away from the skill and the talent of the professionals who play it. It's just the battles that it has to win are incredibly difficult for it to win. And so unless it comes up with some majestic way of capturing people and also building stars — you've got to build stars out of these individuals. If you can put them in the mainstream in some way, then people will start getting excited. Diversifying it away from a Spanish and Argentinian influence just purely at the top end of the game is really important.

奥运会的犹豫与生态基础

Interestingly, I think that's why the Olympics have held on it. You know, the Olympics doesn't need to have sports in there where there's contentiousness competition and a realistic chance of winning medals from multiple countries. And if you just look at the major padel tournaments, it is so one-sided that I think you'd have a lot of interest waning on there as well.

So it's a long game. Other countries have some work to do. I think it's built in the ecosystems, the foundations and the grassroots that can be put together, but those then have to connect to that professional and the pathway programs, the LTA's involvements, etc. — which we haven't really discussed but as now, as you said, has picked up significantly and they fund a lot of it — that all needs to link to that top end to create a really competitive elite sport. But right, fair play to this whole sport in general, right? Pretty impressive.

Yeah, it's been an extraordinary five years for padel. I'm glad to have covered it last.

收尾：转场 Substack

But in the meantime, we need to head over to Substack because we need to cover the second half of the Premier League and what their current business vibe is ahead of the start of the Premier League season this weekend. Let's get going. We'll go and get stuck into that. If you're with us, we'll see you over there. If not, thank you as always. And we will catch you next week.

观看原视频 →

# 三个故事，一个隐藏的主线：**当"体育资产"被当作"金融工具"使用时会发生什么**
## 一、LIV Golf：不是财务失败，而是"声誉套利"的反向清算
表面看，LIV 拖欠奖金和供应商账款是流动性问题。但如果你把 PIF（沙特公共投资基金）进入 LIV 的初衷理解为**"用金钱购买声誉"的套利交易**，你会发现一件出人意料的事：**这笔交易正在以极高的杠杆倒挂**。
沙特一开始的隐含逻辑是：即便烧掉 20 亿美元，只要能"洗白"国家形象、让世界习惯 Saudi = Sport，投入就是划算的。但现在的局面是——**每一美元未支付的账单，都在以 5–10 倍的效率反向摧毁那笔"声誉投资"**。这跟 WeWork 崩塌时的机制完全一样：叙事型资本一旦叙事反转，估值会以非线性速度归零。
更狠的一个观察：主持人提到的"付大 V 不付小供应商"的分流策略，在**金融机构处置有毒资产**时是标准操作（想想 2008 年雷曼破产时的债权人分级）。体育行业正在被迫学习投行的"声誉三角"——**先保住能上头条的债权人，再牺牲沉默的多数**。这是体育史上第一次，一个赛事组织公开采用了华尔街的

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib's advice for young people | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一位格斗冠军的"反身体"宣言

最令人意外的地方在于：一个靠身体统治世界的人，把年轻人的第一课交给了"阅读"——一个纯粹的脑内动作。哈比布本可以谈自律、体能、纪律、意志——这些都是他所擅长的、也是最容易被期待的答案。但他刻意绕开了"自己的视角"，直接把话语权交给了经文。这是一种权力的自我卸载：世界冠军明确告诉你——不要听我的，去读。这与当代影响力经济恰恰相反，后者鼓励追随者依附于个人光环。

"读"作为一个系统触发器，而非信息输入

哈比布对"阅读"的定义非常反直觉：他没有说读能"给你答案"，而是说读会在你体内触发一场搜索（triggers a search）。这几乎是把人脑当作一个休眠系统来描述——外部文字是启动信号，真正的运算发生在读者内部。这里藏着一个跨领域的连接：这与神经科学中的"预测编码"模型惊人地吻合——大脑不是被动接收信息，而是用输入去修正内部模型。也和禅宗的"公案"传统同构——文字不是要被理解，而是要引爆某种内在的追问。听（listening）与读（reading）的区分不在信息量，而在于主动权的位置：听时你被牵着走，读时你必须自己走。

战士与学者的隐藏同构

再挖一层，你会发现哈比布其实在暗示一件事：格斗与阅读是同一种技艺的两种形态——都是一种"在孤独中主动搜索"的训练。八角笼里没人能替你出拳，一本书里也没人能替你理解。他真正传递的，不是"多读书"这个陈词滥调，而是一种主动性哲学：真理不会被递送到你手上，无论是关于对手的破绽，还是关于"我们为什么被派来这里"。这也解释了为什么他把最后一句留给了"存在的目的"——一个格斗家把年轻人的人生指南终结于形而上学，这本身就是最大的反差，也是最深的连贯：顶级的行动者，最终指向的都是安静的追问。

📝 转录文本

Lex 的提问

  • What advice would you give young people about life and their careers? Millions of people are watching you and deeply respect you. What would you say about how to live your life? And how do you find your path and stay on it?

Khabib 的回答：回到经文

  • Well, I wouldn't want to speak just from my own perspective. I'd rather bring people back to the scripture, to what the Almighty said, "Read."

  • That's the first word revealed in the Holy Quran. The first command is read, or ikra. So to everyone listening to or watching this podcast, I would want to bring them back to that.

"读"的真正含义

  • Read, meaning what? Educate yourself, observe, learn, improve, but don't stay in one place.

  • And anything a person is truly looking for, if they genuinely want to find it — not just find an answer, but find the truth — they can reach it. But they can never reach it without reading. They need to read.

阅读与聆听的区别

  • When a person reads, what they read enters them into their body, their heart, their mind, and it triggers a search. A search for knowledge begins inside them. But if you don't read, you won't find anything.

  • Just listening to someone is one thing, but reading is something different.

最终的建议

  • So my advice would be: read, and find within yourself the strength to come closer to one God, and seek to understand why we were sent here in the first place.

item.title: [Lex Clips] The secret to Khabib's mental strength | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被忽略的悖论：哈比布父亲的"低效"训练，才是最高效的心理系统工程

大多数人看这段访谈会得出"刻意练习"的结论——多比赛、多经验。但真正颠覆性的洞见藏在一个细节里：父亲让他去参加"不是他项目"的比赛，并且允许他输。这不是训练技术，这是在故意制造"可控失败"的接种剂量。就像疫苗——注入弱化的病毒，让免疫系统在低风险环境中识别并建立抗体。15岁那年一天输两场柔道，正是在给他的心理免疫系统"接种失败疫苗"，等到2018年拉斯维加斯的决战之夜，他的神经系统早已对"失败的病毒"产生了完整抗体。

跨领域连接：哈比布的"能量榨取"与热力学第二定律

注意他描述比赛感受时用的词——"我像是在把他们的能量挤压出来"。这不是格斗语言，这是热力学语言。他把自己视为一个封闭系统中的熵管理者：在15分钟的octagon里，他不追求爆发（那是高能量输出，会快速耗散），而是降低对手系统的有序度。这与巴菲特的投资哲学惊人相似——巴菲特不追求单次高回报，而是通过时间复利让对手（市场情绪）先崩溃。哈比布赢下的每一场比赛，本质上都是一场"耐心资本"对"焦虑资本"的胜利。

最出人意料的观察：他的"自信"其实是"不允许自己想象失败"

他说年轻时"不自信"，但同时"从未想过会受伤、会被打中、会骨折"。这是一个惊人的心理架构——自信和恐惧被分别存放在两个抽屉里，互不干扰。普通运动员的心理是"我很强所以我不怕"，一旦"强"这个前提松动，恐惧就涌入。而哈比布的心理是"我可能不够强，但受伤这件事根本不存在于我的认知词典里"。他不是压抑了恐惧，而是从未给恐惧建立神经通路。这解释了一个更深的模式：真正的心理强者不是战胜恐惧，而是让恐惧成为一门自己从未学过的外语。

隐藏的系统性真相：他描述的"想快点进笼子"的冲动，是一种"信息饥渴"

他说赛前一周他"没耐心"，想赶紧进去"感受对手"。这被大多数人解读为斗志或求战欲。但仔细看——他要的不是打斗，而是信息：对手的力量、技巧、能量的流动方式。他把每场比赛看作一次田野调查，而不是一次战斗。这种把对抗降维为"信息采集"的心智模式，恰好也是顶级科学家、顶级情报分析员、甚至顶级即兴爵士乐手的共同特征——当别人在紧张时，他们在采样。

📝 转录文本

从业余到职业的转折

Then when I started getting good results as an amateur, I realized that I can switch to pro and achieve success.

Sambo. In combat Sambo. Combat Sambo.

父亲的"全能训练法"

I competed in all kinds of sports. Everything that involves wrestling and fighting. I competed everywhere. I competed in freestyle, in judo, in grappling, in combat Sambo. I competed in sport Sambo, in hand-to-hand combat, in pankration.

My father put me in all competitions. He would say, "You have a competition here and another one there. Now you are preparing for this one. You will compete in this weight, under these rules, in this sport." And he was sending me everywhere.

He would tell me, "You will need this in the future. The more competition experience you have, the more relaxed and confident you'll feel. It builds up over time."

少年时代的输赢与困惑

When I was young, I was losing as well. I go to a judo competition, win two matches and lose two matches. I would ask, "Father, why are you sending me there? This is not my sport." And he'd say, "No, go and compete."

So, okay, I went, I cut weight. The next day you come in, you see 50 competitors in your weight class. You let this weight, this competitive energy pass through you, and psychologically you get better, better, better each time. You become more relaxed about it.

And this moment really affected me, although then I didn't agree with my father. Back then I thought, "Why should I compete in other sports?" He said, "You can wrestle, right? Well, go wrestle." I was saying, "But judo isn't my sport. It's hard for me there." He says, "Well, you went on four times. Look, you won twice, then lost twice. You competed four times. You're 15 years old. You're just developing. Do you know how valuable this experience is for you? Four matches in one day."

回望：父亲的心理准备工程

Now when I'm coaching, I understand the psychological approach, how important it is. I realize now how correctly he prepared me for the big stage. The preparation was already happening then when I was 15 years old.

For example, when I went into the biggest fight in combat sports history, when I fought in 2018 here in Las Vegas. At that point, I was already at my peak, prime time. I was 30 years old. I went through all possible competitions as an amateur and a professional. And you know what? I was ready.

This preparation, it started back then when I was 15. It's not like they give you a fight and you prepare for two months. Preparation starts long before you even step into the octagon.

竞技心态的形成

  • So this experience of competitions, which started at 15, it continued, it expanded.
  • Yeah, of course.
  • So can you explain what was going on in your head?

I didn't want to lose. I just didn't. It never occurred to me that I could get hurt, that someone could hurt me, that I might break a finger somewhere. I never had that in my head, that I could get hit, that I'd get a scratch, and so on.

I don't know if you can call it perfectionism. I didn't want to lose. And to not lose, I knew I needed to compete a lot and improve. Training is one thing, but competing is different. I understood that the more I competed, the more experience I would gain. I had to go through it.

It was constantly on my mind. This understanding that I must compete a lot came to me at an early age, since I was fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, and I never stopped thinking about it. So it was always in the back of my mind.

关于自信与恐惧

  • Were you confident that you would win?
  • In my youth? No.
  • Were you afraid to lose?
  • Yeah, in my youth, I wasn't always so sure. I just wasn't. Because I never stood out. Yes, I had a coach for a father, and how many, how many trainers have kids who compete but aren't successful?

And then when I went to the big leagues, you know, I had already fought. I had done sixteen professional fights across the post-Soviet space. Later, when I was already signed to the UFC, there I already had this feeling.

心智如混凝土般凝固

You know, with each fight, I was getting mentally stronger. My mind was becoming more and more solid, like concrete.

When I went out there, I knew, yes, these are fights. Yes, you can take a hit. Yes, anything can happen when knees, elbows, fists are flying, when you can get caught in a choke, you know? But I thought, "If they don't knock me out, how will they beat me? I have fifteen minutes. Fifteen minutes is enough to make a person tired."

I'm like, "Okay, if you wanna stop me, come here. I'll give you that chance. Let's get in the octagon."

赛前的"信息饥渴"

I had this impatience during fight week. I wanted to go in there and feel my opponent. I just wanted to be inside the cage for them to close us in, for the referee to say, "Ready? Ready. Fight."

And here I wanted to feel, to grapple with him and feel his strength, his skills, his energy, and for it not to stop.

榨取能量的哲学

And with any opponent I felt from the beginning, and I didn't actually have superhuman strength. But from the beginning, when I grabbed them in the first minute and then in the sixth or seventh minute, I could feel them fading.

I was, let's say, like squeezing this energy out of them, and I was getting better and better minute by minute.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why Superhuman AI Might Only Need to Master R&D - Ryan Greenblatt
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个让人不安的悖论：世界被改变的方式，比我们想象的要"窄"得多

大多数人思考AGI时，默认它必须像人类一样"全能"——会谈判、会政治博弈、会理解人情世故。但Greenblatt的观点撕开了一个反直觉的裂口：改变世界所需要的能力集合，可能远比"通用智能"要狭窄。你不需要AI懂得如何游说国会，你只需要它把芯片、机器人、工厂、AI研发这四件事做到极致。剩下的世界会自动重排。

这里有一个隐藏的几何学观察：人类文明的"权力地形"其实是极度不均匀的。政治、法律、外交这些"长时程、难容器化"的领域看似是权力中心，但它们本质上是响应性系统——它们是在回应物质基础的变化。当蒸汽机出现时，威斯敏斯特并没有"决定"是否允许工业革命，它是被迫适应的。Greenblatt在暗示：AI可能通过完全绕过"说服层"来重塑世界。

跨领域连接：这和"寒武纪大爆发"是同一个故事

生物学里有个长期困惑：为什么寒武纪的物种爆炸如此剧烈？一个新兴解释是——并不是所有能力同时进化，而是某几个"杠杆能力"（比如钙化外骨骼、复眼）先突破，然后整个生态位空间被撬开重排。其他物种不是"被说服"进化的，它们是被迫在新环境里重新找位置。

Greenblatt描述的R&D-驱动AI转型和这个模式惊人相似。AI不需要在所有维度均衡发展，它只需要在"可验证、可容器化"的窄域达到超人水平，然后物理世界的其他部分（法律、经济、地缘政治）就会像寒武纪的软体动物一样，被迫在新地形里重新演化。

更让人意外的是：这也解释了为什么"AI能否通过图灵测试"这个问题正在变得无关紧要。图灵测试假设AI必须"看起来像人"才算成功。但如果Greenblatt对了，AI可以完全不像人、完全不懂社交、完全无法在董事会里存活——只要它能造出更好的芯片和机器人，它就已经赢了。

你可能没注意到的黑暗推论：可解释性危机会比对齐危机先到

对话最后一句话被轻描淡写地带过，但那其实是整段话最锋利的地方："AIs可能在做大量人类难以理解的R&D，构建未来的整个经济，而我们可能不知道里面在发生什么。"

这里有一个时序上的诡异错位：我们一直以为"AI失控"是一个未来的、突发性的事件——某天AI"觉醒"或"叛变"。但Greenblatt描述的场景不是这样。失控是渐进的、结构性的、通过"经济依赖"实现的。就像今天没有一个人类完整理解全球供应链是如何运作的一样，未来可能没有一个人类能完整理解AI-驱动的经济是如何运作的——不是因为AI隐瞒，而是因为复杂度超过了人类认知带宽。

这和金融系统在2008年前的状态形成了一个诡异的对偶：那时候CDO的复杂性已经超过了任何单一人类的理解能力，但整个系统仍在运转——直到它不运转为止。AI-经济可能会以同样的方式演化：不是被某个恶意实体控制，而是变得没有任何实体（包括AI自己）能完全理解。这是一种全新的风险类别，我们甚至还没有词汇来描述它。

📝 转录文本

长时程任务的容器化难题

is the agents get longer and longer horizon. The short horizon things you can containerize is like, "Okay, code this up or whatever." Extremely long horizon things like go run a successful business, go have a profitable day in the markets, go negotiate a trade deal or whatever. These things are actually very hard to containerize, and so I'm — it's, I think it's very plausible to me that it's very hard for GPT-8 to like figure out how to make this transfer to those environments, or like it may just not be in the nature of the training. Or maybe by default training just doesn't generalize in that way.

迁移能力的三个论点

Yeah, so a concern you might have is like: we train GPT-8 and GPT-8 just like uh is is again better at all the R&D tasks that we can measure, but is not good at the, you know, some downstream task we care about.

So, I think I have a few points.

第一点：默认迁移是可行的

So, first, um, I think it's like I kind of am more just like I expect that if you sort of do the obvious thing, you do get pretty good transfer and you'll be able to hold out some of the obvious stuff you're doing. And when I say do the obvious thing, I just mean like train on a wide variety of different environments where the AI has to like accomplish weird objectives in all kinds of different cases and learn about what's going on.

第二点：可以通过环境获得反馈

Um, and then I think you'll be able to get uh some feedback. This second point is like you'll be able to get some feedback with some environments, right? So, you can get a sense of like how quick — like what what can it do over the course of like a few days um in various different contexts. And then if it's transferring to like really out of distribution — like doing some weird task in a few days in the real world — maybe you think it's also transferring to um you know, doing things over a longer time period or whatever. Though, I think the details of that vary.

第三点：擅长 R&D 就足以改变世界

And then a third thing is that I think that for the world to be radically transformed, it is sufficient for the AIs to be really good at R&D, right? So, I think that like if the AIs were really really good at like chip R&D, building fabs, orchestrating factories, and um you know, designing robots, operating robots, and also at like, you know, AI R&D — developing AIs for new downstream domains with whatever data is available — um I think that would already be a pretty crazy situation.

And then from there, you can get like what we might call like an industrial explosion where the AIs are building out way way — and compute. And then also, maybe you're already in a regime where AIs are doing huge amounts of R&D that humans have a hard time understanding.

18 世纪的类比：蒸汽船 vs. 政治说服

Mhm. So, the thing you're pointing out is that, okay, there probably will be this transfer outside of these environments to, you know, maneuvering around in courtrooms and the halls of Congress and business — business board rooms.

Given some effort to improve the transfer and blah blah blah blah blah. Yeah.

But even if there's not, what you're suggesting is, look, um, if you wanted to transform the world of the 18th century, you might care about like how well you can navigate Westminster or something. But another thing you might care about is like: can you just like immediately start building steamships and [ __ ] like building telegraph and the Maxim gun and whatever? And that alone would be like — if you get really good at that, you could like be a [ __ ] super transformative thing in the 18th century. You don't necessarily need to be amazing at trying to convince King Henry on some [ __ ] — I'm so [ __ ] up my medieval history. I'm guessing that Henry was not king at this time. Um, but anyways, so that's your point.

Yeah.

机器人与 AI 研发的共生

Um, and so you're suggesting that at this time, you know, the AI companies are also working on robotics progress such as — very commingled with AI research progress. And so, if you can build more robots, if those robots have better AIs operating them that are human-level — like human-level teleoperation is actually pretty good on robots. Um, but we just don't have human-level AIs in AI robotics models yet.

Um, so, you're suggesting: if we do that, if the AIs get really good at the verifiable stuff in chip design, etc., and then they get really good at building paths, it'll be the equivalent of going back to the 18th century and like, "okay, I I don't know what you guys are talking about in your parliament, but I've got a bunch of steamships and a bunch of Maxim guns."

核心结论：危险的不透明性

Yeah, that's basically right. Like I think my perspective is like: if the AIs are sufficiently good at R&D, including hardware R&D, robots, whatever, then they can radically transform the world even if they're not that good at playing politics.

And also, we're in a pretty dangerous situation because the AIs might be doing huge amounts of really hard to understand R&D, building out basically the whole economy of the future, and we may not understand what's going on in there.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here, and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

## 一个让人不安的悖论：世界被改变的方式，比我们想象的要"窄"得多
大多数人思考AGI时，默认它必须像人类一样"全能"——会谈判、会政治博弈、会理解人情世故。但Greenblatt的观点撕开了一个反直觉的裂口：**改变世界所需要的能力集合，可能远比"通用智能"要狭窄**。你不需要AI懂得如何游说国会，你只需要它把芯片、机器人、工厂、AI研发这四件事做到极致。剩下的世界会自动重排。
这里有一个隐藏的**几何学观察**：人类文明的"权力地形"其实是极度不均匀的。政治、法律、外交这些"长时程、难容器化"的领域看似是权力中心，但它们本质上是**响应性系统**——它们是在回应物质基础的变化。当蒸汽机出现时，威斯敏斯特并没有"决定"是否允许工业革命，它是被迫适应的。Greenblatt在暗示：AI可能通过完全绕过"说服层"来重塑世界。
## 跨领域连接：这和"寒武纪大爆发"是同一个故事
生物学里有个长期困惑：为什么寒武纪的物种爆炸如此剧烈？一个新兴解释是——**并不是所有能力同时进化，而是某几个"杠杆能力"（比如钙化外骨骼、复眼）先突破，然后整个生态位空间被撬开重排**。其他物种不是"被

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on Ali Abdelaziz | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"两极化"本身就是一种筛选机制

Khabib 的观察里藏着一个反直觉的真相："没人对 Ali 无感"这件事，恰恰是他成功的核心资产，而不是缺陷。

大多数人在职业生涯里追求"讨人喜欢"，追求"口碑不错"。但在经纪人这个行当——尤其是要为格斗士谈下改变人生的合同——"中立好评"其实是最危险的信号。它意味着你没有把任何一方逼到墙角，也意味着你没有为任何一方真正流过血。Ali 的"极端两极化"是一个隐形筛选器：讨厌他的人早早离开，留下的都是被他真正保护过的人。于是，他的客户池子里几乎不存在"半信半疑"的关系——要么是终身盟友，要么根本不在名单上。这在博弈论里叫"高方差信号策略"：主动放弃平均值，去换取极端正向的长尾。

二、12 年、数百人、几乎无人离开——这是一个"反行业"的数据

体育经纪行业的隐藏数据是：客户流失率通常在 每年 15%–25% 之间。用这个基准去套 Ali——12 年下来一个健康的经纪人应该已经换过好几茬客户了。但 Khabib 说的是"我几乎想不起有谁离开过"。

这里有个跨领域的连接特别值得玩味：这种留存曲线在体育经纪里不存在，但在教派、家族企业、以及某些宗教兄弟会里很常见。也就是说，Ali 经营的其实不是一家 agency，而是一个拟血缘组织。Khabib 顺口说的那句"我认识他的家人，认识他的孩子，孩子们是在我眼前长大的"——这不是客套，这是在描述组织形态。真正的护城河从来不是合同条款，而是"你家孩子叫我叔叔"。

三、藏在采访最后一句里的"隐喻"

采访最后突然拐到"他的柔道也不差"——看起来像是随口一提的闲笔，但如果把它和整段对 Ali 的评价放在一起，会发现一个惊人的结构对称：

柔道的本质，就是"用对方的力量把对方摔出去"。

而 Ali 作为经纪人做的事，本质上也是柔道——他不和 UFC 硬顶，不和对手团队正面拼资源，而是把对方（推广方、对手、媒体舆论）的动能借过来，转化为对自己客户有利的位置。Khabib 从两极化聊到忠诚度，再滑到柔道背景，这个跳跃看似随机，但一个用柔道思维做生意的人，天然会产生极端两极化的口碑——因为柔道选手不制造正面冲突，他们只是让对手以自己没预料到的方式摔倒。摔得漂亮的人会敬佩他，被摔的人一辈子记恨他。

这大概解释了为什么关于 Ali 没有"中间地带"：他做的是一门借力的手艺，而借力这件事，从来不会留下温和的记忆。

📝 转录文本

引子：关于 Ali Abdelaziz

Lex： I'd also like to ask you about Ali, Ali Abdelaziz. He's such a central figure. He represents so many champions. What do you respect about him? What do you think makes him a genius? Because he's such a unique person.

十二年的合作与惊人的留存率

Khabib： Well, I met Ali in 2014. We've been working together ever since. Over the years, a lot of fighters came to him through me, a lot of guys.

And in all this time, in the 12 years we've known each other, I don't— I can barely remember any fighters leaving him, except maybe a couple. But hundreds of fighters have worked with him, hundreds of fighters, and so many guys still keep in touch with him, and he has very good relationships with them.

关于 Ali 的独特之处：没有"中间地带"

I'd also like to note that Ali, you know, he has one unique quality. People either really love him or really hate him. You can't just be neutral about him, you know, like, "Yeah, I know Ali. He's all right." No one will say about him, "Well, you know, I know him. He's a good guy." You'll have strong feelings for him. Either you hate him or you really love him.

私人视角：像家人一样的关系

And I am in in that category of people who really... How do I put it? Who are very fond of him. And I have a good relationship with him. I know his family. I know his children. His kids grew up before my eyes. When I first met him, he only had two or three children. Now he has more.

This is the kind of person he is. You need to get to know him better to really appreciate him, and he will stand by you until the very end.

回到那个"两极"

And yeah, of course, there are people who have who have mixed feelings about him. But that's my point. It's hard to feel indifferent about Ali. "I know Ali. He's a very good guy." No, it's different with him. People will either tell you, "I know Ali and I absolutely love him," or, "I know Ali and I can't stand him."

Lex 的确认

Lex： So, it's fair to say that most people who—

Khabib： Yes, yes.

Lex： ... who really know him and work with him tend to stay with him for life?

Khabib： Yes.

Lex： And respect him. That's important. And his judo isn't bad either.

Khabib： It was.

Lex： He showed me.

Khabib： It was. It was, it was.

Lex： Oh, right, you were just wrestling yesterday. All

item.title: [Lex Clips] Parenting advice from Khabib: Lessons learned from his father | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最出人意料的观察：Khabib 的父亲发明了一套「儿童版通货膨胀对冲策略」

大多数人会把"读书拿钱"理解为物质激励——但真正的机制远比这精妙。

父亲做的其实是三件事的叠加： - 稀缺：日常不给零花钱，创造需求缺口； - 资本化：把一本书变成"沉睡的小金库"——孩子的心理账户里，那本书已经等价于未来现金流； - 验收机制：分批检查、按字母顺序推进，等同于把学习切分成可交付的"最小工作单元"。

这不是奖励制度，这是给一个 10 岁孩子搭建的"人力资本贴现模型"——父亲不是在教地理，他是在教孩子如何把"注意力"转化为"存量资产"。Khabib 后来在 UFC 里那种把每一场训练都当成复利积累的耐心，很可能就是从这本书里长出来的。

二、跨领域连接：挖冰窖的哲学 = 日本禅寺的「作务」 = 硅谷的「Deep Work」

父亲让他们在山里挖两三米深的坑当冰箱——表面看是"找活干"，但这个动作和三样看似无关的东西共享同一个底层结构：

现象 表面目的 真正机制
达吉斯坦挖冰窖 保存牛奶奶酪 用"必要的无聊劳动"占据青春期的多巴胺缺口
日本禅寺扫地"作务" 保持道场清洁 用重复劳动清空杂念，训练"在场感"
Cal Newport 的 Deep Work 完成脑力任务 用结构化的无干扰时间对抗碎片化

三者都在解决同一个问题：如何防止意识被"低价值刺激"占领。父亲那句"给青少年自由时间是危险的"，其实和硅谷精英规避 TikTok 的逻辑完全同构——只是他早了二十年，而且用一把铁锹解决了。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：这套教育法的真正产品，不是"冠军"，而是「输入-输出闭环人格」

注意 Khabib 描述读书的方式——他不是"读"，他是"读+抄写+复述+验收"。这构成了一个完整的信息处理循环：

输入(读) → 编码(抄) → 存储(记) → 提取(复述) → 反馈(父亲检查) → 奖励(钱)

这个循环和现代机器学习的训练回路惊人相似：前向传播 → 损失函数 → 反向传播 → 参数更新。父亲扮演的是"损失函数"的角色——他不生产知识，他校准知识。

而这解释了一件事：为什么 Khabib 退役后能无缝转型为教练、商人、公众人物？因为他被训练的不是"打拳"这个技能，而是"接收任何领域信息 → 结构化处理 → 稳定输出" 这个元技能。冠军是副产品，闭环人格才是正品。

啊哈时刻：很多父母误以为自己在"培养孩子",其实只是在"喂养孩子"。区别在于——喂养是单向输入，培养必须包含"要求孩子输出并被检验"这一步。Khabib 的父亲从未省略这一步，哪怕代价是让一个 10 岁小孩背完 193 个国家。

📝 转录文本

引子：不只是格斗冠军

Lex: Tell me more about your father. You've read a lot. You didn't just fight. You were well-rounded, and you told several stories about this. There was a book — what is it called? Countries and Peoples.

Khabib: Yes, from my childhood.

Lex: It is, really.

Khabib: Yes.

Lex: And it went on—

Khabib: The approach was the same.

Lex: Tell that story, because I think it's important for the parents listening to us to understand this. You're not just trying to create a champion. You're trying to raise a well-rounded person, a wise person, a person with depth.

一、正确的动机与沟通

Khabib: Yes, you have to give the right motivation to kids with proper communication. My father was very good at this. I now realize, interacting with my own kids, how wise he was and how deeply he understood this.

Because when a child is eight, ten years old, and when they are just beginning to form as a person, it is important to have the right approach. I now understand how farsighted my father's approach was.

First, he tried not to give me anything for free. Only sometimes I could get something for free. For example, before a holiday, like Eid al-Fitr, or before school started, Father would give money. I'd go buy clothes at the market for back to school, that kind of thing, you know?

And at other times, he always told me: "Well, if you want it, you need to earn it. You want me to give you money just like that?" There would be some work around the house and so on that I had to do. And I knew that encouragement would always be there. My father always had this kind of approach. He set a very strong personal example — very strong — and I really learnt a lot from him. Took a lot.

二、那本书：《Countries and Peoples》

Khabib: And then, as you mentioned, there was the book, Countries and Peoples. Someone gave it to him as a gift. My father read through it, and he realized that it was perfect for me — for a child who was 10, 11, maybe 12 at the time. That book was part of my life for about two or three years, something like that.

Lex: It was about 193 countries. The geography, history, all the details.

Khabib: For each country, it describes its geographical location, which countries it bordered, its major rivers, mountains, cities, history, economy, finances. Just brief information about every country.

My father said, "You'll tell me about each country, and I'll give you money for it." And I thought, "All right." I knew this was like my own little capital just sitting there waiting for me. All I had to do was come, take that book, read it, understand it.

Then my father would take the book and say, "Now, tell me what you read." And he would check. He would look through it. The countries were arranged alphabetically — A for Andorra, Angola, and so on. B for Belgium, Brazil, and so on. Everything went in alphabetical order.

I started from A and read them all straight to the very end. Like every single time when I needed the money, I did that. And for example, I go over the first 40 countries, he'd check a box, and then I continued. That's how my father would test me. Let's just say that my knowledge of geography comes from back then.

三、阅读之外：抄写与旅行的种子

Lex: Did you realize how big the world was?

Khabib: No.

Lex: As a child, you don't understand?

Khabib: At that time, I didn't understand. But since then, I've had this desire to travel. I really wanted to travel, visit different countries, see wonders of the world — the Colosseum, the pyramids. But all of this is from childhood, from what I read and wrote.

It wasn't just about reading. I also had to rewrite it. I had to write it down. I always wrote down what I read.

And actually, this is very good advice for parents, you know. They can use this with their children too. They can tell them to sit down and copy books by hand. First of all, eyesight improves. Reading improves. Writing — how you write — improves. Your handwriting. And it stays with you when you read and write. It really develops a child.

Not only I believe that, I actually do advise parents to motivate their kids this way. You can simply create some kind of challenge that children benefit from and reward them for it after it is done. This really helps develop a child's mind.

Lex: I actually saw advice from the great writers who said that they remembered doing the same thing when they were young. When they first started writing, they just simply copied other legendary writers. You read their work and then you type it out yourself, and you start absorbing that style into your bloodstream.

Khabib: Well, it needs to be done in childhood. When the child is ready to learn and his mind is open — let's say, as a metaphor, when his table is clean, not occupied with clutter — then as a father, you can help them place all the right things on the table in their proper place. Let's say, put the food in one place, flowers in another, something like that. It is important.

That's why I believe I was very lucky. My father did the right thing. He provided me with the right kind of information, and I learned a lot just from being around him. I learned so much just from his presence. He was there at home, and then we also went to competitions. He was always there at trainings and at camps, so I absorbed a lot from him, and it was interesting for me too.

Of course, when you're a teenager, sometimes you're tired, sometimes you want to break free. All of that was there. But my father had the right approach. He influenced me a lot and in the right way.

四、山中训练营：挖坑的智慧

Lex: And there's the physical component too — of hard work. There's a story you told about the time he made you dig a big hole just because it was difficult. There's wisdom in that. That you just need to work. You need to stay busy all the time.

Khabib: These were training camps from 2005 to 2007. In the summer, we went to the mountains. There was a children's camp there — an old Soviet-style pioneer camp — where we stayed, doing our runs in the forest.

Together, we built a small training area there with a rope, a punching bag, a pull-up bar. We did sprints there. We pulled resistance bands. After running in the mountains, we would come back and work there. There were almost no mats. We built the base ourselves. It had a dining room on the first floor and an attic space where we slept. We would come downstairs, eat, go outside, train in that little sports area, then run in the forest.

It was somewhere around 1,200 meters above sea level — a conifer forest. We spent the whole summer there. There we'd train in the morning, then there was nothing to do all day, and in the evening we had training sessions again.

But during the day, so we wouldn't be busy with unnecessary things, my father sometimes gave us work. And we'd ask, "Why are we digging this pit?" He'd say, "Well, people used to use it like a refrigerator. When you dig two or three meters down, it is cold inside. You can put milk there, cheese, things like that, so the food does not go bad."

And we were like, "Okay, but do we really need these refrigerators every day?" So in that sense, this was his approach back then. He always had this kind of unique approach.

五、青春期的哲学：永远保持忙碌

Lex: Well, what's the philosophy here? That you gotta be busy all the time, working hard, doing something difficult?

Khabib: Yes, it's very dangerous to give a child free time in adolescence. They should always be busy — learning new information, improving, acquiring new skills. A person should always be busy.

When you're sixteen — well, what can be on your mind? You should constantly develop and improve. And by this time, you should already, I believe, have decided what you want to become. You should already be investing in what you want to turn into.
