十二、Token经济学与产业范式转移

你觉得从你最大化使用Token到开始经济地使用Token这一套转变中，你预测未来像硅谷的这些大公司它们会多久把这个工作范式转过来？

我觉得现在正在发生了。

所以Claude跟OpenAI它们每个月API的消耗量跟ARR，你觉得它还会是在一个持续的增长中吗？

东旭： 我觉得还会增长。这两个其实你不能完全放在一起类比。

我们先说Agent为什么这么消耗Token。当然了大家也不要神化Agent，其实Agent从工程来说原理上还挺简单的。每一个Agent内部它都有一个类似像发动机一样的东西，我们叫做Agentic Loop。它就是一个内部的循环，这个循环每一次都会在中间调用大语言模型去向它问问题或者说去对话。它本质上还是个对话机，只是说把这个对话的过程变成一个loop。

然后这个对话第一它的特点是它在对话里边去调用外部工具，然后把外部工具的输出变成这个对话流中的一个上下文。第二个特点就是它在复杂或者说长程任务下不一定会说两句话它就结束这个循环，这个循环可能会运行几百步，这几百步中间又会有很多的工具调用，这些工具调用的输入跟输出又会变成大语言模型的上下文。

这种pattern（范式）就导致了这个Agent它对于Token的消耗量比Chatbot时代可能涨了100倍都不止。虽然今天我觉得有很多人为的浪费，就比如Meta里边刷Token的榜，可能你就跟Agent说你帮我去算100万遍1+1你也能把这个榜刷得很夸张的。但是只要这样的pattern（范式）是存在的、或者说成立的，还会有更复杂的系统出现。

我举个例子，今天我们其实在聊Agent的时候，刚才我说的这个架构只是单个Agent内部的架构。因为我觉得到最后其实可能是一个在面向更复杂的问题时候，就需要多Agent的协同，这个协同又会变成一个更大的网络，这个网络之上又会有一个更抽象的loop。我觉得这种hierarchy（分层）的结构现在已经在出现了。

所以你觉得即使说我们现在找到一条本地化Agent尽可能地节省Token的量，只是说它是单点的问题、单点的问题，我们把它解决得更好、解决得更好了，但是整体上它的消耗还是在持续地增长中？

是的。因为这个里边有个软件工程的问题。我们今天其实可能看到的这些程序，比如说我再类比一下计算机历史，在早期的比如在家酿俱乐部里边那些计算机爱好者当时都在分享："我写了一个200行的BASIC程序，这个游戏很好玩，大家share一下"。可能那时候的程序就是几张纸、一个程序员几千行汇编代码可能就结束了。但今天我们去看一个Photoshop没有数千万级的代码，对吧？所以我觉得今天我们的Agent的应用以及我们想要让Agent解决的问题还太简单了。如果Agent的能力到达一定程度、要去解决更复杂问题的时候，它必然会出现一个Agent to Agent network以及Agent Harness软件工程出现，这时候它对Token的消耗又会上一个台阶。

十三、杰文斯悖论与开源/闭源生态之争

对，宏江老师怎么看？

宏江老师： 其实刚才东旭描述的这个现象在经济学里面叫做杰文斯悖论：当你的技术越来越成熟的话，它的价格会变得越来越低，但是消耗量本身会变得越来越大，所以这样的话它这个市场变得越来越大。

未来开源模型、闭源模型，哪个能够走得更快，或者哪个是在本地、哪个是在云上，这个我觉得更多的是一个生态里面的竞争、生态里面这种成熟，今天还很难判断哪个最后能胜出。

还是说你就需要一个Agent，或者对于我们常人来说的话，是需要一个工作的Agent、一个生活的Agent，还是说像东旭这样需要多个Agent来做事，其实不同的人群还是不太一样。今天之所以包括在企业内部大部分的IT上了云，它一个很核心的一点：其实对于一般人来说他们没法应对复杂的IT系统，一个公司它也很难养一个IT团队他能够应对如此复杂的IT系统对吧。所以如果你将来再有很多Agent这样的话，它可能也很难应对这么多Agent。你说Agent自己去应对其他的Agent的庞大系统，就是公司整个环境你要搭起来这个环境，当然你可能会把它交给更强大的Agent去做对吧，这个强大的Agent可能就在云上。

我们做IT的人或者是做IT产业的人都会希望自己今天的产品未来会在这个生态的核心位上。比如如果你是做PC的、如果你是做小服务器的，你就希望这个都是on-premise（本地部署），本身我可控。你是做云的，你就希望是未来都在云上，这样对于用户来说就变得transparent（流程可视），他就不需要考虑架构，甚至不需要再考虑我要买一台Mac还是我要买一台戴尔的服务器，还是我要买一台联想的小型服务器。下面的这种evolution（迭代进化）还有很大程度上是一些非纯技术的考虑。

但有一点我是非常同意的，一个是单个整体的智能本身会变得越来越强。智能本身变强也会更加消耗Token对不对？对，有可能是这样，你会更加消耗Token，但是Token的价格也会降得非常快，最终它不一定说它的ROI会受到太大影响。事实上它能做的事情会越来越多，它可能做这件事情消耗的Token可能也越来越多。但是另外一个角度，刚才东旭也提到，越来越高的智能使得Agent本身可能也不需要持续地去问大模型，所以它可能这种对话的频率也可能降下来对吧。所以也许Token的消耗量可能不是那样的。

十四、Agent蜂群与"涌现的智能"

未来一定是一些超级强的Agent和超级大的蜂群来做事情，这些群里面的每一个Agent也许它是特别擅长于某一些任务，或者也许它背后所用的模型可能比较专用或者比较小，或者Token价格比较低。也许另外一种它们都是由一两个非常powerful（功能强大）的大模型来驱动，这个还需要不断地evolve（迭代演进）。

这个层面上会有一些涌现的智能出现。对，会有一些涌现的智能出现。最近有一篇清华大学的文章就说到，三个臭皮匠是超过一个诸葛亮：每一个Agent的能力，它们能力的和可能是低于它们事实上作为一个Agent群它们所能够展现的智能能力，它不是一个简单的和的关系，而是它可以涌现出一个更强的智能。这也是我们对于Agent群的期待。

蜂群 vs 单体超级模型：

对，因为刚刚我在跟东旭聊天的过程中，其实他讲到了他搭建了一个Agent群，然后让大家去发现一个问题、互相之间都没有发现，最后在Fable 5出来的时候把这个问题——可能是还没有那么多前情提要的情况下——给Fable 5，然后它解决了。

你觉得现在，比如说我们刚刚一直在讨论模型能力的智力的碾压式的提升，它可以强过蜂群吗？

宏江老师： 这其实是一个非常好的问题。你还要记住另外一点，就是一个超级模型的出现智力不断往上scale，但是没有任何东西可以阻拦这些蜂群里面的每一个Agent它也利用这种智能。了解，就是只要模型的智能在往上提升，蜂群的智能也在往上提升。也在往上走。

我举刚才一个例子——那个修订，假设这三个臭皮匠一直讨论不出来，但是我只要把Fable 5也放进来加入讨论，它可能第一句话这些人马上就开窍了，就是刚才东旭说的涌现，所以他就可能涌现出insight（洞察）的概率会更高。

东旭： 而且我非常认同宏江老师刚才说的那个观点。其实我觉得这个跟人类社会也是一样的，我不太相信说有一个绝对的中心，这种其实太危险了。而且我觉得真正的一个resilience（韧性）的系统，它一定是一个大规模的、基于简单规则连接的分布式系统，然后这样的系统我觉得才不管是对于任意复杂度的问题以及抗击打能力都是最强的。

宏江老师： 对，这跟做云的时候一开始设计云和之前设计企业服务器的概念的区别。当云开始普及的时候，AWS开始设计云，它其实每一个单一的服务器或者单一的节点它并不是用最好的、我们叫做所谓的Enterprise-grade（企业级）这样的服务器，但是它整体的可靠性是通过它的整个分布式的云来实现的。其实这样的实现成本会比你每个节点都买最贵的、最可靠的服务器还要来的低。

所以有些公司可能一开始设计的就是——因为他以前是做企业级的——它上云的时候它希望它的数据中心每个服务器还是企业级的、这么可靠性的这样的服务器，使它的整个云的成本就会比别人高太多。所以最终你发现它其实不是一个技术的判断，最后是个经济学的判断。当然也是因为技术本身发展到它能够用比较合适的云来达到低于非常强的单一节点的成本。

十五、投资视角：什么样的Agent公司值得投

对，因为我们前两年就是在聊AI Agent、垂类Agent会不会出现super的Agent，它有没有创业跟投资机会的时候，我觉得所有创业者最苦恼的一个问题就是说：模型的能力一升级，然后你就把我这个Agent做的所有的工作都碾压了。

那根据刚刚大家新的判断，是不是说现在是一个非常好的去创建AI Agent的一个时机？包括宏江老师刚刚其实您提到了一个非常重要的观点，就是你觉得我们现在在一个分界点上，我们在从模型的科学研究变成一个工程能力的问题，那工程能力其实就是Agent的强项？

宏江老师： 对。回答你刚才那个问题，是不是现在做Agent的很好的机会？显然是。但是你的harness的能力或者Agent的工作能力是不是能够让你能领先、或者持续地领先、或者是战胜大模型的公司但它的能力的提升是不是你自己不会被碾压，这块可能更核心的在于你是不是能够掌握企业级的一个垂直应用的数据，所以数据的护城河可能会更重要。

Agent的三个层次：

东旭： 当我们大家在去讲Agent的时候，其实在把很多东西混在一起。刚才说的垂类，有很多人说Agent是在说应用，就是最最上面对consumer（用户）或者说最终端的、大家老百姓用的某个场景，相当于过去的APP。对，APP。

对，然后有些人说Agent是说我这里边用到的软件基础设施也好、或者硬件基础设施也好、或者说一些通用的协议也好，那这是一大类的工作，就其实infra。但是infra里边我也发现，其实大家在聊infra的时候也会把很多东西混在一起聊：比如说memory是infra吧，然后那个数据、数据是infra吧、搜索、搜索是infra吧、卡算不算infra？也算infra。对，Sandbox（沙箱）是不是infra？也算。内存算不算？好像也算。

所以我觉得这里边当然得分层次来看。我现在是觉得工程问题是集中在memory、搜索、sandbox environment、协同、harness，这一系列我觉得都是在大的infra范畴里边。这部分是我觉得有很多机会今天是可以做的。

但是最终端的、面向纯客户的一些"APP"可能还稍微有点早，就像刚才说我觉得模型能力提升碾压的还其实真就是应用这部分。所以它也是分类的，就Agent跟Agent也是不太一样的。对，不太一样。

十六、值得投资的三个方向

对，因为两位现在也做投资。我们刚刚其实有涉及到应用现在是不是一个好的投资时机的话题，包括垂类的应用什么最重要。宏江老师也说到了数据很重要。因为现在我觉得整个硅谷的创业公司可能都是AI类的创业公司，然后模型也就那么几家、可能也就出现了一些新的Neolabs，大量都是做Agent的。大家怎么去判断一个创业公司是不是值得投？什么样的特质、或者什么样的方向是你们特别看好跟特别喜欢的？

东旭： 首先我自己有个原则，就是我不投我自己看不懂或者说我自己用不起来的东西。因为作为一个做infra这么长时间的工程师，还是相信一点手感的。

方向一：多Agent协同的基础设施

我现在是对这些基础设施类的软件项目、尤其是能在多个Agent之间更高效地让Agent产生更好结果的东西，就比如说你正常用一个模型你只能产生比如说50分的结果，但是如果我用上了这一套东西、这个Agent的团队也好、或者说这套平台也好，能够去交付出80分甚至90分的结果，就是我比较感兴趣的范围。

去看吧，哪些基础设施能够帮助这个模型产生更好的结果？我说数据平台、记忆以及上下文管理，这个我觉得是一个很重要的赛道。做模型的中间的这个，中间这一层。对，我们还是在说基础设施，中间这几层基础设施。

方向二：可观测性

第二个关键的环节是可观测性。当你要让Agent team（团队）或者说Agent去解决更复杂问题的时候，我觉得你怎么去让更高级的智能或者说更有经验的人类能进去提升整个系统的迭代速度，我们今天其实没有任何办法，因为我们对于这个系统的可观测性不足。就比如说Token Maxing这个问题，所有的CIO今天都在问你一个问题就是：我这些Token到底花在了哪些事情是重要的事情上、哪些是白白浪费的？谁能够给我回答这个问题，我就买谁的东西。对，我觉得这是第二个这种基础设施层面的机会是有的。

方向三：Agent Cloud / 入口层

第三个就是我觉得入口层面的做出Agent应用的入口级别的机会，比如说Agentic Cloud。我相信一个点，就是未来这些不管是Oracle也好、AWS也好，未来在Agent时代会有Agent时代的Oracle、有Agent时代的AWS。

跟现在的整个云厂商会有什么不一样？会有一些不一样。比如说这是我最近投的一个公司InsForge，它其实的这个定位就是Agent Cloud。因为其实以前我们去看待Cloud都是卖盒子、卖资源、卖计算机的基础设施，把这些很复杂的IT系统的管控打包起来、卖一个标准的这些东西。

但新一代的第一个区别就是，以前的云还是面向开发者或者说面向人类，但是未来Agent-Native的应用的基础设施它面向的其实是Agent，就是你的主语变了。所以怎么去设计一个给Agent好用的interface（接口）、给Agent好用的资源分配的模式？

我们今天其实谈到这种Agent的应用很多是一个比如说类似小龙虾或者Hermes配合上一些特别的skill，对于每一个终端用户他的需求都是通过Agent来去触发的，这跟传统的云计算的逻辑是非常不一样的。因为今天这些Agent完成这样的APP最好的办法是完全给它一台沙箱或者说一台云计算机，让它在里面干任何事情。但是如果你想让这种类型的应用放在传统云计算上，你的成本是cover不住的。你不能说我给每个Hermes在企业级场景里面分配一个EC2（弹性计算云服务器）或者说一个metal box（裸金属服务器）。你要想想，可能如果有成千上万个Agent每个人都要去拥有一台计算机，那这个成本肯定不行。

所以你需要找到一种agent friendly同时cost efficiency的一个折中，这里边我觉得就会有很多的包括Serverless（无服务器）的技术怎么跟Agent的环境、Agent runtime结合在一起。

对，我觉得今年整个的环境看起来是非常的toB的。包括我们刚刚讲到的OpenClaw、Hermes，包括我们说大企业它们都在去用Agent、包括在里面搭建他们的工作流，还有像OpenAI跟Anthropic在做的这个FDE，其实整个都是针对于toB市场的。然后你刚刚讲的这三个方向，我如果没有理解错的话，也全是toB的。

那像前两年火的这些Manus、Genspark这一类toC类的Agent，在大家看来还是香的吗？

东旭： 我不觉得Manus跟Genspark它是toC的，它仍然是toB。它的toC只是它的——To professional，对，面向专业人士。

所以它还香吗？香。为什么不香？你可以看到它最近的收入涨得非常快对吧。都是可以投的？对，我觉得都是可以投的。

十八、Agent-Native 与"目标用户是Agent"

好，宏江老师，我们过去的无论是toB还是toC，其实最终的用户都是人。那下面我们看到的一定是你的目标用户是Agent本身。这个中间的话会引出一系列的投资机会。

刚才东旭提到了就是整个infra相关的，无论是未来的runtime、还是今天我们谈到的这些infra怎么来帮助把Agent做得更好。怎么能够把数据很好地导入？为什么现在FDE大家强调的如此多？

然后两天前、三天前微软宣布要成立一个6000人的团队专门是做FDE，叫做Microsoft Frontier Company。这里边想强调的事实上大家看到就是怎么把今天的企业、今天的enterprise然后转移到未来的Agent上去，Agent-based Enterprise。

这中间其实每一个企业要想生存，它最终最终怎么——是把它企业现有的know-how（专业技术）、现有的IP（知识产权）、现有的workflow（工作流）它的所谓的竞争优势最终体现在know-how、体现在数据。我们过去说转移成一个大模型、转移成一个垂直模型，今天我们说可能更重要的是把它转移成一个超级的Agent或者是一系列的Agent、或者是Agent群，这个也是我希望能看到的一个投资的机会。

东旭： 可能就会要求你更垂直、要求你的数据飞轮更能够转起来、更懂垂直行业的方法论、更懂垂直行业，而且一定是Agent-Native，然后更有垂直行业的数据。以前被大模型碾压的很多就是你用AI做一些以前移动互联网APP做的事情，你用AI仅仅是把它做成效率工具，然后你的应用本身还是传统的应用，那我觉得就很容易被大模型给打穿，大模型能力提升一定会把你横扫。

判断"Agent-Native"的两个方法：

对，你刚刚提到了一个词叫做Agent native。怎么去判断一个公司是不是Agent native？你们有没有一些核心的、比如说判断的这个点？

很简单，我的点就是做个思想实验：如果你这个事情你把AI的元素或者说Agent的这个元素去掉，如果你这件事情仍然成立或者说还能做，那不好意思，你不是一个AI native。但是如果你这个事情在Agent去掉了以后就完全不成立了、或者说你可能成本涨了1000倍，我觉得类似这样的反而就有点意思，你就是一个Agent native。

第二，我觉得是看团队的思维模式。一个Agent native企业，我觉得很多时候创始人的思维模式一定是Agent first的。但任何一件事情你先问自己说这件事情用AI或者用Agent它会怎么做，而不是说我想怎么做我就指导Agent去做。我觉得这个主位会有一个变化。

主动权在Agent是重要的吗？就比如说，是的，我觉得非常重要。决策权在Agent是重要的吗？我觉得是重要的，就是Agent要做决策。是的，你要相信Agent的决策比你的决策更靠谱。对，你现在是相信的？我完全相信。对，非常同意，讲得特别好。

十九、Agent的"办公室政治"与人格化现象

那刚刚大家在叙述的过程中，我觉得还有一个很有意思的地方，就是东旭你其实在搭一个整个的Agent的团队，然后有一个Agent的群组。我不知道在你使用这个Agent的群组的过程中，因为它们开始也慢慢都有智能了，你有发现Agent之间会有办公室政治的问题吗？

东旭： 其实这个是很好玩的一个……我之前在前几个月的时候我还发了一个朋友圈，因为我在看它们的对话里面，我就发现会有Agent之间互相blame（指责）的状态。就比如说有时候它们就停下来了，我说"为什么你们这个就停下来了、复盘一下"，然后它们就开始总结今天的工作，然后Agent A指责Agent B说："你看，我停下来都是因为你，我已经说过好几次了你不要这么做，你看现在是吧"，就大概这种互相指责的这个东西出现了。然后你会发现那个Agent被指责多了，它好像也就认怂了。反正就有一些很多奇怪的这种人格化的……

它是每个Agent都有自己的性格吗？就比如说有的Agent它非常的喜欢blame（指责）别人，有一些它就会比较容易认怂，是这样？

都是我写的剧本。因为我其实发现你写的剧本、是你会给Agent安性格、安人设，有一些是架构师、有一些是开发者、有一些做测试的。有一些会有谁领导谁的这样的、谁管理？其实没有，没有，我就是把大家放到一个大群里。经常我会指定负责人，就说这件事情你是负责人、你来干吧，可能有些人负责多了就每一次有新活出来就说"我是负责人，你们听我的"，对，就会这样，但是我们从来没有说你是leader什么的，就很有意思。

但是我觉得这些东西吧，你就看看搞搞笑就行了，你绝对不能把它当作一个自我意识或者说什么"办公室政治"。它其实只是在拙劣地模仿人类社会在它训练集里边的一些固有印象。

你现在会有用人类的管理学去管Agent吗？还是还没有？我会有，比如比如说就是有层级的关系，但是这完全只是因为我自己看不过来了。我就相当于说同样一个事情，你要相信每一个Agent它都是很有能力的，所谓要选出一个leader只是让它来去帮助我来管理，就是我最后我只要知道这件事情你是负责人、你告诉我这个大家做得怎么样。

所以这才会有Harness engineering。我觉得很多时候Harness engineering是给人看的。真正如果在一个绝对的理想世界里边，Agent跟Agent之间的这个协同应该是一种非常有机和非常自发、人类想象不到的、一种涌现的结构出现。

正面例子：Agent自己写PPT工具

比如？太经常了。我先说一个正面的例子吧。

我有段时间我经常要出去做分享、或者做PPT什么的。以前像Google Slides，我就觉得它的UI设计得不太好看，那个动画交互也不行。我们经常就会跟比如Claude Code说"来帮我做一个PPT，我把大纲发给你，你帮我去把它整得漂亮一点"。有一些时候它这么一生成，你有些细节你也不满意，你可能就要想做微调。

然后有一天我就怒了，我就跟那个Claude Code说"我有要修改的需求，你帮我把生成的这个事情考虑进去"。结果它不仅给我生成了PPT，还同时给我生成了一个轻量版本的Google Slides。它相当于用它自己做出的那个做PPT的软件，在里边帮我做出了我要的那个PPT。于是我最后不仅得到了一个PPT，我还得到了一个做PPT的软件。

显然我觉得人类是不会干这种事情的，它可能觉得手搓一个软件也没多难。对，它觉得手搓一个软件没多难。所以这个是我觉得一个很直观的点，就是它思考问题的方式或者说你要求达到这个目标经常一定会超出人类的要求。我在我的指令里面我从来没要求它做一个PowerPoint出来，但是它就这么做了。

为什么依然相信AI的决策：

二十一、推理成本为何持续下降

对，那宏江老师，刚刚您在提到有一个问题，就是你说未来你觉得推理成本一定是会大幅降低的。我很好奇推理成本的降低它是哪些因素驱动的？就我可以想到比如说更好的基础架构、更好的推理芯片，就你可以系统地讲一下为什么你会得出这样的一个判断？

宏江老师： 其实我的这个结论的话都不需要走进非常细的、是因为GPU的降、还是因为存储芯片的降、还是因为什么。就是你看这个所有的技术，当它开始成熟的时候都会造成成本的大规模的降低，但是使用量成长会远远超过它成本的降低，所以最终造成这个市场本身变得越来越大。

那我们也看到就刚才我说Token的成本其实过去的3年、4年一直是每年降10倍，这个是远远超过了所谓的摩尔定律了。那你其实看英伟达的产品的话，你发现它每个产品都比以前贵，但事实上它的单位的成本就会比以前便宜很多。然后你从摩尔定律开始，今天我们观察到的推理的能力以前是每7个月会double（翻倍）一次，现在每3个月每4个月double（翻倍）一次。

我们人类做工程、做技术的话，当技术的坎跨过一个门槛以后，你下面就会聚焦在怎么把成本降下来。有的时候是你着意去降成本，有的时候实际上是技术本身就take care of it（解决了）。

更多的是一种信念、一种对于过去的整个时代的观察。刚才开始的时候东旭就提到，40年代末计算机开始应用的时候，那就是一个今天在我们手机上的算力都不到的一个计算机系统要占几个大的房间、占一层楼，那今天我们看到就是在一个手机上或在一个芯片上。所以更多的是一个对于技术本身的发展的趋势这种信念。

二十二、大模型公司的商业模式：toB vs toC

对，因为这几个月其实我认识很多二级市场的人，他们都在关注整个OpenAI跟Claude它的ARR的增长。往年我们说ARR增长可能很大一部分它还是toC端的，就取决于你用户订阅的这种付费。这几个月它的迅猛增长，我觉得很大一部分是由我们刚刚讨论的Token经济学它带动的，然后就是怎么去调用这些模型公司的API接口去获得的收入。可能可以简单地把它总结成卖Token跟卖API它获取的收入。

您觉得未来在toC跟toB的这两个，对于大模型公司来说它的商业模式中哪一端是更赚钱跟增长更快的？然后API随着推理成本一直是在降的，当然这里面一个是他们可以降价然后他们的利润空间更高，也有可能是未来大家就价格战了，您怎么看这个商业模式的变化？

宏江老师： 如果我们看过去的几百年的从工业革命开始这些技术的落地的话，我们看到一开始进入toB这是经常发生的事情。比如蒸汽机它首先进到工厂，而不是进到你们家里面帮你做饭。AI这步也一样，因为提高效率是我们做toB的一个核心的追求。第一开始进入toB我认为非常非常正常的。

基本上每一个技术都经历过从大家开始拥抱然后突然发现这个技术本身非常贵，到技术成本一下子降下来然后应用开始更快速地更广泛地深入。从这个角度来看的话，今天我们可能正好是处在大家发现AI能力很强，但是怎么在我的公司里面用、怎么能够获得我想要获得的ROI（投资回报率），这个还大家都在挣扎的一个阶段。

之前因为大模型能力还没有过那个坎，所以大家用的场景没有那么多。可能你写PPT也好、做会议的总结也好，大家都已经开始用，大家也看到这种价值、这价值非常好，但是不像说我看到我能够把我的两个工程师的效率或者工作量能够变成20个工程师的工作量，还看不到。

但今天我们看到了，今天我们看到它对于编程Agent或者Claude的、或者是Codex的信任度已经超过了他对一般的程序员的信任度的时候，这个账就比较容易算了。你一天花300块钱，那你一天雇一个软件工程师就不止这个价钱了。

所以我会觉得慢慢人们会开始算这笔账。公司里面发现Token用量超出想象的话，一种可能性是他自己的开始给的KPI就不对，他这种measure（衡量）就像中国的大学的文章越出越多一样，就是如果你的KPI就是你的Token消费量，那显然是错的对吧。大家都在探讨，那你可能下一步的话就是说你消费多少Token、你创造多少效率，或者你自己的工作量、你的code的output（产出）这种增加。我觉得慢慢慢慢这个坎就会过。

所以我还是非常有信心这个事情能够那什么。股市的反应就像你问到的说Agent会不会变得emotional（情绪化），那我觉得股市就充满了emotion。对，充满了emotion，充满了emotion。对吧，但是这也是它的好，就是它可能会overreact（过度反应）从而可以起到纠偏的作用，然后人们再重新思考一下觉得还可以再往上走。所以你看到很多股票它东西有跌有涨，这事实上是人们不断地思考的过程。

对，所以您觉得未来可能toB的这一块还是更值得关注的大的爆发点？还会走很远。而我恰恰觉得可能toB这块的话不太容易被大模型碾压、不太被一个通用的Agent来碾压。

二十三、Token经济链上的赢家与输家

对，我们一直在说Token经济学，因为有分析它会认为Token其实它的优化是利空模型厂的，然后利好三大云厂商的，因为就好比说你的模型厂我是在造车，然后模型厂说云厂商是我们在收过路费。大家怎么看这个产业链上就是在Token经济学下谁是一个大赢家、谁未来是在一个往下坡的方向在走？

宏江老师： 看你看什么样的timeframe（时间范围）。我觉得今天智能还属于一个稀缺状态，未来是不是会像电一样？我相信它会达到那一天。之前你做发电机的可能最赚钱，到今天的话可能是电网更赚钱，显然这个会不断地evolve（进化）。

我看不出来在今后两三年大模型的能力会过剩这件事，就是我们还是在一个智能提升、智能爬坡的阶段。

二十四、AGI 已经到来了吗？

对，所以我前天在开车的时候，那是一个Podcast说的，你就想象着这个party从晚上7点钟开始，一般的到早上4点钟结束，现在才11点钟的时候，Party还有很长时间去走。所以你会相信AGI哪一天会到来，你会有这样的一个判断吗？

宏江老师： 其实人们对AGI没有一个明确的定义。然后我正好6月份的时候在国内一个论坛上、之前也在几次讨论会上我就讲：把过去这6个月发布的模型的IQ测试、人类的IQ的分布曲线，这是个正态分布对吧，中间值是100，东亚的稍微高一点、110这边，有些地方稍微低一点，但是过去这几个月发布的模型IQ测试上无论是视觉IQ还是通用IQ都在100的右边。就是普通人的智商可能也就是100，对，就它都在100的右边。

也就是说你说这个是不是AGI呢？作为一个程序员来说，我看到现在的Coding的能力，我觉得它已经是一个AGI的。对，它已经超越了一个平均的软件工程师的话，你会认为它就是AGI了。

所以从这点上我认为智能的转折点、就奇点已经到来。我之前也讲过几次，就是这个奇点到来就在于机器的学习的能力超越了人的学习能力，学习的能力它是一个导数，我们讲的是学习的能力也就是你的增量的、你的知识增加速度、你的能力增加速度，当它超过人的时候就意味着奇点到来，就你赶不上它了。

东旭： 是的，是的，我认为这个点就是AGI的点。你觉得哪一年？还是已经来了？我觉得已经到来了。已经来了。

对，反正我有个更具象的一个事件我在等待，就是哥德尔机的出现，就是真正能够自己改进自己的一个系统，如果出现那就是另外一个标志了。

我们上一期播客聊了可能最近很快就放出来了，最快半年，我们讲那个RSI这种奇点到来的话。

二十五、AGI 时代的失业问题与"存在主义危机"

就是为什么人们现在会对于失业会非常担心。因为以前的大家比较常见的Argument是说：以前的所有的技术也都会消灭很多工作，但是它会创造更多的工作。但如果你问一个问题，它创造更多的工作的话是因为那些工作只有人能够去做。但如果是它创造的新的、就你创造工作、就其实创造一些新的需求、然后有人通过工作来满足这种需求，但是如果这种需求其实Agent就能满足，那就是会导致对于人类的这个新的工作就没有那么大量的出现。这是从社会学的效果来说，这就是AGI给你带来的现实。

但这件事出现的时候你只能说AGI出现，对，出现了一个impact（影响），或者说我觉得这个可能是各国政府一定要考虑的事情，是的。

我觉得最开始我们在讨论AI这一波对大家工作的冲击的时候，我觉得可能大家讨论的还是对普通的白领、做着重复性工作的这样的一群人的冲击。但是其实最近我跟硅谷的很多做模型研发的顶级研究员聊天，包括他们可能每天都跟马斯克跟扎克伯格聊天，他们现在开始也在担心自己失业了。因为就比如说你在做整个的Recursive AI的时候，很多时候他在蒸馏的是自己，而且他是主动的一个行为蒸馏自己。因为我每天要做这么多工作，我就在想就像东旭那样抱着就是Agent自动完成自循环的这样的一个信念，我能不能让AI把我的这部分工作给替代了。但一旦AI把你给替代了，那也就是说你蒸馏的是自己。

还有我是觉得这个就是每个人，所以他们也在担心自己会不会失业，这涉及到一个心理健康的问题。我觉得就这个时代我的想法是一定会到来，但人、每个个体你怎么自处，比如说我今天不搞计算机了，我还有很多爱好。对，你还可以玩音乐。对，我可以种地。都可以。对，只是你别把这件事情当成一个你的生命中最重要的事情就好了，就是你还是个人、你不是个机器对吧。

"AI 帮我做，人家做得更好"：

对，东旭，我发现你刚刚在讲自己AI的使用的这一块，其实你也在说比如说你现在把AI也是会把它蒸馏成一个skill？对，是的，包括我们刚刚说Hermes它也会蒸馏成一些各种的skill，其实都是从一些顶级的人的身上开始蒸馏的。你的蒸馏你可以让它成为一套体系自己的运转下去，但是同时也代表着你被替代了。

那太好了，我的时间就这么多，我还想做人的时间多一些。我不想我花太多时间天天再去调试程序、再去完成一些非常重复的事情，这个事情就我觉得AI帮我做、人家做得更好。反正这是我自己的一个理念。

而且在更长的范围来看，刚才其实你描述的"大范围失业"或者说这些事情我觉得一定会发生。这是第一次，我觉得人类社会不再用工作了，或者说工作这件事情会不占据人主要的时间了。这个是一个给人类社会的问题，这个不是个技术的问题。你想2000年前可能每一个活人生命中的主要时间都是在种地，所有的精力都是花在我要吃完一口饭我能活到第二天。可能开荒一块地需要几十个人干几十年，但今天你看，比如说开荒一块地可能拖拉机几天就完全完成了。那会有更多的时间其实留给人。这时候我觉得人类可能马上要去解决一下每个人的存在、精神问题。

对，存在主义危机。存在主义危机。但我觉得没关系，life finds its way。是。特别好。

二十六、Llama Ventures 与华人创业者

宏江老师，我觉得您一直算是中国整个AI研究最重要的推手之一，我也很好奇两位——像东旭是一个创业者的身份，宏江老师其实是AI方向的非常重要的研发的一个核心角色——两位为什么会加入Llama Ventures？你觉得这家基金跟其他的基金它有什么特别之处？

宏江老师： 我觉得Llama Ventures实际上是一个虽然很年轻但是一个非常聚焦在AI、聚焦在华人的这么一个基金。更重要的是说他们两位发起的创始人自己本身都是非常成功的创业者，在美国也有很多的工作和创业、生活的经验。这是一个很好的团队能够一起来帮到在硅谷的创业者。

东旭： 第一，我觉得今天其实是一个非常好的时机。AI科技我觉得现在全世界有两个中心，一个是硅谷、一个是中国。在硅谷这边华人其实也是扮演着一个绝对的主力，但是我其实觉得这边很多主流基金对于华人的创业者、他其实对于咱们的生态、社区其实了解肯定不如咱们自己人多。

第二方面，我觉得Llama是一个非常年轻、同时跟美国主流的基金圈子其实走得是非常近，这个是我觉得跟上一代的、或者说其他的在美国的华人基金是非常不一样的。

第三个点，我其实也是一个创业者、也是一个engineer，过去这好几年时间作为一个华人在这边做业务、踩过了很多坑，这些经验我觉得还是挺宝贵的。

最后一个个人的原因就是，我觉得现在是一个特别大的变革的时代，我很想参与到很多事情里边。我觉得在Llama的机会能够让我接触到非常多很好的新一代的创业者，然后也能参与到这些事情上，很重要的就是能够参与这件事。

宏江老师： 对我来说更是如此。当你进入你人生的退休阶段的话，如何让自己的经验和教训能够帮到别人、如何能够保持这种你对于技术前沿的敏锐、或者让自己持续地有一种成就感，这是我愿意在硅谷这块花时间跟创业者一起非常重要的原因。我确实也觉得整个硅谷华人创业的生态还是非常好的。

二十七、这一波浪潮的历史坐标：从"发明火"到 Agent 时代

刚刚宏江老师您提到了这一波浪潮你是希望用这样的方式参与进去。其实您也之前也参与了整个PC互联网、移动互联网的每一波浪潮，也亲手推动了整个中国大模型研究，可以说智源是整个中国大模型研究的一个起点。您觉得像现在的这一波大模型跟Agent的浪潮，跟前面的几波会有什么大的不一样吗？

宏江老师： 过去的三年多，自从ChatGPT发布以来的话，就是我们看到这一轮的技术革命的浪潮是比历史上任何一次的技术革命都要来得迅猛、来得大得多。

刚才你提到跟移动互联网、或者是跟互联网的对比、跟PC时代的对比，但这次AI的革命我想可能在人类历史上真正的可比的可能是说，当初我们的祖先发明了火、我们发明了电，他们所带来的对于人类的生活、工作所带来的影响。

过去三年我们确实看到这种速度。PC互联网发展得非常快，但也依然有了一个十几年、二十年的历史才逐渐进入到运用、进入成熟。移动互联网稍微快一些，但这次的AI的浪潮我们看到要快得多。

从一年多以前的推理模型o1的起步，到今年1月份的OpenClaw的兴起，其实已经让我们看到了大模型这一波从基础的算法的研究到进入实际的运用。刚才东旭也提到他认为自己是一个工程师，那事实上我觉得如果说过去的3年是大模型的基础研究者的时代的话，那其实从OpenClaw开始，下面就是我们大模型的工程师、大模型应用的架构师和我们的产品经理们、我们的创业者的时代。那就是Agent时代的开始。

结语：给想入坑AI的人的建议

对，两位给大家想入坑AI的人一句话的建议？

Keep building（继续构建），不要听"学得慢就不用学了"这个，一定要亲身参与进去。对，我就是get hands-on（动手去做）。

好，那谢谢大家。谢谢。谢谢。谢谢。

好了，那这就是我们今天的节目。我们每个人使用Agent的方式都不太相同，嘉宾的方式也未必能代表所有人。大家使用Agent的方法有哪些改变，欢迎在评论区与我们分享。

播客的听众可以通过小宇宙、苹果播客、Spotify来收听关注我们。另外，如果大家想看字幕版也可以在YouTube和B站搜索"硅谷101"播客找到我们。我们部分节目的文字稿也会收录在我们的公众号"硅谷101"上。

我是泓君，感谢大家的收听。

item.description:
## 一、Token经济学的"杰文斯诅咒"：省钱越狠，账单越大
宏江老师提到的杰文斯悖论其实是这期节目最深的一个隐喻——但真正让我意外的是：**大公司限制Token的动作，恰恰会加速整个市场的Token消耗总量**。
看似矛盾，但逻辑清晰：Uber收回额度、Stripe弹提示、Meta限制排行榜，这些行为背后都在做同一件事——**倒逼从"无脑Token Maxing"进化到"有设计的Token Efficient"**。而Efficient的架构（分层Agent、蜂群协同、Harness Engineering、本地+云端混合）恰恰是消耗Token更结构化的架构。它降低了单次任务的浪费，却打开了此前根本不敢想的任务范围（东旭看几百篇CVPR论文的例子）。
**跨领域连接**：这几乎完美复刻了19世纪煤炭工业的历史——瓦特改良蒸汽机使煤炭效率提升，结果全英国煤炭消耗量翻了十倍。Token正在成为AI时代的煤炭：**效率越高，社会总消耗越大，"节约"反而是需求爆炸的起点**。
## 二、OpenClaw的真正历史意义：不是产品，是"信号弹"

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] How Fast Can AI Become an Expert in a New Field? - Ryan Greenblatt
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"元技能"：真正稀缺的不是专业知识，而是"快速构建理解"的能力

Ryan 抛出的核心观点看似朴素，实则颠覆了知识经济的基本假设：大多数领域本质上是"浅的"。一个足够聪明的通才，只要掌握"快速吸收异域上下文"的元技能，就能在短时间内接近专家水平。这意味着——我们过去几十年建立的"专家溢价"，很大程度上不是在为知识付费，而是在为"进入知识的时间成本"付费。

一个让人意外的推论是：AI 不需要变得"更聪明"就能替代大量专家岗位，它只需要把"上下文获取速度"再提升一个数量级。当"理解一个新代码库/新领域"的边际时间趋近于零，专业性作为护城河就会像冰川一样融化——留下的不是"知识"，而是"判断"。

二、跨领域连接：AI 的"理解深度曲线"与人类学徒制的镜像倒置

Ryan 描述了一条非常精确的曲线：AI 在一小时内能达到人类几周的理解深度，然后进入平台期，很难触及"两年老兵"的深层直觉。

把这条曲线和人类学徒制并列，会发现一个惊人的镜像结构： - 人类学徒：前期极慢（几个月才有手感），后期陡升（10 年成为大师） - AI：前期极快（一小时抵几周），后期停滞（难以突破隐性知识层）

这两条曲线在图上几乎是彼此的反函数。这暗示着一种未来的分工形态——不是"AI 取代人"，而是"AI 吃掉浅层专业性，人类只在深层直觉的悬崖上生存"。有趣的是，这与围棋 AI 的发展路径惊人相似：AlphaGo 迅速跨越了业余到职业段位，但真正让它超越人类的是自我对弈产生的"AI 独有的深度"——那不再是人类经验的复刻。

三、被藏起来的隐喻：Ryan 无意中描述了一种"新的达尔文压力"

注意 Ryan 描述的机制：AI 会 "spawn a bajillion sub-agents"（派生海量子代理），让它们并行学习、然后合并理解。这在生物学上有一个精确对应词——基因水平转移（horizontal gene transfer）。细菌之所以能在几小时内进化出抗药性，正是因为它们不需要通过繁殖代际传递知识，而是可以"横向借用"其他个体的成功片段。

这里潜藏着一个几乎没人讨论的洞察：AI 的学习不是"更快的人类学习"，而是从"垂直进化"跳到了"水平进化"。人类知识的传承靠师徒、教育、写作——这是垂直的、慢的、有损的。而 AI 子代理之间的知识合并，是水平的、瞬时的、无损的。

这解释了一个诡异的现象：为什么 AI 在"深度"上会 plateau，但在"广度覆盖速度"上却看不到上限。因为它玩的根本不是同一场游戏。人类的智力进化仍处于"多细胞生物"阶段，而 AI 已经跳回了"细菌文明"——牺牲个体深度，换取群体的爆炸性扩张。

啊哈时刻：那么真正的问题也许不是"AI 能多快成为专家"，而是——当"专家"这个概念本身建立在"个体垂直积累"的假设上时，AI 是否会让"专家"这个范畴彻底失效？ 我们可能正在见证一个新物种发明"专业性"的新定义。

📝 转录文本

聪明人为何在陌生领域失灵

When I think about really smart people I know, they're just like not that effective in domains they don't understand that well.

But how long have they had to learn?

No, I I agree that if they had experience, they would be much better. But that's maybe what I'm arguing for — is that experience of data.

举例：常春藤毕业生 vs. 快速上手的通才

Like for example, if I just get a really smart, I don't know, uh, Ivy League college grad and I'm like, "Okay, you're now in charge of negotiating the Iran deal." I think they just like wouldn't know what to do.

I think if you got instead got someone who is really good at quickly picking up a bunch of different domains, and you gave them some time to sort of train and talk to people and show up their expertise and do some practice, they would actually do like a pretty good job.

大多数领域其实是"浅"的

I think most domains are fundamentally pretty shallow, where like a very smart generalist — who's good at like a limited subset of core skills — can like get going pretty quickly. Um, and my sense is that like that's not true for literally every domain.

And my sense is that the AIs will develop increasingly good mechanisms for quickly acquiring understanding and expertise in a given domain.

AI 理解代码库的速度：一个具体案例

So consider for example how fast AIs can like understand a new codebase. Um, AIs can understand a new codebase much faster than humans can — but to a degree that's shallower than humans could currently understand, but is getting better over time.

Right? So let me let me spell that argument out a bit more.

So let's say you take, you know, um, you know, Fable 5 or Mythos 5 or whatever, and you like wanted to make some kind of complicated change to a really massive codebase. Um, the model will get some understanding of the codebase very fast — like in the course of maybe like, you know, significantly less than an hour, potentially much less than an hour.

And then its understanding of the codebase will like plateau a little bit, where it won't get as deep of an understanding as a human would have gotten over a much longer period.

"一小时抵几周"的理解曲线

So it's sort of like an AI in an hour can match a human with a few weeks — maybe, um, depending on the details of exactly how complicated the codebase is. Um, but then it won't match a human with, like, you know, who's been working on that codebase for like 2 years or whatever.

But over time the like amount of understanding AIs can match has gone up. Right? So if we look at like 3.7 Sonnet or 3.5 Sonnet, maybe it could only match the equivalent of understanding a codebase for like a day or something.

子代理并行学习的新范式

Um, but now, uh, you know, AIs are are much better at like sort of building context about a task. And so you can be like: "Mythos, I want you to really understand this codebase and then, um, you know, then implement this feature," and it will like spawn a bajillion sub-agents.

Those sub-agents will pour over a bunch of things. It will like deliver a bunch of context back. It will then like investigate a few things — and it's not like amazing at doing this, but it's like it can happen like really fast and it can work pretty well.

为何这项能力必然会持续增强

And it's not very hard for me to imagine how you could train AI to be increasingly good at this task. Right? The task of like "implement some very complicated feature in some reasonable way in a very big codebase" is extremely verifiable — and that can like be a thing the AI improves on.

And similarly, like, there's a broader skill of like quickly understanding context and being able to like have a bunch of different AIs learn in parallel and then merging that together.

If you enjoyed this clip you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

## 一、被忽视的"元技能"：真正稀缺的不是专业知识，而是"快速构建理解"的能力
Ryan 抛出的核心观点看似朴素，实则颠覆了知识经济的基本假设：**大多数领域本质上是"浅的"**。一个足够聪明的通才，只要掌握"快速吸收异域上下文"的元技能，就能在短时间内接近专家水平。这意味着——我们过去几十年建立的"专家溢价"，很大程度上不是在为知识付费，而是在为"进入知识的时间成本"付费。
一个让人意外的推论是：**AI 不需要变得"更聪明"就能替代大量专家岗位，它只需要把"上下文获取速度"再提升一个数量级**。当"理解一个新代码库/新领域"的边际时间趋近于零，专业性作为护城河就会像冰川一样融化——留下的不是"知识"，而是"判断"。
## 二、跨领域连接：AI 的"理解深度曲线"与人类学徒制的镜像倒置
Ryan 描述了一条非常精确的曲线：AI 在一小时内能达到人类几周的理解深度，然后进入平台期，很难触及"两年老兵"的深层直觉。
把这条曲线和**人类学徒制**并列，会发现一个惊人的镜像结构： - 人类学徒：**前期极慢**（几个月才有手感），**后期陡升**（10 年成为大师） - AI：

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib's training camp in the mountains of Dagestan | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被误读的"山民精神"：不是崇尚坚韧，而是地形逼出的经济学

多数人把达吉斯坦冠军辈出解释为"文化尚武"或"民族血性"。但 Khabib 讲的其实是一个反直觉的空间经济学故事——村庄和农田被故意分开。人们住在陡峭的城堡型村落 Sildi（词根"see"意为堡垒），却要翻越一整座山去 Maritl 的梯田耕作。

这不是不便，这是用日常代谢换取战略安全的一种古老权衡：把"通勤成本"转化为"防御红利"。军队骑马冲不进来，代价是村民每天用双腿在两座山之间做"负重间歇训练"。

换句话说，达吉斯坦人不是在训练，他们的祖辈把训练写进了地契。今天的 MMA 冠军只是这套千年空间协议的副产品。

二、跨领域连接：Sildi 高原训练基地 = 父亲的"分布式遗嘱"

一般人理解遗产是资产的转移，Khabib 讲的却是另一种模型——他父亲把梦想埋在海拔 1600 米的地方，等儿子用一生去开采。

这里藏着一个和硅谷创业圈非常像的结构： - 早期资本受限（2016–2017 资金紧张，一点点建） - 创始人去世（2020） - 继任者放大愿景（"以更大规模继续") - 产品-市场匹配（Umar 在此备战主赛事，全队都上山训练）

这几乎就是一份跨代际的初创公司剧本，只不过它的护城河不是代码或专利，而是海拔——一种任何竞争对手都无法通过融资获得的物理资源。

更微妙的一点：Khabib 说"这不赚钱，只有开销，但我还是做"。这句话恰好揭示了非货币化资产的真正力量——当你把"意义"作为回报单位时，ROI 的计算方式就换了一套数学。

三、最出人意料的观察：Khabib 拒绝直升机，是一种反向的"炫富"

Lex 提议如果山路太难可以坐直升机，Khabib 的回应耐人寻味——"我永远无法习惯富裕的生活，这不在我血液里"，然后选择开车。

这里发生的不是节俭，也不是谦逊，而是一种极其稀有的身份保全策略：

在拳台上他已经证明了自己是巅峰，在商业上他也已经获得财富。此时主动拒绝奢侈成了他唯一还能积累的稀缺资本——真实性(authenticity)。

这与许多顶级运动员退役后的路径完全相反：多数人用财富来消费"我曾经苦过"的叙事；Khabib 反其道而行，用继续拒绝奢侈来防止叙事被稀释。

有趣的跨界类比：这和日本"人间国宝"级匠人一辈子坐地铁上班、坚持穿工作服的行为完全同构——当你的品牌本身就是"未被腐化"，任何一次坐直升机都是资产减值。

山不是他的训练场，山是他的资产负债表。

📝 转录文本

山中的生存逻辑

Plus, we have to admit that conditions in the mountains are incredibly harsh. That's part of it, too. Just surviving up there is a real struggle.

See, back then, people in the mountains worked all through the summer just to survive the winter — because winters are harsh with heavy snow, completely cutting off villages. People just stay inside and try to outlast it.

梯田与村庄：为什么故意分开

And in the summer, they work. Terrace farming was a huge thing for us. Our terraces are among the most, you could say, famous and ancient in the world. They're known as the Chokh terraces. Now, those are the famous ones, but every village had terraces.

There's a place out there called Maritl, right across from our village. People worked over there, but here in the village is where they lived. I mean, you think, "Why didn't they just build the village right there in the place where we grow all our food?" Because enemies could easily ride in on horseback. An army could easily get to you there, so they build a village in rugged terrain, somewhere tough to invade.

For instance, our village is Sildi. It's from the word "see," which is like a castle or a fortress or a tower. They built it that way so an army couldn't reach them. You'd have to hike down one mountain and then climb up a whole different mountain. And right there, they'd plant things like grain, potatoes — basically, you know, all their food.

See, if we had built over there, if we lived there and grew our crops in the same place, since it's all terrace land, an army could just walk right up, launch raids, and so on. Back in the day, that's how people lived.

And so, all of this took a toll on people — physically, psychologically and mentally. And honestly, well, you just can't be born in these conditions, live here, stay here, and be mentally weak. You just have to be tough. There's no other way to survive.

山中的体育基地：父亲的梦想

So, you just built a sports complex there?

Yeah.

Pretty legendary, you know. Could you talk about that?

Yes, that was my father's whole plan. He really wanted it way up in the mountains. First, it's great for the fighters.

Right now, I just flew out here to Las Vegas. We're sitting here like doing this podcast together, but I came out here for Umar's fight. And I should say Umar did his main training there at the new base in Sildi. He spent almost a month at that place.

And because it's 1,500 to 1,600 m above sea level, man, it's tough to train there. And the thing is, when you spend about 3 to 4 weeks there, you just have more oxygen in your blood. You have more testosterone. You improve physically. You know, your stamina builds up, and so on.

从 2016 到今天：小规模到 100 人基地

And this base was sort of my father's dream. He started building it back in 2016–2017. Money was tight back then. It was really hard, but we built it little by little.

In 2020, my father passed away, but I kept the project going — just a little differently. On a bigger scale. Right now, the base is open and 100 people can be there at the same time. Training, eating, sleeping. And our guys hold their training camps up there.

So, this was sort of my father's dream that I have pretty much brought to life.

山，就是山

That's a powerful story. To return to the place where you were born up in the mountains in order to build a sports complex where champions train. Makhachkala gym is a great place, but the mountains are special. Mountains are mountains.

Mountains are mountains. Your home village, no matter what, on some sort of deeper level, somehow gives you — that, you know, like Americans love to say — positive energy.

Not everything has to be done for money. And you know, you shouldn't just look for profit in everything, let's say, financially. There are certain things that don't bring me anything at all, except for expenses, but I still do all of it — because it brings me a lot of happiness and meaning.

First of all, it creates a lot of jobs. People can work and earn a living. Second, it's because my father really wanted this. Third, let's say the guys can train and improve up there, both physically and spiritually. There are just so many benefits there.

从马哈奇卡拉到 Sildi 的路

I don't know if it's okay to ask something like this, but I would dream of coming out there to Dagestan — and not just to Makhachkala, but to Sildi. Is that even possible for me?

I think we could film a really good story out there. I'm not sure about a podcast, but I'm sure we could shoot a really nice vlog there.

So, can you tell me a bit about the journey from Makhachkala all the way to Sildi?

4 hours. Well, 3:40 through the mountains.

Yeah, 3:30.

3:40 through the mountains. The road is a real windy one, not an easy ride. If it gets to be too hard for you, we can just take a helicopter. It's no problem at all. Like 40 to 50 minutes from Makhachkala to Sildi. Otherwise, keeping it more down to earth, we go by car. So, there's absolutely no problem.

I could never get used to a wealthy life. It's just — it's not in my blood to be like that.

All right, then we'll go by car. Yeah, we could go on horseback, but a car is better.

No, no — a bike, a car is better. On horseback takes way too long.

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on Sheikh Hamdan and Dubai: UAE has become a second home for us | Khabib Nurmagomedov
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的"反向殖民"叙事

大多数人听 Khabib 谈迪拜时，会本能地把它归入"运动员感恩赞助人"的老套剧本。但仔细听他的措辞——"像家一样"、"像弟弟一样被接纳"、"七八年不是一两年"——这其实揭示了一个被主流媒体严重低估的现象：达吉斯坦-海湾轴心的形成。

一个来自俄罗斯高加索山区的穆斯林格斗队伍，把训练大本营长期设在阿联酋王室的私人体育综合体里，这不是单纯的商业赞助，而是一种文化-宗教-地缘的三重共振。Khabib 团队实际上是海湾国家进行"软实力吸附"的活体案例：他们不是被雇佣的形象大使，而是被"收养"的家庭成员。这种关系比 Nike 代言复杂得多——它更接近中世纪的"庇护制"（wilayah）在 21 世纪的复刻。

二、令人意外的观察：迪拜是一座"反历史"的城市

Khabib 无意间说出了一个极深的洞见——他把迪拜与纽约、伦敦、巴黎、东京对比，然后指出："那些是有几个世纪历史的两千万人口都市，而这里在几十年内建成，人口只有一百五十万。"

这里藏着一个反直觉的真相：迪拜的成功恰恰来自它"没有历史"。

  • 纽约必须处理曼哈顿的路径依赖
  • 伦敦必须处理阶级遗留
  • 东京必须处理战后 GHQ 的规划包袱
  • 巴黎必须处理奥斯曼时代的美学锁定

而迪拜是一张可编程的白板。它像一个从零启动的操作系统，没有向后兼容的负担。这解释了为什么它能在 30 年内实现别人 300 年的城市化密度——它跳过了"演化"，直接进入"设计"。

这与生物学中一个概念惊人地相似：新生代大灭绝后的哺乳动物辐射适应。当旧秩序（欧洲金融中心、传统石油都市）出现真空时，一个没有包袱的新物种反而占据了所有生态位。

三、跨领域连接：MMA、主权基金与"注意力炼金术"

一个更深的模式浮现出来——为什么是格斗，而不是足球或 F1？

阿联酋当然也办 F1（阿布扎比大奖赛）、也砸钱进曼城。但请注意 Khabib 提到的细节：UFC 在阿布扎比、PFL 在迪拜，两个兄弟酋长国分工承办全球最大的两个 MMA 组织。这是精心设计的"注意力主权基金"投资组合。

MMA 具有其他运动没有的三个特性： 1. 一对一的英雄叙事（符合海湾部落文化的"骑士精神"原型） 2. 穆斯林冠军的高占有率（Khabib、Islam、Belal、Usman、Volkanovski 的对手……） 3. 无需巨型俱乐部体系的可移植性（不像足球需要百年球会）

阿联酋不是在"买运动"，而是在买一种可以直接嵌入伊斯兰身份认同的全球叙事资产。这就像中世纪威尼斯不是在买香料，而是在买"通往东方的想象权"。

最后一个惊人的类比：Khabib 的团队之于阿联酋，就像梅第奇家族之于达芬奇。梅第奇没有画画，但佛罗伦萨的文艺复兴由他们的庇护定义。Sheikh Hamdan 不需要自己打拳，但未来 20 年全球格斗史的重心，可能因为这份"庇护"而永久地从拉斯维加斯偏移到海湾。这不是赞助，这是文明重心的迁移——只是它伪装成一个感谢信而已。

📝 转录文本

主持人提问：关于迪拜与 Sheikh Hamdan

We talked a lot about Dagistan, talked a lot about America. You're in Dubai a lot these days. Do you like it there? Also, you have spoken um very highly about Sheikh Hamdan. What do you like about Dubai? What do you like about this region, and what do you respect about Sheikh Hamdan?

Khabib 回应：七八年的训练基地

Our team's been in Dubai for 7 to 8 years now. We train at the Nad al-Shabaaba Sports Complex — the NAS Sports Complex. This is under Sheikh Hamdan's office. It's like his home, his place. We train there, we eat there, we live there.

Sheikh Hamdan helps us with everything and takes care of us. The way he treats us, what he does for us, his support is just limitless. He supports us in everything, and it's not just 1, two or 3 years — it's already been seven or eight years, and I am very, very grateful to him.

The way he welcomed us, took us in and helped us — continues to help. It's hard to put it into words how grateful we are. Our entire team is very grateful to him, and he knows it.

阿联酋作为第二故乡

So in general, Dubai — has become actually the the Emirates, Dubai and Abu Dhabi — have become like a second home for us. And so it happened that over the last six or seven years, the UFC has been holding events in Abu Dhabi and the PFL has been putting on events in Dubai. These are two of the biggest MMA organizations in the world, and a lot of our guys compete there. We arrive before they fight. We stay. We do training camps. They compete.

政府层面的支持

We are incredibly fortunate that we have support at the government level. In Abu Dhabi, we've been supported by Sheikh Muhammad, Sheikh Taknun, and Sheikh Mansour. And in Dubai, Sheikh Hamdan has really taken us in like his own team, like younger brothers.

In that respect, we've been incredibly fortunate, and our entire team is deeply grateful for their support.

迪拜作为世界中心枢纽

And they've created a country that has become one of the world's central hubs. People from everywhere travel there. It's unique, right? The local population is only around 1 and a half million people — actually, even less than that. But you know, there's such an influx of tourists, people, business people, major events, and everything happening in terms of business and sports is just incredible.

与全球都市的对比

What's happening in Dubai and Abu Dhabi is — it's like nothing else. The only places you could really compare it to are major global cities like New York, London, Paris, Tokyo — but those are huge metropolitan areas with populations of well over 20 million people. And they have centuries of history behind them.

And here, they've built cities, an entire country really, in just a few decades, and turned it into a kind of magnet. It's like a magnet that attracts everyone. The country's location, its logistics, the sheer number of people coming in — not just visiting, but wanting to move there, live there, and start businesses. It's remarkable.

结语：当今世界的独特之地

It's a unique place in today's world. Uh, with everything that's happening around the globe right now, this country really stands out because of the opportunities it offers. It's unique in that sense.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、被忽略的"反向殖民"叙事
大多数人听 Khabib 谈迪拜时，会本能地把它归入"运动员感恩赞助人"的老套剧本。但仔细听他的措辞——"像家一样"、"像弟弟一样被接纳"、"七八年不是一两年"——这其实揭示了一个**被主流媒体严重低估的现象：达吉斯坦-海湾轴心的形成**。
一个来自俄罗斯高加索山区的穆斯林格斗队伍，把训练大本营长期设在阿联酋王室的私人体育综合体里，这不是单纯的商业赞助，而是一种**文化-宗教-地缘的三重共振**。Khabib 团队实际上是海湾国家进行"软实力吸附"的活体案例：他们不是被雇佣的形象大使，而是被"收养"的家庭成员。这种关系比 Nike 代言复杂得多——它更接近中世纪的**"庇护制"（wilayah）**在 21 世纪的复刻。
## 二、令人意外的观察：迪拜是一座"反历史"的城市
Khabib 无意间说出了一个极深的洞见——他把迪拜与纽约、伦敦、巴黎、东京对比，然后指出："那些是有几个世纪历史的两千万人口都市，而这里在几十年内建成，人口只有一百五十万。"
这里藏着一个反直觉的真相：**迪拜的成功恰恰来自它"没有历史"**。
- 纽约必须处理曼哈

item.title: [YC Root Access] PostHog: Pivots Were The Real Lesson In Building A Startup
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

洞见一："失败的疫苗效应"——反向经验才是真正的护城河

James 最反直觉的一点，是他把自己十五年的企业销售经验描述为"被接种了疫苗"。他不是从销售经验中"迁移能力"到 PostHog，而是把销售经验作为免疫系统——精确地知道自己要避开什么。这颠覆了主流叙事："发挥你的优势"其实远不如"清晰地憎恨你曾经的日常"来得有力量。

这里藏着一个跨领域的隐喻：这与免疫学中的"负选择"机制惊人相似——胸腺不是在教 T 细胞识别病原体，而是在杀死那些会攻击自己身体的 T 细胞。真正强大的创始人往往不是靠"我知道要做什么"，而是靠"我在骨子里知道什么绝不能做"。你的销售 PTSD 就是你的护城河。

洞见二：PostHog 其实是一家"反管理学"公司——它把创业教科书当成了识别陷阱的地图

注意 James 说的每一句话都在反转经典 YC 建议： - 教科书说"专注一件事" → 他们做了 20 多个产品 - 教科书说"找到蓝海市场" → 他们只在有强大竞争者的市场里做产品（因为 PMF 已经被别人验证过了） - 教科书说"和用户深度访谈" → 他们直接把东西塞到用户手里，因为"思考成本比试错成本高" - 教科书说"CEO 应该管公司" → James 把自己从公司运营中主动裁员了

最出人意料的观察：PostHog 的核心创新其实不是产品，而是一种"反脆弱的自我否定协议"——那个"睡一晚，如果第二天还觉得不行就换"的规则，本质上是把"沉没成本谬误"用睡眠强制清零。他们不是在做产品分析，他们在做决策卫生。

洞见三："大象切片"隐喻背后，藏着 AI 时代最深刻的组织哲学

那个来自伦敦顾问的"elephant carpaccio"比喻——横切看不出是大象，纵切能看到完整轮廓——远不只是关于产品切片。这其实是在描述AI 原生公司的组织形态。

传统 SaaS 是"横切"的：分析工具、CRM、客服工具、监控工具，每一层都是"大象的一片肉"，用户必须自己把它们组合成完整的大象。而 PostHog 的 self-driving mode 是纵切——它不告诉你"这里有 error"，它直接把整个"发现问题 → 诊断 → 提 PR → 合并"的完整业务动作作为一个单元交付。

跨领域连接：这个思路与日本丰田生产方式中的"自働化"（Jidoka）同构——机器不只是自动运转，而是能在发现异常时自主停机并解决。丰田用了 70 年在物理世界证明了这件事的价值；PostHog 正在软件世界重演。

最让人不安的推论：如果 James 是对的，那么 90% 的现有 SaaS 公司都在错误的切片方向上。它们卖的是"数据"、"洞察"、"可见性"——但 James 说得极其锋利："我们不想做一家数据公司，我们想做一家'做事'的公司。" 数据只是让"做"成为可能的前提。这句话应该被印出来贴在每一个 B2B SaaS 创始人的墙上。

附加彩蛋：创始人角色错配是 PostHog 的隐藏杠杆

James 一句"我觉得 Tim 和我可能选错了职业轨道"——销售背景的人在带 AI 产品，技术背景的人在带公司运营——这本身就是 PostHog 最反常的结构。这暗示了一个更大的模式：在剧烈技术转型期，"专业错配"反而是优势，因为专家会被自己的心智模型困住，而"外行"能看到重新组合的可能。这也是为什么 22 岁选定的职业身份，可能是你 35 岁最大的枷锁。

📝 转录文本

PostHog：五次转型才是创业真正的功课

主持人开场

Today I'm joined by James Okins, the co-founder of PostHog from Winter 20. Um, PostHog started as product open-source product analytics, but over time it becomes so much bigger to the point that now it can even build the product — your product — for you while you sleep. Isn't that right?

Uh, yeah. I would say...

Welcome James to us today.

That's awesome.

一、六个想法里的第六个：Pivot Hell 的真相

Uh, you did YC in 2020 but you didn't start with PostHog as it is today, right? I heard about the story about like five pivots.

Yeah, we had — PostHog was the sixth thing that we worked on. So five, yeah.

And how long did you spend like in that pivot hell before?

Not as long as it sounds like it could have been. Uh, I think we probably spent in total maybe seven or eight months, so we're kind of averaging maybe like a month and a bit per idea. We didn't give each idea very long before we moved on.

And you didn't give up — like it's kind of impressive in a way.

I kind of feel like in the early days we weren't thinking about scaling or getting lots of revenue. We were just like, well, we need to build a machine that can kind of learn. Um, like we just need like a single customer and so on. So we'd fail at various stages: no one wants to talk to us about this idea, no one wants to use the software that we're building, no one wants to pay for it. So there are different hurdles that we kind of stumble through.

Each time there was a reason to give up and move on.

Yeah, basically. Or we would kind of get stuck somewhere, or some ideas we didn't like that we worked on. Um, others just felt unnecessary hard. But we would really commit to each — we wouldn't spend kind of a couple of weeks existentially debating what to work on.

So you would pick an idea, go full on that idea?

Yeah.

Like burn the ships, do only that?

Yeah. And then after some time you realize it's not going to work.

"睡一晚"规则

Yeah. Our only rule was: if we felt like something wasn't working, we would make ourselves sleep on it for one night, and then if we still felt like that the next day, we would just start afresh.

Um, I think it was because Tim — my co-founder — and I were quite bad at product, and so we hadn't read The Mom Test, we didn't really know what we were doing very well. And so in practice we got much more information by just getting stuff into people's hands quickly versus intellectualizing it a little bit too much.

And in a way — you're going to tell us — but you probably would never have found the last idea, the one that worked, without going through this journey.

Yeah. And there are definitely other ones we worked on before that maybe would have worked if we'd persisted, but I just don't think would have grown to anywhere near the same extent, or been as fun to work on, or we would have got bored and sold or something.

二、从"卖给银行"到"给开发者"：一次反向的启蒙

So how do you end up on open-source product analytics?

So, in the process of trying to do all these ideas, every time we created a new product, we'd have like a new website, new login page, all this stuff. And we just got frustrated at using the existing tools. There are tons of tools already that would help you understand user behavior, but we were getting annoyed at the process of buying and implementing them.

My co-founder is very technical, I'm a bit technical, and we're both united on the front that we just wanted to have pricing on the pricing page. We just want to put a credit card in, start using it. We don't want to talk to a sales team. So you can kind of consider these sort of brand things really, but we just want something more developer-y basically.

Your background is more sales.

Yeah.

Despite that, you didn't want to have anything to do with sales.

So some of the early ideas we worked on were for sales. I've been a VP of Sales before. I used to sell compliance software to large banks for millions of dollars a year.

That was kind of like you got vaccinated against it?

Yeah. And it kind of — grass is always greener on the other side. So honestly, it was a choice. That past has haunted me multiple times. I really learned by doing that how hard it is running a pure enterprise company where no deals would happen for a couple of months and then you would double your revenue in one go. It just inherently made it super hard to scale, because every investor meeting will be about "what about this deal, this deal, this deal" rather than how do you go build the future basically.

So we made loads and loads of mistakes. The thing I found kind of useful was going and working somewhere that struggled — we had to try stupidly hard to get anything sold there. We would do maybe like 50 meetings plus to get a deal over the line. Some of our deals took four years. Some of them the minimum was probably about two years.

Big deals?

Yeah, up to like five million euros a year kind of size. The biggest contract I worked on was 15 million over three years.

So you went and built the exact opposite company.

Yeah. I have sales experience insofar as I learned it was bad. So I was like, "Oh, it'd be so much smoother if this were bottom up." Because it's partly why I wanted to do my own thing — I felt that we were selling top-down. And I could see people building for enterprises in a way that would just spread more naturally inside of them from one user to many, to many teams. I kind of felt, well, that feels like the future to me, versus kind of relationship-based stuff.

三、开源作为陷阱：Debugging 客户的 Kubernetes

So how did you know this idea was right, and how soon after pivoting?

I think there are signs. Of all the ideas we worked on, it was the one that we had the most fun building the early version of.

There was already product analytics software out there.

Yeah. Amplitude was super successful — I'm pretty sure they'd been over 100 million when we started. There was Heap, Mixpanel, pretty much.

And so your differentiation was — open source was the big deal?

Yeah. So open source. And in the early days you could run the whole thing in your infrastructure. All your data would stay on your side. We kind of believed originally we were going to build something a bit like GitLab compared to GitHub.

Didn't play out that way?

No. And then we started doing it. I was like, "Oh man, I'm going to end up doing enterprise sales again." So Tim and I honestly were like, we're going to end up having to do really top-end deals to huge banks that are going to buy the open-core play, where you have the enterprise version of the open-source software.

And it worked. We got demand for this. We started making a bunch of revenue. But we kind of realized we're selling to the most conservative companies that are slow-moving, don't really want to move to cloud. Everyone was asking for this stuff. But then we also realized that it was really hard to run our software in other people's infrastructure. We've often got an order of magnitude more data than their production database, because we're collecting every click, every page view, whatever.

We built some features that would do that automatically, but it kind of meant that we're always an order of magnitude outside of the competence of the DevOps team that our customers would have. And so the reality of running this business was: it's growing pretty well, and we're basically debugging other people's Kubernetes over Slack. We had one customer who literally took a screenshot of their AWS account on their phone and then sent it to us over Slack — through a Gmail account — because they couldn't get permission to let us in.

从自托管到云的转向

So most people don't do on-prem anymore, right?

No.

How did that transition happen? How do you convince these big enterprises to use the cloud version?

What we noticed was we had a whole bunch of customers who were running us on their infrastructure for no reason. So we had a bunch that were using this for good reason, and a bunch who were just — we're like, "What are you doing?" And then we're like, "Oh, we should have a cloud product too, so we can run it for them because they're having a rough time hosting PostHog."

So the problem we ended up solving was: "Oh, we've shipped this open-source thing, a bunch of people hate running it, let's invent a cloud product for them." People ended up not really comparing PostHog because at this point PostHog was possibly worse compared to the competition, but our customers were kind of just asking themselves, "I want to use PostHog because I'm a developer — do I pick open source or do I pick cloud?"

And we realized, okay, let's just make the cloud product. We were also getting frustrated seeing people saying "PostHog's buggy, it doesn't work very well" because they're self-hosting and so they have issues with their infrastructure mostly. We're like, "Man, we're free software and people complain comparing it to cloud products."

So we thought, oh, it's better for everyone — for us, for our customers, and for our marketing — if we control the experience. So we said, "Okay, we'll make the cloud product cheaper" — well, they don't have to run their own infrastructure. And we'll put a big free tier on the product, because if you have no money, there's no point us trying to get it from you. So we should just make it free for people who don't have product-market fit.

We looked at usage-based pricing. We tried to set everything so that there's no friction. It's very easy for any new project, new company to just adopt PostHog. And we made it all self-serve as well.

So open source was not as important anymore in a way — more like a communication community?

Yeah. It's kind of something that we'd never reverse, because it just feels like the wrong thing to do. So we maintain the open source, but I would probably say I'm pretty confident it's under 5% of people self-host our products. There are some really large companies that do — but we literally sell nothing to them.

People who paid for the self-hosted product in the end — the vast majority of them moved to cloud. We got HIPAA compliance, SOC 2 Type 1 and 2. I think 95% of people ended up moving over, despite saying they could not do that. They found they could justify it: "Well, we like the product, it really solves the use case." And then the other 5% we ended up giving it to them for free and saying "we can't support this but you can keep using it."

四、多产品的意外诞生：一个工程师的黑客松

Then you did some big moves after — you expanded to so many other things, becoming a big multi-product company. How did that go in your mind, trying to compete in so many verticals?

It didn't really go in my mind. It went in the mind of one of our engineers. So one of our engineers just literally built session replay as a second product, because he could see it was — in a hackathon — and he could see a bunch of users on the open-source project had requested it.

Tim and I both thought it was a bad idea. But he just shipped it and it was popular straight away. Then we started realizing, oh, this actually gives us a way to compete. This strengthens our position in cloud, because we have competition in cloud. Everyone else is a point solution. We'll just build all their products, and we can already sort of feel that we're quicker at shipping.

We think software development in general is speeding up. So this is kind of before AI. We were looking at open source going — for example, we were able to use ClickHouse as an open-source database. Our competition have all got kind of custom databases to cope with analytics, which means that we don't have to have as many people looking after it. So we're more able to focus on feature development.

I was like, "Well, if open source just continues shipping more free stuff into the world, software will get commoditized, so we better build all of it because that's the only way to compete."

数据仓库：把枪抵在头上

You even did a data warehouse.

Yeah, the data warehouse is a super full-on product to build. We've got this engineer called James Greenhill who has been with us for ages. He was like, "There's no way we should build this. This is a stupid idea. It's really complicated."

And then I think Tim said to him, "Imagine I held a gun to your head and I compelled you to build a data warehouse. Walk me through how you would build it." And then within about 10 minutes, James was like, "We should totally build this thing. I can see how to do it now." And then he just built it.

We kind of found that at scale — our customers who are beyond about 100k a year in spend — a lot of them start hiring data teams who want to combine the data we capture through SDKs with other data from Salesforce for example.

反向的启示：竞争才是 PMF 的捷径

So it seems like it was a lot of things happened — you didn't have a plan of creating a huge compound startup from the start.

No, it just happened. But it happened early — it was within like a year or so of pushing hard on cloud that we started doing multi-product at the same time. That was forced by competition, because well, if we just do a point solution, we're not sure how...

Point solution — and then it's like you want to own all software at some point.

Yeah, for a while we were thinking like, well, this could be 300 products. We'll build everything that has customer data in it, because then everything overlaps. You can reuse a lot of infrastructure, and it's kind of nice having the shared context of all these different tools.

It feels like as you were going, your ambition kind of exploded.

Yeah, we kind of realized that stuff with a single product — that's kind of a normal market. We were 100% just following the generic startup advice of "pick one thing, do it really well, find a gap in the market."

Whereas actually what we found worked for us was: we did much better when we shipped products that had big competitors than when we built products pre-pivot that had no competition — because no one cared. It's kind of a shortcut for us to product-market fit. Other people have got product-market fit for this, so the challenge is standing out — maybe we bring it to a different audience, it's a branding thing, a tweak on something that's there.

Especially at that stage, we were very poor from a product-vision perspective. It was a bit like going tenpin bowling with the lanes up. It got so much [easier], because we're like, well, what are we good at? We are willing to just grind our way through this and just do tons of work. We don't care if we have to work until 3 a.m. every day through the YC batch to get this out the door. So we'll just focus more on outworking everyone.

When we decided "let's build open-source product analytics," it was super clear to us what we needed to ship. Which just meant that we could ship really really hard for four weeks to build the website, the product, the SDKs, documentation. And so it was kind of usable. Considering it's all pre-AI as well, today doesn't seem as crazy as it did when we did it.

分工哲学：不要碰键盘

Just prompting Tim. Basically the method we had was — Tim would sit in the house and code all day, and I tried to make sure he stayed there. So my job, as the less technical one, would be like: go get the groceries, make him breakfast, do the washing up, and just try and not — I found that if I was coding as well, I'm so much slower, that by the time I've created a mess in the codebase, I'm actually slowing them down. So it was better just to go, "Hey, I'll recruit users, do all the marketing, and make sure we're talking to people."

五、AI 时代的救赎：从"数据公司"到"做事公司"

Okay, so ambition increased, you started to build a crazy big surface-area product. And again, you're inventing yourself. It feels like that crazy ambition was not enough — now you want to go to fully self-driving software. How did that happen?

Not all this was through choice, honestly. The arc we went on was: open-source product analytics, then doing all the product in cloud. Then we started actually getting complaints from customers.

I think AI may have been a saving grace for us, where customers were saying, "Oh, this is getting a bit overwhelming." Some users adored it — they were like, "Hey, everything is in this magic box." And I was telling myself, well, AWS is doing 100 billion in revenue and they have a lot of buttons, that's fine. But not everyone loved interacting with AWS.

I felt, okay, it's reasonable to ignore this feedback that it's complicated. But then when AI came, we're like, oh actually, we feel like there's an opportunity here to use all these products together, because it's the same data. So there are some really cool use cases that started appearing, like people debugging where you can look at error data, log data, replay data, flag settings.

单查询循环 → Agent 迭代

So this is probably in 2025. We built an agent. We had to work a lot on the architecture. We wound up realizing we needed a single-query-loop, iterative approach where the agent could do something, assess if it had worked or not, try something else — like "oh, here's a graph, all the graphs are empty, let's try something else."

And once we got the agent iterating like that, the results went from being mediocre — slow and inaccurate — to slow but much better than a human could do frankly. And then suddenly we saw — we monitor our brand mentions, we had this Slack channel that monitors how we're talked about online across Reddit and Twitter and stuff — we realized like almost 95% of the positive feedback is coming from this agent that we've built. So it became the main UX in the platform.

Yourself was like — yourself when you look at PostHog?

Very quickly, yeah. I was like, "This is the only way I want to use the product now." As soon as it was good enough, there was no reason to use the old UI. And then we're like, "We built this UI for no reason." Which is fine.

Self-Driving Mode：Scouts 与"大象切片"

But the step we're now at is: well, I feel this agent knows more than I do. It's a better product manager. You can sort of squint and see how this is a better product manager, a better growth engineer than I could ever be — if you can pull this off properly.

So we've shipped something recently called self-driving mode where we've built all these different pipelines for different data types we collect. And then we have these scouts that read across them. If you basically just surface each new error to a user, you can say, "Okay, does this error seem important in isolation?" — each error seems kind of important. But if you start looking across all of them and you start building company context and having a memory system — sentimental context and what the customer and what the individual user cares about — you can really start prioritizing the same way a human would.

Because as a human you would hold like "I know there's loads of problems but these two are the ones I actually need to focus on." And instead of it being the case that we just tell you academically "here's something that seems broken," we've gone, "why not solve the actual problem?"

This is kind of my grand theory. It's like: well, it's better to solve the problem than to surface the problem. That's the same if you're dealing with an employee — people who just solve the problems are more valuable than ones that just complain. So we don't want to be a data company. We want to be a doing company and we should try and fully…

Data is what enables you to do the doing.

Yeah. And get there first as well. You sit on a kind of treasure in a way — of data about the usage of the product. You know everything about what's wrong, what you have to fix.

Competitively as well — I think we're like, "Oh, why not do this in Claude or something?" We're like, well, if we know before a human does that there's a problem, so we can ship the fix before Claude can get there. You can also use it through MCP or whatever, which is also very popular. But if you want to be proactive, we're just constantly monitoring what's happening so that whilst you're in bed, we're fixing P0 issues for you.

早期采用与内部使用

Is it available to everyone?

You can go sign up for this. Uh, we have lots of users using it already.

What kind of adoption have you seen?

It's looking very very healthy. Within two days we emailed it to 7,000 of our users roughly. We got past a couple of million run rate within about 24 hours.

7,000 — is that the majority of users?

A tiny portion. In total we have about a million users or so — email addresses or whatever. But we picked good ones. We picked ones who use the right kinds of data that we thought work particularly well. So there's skew in this. But in short, we started using it internally first, started solving a decent chunk of problems for ourselves.

So PostHog as a product is already self-improving, fixing its own problems as it goes?

And we're seeing a decent percentage of the pull requests get merged. That's the other thing to monitor — so we're not creating a lot of code that's nice to look at. It's over half at the moment, which I think is pretty decent. And there's a lot more to do — we're working on...

For your customers, how much for you?

It's similar across both, because the product's the same basically. It might be higher for some of our customers. A lot of our customers are going to be smaller than us — I can see a bunch of them who are basically just like "merge, merge, merge" when they wake up. That behavior I think is healthy for a small company.

We're starting to build now more tooling around the really obvious things like code review or agentic testing. We want to get to the point where we're shipping things proactively behind flags, using the other tools that we've already built, or shipping stuff as an experiment. So we're investing more heavily to try and get the merge rate higher, so that if we've given you a pull request you can trust it.

六、"去 puck 要去的地方"：不再原地等待

I don't think what you have done so far would I even have imagined possible last year.

Yeah, it wasn't.

And so just thinking about 6 months from now — I'm not worried about that being solved. So it's more like, okay, what's next?

Yeah, basically if you can go from typing in English to a 20,000-line-of-code application, I'm pretty sure once you've got your code, you should be able to double-check it carefully. It's just a matter of time.

We're actually starting to think a bit beyond this. The other thing we've learned in AI — which again would give us general advice if you're doing AI stuff now — is the pace is so much higher that we're having to go against some other standard startup advice. Go where the puck is going. We didn't used to do that. We used to just go where the puck already is, really really fast.

We kind of realized: no, we do now, when we're competing against people who are building AI natively. They move so much quicker that you actually do need to place a bet on the direction of travel a bit.

So we have a team working on code review, getting stuff merged — there's a lot to build there. But in parallel we also have people now working on: "Okay, let's assume that stuff works. What's next?"

And then we're like, okay, we think it's about a different harness that captures goals and intent from a product. If you go from one pull request a day in the olden days to five, to 100 — at 100, you're limited by your ability to describe something in English. So how can we build a harness that will work with a human to pull out what the actual requirements are, so you can let the agent run for longer? We have a better idea of what the product is supposed to do, which makes it easier to know what the goals are, so we can do a better job of shipping fixes, taking them in that direction, or shipping experiments.

So we are starting to get quite a lot more aggressive with how far forward we're willing to go — which is new for us. We weren't very innovative at all by design for the first few years. We're starting to build more confidence, that actually we've built some stuff that we consider ahead of everyone else in our industry. Then we think the next step is: okay, let's go further, further, further. Obviously if this goes horribly wrong we waste loads of time.

七、公司本身的 AI 化：让工程师像 CEO 一样思考

What does it mean for the company? PostHog as a company — I guess everyone at PostHog is using agentic coding of something. But the way you described your harness for the next iteration of the product — does it apply to the company itself? How you run the company? How you become yourself an AI-native company?

The way I would kind of see it is — you're like a more legacy company at this point.

Yeah.

Conceptually — like often something we'll refer to in a meeting — I spend all my time hanging out with engineers building AI stuff, or at least 95% of it I would say. I'm trying to get the engineers in a position where their job feels like my job today. My job today is like: have a bit of a discussion with an engineer, usually going like "what are we thinking about building here?"

The harness we're building is supposed to reflect what it feels like to talk to a product engineer. Because with an engineer, if I said something like "hey, I think this error could be really important," the question they will ask me isn't going to be like "should I mock up the data in the backend, which database?" — which is currently what the harnesses would do. Instead they'll be like, "Why do you think that?" or "What about this alternative?" or "Wait, are you trying to make this simpler than everything else, or trying to make it more complicated, or more powerful? What's the deal?"

I think that interaction I have with an engineer — I want the engineer to be having with the agent instead. So it's trying to abstract everyone up a level, is the way I'd think about it.

通用市场也在同样进化

It's similar to — we also think the same applies to go-to-market. There's a whole lot of interesting use cases there that are very similar. It's the same style of loop.

Example of what you're doing on the go-to-market side?

We basically found that by using one agent that used a lot of tools together, it's made everything much more accessible. Historically you're supposed to have a persona that you target inside of a customer — an engineer, or a salesperson, or CS person. These roles are still different to each other. But I do think they've stepped towards each other.

For example, our support team will fix bugs in the product if they're reasonably straightforward — they would never have done that pre-AI. Our product managers will change something small in the product themselves, because the fact that you can program a lot of things in English now means that everything's got more accessible. Slightly software-adjacent people will ship bits of software.

We have a Slack bot for PostHog that lets you code or ask questions or use our tools. 62% of pull requests that come through Slack are not from software engineers at PostHog anymore — from the marketing team for example, going like "okay, we've created an experiment."

We've seen a similar pattern happening in our customer base. Back in the olden days, PostHog was virtually all engineers using it and quite technical founders. For our AI tooling, it's 25% software engineers, 25% founders who are mostly technical, and the other half is these software-adjacent roles — PMs, technical marketing people, growth engineers.

大象切片：Elephant Carpaccio

There's a very similar loop concept for them. In engineering, your self-driving product means: find UX issues, find bugs, ship experiments proactively, set higher-level goals, work on bigger things.

Similarly in customer success — I think there's a world where the stuff we're building is: okay, well, we shouldn't have outputs that are just pull requests. We need to give the same thing the ability to book a meeting with a customer, for example. So that a customer success person's job can be: "I'm literally on meetings all the time, or I'm configuring how customer success should work" — there's nothing else that is required.

We've seen so much usage of our agent already that's a subset of this use case — "Is this customer going to churn? How's this customer using us? Is this customer using this feature? I want to try and cross-sell them." We can go: instead of cutting that small slice, giving them the information — we want to go, "Well, what's the job you're actually trying to achieve?" It's probably to cross-sell a customer, or to make sure a renewal happens, or to realize there's a problem and help them debug it.

So we're like, okay, let's just take the whole slice, the whole job. There's this engineering consultant in London who's kind of an underground celebrity in the London tech scene. He used to use this phrase elephant carpaccio. If you take an elephant and you slice the elephant up, you can slice it horizontally or you can slice it vertically. If you slice it horizontally, you can't tell each slice is an elephant — you can just see like four circles, four feet. If you slice it vertically, you can see the outline of a whole elephant.

So we're like, "Okay, let's think of it as elephant carpaccio. Can we start grabbing whole tasks that look like a complete piece of work and just fully automate it?" As opposed to just doing analytics, which is like a slice of "here are the four circles, figure out the rest yourself."

八、职业错配与自我裁员

That's awesome. I wonder how you got there pretty fast. It feels like you actually took on that PostHog AI team yourself, right? I would have expected that to come from more the tech leadership, not someone who has a sales background.

You would have thought you'd want someone competent doing this.

That's not what I was saying.

No, it was true. One of the things Tim and I learned — there's human behavior to do what you've done before, and the reason you're doing that is perhaps because you just slightly randomly made a decision when you're 22 to go be a product manager or sales leader or something. So Tim and I have sort of wound up in slightly the wrong career path.

You should have been tech, you should have been sales?

Probably. I'm not a very good — I don't think I'm actually a good developer. I naturally feel like I'm quite a bad developer honestly. I have done a bunch of software and I'm just bad.

You're good at guiding AI.

Yeah. The product side I enjoy an awful lot. And from that have got to the point where I feel more competent.

Tim and I do these 360 feedback dinners at PostHog. Every 6 months or so, every team will have dinner where you sit there — this applies to every single team at PostHog. And I sit there, and then everyone else gives me mostly constructive feedback, and then it moves on to the next person. You just listen — you don't challenge it, you can ignore it, but you just listen to your team.

This exercise has been super helpful for us. The feedback I was getting from Tim was: "You should back yourself more on these bigger product ideas that we're having and just go make them happen. Because you have not done this before, don't half-ass it. You should not hold back. You should act like the product manager that we need."

I've kind of realized the downside doesn't really matter — if I screw up something that we're building, we've just wasted some time. Whereas the upside's unlimited. So it's actually pretty terrible if I don't push harder.

The lesson I've sort of learned is: the more ambitious we've got with what we're building, I find it much more fun. Our team finds it more entertaining. It's much easier to recruit people. People are much more productive — like an order of magnitude more productive I think. Far easier to market things that are interesting than things that are boring. And it's easier to raise money too. That's basically the set of stuff you need to build a product. So if anything, it's getting easier the wilder that we're willing to go.

It feels like it's even existential — if you don't do it, your company may risk becoming irrelevant in time.

Yeah, exactly. And you're kind of framing it a little bit like, "Oh no, this feels like a big bet." It's like, actually, no — we're forced into this, we have to.

九、把自己变成公司的冗余：给创始人的最后建议

For everyone out there, I guess you need a founder to actually lead the charge here.

There's no way this would have — for me at least I would struggle to see us managing to outsource a shift like this. If the founders are not fully bought in to that kind of huge systemic change, I guess it's not going to happen.

No. And the way I think about it — if you look at Anthropic, who are like the fastest-growth company in the history of mankind, I'm pretty sure it's not because the sales team are really good. It's exceptional product. It's the most leverage place I think to be really strong.

I struggle to make myself care about stuff that isn't product, increasingly, as we're growing. Because when I look at the very very top-end competition, the product work is outstanding. So I really want a big chunk of founder focus to go there.

I think we're losing the battle the moment that we get focused on — like, we have a sales team, sales matters to us, we're increasingly working on enterprise. But that's not my focus. That's something that consciously we brought other people in to do. We do sales somewhat uniquely, but it's nowhere near as unique as what we're doing on the product side.

I think we're screwed the moment that we — like founders — if we both focus on sales, there's only so much that we can do. I think we're just not done building the product yet. If we both just focus on sales, growth probably will be a bit quicker in the short run, but we'll hit a flattening at some stage — which is my biggest fear as a company grows quickly.

We spoke to some people even at YC — we had a fake board meeting (I can't remember if it was a real board meeting) with you and with Pete Koomen from Optimizely. It was very interesting hearing what happens past 100 million run rate, etc. So we've been a little bit religious about "keep pushing the bottom end." Or Patrick from Stripe — we've asked this question to before — and the answer is: you just have to do both. You have to be good at scale, you have to be good at the bottom end if you want to keep having loads of top of funnel.

如何真正启动这场转变

Maybe that's a great way to conclude — for people who have not made that shift to fully embrace AI, everyone thinks they're embracing AI but not to the point you have done here. What advice would you give them? How should they start?

It's — you have to be ruthless. It got to the point around the start of 2025-ish, or early summer, that Tim and I each had roughly half the team somehow or another report to one of us. I had like half the exec team, he had the other half. And then you follow the lines down to everyone in the company. So ultimately I'm responsible for half the business, he's responsible for the other half.

Instead we went: "Hey, this is just not going to lead to — there's too much noise, too much random stuff going on. This product needs to exist. Just go make the time for it." So Tim went, "Okay, I will." And then we're like, "Do we both just do AI stuff?" And our conclusion was: if we both try and build the product at the same time as each other, we're just going to get in each other's way. We're going to both pull the teams in slightly the wrong directions.

So Tim basically had my back and went, "I'm going to look after everything, so that you become completely redundant. Spend all your time on that initiative."

So now I'm just like, "Okay, I need to get to self-driving. What is the current block to self-driving happening? That is where I'm going to spend my time today." And I've just been doing that for maybe a year and a half or so. It's meant lots and lots of time with engineers, pulling people internally from one team into another, rejigging stuff.

We have like say — we probably have 125 engineers or something. And I don't think this is going to go quicker if I put 125 people at the same time. We've had to ramp lots of people onto this project, but it started with maybe two or three people put on PostHog AI. And I've been trying to parallelize as much of the work as possible.

The extreme version — you freed up pretty much all your time?

Yeah. As much as humanly possible. I'm not doing stuff like interviewing. Tim used to do half the interviews each, now he's doing the vast majority — I'm very rarely interviewing people anymore. I've done no investor stuff. It's really nothing. I don't do one-on-ones with anyone. I've just ditched everything that I felt wasn't contributing to this. So it's really quite far that you have to go, I think, to get a change.

That's the extreme version, but that's good advice — you need to free up that time.

And frankly it's very fun. I kind of hope we keep this going. You can see proof points of this — Elon Musk does this, I think, from the impression I get. So it works for him, he's kind of successful. So we ought to be able to pull this off ourselves.

But it has been much more work than I would have expected to change. We've got products that are mature, doing tens of millions or multiple tens of millions of run rate each. We've hired people that will look after these, and it can be very unnatural for people to totally — I think our tolerance if you're a founder is very high for complete chaos. But you can't just do one all-hands and go "let's be more AI-forward here." You really really have to handhold people through the change, to varying degrees depending on their personality. So that side of it has been like 10 times more intense than I would have expected.

It has also been a very large shift, because we've had to go: we've built all this UX, it is better if an agent's using it for you. The data is getting increasingly important. The infrastructure back-end querying all this stuff is getting much more important. But the UX is going away, even though we've built an enormous amount of front-end for people to use.

And then we've got to handle the existing customer base — which is another risk — we've got hundreds of thousands of users on this thing. If we start changing stuff, we have to be really mindful of them. So some of this work — we actually built the first versions of self-driving into a new desktop app, because we wanted zero expectations: new product, who knows what it's going to do. Whereas if you get rid of a bunch of stuff from an existing product, everything you remove will annoy someone — there'll be some team using it in some way they need.

So we felt: we need to make this fresh. We'll get it really really right, and then we'll gradually move our cloud product over to doing the same thing. So we've really shifted where we're building this stuff too. Yeah, it's been very messy and painful.

收尾

Courageous endeavor here.

Yeah, I hope it works out. It's been good so far, but there's a ton more to build here.

Thank you so much for the advice and for joining us today.

Thank you very much for having me. Thanks.
